421.title: /continual-progress — trackable, always-PR’d, continually-committed work
421.content: Skill continual-progress: Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Sibling agents and the author can only coordinate with work they can see. This skill makes every in-flight task trackable in real time: the PR is open from the first commit, progress lands as a stream of small pushed commits, and the PR body carries a live status checklist. It is the visibility complement to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) (which triages across PRs); this one governs how your own PR stays legible while you work.

422.title: The four invariants
422.content: . | Always have an open PR (from commit #1). Branch, make the first (even stub) commit, push, open the PR — before further work. The PR is the durable, visible artifact; the chat session is ephemeral. Never accumulate work on a local branch with no PR. Never ask permission to open one — branch, commit, push and PR are all pre-authorised. | Commit + push small, coherent increments — continuously. Each logically distinct change is its own commit (a single fix, a single module, a single unit of work). Push after each commit (or every 2–3 if moving fast). A watcher should be able to git log your branch and see a legible, bisectable trail — not one giant drop. Target: no more than ~20–30 min of work between pushes on a long task. | Keep a live status checklist in the PR body. Maintain a - [ ] / - [x] checklist of the task’s sub-parts in the PR description (or a pinned top comment), updated as each increment lands. A sibling or the author should be able to read the PR body and know exactly what is done / in-flight / remaining — without reading the diff or asking in chat. | Post brief intent — on your PR and overlapping siblings. One short intent line on PR-open (“doing X on <files>; will touch <scope>”); a one-line comment on any sibling whose scope overlaps (“starting <theme> on <files>; flag conflicts”). Don’t stream comments — update the checklist (invariant 3) for routine progress; comment only for genuine coordination (overlap, a blocker, a handoff-relevant finding). Defer to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) for the full cross-PR triage protocol. New work posts its intent only after the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” has been run and recorded in the workplan work item. | . Bean edits are pushed to the state branch, not the PR . Work item and workflow-instance edits (beans/defs/*.md, beans/workflows/*.json) do not belong in the PR’s commit set. The code PR contains code, test, and documentation changes destined for main. Work-plan progress, work item claims, status updates, and notes are written directly to the work-plan store through its configured Tool (work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan); on a git state branch, bun run cat state:push per work-plan-store-git-branch). The PR description references the work item via Closes-bean: <id> (or in the status checklist), but commits on the PR branch must not bundle work item file edits. This avoids merge conflicts on work item files and prevents work-plan edits from triggering code CI workflows.

423.title: The fifth invariant, and the one agents get wrong
423.content: . | Do not hold a green change proposal back waiting for someone to look at it. This is the rule that gets inverted in the name of care, and inverting it is not caution — it is a blocked reviewer. | . An agent that has built something it cannot fully verify — a rendered page, a diagram, a UI — must not leave it open and ask the human to confirm from a preview first: . A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it, and a preview pasted into chat is a strictly worse proxy than the deployed thing. Holding the merge does not transfer the verification to them — it withholds the only form in which they could do it, and asks them to adjudicate from a screenshot. Link the PAGE, never the site root . When you ask somebody to look at a rendered artefact, link the artefact. Not the site it is on, not the preview’s front door — the exact URL of the thing you changed. Linking the root makes the reader reconstruct a route the agent already knew, and every extra click is a cost passed to a reader who may type with difficulty. It also hides a real failure: an agent that links the root has not checked that its page is reachable at all. So: . | One link per thing to look at. Two changed pages is two links, each labelled with what to look for on it — not one root and a sentence of navigation. | Deep-link past the index. If the change is on /docs/<iris-replica>/kg-to-portal.html, that is the URL, not /docs/<iris-replica>/. | Take it from the preview’s page list, never from memory or a source path: a branch slug is exactly the kind of string that is almost right. The rule, and where the list comes from, is feedback-deep-links. | The root is the right link for precisely one thing — a change to the landing page itself. | . This is the same rule as the invariant above, one step further on. A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it; they also cannot assess it from a link to somewhere near it. What to do with the thing you could not verify . Say it in the body, and merge anyway. ## Not verified is a real section and an honest one; an unmerged proposal is not a substitute for it. Reversibility is what makes this safe — a docs or content change is one revert away, and the cost of reverting is far below the cost of a human blocked on a decision they have no artefact for. A pipe discards the exit code — so a piped run cannot verify anything . cmd | tail makes $? the status of tail. Every claim that a command PASSED must come from a run without a pipe, or from ${PIPESTATUS[0]}. This is mechanical rather than a matter of care, because care does not prevent it. A command whose output sounds like a failure, run through a pipe, reads as a silent pass, and one whose output sounds like a pass hides a failure; a silent pass is what this repository treats as worse than a loud failure. So: when the question is “did this pass”, run it bare. When you want both the output and the verdict, run it twice or capture the status first. Reading a verdict off prose you piped is the same error as quoting a count from prose. A template is not a page — verify the BUILD, not the source of it . The invariant above says a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. This is its twin, and it is the one an agent breaks: . An agent cannot assess a rendered artefact from the template that generates it. A correct template and a correct page are different claims, and only the second is what a reader loads. Every source gate can pass over a defect that exists only in the build’s output. For example, a Liquid -%} that strips the space between two attributes makes Kramdown stop treating a block as HTML and escape it into visible text, while unit tests, lint, type checks, gates, e2e and accessibility suites all read valid sources and pass. So the rule is mechanical, not a matter of diligence: . | When the artefact is a built page, the evidence is the built page. Build the site and read the output. Reading the template proves the template. | A screenshot of a scratch render is not a screenshot of the build. If the real build cannot run locally (here the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway — a pass-through _layouts/default.html is enough to see what Kramdown did. Stub the part that cannot run; never substitute the part under test. | State which one you looked at. “Rendered and checked” is ambiguous between the two, and the ambiguity is where this hid. | . check:escaped-markup, run in docs-site.yml against the assembled _site/, covers the escaped-markup case, because the assembled site is the only place the answer exists. It does not retire the rule: the next defect of this shape will be in whatever the build does that no source gate can see. The exceptions, and none of them is “I am unsure” . | Never merge red. A failing or unrun required check is a real blocker. | Never merge over an unresolved review thread you have not answered. | Where the repository requires explicit merge permission, that wins, and nothing here relaxes it by a word. Some folios require an explicit “merge it” from the author for every merge to the default branch. There the rule reads: get it green, get it mergeable, say once that it is ready, then stop — do not re-ask on a timer, and do not let “not merged yet” become a reason to stop pushing. | . Green means handed to the Merge Steward — an agent never merges to main here . The merge policy for folio-assistant. It is the “explicit merge permission” case above, made into a hand-off rather than a question: . | Never merge to main yourself — not with gh pr merge, not with the MCP merge tool, not after a green run, not under a standing “merge it” from earlier in the session. | When CI is green on EVERY job (the run list, not the PR page — see prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”; on a draft, the fast tier), and when the queue allows (§”Pace the ready marking” below): mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha> — the full sha of the head that went green, so a push after it is visibly not what was declared ready. | Ask the merge manager to merge, in six lines (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). First check that a merge manager is active and live: the latest merge manager: <session id> announcement, and that session answered within the stall window. Send it the PR URL and full head SHA, your session URL, 1-3 sentences on what changed, the rendered preview URL for that head (or no preview: <reason>), what to look for in the preview, and full tier green as judged. It posts them in its chat and asks the owner by card. An approval the owner gives in your own session does not authorise a merge. With no live merge manager, follow merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first”: measure whether one is needed, then either manage your own PRs or elect one with your siblings. If your request is not acknowledged within the stall window, the merge manager has stalled: re-elect without it. The format is in §”The merge request: six lines” there. | The Merge Steward session (“Separation”) merges. It brings main in, runs regen, re-checks and merges. That is its lane, not yours. | If it reports red, it is yours again: fix, push, wait for green on every job, then re-label and comment ready: <new head sha>. | . Wherever a merge does happen, it is the merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) sub-process: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded, then the merge. So “merge anyway” in §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” reads here as mark it ready anyway, and “merge it as soon as it is green” in the fix-forward section below reads as hand it over as soon as it is green. The point of both is unchanged: a green PR is not held back. Pace the ready marking — the runner pool is shared . The Actions runner pool is shared across the owner’s repositories. A draft PR runs only the fast tier, and marking it ready starts the full tier, about 10 jobs. So the number of PRs marked ready at once is what fills the queue: . | Open every PR as a draft. | Mark it ready only when its own change is done and its fast checks pass. | Check the queue first: gh api "repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs?status=queued" --jq .total_count. If it is more than about 2 queued runs per runner (5 runners on 2026-10-24, so more than about 10), hold the marking and check again later. | At most 3 ready, CI-pending PRs per agent per repository. Hand one over or let it finish before you mark another. | A fix that unblocks other work may jump the line: a link in the repin chain, or a fix for a red main. | . Holding a PR as a draft for pacing is not holding back a green PR: the fast tier is green, and the hand-off above waits for the full tier. The merge manager enforces this rule (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Cancel CI”). When the runners are saturated, it closes superseded PRs, cancels stale queued runs that never started, and asks the owners of the lowest-priority PRs to return them to draft: merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Runner relief”. A new gate is proven downstream before it lands . A PR that adds a gate or check:* script to a lower layer passes on its own main, says how downstream layers run it, and shows a dry run over a fresh folio-assistant mount. Otherwise the next re-pin inherits the breakage (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). One pusher per PR branch . Only the session that owns a PR pushes to its branch (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Anyone else sends the owner the change, on the PR’s thread or by message. Every push restarts the full CI run: on 2026-11-07, three sessions pushed to folio-assistant#2985 within 10 minutes, and each push restarted it. Stack instead of waiting . Do not wait for a dependency to merge before starting work that needs it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “they dont need to wait for a merge to start working on a feature branch needing a dependent feature branch. They can stack”). The process is the first row of merge-request.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | In the same repository: branch from the dependency PR’s branch, and open a draft PR whose base is that branch. Pull later changes of the dependency in with merge commits. Never rebase or force-push another session’s branch. | Across layers: develop against the dependency’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft may pin the dependency PR’s full head SHA (never a branch) so that CI sees it (remote-mount §”Stacking across layers”). | A re-pin is its own PR. Put the pins, and nothing else, in one PR, and stack the work that needs them on it. A fix the re-pin needs lands in its owning layer first (owner ruling, 2026-11-07; remote-mount §”Re-pinning”). | Say so: write stacked on <repo>#<n> in the PR body, and list the order in the merge request. | When the base lands: retarget the PR onto main, merge main in (across layers: re-pin to the dependency’s merge commit on main), then mark it ready by the queue rule. Never merge the stacked PR into its base branch, and never mark it ready while it pins an unmerged commit. | . Two green PRs can merge into a red main, and the answer is to fix forward . A PR is tested against the main it last merged, not the main it lands on. Two PRs that are each green can still combine into a failure that neither branch contained, and no regen on either branch can see it. The policy is to fix forward, not to add a merge queue or an “up to date” requirement. So: . | Watch main’s CI after every merge of yours, not only your PR’s — whoever pressed the button. “My PR was green” does not mean main is green. | A red main whose failure your diff did not cause is still yours to fix when you find it. Establish the cause from the failing run and each parent’s history first, then regenerate or repair in a small PR of its own, and merge it as soon as it is green. | Do not blame the last merge because it is the last merge. Check whether the parent was already red. | .

424.title: Why — the failure modes this prevents
424.content: . | Stepped-on work. A branch that hoards uncommitted work collides with siblings the moment it lands. Continual push surfaces intent from minute 1 so siblings triage around it. | Lost work on session reclaim. Cloud sessions are ephemeral; an uncommitted change vanishes when the container is reclaimed. Push it. | Opaque progress. “What’s the status?” should be answerable from the PR body, not a chat scrollback. The checklist is the source of truth. | Un-takeoverable tasks. If you go idle/blocked, a sibling can pick up a continually-committed, checklist-annotated PR; they cannot pick up an opaque local branch. | .

425.title: Checklist (run this as you work)
425.content: . | PR open? If not: branch → stub commit → push → open it now. | Anything uncommitted older than ~20–30 min? Commit + push it. | Does the PR-body status checklist reflect the current state? | Any sibling whose files I just started touching un-notified? One intent line (not a stream). | Blocked or going idle? Update the checklist + a one-line “blocked on X / handoff-ready” note so a sibling can continue. | .

426.title: Relationship to other skills
426.content: . | pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc): what the PR body says ABOVE the status checklist (the problem, why, approach, constraints, solution, usage, what is not done), for a reader who was not here. | /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — cross-PR triage (scope map, sibling intent, cherry-picks, ledger). continual-progress keeps your PR legible so /coordinate (yours or a sibling’s) has something to triage. | A folio’s own AGENTS.md may carry these rules for that repository, and a stricter merge gate — litlfred/qou §”Branch + PR workflow” is the worked case. This skill is the platform-side statement; where a folio is stricter, the folio wins. | /todo-manager — the session work-plan; the PR-body status checklist (invariant 3) is its externally-visible projection, so a watcher needs no access to the session’s work item queue. | .

428.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
428.title: Contributor feedback on a working draft
428.content: Process_ContributorFeedback · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A document is still being written, and the Authoring Committee gives feedback on it in a shared Contributor Feedback sheet. This is what happens to ONE change set, one row of that sheet: a member starts it with a title, the sections it is about and their feedback; the agent proposes a direction; an Editor lets the agent edit; the agent makes the edit in the row’s one pull request, whose staging preview shows what changed; the committee answers on the row; and an Editor lets the agent merge. If the row’s feedback changes after the agent wrote its proposal, the proposal is marked stale and the row’s Ready for agent goes back to No, so the agent proposes again and an Editor decides again. The sheet’s colours follow the lanes: Blue for the committee, Green for the agent, Orange for the Editor. Skill: review-sheet-script. i i i i i i i i i

440.title: Working on materialized content — copy it out
440.content: Skill copy-out-materialized: Materialized content is read-only. To work on it you take a copy into your own folio/, and the copy records what it is a copy of — the local-provenance edge, which is not the upstream one. Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes . Materialized content is a copy of somebody else’s bytes, and this repository does not edit it in place. The contents of a materialized <stub>/<sub-graph> are immutable, and the rule is enforced: to work on them, copy them into your own folio/. Diagram: copy-out-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

441.title: What the rule protects, and what it does not
441.content: It protects the CLAIM. A materialized record asserts “these bytes are what upstream published”. Editing them in place leaves that assertion standing over bytes it no longer describes — and check:materialized-fixity is what catches one that happened, by hashing the bytes against the digest the record carries. It does not protect against the copy being wrong, stale or badly chosen. Those are the five gates’ job, at materialisation time (materialize-remote), and a copy-out re-opens none of them: you are copying something this repository already decided it may hold.

442.title: Who may copy out
442.content: Any reader. This is deliberately not a permission: refusing a copy would not protect the original, because the original is protected by being read-only. A gate here would only stop people working. What copying out does NOT confer is the right to publish. The copy inherits its source’s restrictions and copyright verdicts, and it is a new artefact in your folio whose publication is your folio’s decision, judged the way any other authored content is.

443.title: Where the copy goes
443.content: Into the copier’s own folio/, with provenance — never a scratch area, which makes the copy publishable by accident: a directory nobody declared is a directory nobody gates.

444.title: The copy records what it is a copy of
444.content: This is the part that is easy to leave out and impossible to reconstruct later. materialization.provenance is a pair: . | field | points at | . | upstream | the remote thing — a URI, upstream | . | local | the original in this repository it was taken from | . A copy-out writes local. It does not overwrite upstream, and it does not reuse upstream for the local original. Without local, one rename later a copy is indistinguishable from original work. That is the whole failure this step exists to prevent, and nothing downstream can repair it: the information was never written down.

445.title: The copy is NOT read-only
445.content: A materialized node is frozen because it is a claim about somebody else’s bytes. A copy in your own folio/ is yours, makes no such claim, and is ordinary authored content — so it is writable, and its directory’s readOnly is false. If it were frozen too, the copy-out would achieve nothing, and the next person would need a copy of the copy.

446.title: The exception is “say what you did”, not a list of who may skip
446.content: The exception — for publication workflow purposes and the like — is a rule, not an allowlist of writers that would go stale: . A step that rewrites a materialized artefact records the new fixity in the same change. Then check:materialized-fixity passes and the record describes what is actually there. A step that rewrites without updating fixity fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream without saying so — which is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. The check asks a question about BYTES and never about who wrote them, so it needs no attribution of a commit to a process step. Where it applies . refresh-materialized.bpmn’s Task_Apply is the one step in the declared corpus that rewrites bytes a materialization record describes, so it writes the new fixity in the same change; otherwise a correct run of it would fail the gate as an unannounced edit. No publication process writes to materialized content. kg-to-portal.bpmn’s S_Sign signs a subgraph cut from the KG — derived content, not held upstream bytes. So the publication case is a rule with no instance yet, stated here rather than drawn as a step no diagram does, because a declared-but-absent step makes a consumer report a clean run over nothing.

447.title: What to check afterwards
447.content: . | bun run cat check:materialized-fixity — the original still hashes to its recorded digest. If it does not, the copy-out was an edit in place. | bun run cat check:read-only-graphs — your folio’s directory is not accidentally declared read-only, and the source’s still is. | .

449.doc: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else's bytes
449.title: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes
449.content: Process_CopyOutMaterialized · strict · 5 step(s) . Somebody wants to change content this repository holds a read-only materialized copy of: copy it into their own folio/, recording which original it came out of. Materialized content is read-only, and that is enforced, not advised. STRICT, and the reason is narrow. Only one step here is a gate, and it is Gateway_Frozen: whether the target is read-only at all. Everything after it is mechanical. What makes the process strict is that skipping it does not fail loudly — an edit in place succeeds, and is only caught later by check:materialized-fixity hashing bytes against the digest their record carries. A process whose omission looks exactly like compliance cannot be advisory. The copy-out re-opens NONE of the five materialisation gates. Those were answered when this repository decided it may hold these bytes at all (materialize-remote.bpmn); copying something already held is not a second acquisition. What the copy does inherit is the restrictions and copyright verdicts — the copy is a new artefact in the copier’s folio, and publishing it is that folio’s decision. The three states, the five gates and the provenance pair are folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i

455.title: Corpus — committing an accepted edit
455.content: Skill corpus-commit-contract: The contract the corpus role is held to when an accepted edit is committed into it: take the write only on the editor’s acceptance, as one change with its QA sidecars, under the commit-hygiene requirement and with no relaxing of that policy. The narrowest contract the editing diagram requires. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Editing and HCI validation . corpus (declared below this layer) is played by a mechanical actor: the versioned content store, which is written to and decides nothing. A role played by a machine is still a role, and its skills are its contract: the responsibilities it must perform, which a test can hold it to. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s diagrams rely on, and nothing more.

456.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
456.content: Lane_Corpus in editing-hci-validation names this role and holds one activity, Task_Commit. What that lane’s documentation and the task’s say is the whole contract.

457.title: What it must do
457.content: . | Receive the write only after the editor accepts. Task_Commit is reachable from no path except Gateway_EditorDecision’s accept branch (the lane’s documentation). A change the editor discards, or one that has not reached the editor, never reaches the corpus. | Take the change together with its QA sidecars. “Only now does the change become corpus content, together with its QA sidecars” (the task’s documentation): the block and the findings about it arrive as one change. | Hold the commit to the commit-hygiene requirement (req:commit-hygiene), and allow no relaxing of it: the task’s policy is relaxable="false", because this is the one step that is irreversible in a way nothing upstream is. | .

458.title: Not its responsibility
458.content: Drafting the change, validating it, or deciding whether to accept it. Those happen in the author’s, the pipeline’s, the reviewer’s and the editor’s lanes before anything reaches the corpus. Resolving the bean afterwards is the work plan’s.

461.title: Corpus-Grep Skill
461.content: Skill corpus-grep: Pre-declaration corpus check. Before declaring any item “open”, “gap”, “TODO”, “open problem”, “pending derivation” — or asserting in chat that something is unresolved in the corpus — run the four-path grep checklist. A source file’s ## Status note lags the corpus by weeks; the corpus is the source of truth. An item is open only after all four paths come back empty (modulo the originating file itself). Named by: Hand back to the discussion . Disambiguation. This skill formalizes the backward check (“has this already been resolved somewhere in the corpus?”). Its forward complement is the formalize-first discipline (“can a structural claim prune the hypothesis class before I run a wide search?”). Run corpus-grep before declaring an item open; run formalize-first before launching an expensive numerical scan. The two are duals — backward against known results, forward against the hypothesis class.

462.title: Role
462.content: Gate every “this is open / unresolved / a gap” declaration behind a mechanical four-path search of the corpus. The originating source file’s status note (## Status, Open question, Phase 3 open, a TODO in a code or formal-source file, a PR-description “still open”) is not authoritative — prior agents routinely land a resolution as an audit doc, an adjacent chapter’s block, an implemented witness script, or a coordination ledger entry weeks before the source file’s note is updated. This skill catches that lag.

463.title: When to run this skill (STRICT)
463.content: Run the checklist before any of the following land in a durable artifact (audit doc, content block .md/.ts, code or formal-source comment, PR description, coordination ledger) or are asserted as fact in chat: . | “X is open” / “Open X” / “open problem” / “open question” | “TODO: derive X” / “pending derivation” / “still missing” | “this is a gap” / “no proof exists” / “not yet implemented” | “X is not wired into compute” / “nothing computes X” | . If you are about to type any of those about a corpus topic, stop and run the four paths first.

464.title: When NOT to run it (scope boundary)
464.content: The checklist gates factual corpus-status claims only. It does not gate, and must never be used to suppress: . | Skeptical assessments — “this looks fitted”, “this is numerology”, “hidden degrees of freedom here”. | Outside-view critique of a derivation’s rigor. | Reception / publishability / referee forecasts. | . Those are critical-distance judgments (see the repo’s Critical-distance license), not open-item declarations, and are never gated by this skill. Voicing them in chat does not require running corpus-grep first.

465.title: The four-path checklist (run all four)
465.content: | # | Path | What it catches | . | 1 | grep -rln <topic> docs/audits/ | Owner-authorised resolutions land as audit docs ahead of the source file’s status note being updated. | . | 2 | grep -rln <topic> content/ (full tree) | Related conjectures / propositions cross-cut chapters: a block in one chapter may answer a question raised in another. | . | 3 | grep -rln <topic> folio-assistant/computations/ | Implemented code may already discharge the content. | . | 4 | docs/coordination/<theme>.md | The coordination ledger — a prior agent may have already closed the item. | . Search the full content/ tree, not just the chapter you started in. The whole point of path 2 is that the resolution lives somewhere you did not expect.

466.title: Mechanical recipe
466.content: Pick a TOPIC that is the keyword / regex of the claim (an identifier, a label fragment, a phrase — e.g. delta_lambda, bring_color, c_3.*Taylor, kashaev.*density). Then run all four paths in one sweep: . TOPIC='delta_lambda' # ← keyword or regex for the claim under test for d in docs/audits content folio-assistant/computations docs/coordination; do if [ -d "$d" ]; then echo "=== $d ===" grep -rln -e "$TOPIC" "$d" 2>/dev/null fi done . Prefer the harness Grep tool (output_mode: "files_with_matches", one call per path or a single call with path set to the repo root and a glob) over shell grep when running inside an agent — results integrate with the permission UI and file links. The shell snippet above is the portable fallback. Widen the topic if the first pass is empty: try a synonym, the formal declaration name, the block label, the function name, and the witness-JSON key. A single spelling is not a clearing.

467.title: Decision procedure
467.content: . | Any non-trivial hit in (1)–(4) ⇒ the item is NOT open. Read the hit, then document the existing resolution instead of declaring a gap. Cite the file (audit doc / block .md / witness / ledger entry) that resolves it. | All four empty, modulo the originating file itself ⇒ you may declare the item open. “Modulo the originating file” means: a hit that is only the source file you are auditing does not count as a clearing — it is the very note you already mistrust. | Unsure whether a hit is the resolution ⇒ open the file and read it. A filename match is a lead, not a verdict. Treat a hit as resolving only if it actually discharges the claim (an audit verdict, a proved block, a passing witness, a ledger “CLOSED”). | .

468.content: This skill is the canonical, self-contained statement. It is invoked by, and consistent with, these codified instances: . | The folio’s own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, where it states the rule for its corpus. | A content type’s own audits, which apply the checklist to their declarations. For a paper folio these are the science layer’s proof-gap-audit §K (proof-gap declarations), compute-author and compute-audit (before declaring a statement “not wired into compute”) and lean-environment-setup (before declaring a capability unavailable). | .

470.title: Covered is not reachable — and check:tools cannot tell you which
470.content: Skill covered-is-not-reachable: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism is reachable from no Tool node. Read before concluding from check:tools that a command is reachable, and before adding a Tool node or a maintains claim. Named by: Code node review . A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing. check:tools reports the skill as covered and is right to: coverage is a relation between a Tool and a skill, never between a Tool and a command. For example, kg-export can be satisfied by a publishing node, a serving node and schema carriers while no node runs an export; translation-manager by extract, inject, status, signoff and validate nodes while none reaches the round-trip QA.

471.title: The two questions, kept apart
471.content: “Does this skill have a Tool?” — bun run cat check:tools, and bun run cat tools:coverage for which of the uncovered ones warrant one. “Is this command reachable by asking the graph?” — no instrument answers this yet; it has to be measured by hand. A skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Do not use the first question to answer the second: the cause of an invisible mechanism is structural, because nobody asks the second question.

472.title: What to do when you meet one
472.content: Add the node for the mechanism. Then two things not to do: . | Do not widen an existing node’s satisfies to make the gap look closed. That makes the graph assert a node does something it does not. | Do not give the new node the same I/O as an existing one unless it really is a substitute. Alternatives are derived from a shared skill plus an identical I/O signature (deriveAlternatives), and export-then-publish-then- serve are complementary steps, not competing arms. | .

473.title: Two reasons NOT to write maintains
473.content: maintains.artefact is a single path. A generator that writes one file per subject — gen-skill-docs, gen-schema-docs, gen-block-jsonld — has no single artefact to name. A declaration naming one file out of tens is worse than absent: it looks like a complete provenance record. A maintains claim asserts the artefact is published. Verify that by reading the build, not by assuming: cat-harness/ns.jsonld is a real claim because .github/workflows/docs-site.yml writes it. Remove a claim in the same change that retires its artefact: a claim outliving its artefact is the same 404 from the other side. An artefact nobody publishes is exactly the 404 the drift check exists to prevent. And the drift check only covers its own producer . kg:schema:check reconciles maintains both ways, but its unproduced direction runs only over artefacts whose declaring Tool invokes bun run cat kg:schema, because a maintained artefact is not necessarily produced by the schema exporter. So a maintains claim on any other producer’s artefact is unchecked: it can rot to a 404 and nothing notices. The fix — not yet built — is to assert every declared artefact is present after _site/ is assembled, with could-not-determine kept distinct from present.

474.title: Adding a Tool type is fail-closed, and that is deliberate
474.content: check:tools refuses a command-line input whose type could express a shell payload, against the membership list in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts. A newly added type is absent from that list and therefore unsafe by default. Adding it is a deliberate step, not an oversight to route around — and the fix for an enumerable input is the enum, never a looser type that happens to pass. Where the enum duplicates a union declared elsewhere, guard it in both directions: satisfies catches a member that stops being valid, and a conditional type catches a member added to the union and not here. An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not — see directory-conventions.

475.title: Five cases, most invisible to the instruments
475.content: | case | what exists | what is missing | what sees it | . | 1 | a skill | a Tool | check:tools, tools:coverage | . | 2 | a skill and Tools for its neighbours | a Tool for the mechanism | nothing — this skill | . | 3 | a mechanism | any skill stating the capability | nothing | . | 4 | a skill, a mechanism, a Tool | a command — it runs in-process only | nothing | . | 5 | a skill, a mechanism, a command | anything that invokes it | nothing | . Case 5 is case 4’s inverse — the entry point is present and the callers are absent — and it is discussed under §Reachability is PLURAL below, because the useful question there is how many dispatch points this should have. A script whose only references are its own usage string and a line of skill prose telling a human what to type is case 5: its mechanism is inlined in prose.

476.title: The third case: a mechanism with no skill at all
476.content: A generator that renders theme and avatar nodes into the site’s stylesheets is a textbook maintains pair, and yet no generic skill need state the capability. tools:coverage cannot see this: it enumerates skills and asks which lack Tools, so a capability nobody has stated is absent from the list it walks. (site-presentation-assets is the skill that now states that one.) . satisfies requires at least one skill, so a node cannot be written without one: . | Do not stretch a neighbouring skill to make the node validate. The resulting satisfies edge is simply false. | Do not write the skill as a wrapper for the command. A skill states a capability generically and names no script; one that exists to give a script somewhere to point is a Tool with front matter. | . Authoring the skill is a design act — a claim about the platform’s capability vocabulary, inherited by every dependent layer — so it goes to the owner rather than being decided in passing. Write the skill before the nodes. Once the gap is closed, remove any note announcing it: an agent that believes a stale gap either avoids the capability or rebuilds it.

477.title: The fourth case: a mechanism with no command, reachable in-process only
477.content: Cases 1–3 are about a missing node or a missing skill. This one has both, and is still unaskable: the mechanism has no command, so no CI job and no person can run it. For example, checkFolioProfile in pipeline/profile-check.ts catches what schema validation structurally cannot — a block valid against its own schema but wrong for the folio’s content profile, because adapters partition disjointly while profiles nest. Its only caller is the MCP tool registration, so it is reachable by an MCP-connected agent and by nothing else: not a gate, not a sweep, not a person at a shell. Every instrument that asks “can this be reached” answers yes. Ask which callers, not whether. “Reachable from MCP” and “reachable from CI” are different claims, and a durable verdict needs the second. Giving a library function its first command . Prefer a qa-sweep axis to a one-off check script: a sweep verdict is durable where a printed one is not — a printed verdict cannot distinguish “wrong since it was written” from “broken in the commit under review”. Watch the library’s defaults. checkFolioProfile resolves through readFolioProfile, which turns an undeclared profile into "paper" — correct for a validator, which validates against the wider vocabulary, and wrong for a reporter, which must use readDeclaredFolioProfile or report pass on a folio that declares no content type at all. A library’s defaulting is usually what erases the third state. When you give a library function its first entry point, the value it resolves for its own use is not the value a verdict may report. Check which of the two you are reading — by running it, not by reading it.

478.title: Reachability is PLURAL — “which caller should this have?” presumes one
478.content: One mechanism can have several dispatch points, so the question to ask is not which caller should this have but: . What should be able to start this — and is each of those a trigger or a Tool? . The two are different objects, and which one a dispatch point is follows from who initiates: . | dispatch point | it is a | because | . | a named command | Tool | a caller invokes it; that is what a Tool node IS | . | a BPMN activity | trigger | the process fires it when the step is reached | . | a QA sweep axis | trigger | the sweep fires it per subject | . | a schedule or a watcher | trigger | time or an event fires it | . None of them is an alternative to another, by the same argument deriveAlternatives makes about sharing a skill: they are different ways the same work gets started. Enumerating the dispatch points also finds the ones already built. For each candidate, check whether it exists (an activity may already carry the skill, so workflow_next already hands it to an agent), whether it is possible (a sweep cannot run a check whose verdict originates outside it), and only then what is missing. Presented as a choice, the options waste proposals; enumerated as dispatch points, they are a short audit with one action. Read the mechanism’s entry point before proposing dispatch points. A name and a position in a diagram say what something is for; an argument list says what it does — for example, whether it performs a check or only records a verdict somebody else produced.

479.title: The same failure one level out: a KIND, not a mechanism
479.content: Ask what is missing of a kind of node and the same mistake appears: counting kg-qa sidecars over the work item store, finding zero, and calling work items unaudited when several gates audit them. Coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for — see audit-coverage, with bun run cat audit:coverage as the second question.

The stakeholders sign off, the BA confirms every criterion is met, the feature lands on main through the merge-to-main sub-process, and only then does the agent close the issue. Never the other way round: an agent must never assume completion. i i i i i

487.title: CRDM — the data-modelling phase
487.content: Skill crdm-data-model: The CRDM data-modelling phase — when in the requirements process a model is built, what it is built from, who confirms it, and what it hands to the phases either side. The technique it invokes is data-modelling; this skill carries only the sequencing and the sign-off. Named by: CRDM data model . This skill says WHEN and WITH WHOM. It does not say how to model. That is data-modelling, and it is deliberately free of CRDM so a folio modelling data outside a requirements process can read it without inheriting a methodology it is not running. Where the two disagree, the technique wins and this page is wrong.

488.title: Where it sits, and why there
488.content: Between requirements (phases 2–4) and sign-off (phase 5). Requirements are statements about things; the model says what the things ARE. The entities come from the business-process analysis (phase 2), and phase 5 must not sign off requirements whose nouns were never pinned. Drafted too early, the model is invented from nothing; drafted too late, two stakeholders approve the same sentence meaning different things. Call_DataModel in crdm-requirements.bpmn is the callActivity after Call_Requirements and before Call_Signoff.

489.title: What it consumes
489.content: | from | what | . | phase 1, needs | the domain vocabulary the BA actually used | . | phase 2, BPA | the activities — every verb whose object is a candidate entity | . | phases 3–4, requirements | each requirement’s nouns, which the model must be able to express | . A requirement the model cannot express is a finding, not a modelling failure. It means the requirement is about something nobody has named, and the remedy is to name it. That is why this phase sits after requirements rather than before.

490.title: The sign-off, and who gives it
490.content: The agent drafts; the BA confirms the entities are the ones they meant; the stakeholders confirm the cardinalities. Those are two different questions and are asked of two different lanes on purpose: . | Are these the things? — a naming question, and the BA owns the domain vocabulary. | Is it really one per? — an operational question, and the people who run the process know where the exceptions are. | . The agent asks both and decides neither: the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess, because a wrong cardinality is invisible until the data arrives.

491.title: What it hands on
491.content: A declared model, readable by a tool, per step 6 of the technique. Phase 5 signs off requirements against it: whether each requirement is expressible, not only whether it is wanted.

492.title: The loop, and when to leave it
492.content: Like every other CRDM phase this one loops until confirmed, and the gateway is the phase. Leave when the BA recognises the entities and the stakeholders have answered every cardinality — not when the model looks complete, because an unanswered cardinality is a hole exactly where the exceptions live.

493.title: Not decided by this skill
493.content: Whether the model is expressed as Zod, JSON Schema, a class diagram or prose is placement’s question and the folio’s choice. This phase requires only that the artefact is declared, so the next phase can read it rather than be told about it.

501.title: CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance
501.content: Process_CRDM_Deliver · strict · 9 step(s) . One phase and not three, because the loops say so: an increment the BA rejects, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation. A subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished, so splitting this region would have changed what the diagram says. i i i i i i i i i

503.title: Lanes — who acts
503.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | BA / Feature Requestor | business-analyst | Every signal that can send the loop back to A_Implement is filtered through this lane first: BA_ReviewIncrement judges behaviour rather than code, GW_MVPReady decides whether accumulated increments are worth showing stakeholders at all, and BA_TranslateFeedback is the only step that turns S_TestMVP’s raw findings into direction the agent can act on. Nothing stakeholder-facing reaches Lane_Agent without passing through here. | . | Agent | authoring-agent | Every loop-back in this phase — a rejected increment, an MVP not ready, stakeholder feedback — lands on A_Implement rather than on Call_OptionsAnalysis, so this lane always reworks an approach already chosen and never re-selects one. Deciding that the APPROACH itself is wrong is not this lane’s call: that belongs to the calling step in crdm-requirements.bpmn, one level up. | . | Stakeholders | stakeholder | Tests in the stakeholder’s own workflow and data rather than against the acceptance criteria BA_ReviewIncrement already checked — a second, independent pass rather than a repeat of the first. GW_StakeholderOK’s findings branch does not hand the agent anything directly; it hands raw results to BA_TranslateFeedback, which is this lane’s boundary: it reports what works and what does not, and translating that into direction is somebody else’s lane. | .

By Phase 6 the needs, requirements and data model are signed off, which is exactly the evidence an options analysis needs and the reason it belongs here rather than earlier: at Call_Needs there is nothing to weigh, and after A_Implement the choice has been made in code.The three loop-backs into A_Implement — _5 (increment rejected), _7 (MVP not ready), _13 (feedback translated) — deliberately BYPASS this call. Routing them through it would run the subprocess on every iteration of the inner loop, which is the ceremony this design refuses: a gate invoked on every pass stops being read. An iteration reworks an approach already chosen; if the APPROACH is what is wrong, that is not a loop iteration and it belongs to the calling step in crdm-requirements.bpmn.Contrast upstream-version-adoption, where the loop DOES re-enter the analysis. There the loop-back returns to A_Impact, which re-gathers the evidence, so the second pass weighs genuinely different inputs. Here the loop returns to implementation with the evidence unchanged.A_Implement carries a note on the bean (its claim is the OPEN that Process_CRDM calls first); this step carries no bean op, because Process_OptionsAnalysis ends with its own decision-audit note on the bean the caller claimed. | . | Phase 6: Implement (feature branch + PR)A_Implement | Agent | continual-progress | Inner loop: agent claims a bean, implements onfeature branch, opens PR, posts summary to the issue.When the requirement changes a rendered surface, implement against thewireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4(Process_WireframeDesignReview, called from Process_CRDM_Requirements), notagainst a fresh design; and the delivery summary links the chosen candidatebeside the after-screenshot, so the reviewer can see the build matches what wasapproved. | . | Audit the code nodes the increment addsA_CodeAudit | Agent | calls Review task | Descend into the review task for what this incrementCHANGED IN THE GRAPH — Tool definitions in tools/ and schema definition nodesunder schemas/. Staging URL, demo, or walkthrough. | . | Test MVP in own contextS_TestMVP | Stakeholders | — | Stakeholders test the delivered feature in their ownworkflow, with their own data. 507.title: Feature-request detection (CRDM trigger)
507.content: Skill crdm-detect: Detect when a request needs requirements agreed before anything is built, and which of the two parallel requirements methodologies governs it. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Detect when a user request is a feature request (platform capability change) rather than a content request (writing, editing, reviewing folio content). When a feature request is detected, the agent works through requirements rather than implementing directly.

508.title: Applies when
508.content: Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, on work tied to a folio’s domain — WHO SMART Guidelines, an IG, a programme’s content. The requester is a content developer working through a BA, and the answer depends on what the folio says. Not for a platform capability change raised by somebody building the tooling with a content-agnostic answer — that is spec-kit.

509.title: Which requirements methodology — the fork this detection now carries
509.content: Detecting a feature request does not select CRDM by itself. There are two parallel requirements methodologies, and methodology-adoption forbids blending them. The signals below tell you a request needs requirements; this fork tells you whose. |   | governs | requester | the answer depends on | . | crdm — this methodology | stakeholder-facing WHO/IG work: needs assessment, BPA, stakeholder sign-off | content developers, via a BA | a folio’s subject matter | . | spec-kit (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | folio-assistant feature development; software-development best practice, closer to a scrum process | tool developers | nothing a folio says — content-agnostic | . Most of the signals listed below are spec-kit’s, not CRDM’s — the “Platform-level change requests” and “Direct capability requests” categories especially, since both describe somebody building the tooling. Read the categories as this needs requirements, then apply the fork. Two things bind under either methodology and are not a reason to pick one: the issue-association rules at the end of this file, and the spec-before-code gate.

510.title: Detection signals
510.content: Scan every user request for these categories of phrasing. A single match is enough to flag; two or more from different categories is high confidence. Direct capability requests . Phrases where the user explicitly asks for new functionality: . | “I need a way to …”, “can you add …”, “we need a tool that …” | “there should be a skill for …”, “add a QA check for …” | “the renderer should support …”, “make the pipeline do …” | “can we add a new block kind for …”, “we need a content type for …” | “it would be great if the agent could …” | “the agent should …”, “the agent needs to …”, “we will need to …” | “build me …”, “create a tool …”, “develop a feature …” | . Workflow gap descriptions . Phrases where the user describes a process that does not work today: . | “right now I have to manually …”, “there is no way to …” | “the current process for … is broken”, “this workflow doesn’t handle …” | “we can’t do … yet”, “it’s missing …”, “it doesn’t support …” | “every time I need to …, I have to …” (manual workaround pattern) | “other people need to be able to …” | . Platform-level change requests . Phrases that imply changes to folio-assistant itself (not folio content): . | “change the schema to …”, “modify the pipeline …” | “add a new adapter …”, “the constraint should …” | “update the CI to …”, “the workflow should fire when …” | “the MCP tool needs to …”, “register a new tool for …” | “the upstream change requests to …”, “upstream asks” — a change asked of a tool this platform DEPENDS ON is still a platform change; the folio is not where it lands either way | References to files under schemas/, pipeline/, adapters/, src/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ | . Cross-cutting concerns . Phrases that affect multiple folios or content types: . | “for all papers …”, “every folio should …”, “across all content types …” | “when any user …”, “the platform should …” | “this needs to work for both document and paper folios” | . Review-surfaced needs . Phrases that emerge during content review: . | “this review process would be easier if …” | “we need a way to triage these comments …” | “the feedback workflow should …” | “stakeholders need to be able to see …” | “can we make the review process more …” | . A request for a plan . A request for a plan ALWAYS produces a requirements document and a work plan for review before implementation. | “plan”, “make a plan”, “plan the …” | “approach”, “what approach would you take” | “proposal”, “propose …” | “how would you …” | “come up with …” | . A plan request needs requirements under either methodology, and content requests are not exempt: “plan the edits to chapter 3” triggers it as surely as “plan the new validator”. The fork above still decides WHOSE requirements — this signal never selects a methodology and never blends them. The operation is the same for both and lives in the content layer, in the plan-request-gate skill (skill_fetch plan-request-gate): produce a requirements document and a work plan, put them where this methodology says (CRDM: committed under docs/proposals/), hand both over as absolute GitHub permalinks, and stop until sign-off is recorded on the issue. The definition of a requirement both methodologies share is the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition). Self-declared genre . The mirror of "Migration record: …" below. Some documents say what they are in their own first line, and a proposal or a design document argues for a change that does not exist yet — which is a feature request whichever category its sentences fall into. | “Proposal: …” as a document’s OPENING line | “design document for …” | . Anchored to the opening line. On the adjudicated corpus an unanchored proposal adds no false alarm and catches one more item (a change register for pipeline changes not yet built). The anchor stays until an owner decides, because changing a detector to fit its own 27-item eval set is tuning to the test.

511.title: What is NOT a feature request
511.content: Do not trigger CRDM for: . | “Write the next section of chapter 3” — content authoring (but “plan the next section” is a plan request — see §”A request for a plan”) | “Fix the typo in the overview” — content editing | “Run content_validate” — tool invocation | “What does this block kind mean?” — information request | “Review chapter 5” — content review within existing workflow | “Create a bean for …” — work-plan management | “Migration record: …” — a record of work already DONE, not a request for work; the tense is the signal | Bug reports about existing features (unless they imply a redesign) | .

512.title: On detection — what to do
512.content: Do NOT use the term “CRDM” with the user. It is internal methodology jargon. If new session and the first request is a feature: . | Acknowledge the request as a feature/capability change | Explain that you will help them work through the requirements before building | Start Phase 1 (needs assessment) | . If existing session and the user is already in a CRDM cycle: . | Incorporate the new request into the current requirements document | Continue with the current phase | . If existing session and the user is doing content work (not in CRDM): . | Synthesise what you have heard as a feature need | Ask the user: . | “This sounds like a platform change rather than content work. Would you like to pause and work through the requirements now, or should I note it for later?” | If pause: enter CRDM Phase 1, return to content work when done | If later: create a work item with as much context as possible, linking to any relevant GitHub issue | . | .

513.title: Issue association
513.content: Feature work should be linked to a GitHub issue: . | Scan open issues for a match — search by title/body keywords | If match found — ask user: “This looks related to #NNN — should I add your requirements there?” | If no match in open issues — scan recently closed issues | If no match at all — ask the user to create an issue (do NOT create without permission) | Do not proceed without an issue link — the issue is where stakeholders do feature sign-off; without it, there is no review surface | . Requirements may span multiple issues. The agent should link to all relevant ones and note the relationship.

514.title: After implementation
514.content: When a PR is merged that addresses a feature from this process: . | Post a summary comment on the linked GitHub issue describing what the PR accomplished | PRs are for code review (agent and human coders, code reviewers) | Issues are for CRDM stakeholders — the requestor, the BA, and updates from the coding team for feature sign-off | Many work items per issue — they are not synonymous | .

515.title: A feature is a COLLABORATION you are joining, not a fix you are making
515.content: When a feature comes up in conversation, it starts or joins a collaborative design between this user, other users and authors, and other agents. It is not a one-off fix: put it into epics and stories, create or update the artefacts it needs, and link them from the owning harness’s docs/ page. The default that is wrong . A feature surfaces mid-conversation, the agent understands it, and the agent builds it, with the conversation standing in for requirements. Everything needed to review the decision — the alternatives, the reason, who else it affects — stays in a chat log nobody else will read. What to do instead . 1. Assume the conversation is not the first. Before treating a feature as new, look for the collaboration it belongs to: an open issue, an epic, a work item, a sibling session’s branch, a spec. This repository has many of each and they are cheap to search. A feature that arrives without a home usually has one. 2. There are OTHER PARTICIPANTS, and they are not all present. Other authors, other users, other agents working other branches. Two consequences: . | the record has to be legible to somebody who was not in the conversation — which is what the issue is FOR, as against the PR (code review) and the work item (work plan); | a sibling session may already be solving it. Check before you build, and if their answer differs from yours, that is a design discussion to have on the issue rather than a merge conflict to win. | . 3. Structure it: epics and stories, not a task. A feature that is worth doing is worth a place in the roadmap. This store’s hierarchy is milestone → epic → feature → task, and check-bean-parents enforces that every open work item has a home. A feature filed as a bare task with no parent lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section, where it stops being planned. An epic cannot parent an epic here. When the subject already has an epic, the new work is a FEATURE under it — a second epic beside it splits one subject across two roots, which is how a roadmap becomes unreadable. 4. Write the artefacts, and LINK them from docs/, because an artefact nobody can navigate to is one nobody reads. The harness that owns the capability owns the link — so a change to cat-harness’s pipeline is linked from cat-harness’s docs/, not from wherever the agent happened to be working. Which harness owns it is usually answered by which layer declares the directory the change lands in. The test . If this session ended now, could somebody who was not in it pick the feature up — find what was decided, what is still open, and who else is affected — without reading the chat? . If the answer is no, the collaboration has not been joined yet, whatever has been built. What this does NOT mean . It does not mean every small change becomes an epic. The trigger is the same one opening-brief uses: irreversibility and surprise, not size. A one-line fix to a typo in a generated file is a fix. A one-line change to a schema that three layers resolve against is a feature, because other people have to live with it. Nor does it mean stopping work to do paperwork first. continual-progress still holds — branch, commit, push, open the PR from commit #1. The point is that the record is collaborative, not that the work pauses.

516.title: Related work first
516.content: When a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, find the related work before anything else. That means work items, issues and open PRs, each categorized and summarized, followed by one question to the user about whether and how to coordinate. The procedure is related-work-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), and crdm-issue-linking.bpmn calls it as Process_RelatedWork.

518.content: Skill crdm-impact-analysis: Guide for CRDM Phase 4 — Impact Analysis and Migration Planning. 519.title: The 7 impact dimensions
519.content: 1. Schema impact . Scan schemas/*.ts: . | types.ts — are any types added, removed, or changed? | block-kinds.ts — does a block kind change? (triggers adapter cascade) | constraints.ts — new or modified constraints? | builders.ts — new or modified builders? | folio-config.ts — does the config schema change? (affects all folios) | . rg "YourChangedConcept" schemas/ . 2. Pipeline impact . Scan pipeline/*.ts: . | Validators (validate.ts, profile-check.ts) | Renderers (render-markdown.ts, render-latex.ts) | Extractors/codemods (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts, citations.ts) | Content graph (content-graph.ts) | QA criteria (qa-criteria-registry.ts) | . 3. Adapter impact . Check adapters/ routing and inheritance: . | PaperContentAdapter extends DocumentContentAdapter | adapterForKind must stay total and unambiguous | Adding a kind: which adapter owns it? | Profile vs adapter distinction (AGENTS.md §”Content types, and starting a folio”) | . 4. Folio impact . For each active downstream folio: . | Does it use the changed schema/pipeline? | Does it need a migration? | Will content_validate still pass? | Is init-folio affected? | . 5. Skill impact . rg "affected_file_or_concept" cat-harness/skills/ . Check .claude/agent-memory/ for rules/traps that reference the changed area. 6. Migration assessment . | Does this need a codemod? (codemod-*.ts) | Schema version bump? (schemas/package.json) | Data migration for existing folios? | Rollback strategy — what if the migration fails? | . 7. Test and documentation impact . | scripts/tests/ — which tests need updating? | E2E tests — affected scenarios? | Jekyll docs under cat-harness/docs/ — pages to update? | BPMN diagrams in cat-harness/processes/**/*.bpmn — workflows affected? | .

520.title: Structured output format
520.content: Post this table to the GitHub issue: . ## Impact assessment — [Feature name] | Dimension | Affected? | Files | Risk | Migration needed? |---|---|---|---|---| Schema | Yes/No | `schemas/types.ts` | High/Med/Low | Yes/No | Pipeline | Yes/No | `pipeline/validate.ts` | ... | ... | Adapter | Yes/No | `adapters/paper/` | ... | ... | Folio | Yes/No | `qou`, `who-smart` | ... | ... | Skills | Yes/No | `skills/process/crdm/` | ... | ... | Migration | Yes/No | — | ... | ... | Tests/Docs | Yes/No | `scripts/tests/` | ... | ... | ### Consumer impact - [List fields added/removed from published artefacts] - [List IRIs or filenames that move] - [List conventions a consumer must learn] ### Test plan - [Tests to add or update] .

Folios # Check folio.config.json in each active folio # 5. Skills rg "CONCEPT" cat-harness/skills/ # 6. Tests bun test 2>&1 | tail -20 # 7. Docs rg "CONCEPT" cat-harness/docs/ .

530.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment (detail)
530.content: Skill crdm-needs-assessment: Facilitate Phase 1 (Needs Assessment) of the CRDM requirements workflow. Guide the BA through stakeholder identification, source material gathering, and synthesising a domain-language needs statement. Post to the GitHub issue and iterate until the BA confirms the need is correctly captured. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Options analysis, SWOT situation analysis, Questionnaire wireframe review, Guideline Updates, DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . This skill expands the Phase 1 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md. The agent facilitates; the BA provides domain knowledge.

531.title: Identifying the requester
531.content: Determine who is asking and their role: . | Role | What they bring | . | BA / Feature Requestor | Domain knowledge, stakeholder access, sign-off authority | . | Content Author | First-hand experience with the gap | . | Managing Editor | Cross-folio perspective | . | Technical Reviewer / SME | Deep subject-matter expertise | . | Programme Lead | Strategic priority, resourcing | . The requester is the BA for this CRDM cycle. They interact with the agent; stakeholders interact with the BA.

532.title: Identifying stakeholders (systematic 4-step approach)
532.content: . | Check each active folio’s <name>.config.json roles — authors, editors, reviewers, contributors, affiliations | Check .github/CODEOWNERS — subsystem ownership | Check recent activity — gh issue list --search "...", gh pr list --search "..." for who’s been working in the area | Ask the BA directly: “Who else is affected by this change?” | . Categorise stakeholders: . | Approvers/Governance — must sign off (e.g. review committee) | Direct Operators — will use the feature daily | Downstream Consumers — affected indirectly (e.g. country adaptation teams) | .

533.title: Gathering source material
533.content: The request may arrive through any of these channels: . | Source | How to access | . | Chat messages in the current session | Current context | . | GitHub issue body or comment | gh issue view <number> | . | Uploaded document (Word, PDF) | uploads/ directory | . | Referenced document in library | library/ directory | . | Issue comment attachment | Download via gh | . | Pasted Teams/email discussion | Current context (motivation, not spec) | . Probing discipline: begin with the end in mind. Distinguish: . | Symptoms vs root causes | Workarounds vs missing capability | One user’s need vs shared need | .

534.title: Synthesising a needs statement
534.content: Every needs statement follows this structure: . | Current state — what exists today (specific, not vague) | Gap — what is missing or broken (the actual problem) | Desired outcome — what should happen after the feature | Who benefits and how — named roles, concrete improvements | Workflow rationale — how this fits the broader process | . No jargon (STRICT) . Write for business stakeholders and domain experts, not developers: . | ❌ Avoid | ✅ Use instead | . | Zod schema validation | “the system checks the structure” | . | AST traversal | “scanning the document” | . | TypeScript types | “the data format” | . | Pipeline stage | “processing step” | . | CLI flags | “options” | . | MCP tool | “assistant capability” | .

535.title: Posting to the issue
535.content: . | Scan for existing issue first — gh issue list --search "..." | Never create an issue without BA permission | Post the needs statement as a comment: gh issue comment <number> --body-file /tmp/needs-statement.md . | .

536.title: Requesting feedback
536.content: After posting, ask the BA: . | “Does this capture what you need?” | “Are any stakeholders missing?” | “Is the desired outcome specific enough to test?” | . The BA coordinates with stakeholders. The agent does not contact stakeholders directly.

537.title: Exit gate
537.content: BA confirms the needs statement before proceeding to Phase 2.

546.title: Requirements from a recorded walkthrough
546.content: Skill crdm-recorded-walkthrough: Turn a recorded requirements walkthrough (a video call where a business analyst demonstrates a feature and a stakeholder asks for changes) into CRDM Phase 3 requirements with evidence: transcripts compared, an independent transcript where one can be made, screenshots cut at the moments the speakers point at the screen, and every requirement traced to a timestamp. Use when someone uploads a meeting recording, a Teams/Zoom transcript (.vtt, .docx) or both, and asks for requirements from it. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Options analysis, SWOT situation analysis, Questionnaire wireframe review, Guideline Updates, DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . A walkthrough recording is the best source a CRDM round can have: the stakeholder reacting to a working thing, in their own words. It is also easy to over-trust, because a transcript reads like a record and is not one. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/meeting-recording.py (stdlib + ffmpeg; --help per subcommand).

547.title: 1. Inventory what was actually uploaded
547.content: List the files before promising anything, because a request can promise a video that was not uploaded. A Teams .docx transcript never contains the shared screen; its images are speaker avatars. Say what is missing, do what can be done, and list what waits for the missing file.

548.title: 2. Two exports of one recognition are one transcript
548.content: meeting-recording.py compare A B gives word similarity and where they differ. | pair | similarity | what the differences were | . | Teams .docx against its .vtt | 0.980 | interjections in another cue; words joined at a .docx line break | . | Vosk small-en (independent) against Teams | 0.802 | mostly Vosk’s errors, but also Teams’ (“Lightner” → Leitner, “philtres” → filters) | . The first number is not confirmation: both files carry every word Teams misheard. Only an independent recognition can disagree with it. A lower similarity from a weaker model is expected and still useful, because what you read is where they disagree, filtered with --keys to names and domain terms. Record the names the recogniser mangled (“Tini”, “Jiun” for Chinni; “Saroop” / “Swarupu” unresolved) in the requirements document, and ask rather than guess any name neither transcript settles.

549.title: 3. An independent transcript, offline
549.content: meeting-recording.py transcribe VIDEO --model DIR --out vosk.json needs the vosk package (PyPI) and a model directory. It downloads nothing. In a sandbox whose proxy refuses Hugging Face and the Vosk model host, find a model already packaged somewhere the network allows, take only the model files, and never run code that came with them.

550.title: 4. Screenshots: where the screen changed and where a speaker points
550.content: . | scenes VIDEO --min-gap 10 lists when the shared screen changed. | Grep the transcript for deictic phrases: “you can see”, “here”, “this”, “looking at the screen”, “select these”. Their timestamps are the candidates; a scene change a second or two later is the frame to take. | frames VIDEO --at 1:52,2:26 --out DIR --crop W:H:X:Y --width 1280 --webp. Crop out the participants’ camera tiles: a requirements document needs the screen, not the faces. Check the crop on one frame first. | Look at every frame you keep. A frame cut for one thing can show a defect or a requirement that is already half-built, and either changes the requirements document. | WebP at quality 80 cut nine 1280-wide frames from 2.8 MB to 476 KB. | .

551.title: 5. From transcript to requirements
551.content: Follow crdm-requirements-template. In addition, for a recording: . | Every requirement cites a timestamp, and every defect the demo exposed is listed separately from the requirements, with the timestamp and “not yet reproduced” until it is. | Say what already exists (Today:) for each requirement, measured against the code or the data, not recalled. | Who signs off is part of the requirement set. Ask who it is if the recording does not say. | Do not build from the recording. A speaker telling the recording agent “implement them on a staging site” is a requirement about the process (P-1), not approval of the requirements. | .

559.content: Skill crdm-requirements-template: Guide and template for CRDM Phase 3 — Requirements Definition. Helps the agent structure requirements from conversation using a REQ-### format with acceptance criteria, priority, and traceability.
