This skill expands the Phase 3 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md and applies the crdm methodology.

560.title: Requirement format
560.content: One definition, shared with spec-kit: a statement, a conformance level, a source, at least one success criterion with its verification method, and a sign-off owner — the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) in the content layer. The fields below are CRDM’s rendering of it; Acceptance criteria are the success criteria. A requirement with none is not ready to post. Each requirement has: . | Field | Format | Example | . | ID | REQ-### | REQ-001 | . | Title | Short phrase | “Beans filtered by epic type” | . | Description | Plain language, no jargon | “The agent can filter work items by their type (epic, story, task)” | . | Conformance | SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT (RFC 2119 / RFC 8174) | SHALL | . | Acceptance criteria (= success criteria, ≥ 1) | Testable, measurable, each with a key and a verification method (test / inspection / review / analysis) | “SC-1 (test) — Given an epic with 3 child stories, when filtered by epic, then all 3 appear” | . | Sign-off owner | Who says it is met — a named person or role | “The BA” | . | Priority | Must-have (High) / Should-have (Medium) / Nice-to-have (Low) | Must-have (High) | . | Source | Phase 1 needs statement / Phase 2 process activity ref | “Needs statement §2 — BA cannot see work grouped by release” | . | Impact | Phase 4 footprint | “Schema: new type field on bean. Pipeline: none” | . | Estimated scope | Work item count / PR sizing | “2 beans, 1 PR” | . Priority scale and conformance keywords . CRDM separates implementation priority (how essential a requirement is when sequencing work or trading off scope) from normative conformance (how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement): . 1. Priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . Aligned with PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH & PHII (2012) (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1): . | Priority label | PHII / PATH CRDM scale | Meaning | . | Must-have (Must) | High | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Should-have (Should) | Medium | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Nice-to-have (Nice-to-have) | Low | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 2. Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the separate Conformance field uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14 — library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels (RFC 2119) and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words (RFC 8174, specifying that only UPPERCASE words carry RFC 2119 normative meaning): . | SHALL (MUST) — mandatory requirement of the specification | SHOULD (RECOMMENDED) — recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed | MAY (OPTIONAL) — truly optional capability | SHALL NOT (MUST NOT) — absolute prohibition | .

561.title: Generating from conversation
561.content: 4-step elicitation . | Listen and deconstruct — identify the nouns (entities), verbs (capabilities), and adjectives (qualities) in the BA’s description | Disentangle what from how — “I need to see beans grouped by release” is a requirement; “use a Jekyll page” is an implementation choice | Formulate testable criteria — every requirement must have a Given/When/Then or a checkable statement | Validate with the BA — read it back. “Does this capture what you need? Anything missing?” | .

562.title: The document is a requirement set
562.content: The requirements document as a whole is a RequirementSet (bootstrap-tools/schemas/requirement-set.ts, published as bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json): reqset:<slug>, the methodology, the issue, a stage — draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded — its members (req: references, each with its own decision), its work plan (work item ids) and its sign-offs. Commit it beside the proposal as <slug>.requirement-set.json, or as a requirementSet: key in the proposal’s front matter; check:requirements judges it. The set’s stage and each member’s status are independent — a requirement outlives the document that proposed it — with one link enforced: a set is accepted only when every member it approved is in-force. The stage moves only through a sign-off (Phase 5’s BA_Signoff, close-out’s BA_Confirm), and check:requirements refuses approved/accepted without a human sign-off, planned without work items, and cancelled without a reason.

564.content: Format as a markdown checklist: . ## Requirements — [Feature name] ### Must-have - [ ] **REQ-001** (SHALL) — Beans filtered by epic type - _Source:_ needs statement §2 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (test) — Given an epic, when `beans list --type epic`, then only epics appear - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR - [ ] **REQ-002** (SHALL) — Release lifecycle skill - _Source:_ needs statement §3 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (inspection) — Skill exists at `cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/release-lifecycle.md` - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR ### Should-have - [ ] **REQ-003** — ... ### Deliverables summary | ID | Title | Priority | Beans | Status |---|---|---|---|---| REQ-001 | Beans filtered by epic type | Must | 1 | ⬜ | REQ-002 | Release lifecycle skill | Must | 1 | ⬜ | . UI / wireframe . Every requirement set carries this section, filled or marked not applicable. When a requirement changes a rendered surface (a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen), the wireframe is designed and chosen before implementation, by wireframe-design-review in Design use; its output (schemas/skills/wireframe-design-review/output.schema.json) supplies every row: . ### UI / wireframe - _Surface:_ the review page's heat map (REQ-004, REQ-005) - _Candidates:_ `docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/` — assets of this proposal - `a.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-mobile.png) - `b.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-mobile.png) - _Chosen:_ `b` by @requester ([where they chose](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6): the conversation, the issue or the PR), because …; `a` rejected because … . Once a feature request is detected (see crdm-detect.md), the agent follows this workflow to gather, validate, and implement requirements collaboratively.

570.title: Method origin and how this workflow adapts it
570.content: This workflow adapts the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) developed by the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and applied to health information systems by PATH & PHII (2012) — see the crdm methodology node and the canonical SKOS glossary concept https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology: . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (library/phii-2023-crdm) | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide) | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm) | . The relation to PHII and PATH CRDM is adapts: . | Phases that follow PHII & PATH CRDM: . | Phase 1 (Needs assessment) and Phase 2 (Business process analysis & redesign) follow PHII’s first two concentration areas (1. Business Process Analysis — think: How do we do our work now? and 2. Business Process Redesign — rethink: How should we do our work?), using swimlane task-flow diagrams across pools and actor lanes and a business process / gap matrix. | Phase 3 (Requirements definition) follows PHII’s third concentration area (3. Requirements Definition — describe: How can an information system support our work?) and PATH (2012)’s separation of activity-linked functional user requirements from cross-cutting non-functional / general system requirements, together with PHII’s priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) and validation walkthroughs (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review). | . | Phases and mechanisms that are the platform’s own extensions: . | Agentic BA-only facilitation channel: An LLM agent facilitates the process with the human BA (Role_BusinessAnalyst) over issues and pull requests rather than a multi-day in-person workshop. | Phase 4 (Codebase impact analysis): 7-dimension impact analysis across the repository’s schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers (crdm-impact-analysis.md). | Phase 4b (Capability area dependency ordering & formalize-first rule): Grouping requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …) ordered by a dependency DAG and formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new features. | Phase 5 (Work-plan decomposition & specification filing): Creating agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and filing proposals from docs/proposals/<slug>.md to docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | Phase 6 (Implementation, branches/ preview & merge sign-off): Feature-branch delivery, automated verification gates, branches/<branch-slug>/ review, and explicit human owner confirmation before merging (merge-to-main.md). | . | .

571.title: Actors
571.content: | Actor | Role | Swim lane | . | BA / Feature Requestor | The person who identified the need and coordinates the CRDM process. Acts as Business Analyst: interacts with the agent, reviews increments, translates stakeholder feedback into agent-actionable direction. May be an author, editor, programme lead, or reviewer. | BA / Feature Requestor | . | Agent | The LLM agent running in the folio-assistant harness. Facilitates the process, synthesises inputs, implements on feature branches, posts summaries to the issue. Interacts with the BA only, not with stakeholders directly. | Agent | . | Stakeholders | The people affected by the feature who must review and approve it. They participate at defined checkpoints (needs confirmation, requirements approval, MVP testing, feature sign-off) — not in the day-to-day development loop. Examples: review committee, country programme managers, IT teams, end users. | Stakeholders | .

572.title: BPMN reference
572.content: processes/process/crdm-requirements.bpmn is the outer process — detection, the Feature? decision, then six phases, each a real subprocess in its own file: . | phase | file | what happens | . | Link the work to an issue | crdm-issue-linking.bpmn | scan, then link or ask; never create without permission | . | Phase 1 — needs | crdm-needs.bpmn | stakeholders, needs statement, loop until recognised | . | Phases 2–4 — BPA + requirements | crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn | current workflow, requirements, impact, loop until approved | . | Phase 4b — prioritization | (inline in Phase 4 exit) | dependency-order capability areas, formalize-first rule, BA confirms | . | Phase 5 — work items + sign-off | crdm-signoff.bpmn | requirements become work items, BA signs off, branch announced | . | Phase 6 — implement + acceptance | crdm-deliver.bpmn | implement, review increment, share MVP, take findings | . | Close-out | crdm-close.bpmn | stakeholder sign-off, BA confirmation (an adjudication, recorded as a requirement-signoff attestation that moves the set to accepted), then the close | . workflow_complete takes step ids such as A_Implement, A_Close and BA_Signoff by name; the interpreter enters a phase by itself and workflow_next tells you which one you are in (inside: Phase 6 Implement + acceptance). You cannot complete a phase — a phase is done when its steps are. Phase 6 is one subprocess, because a rejected increment, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation, and a subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished.

573.title: Every question you put to the BA carries its context first (STRICT)
573.content: Every phase of this process hands the BA a decision they were not inside the analysis for. The ordering rule in interaction-modality.md §4.1 governs this whole workflow, not just its explicit checkpoints: context → options → recommendation → question. Its test applies unchanged: . Can the BA answer without opening anything? . Terms the agent coined during its analysis feel defined to it and are new to everybody else. Three traps: . | An option name you invented. “Prefix-at-rest or prefix-at-install?” names two things that exist nowhere outside your own head and your own issue. Describe what each one does instead, and put the coined name in parentheses if it earns its place at all. | A question that resolves to “go read the issue”. The issue is where the BA goes for depth. It is never where the question’s terms are defined, and a question that needs it read turns a quick decision into a long one. | Options without their costs. “A or B” is not a choice; “A, which changes nothing here, or B, which rewrites every bootstrap.processes:skill ref in the diagrams” is. The BA is deciding on the consequences, so the consequences are the question. | . This applies to every surface this workflow uses: the chat, the summary comment posted to the issue after each round, the PR body, and a work item’s ## Done when.

574.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment
574.content: Input: the feature request (from chat, issue, discussion, or upload) . | Identify the requester — who is asking? | Identify stakeholders — who else is affected? Check: . | <name>.config.json roles across active folios | GitHub CODEOWNERS | Recent activity on related issues | . | Gather source material — the request may come from: . | Chat messages in the current session | A GitHub issue body or comment | An uploaded document (Word, PDF) in uploads/ | A referenced document in library/ | An attachment to a GitHub issue comment | . | Synthesise a needs statement — write a clear, jargon-free statement of what is needed and why, with rationale linking to a concrete workflow | Post to the issue — the synthesised needs statement goes on the GitHub issue as a comment, not in chat | Request feedback — ask the requestor and stakeholders to review | . Loop: iterate until the needs statement is approved.

575.title: Phase 2 — Business process analysis
575.content: Input: approved needs statement . | Find the current workflow — check processes/**/*.bpmn for existing process diagrams that cover the affected area | Map the gap — where in the current workflow does the need appear? Identify the specific activity or decision point | Document current state — if no BPMN exists, document the as-is workflow in prose or create a new BPMN fragment | Identify bottlenecks — probe for the real pain point behind the stated request | . Post to the issue: current-state workflow description with gap identified.

576.title: Phase 3 — Requirements definition
576.content: Input: current-state analysis with identified gap . For each requirement: . | Functional requirement — stated as “SHALL” / “SHOULD” / “MAY” | Proposed implementation: . | Skill file (name, location, description) | MCP tool registration (if applicable) | Schema changes (Zod types, block kinds, constraints) | Pipeline changes (validators, renderers, scripts) | . | Acceptance criteria — testable conditions | Consumer burden — see below. A requirement that shifts work onto the consumer is not done. | Cross-references — link to related documentation pages under docs/source/, existing skills, existing workflows | Wireframe candidates, when a requirement changes a rendered surface — a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen. Before anything is built, run wireframe-design-review in Design use (Call_Wireframe in crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn): at least two candidates, each with a web and a mobile layout, committed as assets of the proposal under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, and shown where the requester will look, chosen from context — the conversation, the issue the request came from, the PR, or several — each place carrying the same branches/ deep links and screenshots (feedback-deep-links, point 5). The candidates are the options Phase 4’s comparison lays out; the requester or BA chooses one at the review. Record “N/A — no rendered surface” in the template otherwise. The wireframe is part of the design process for adjudication (wiregen). | . Consumer burden is a requirement, not a nicety (STRICT) . Every requirement states what a downstream consumer must do to use the result — and the target is nothing. The standing rule: a downstream consumer must never have to string-manipulate, re-derive, or assume a rule in order to use what we publish. If an artefact makes a consumer parse a name, strip a prefix, substitute a base URL, or know a convention that is written down only in prose, the requirement is not met. Ask it in this form, because the failure is always phrased as a saving: . “We don’t need to emit X — it can be derived from Y.” . That sentence is the smell. A rule a consumer has to know is a rule a consumer can get wrong, and the cost is paid by someone who cannot see the code that made the assumption reasonable. Emitting the derivable field costs bytes in a regenerated artefact; the derivation rule costs correctness in every consumer. So emit the derivable field. For example, a preview knowledge graph’s nodes each carry an explicit prov:alternateOf link to their canonical counterpart, rather than relying on a documented base-URL substitution: a consumer should follow a link, not implement a substitution. Three checks that catch most of it: . | Would a consumer in another language need our source to understand this? If yes, emit the field. | Is the convention stated anywhere a machine can read? Prose in a skill is not machine-readable. A typed term in a @context is. | Does the artefact answer “what am I?” from itself? A preview that needs an external convention to be told apart from the canonical version fails this. Put it in the type, not in a filename or a path segment. | . This is also why the declaration file keeps a fixed name while artefacts are stub-named: a consumer must be able to open a repository it has never seen without first deriving a filename. See directory-conventions §Naming. Post to the issue: structured requirements with acceptance criteria.

577.title: Phase 4 — Impact analysis
577.content: Input: defined requirements . | Schema impact — which types, constraints, builders change? | Pipeline impact — which scripts under pipeline/ are affected? | Adapter impact — paper, document, dak? Does it ripple? | QA impact — new criteria? Modified criteria? Registry changes? | Folio impact — which active folios need migration? | Consumer impact — what must every downstream consumer change, and what must it now know? An impact analysis that lists only our own files has measured half the change. Enumerate: fields added or removed from published artefacts, IRIs or filenames that move, conventions a consumer would have to learn. A convention added is an impact, even when no file changed shape. | Test plan — what tests to add or update? Include at least one that asserts the consumer-facing contract, not only the internal one — a test over the emitted artefact, not over the function that built it. | Migration plan — steps, rollback, what breaks without it | . Post to the issue: impact assessment and migration plan. When the analysis yields more than one viable approach . Phase 4 often ends with a choice rather than a plan, and that is the moment the BA is handed a decision. Not a list of approach names with the analysis linked: a comparison, per decision-comparison — per option its pro, its con, what it changes downstream and how reversible it is, laid out where the rows can be read against each other, then one recommendation and a stated default. Items 1–6 above enumerate the downstream question for the change as a whole; the comparison asks it once per option, so an empty downstream column discards work already done.

578.title: Phase 4b — Prioritization and dependency ordering
578.content: Input: impact analysis complete, possibly multiple capability areas identified . When a feature request decomposes into more than one capability area (as most non-trivial requests do), the agent must explicitly order them before creating work items. This is not optional: a flat work item list has no implementation sequence, so the next session either guesses the order or asks the BA a question the analysis already answered. The prioritization protocol . | Identify capability areas — each is a coherent cluster of requirements that can be implemented and reviewed independently. Name them. | Map dependencies — draw the dependency graph: . | Does area A define concepts that area B assumes? | Does area A produce artefacts that area B consumes? | Does area A change structure that area B builds on? If yes, A must precede B. | . | Apply the formalize-first rule — within the dependency order: . | Structural/organizational work first (taxonomies, indexes, schemas) | Process/policy formalization second (skills, workflows, conventions) | Implementation third (code, pipelines, tools) | Visualization/UI last (dashboards, pages, views) | . Only the UI’s build comes last. Its wireframe is designed and approved in Phases 3–4 (step 6 of Phase 3), so the order fixes when it is implemented, not when it is decided. This is not arbitrary — a visualization built before the process is formalized will be rebuilt; a process formalized before the structure is organized will reference the wrong paths. | Present the order to the BA — as a dependency chain, not a list: Area 5 (structure) → Area 2 (process) → Area 3 (review) → Area 4 (planning) → Area 1 (visualization) . With one sentence per arrow explaining why the dependency exists. | BA confirms or reorders — the agent proposes, the BA decides. The BA may override the dependency order (e.g. “I need the visualization first even if it’s throwaway”) — that’s a legitimate business decision, and the agent records it as such rather than arguing. | . What this step produces . | A numbered list of capability areas in implementation order | A dependency rationale for each ordering decision | An estimate of scope per area (work item count) | A recommendation for which areas constitute the MVP release | . Post to the issue alongside the impact analysis. This becomes the input to Phase 5’s work item creation — work items are created in dependency order, not in the order the BA mentioned them. Cross-domain applicability . This step applies identically to code features, paper milestones, and project deliverables. The formalize-first rule is domain-independent: a paper’s structure (chapter order, block kinds) must precede its content (prose), which must precede its presentation (PDF layout).

579.title: Phase 5 — Sign-off and bean creation
579.content: Input: requirements + impact analysis reviewed and approved by stakeholders . | Post sign-off summary on the issue — what was agreed, what was deferred — and record it. BA_Signoff is an adjudication: the BA answers approve, amend, reject, defer or cancel, and A_RecordSignoff appends a requirement-signoff attestation for the requirement set (who, when, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the set to, the reason, and the permalink to the issue comment). GW_SignoffRecorded reads it back, so the phase cannot continue on a sign-off nobody recorded. An agent records the BA’s decision; it never makes it. | Create work items for each implementation unit — each naming the req: statements it delivers, with ## Done when copied from their success criteria, and listed in the set’s workPlan (a set at planned with no work items is refused): . | Follow the check-before-create protocol (see todo-manager.md) | Scope to a single PR-sized unit | Reference the parent issue in each work item | . | Offer the knowledge-graph destinations for the agreed set — A_OfferKg, BA_ChooseKg, A_RecordKg in crdm-signoff.bpmn. This step is not optional and its default creates nothing. See below. | . The agreed set is an ASSET, and Phase 5 is where it gets a home . The agreed set is a design-memory asset, so it goes into docs/; when it relates to a harness, feature or tool, its detailed design and planning go into that harness’s docs/. Without this step requirements end as an issue and a conversation: requirements are produced while building, and they are not the thing built. Three rules, and the first is the one a run skips: . | Ask; never pick silently. The destinations are DERIVED from the owning layer’s declared graphs at the time of asking, none is a listed answer, and if nobody answers nothing is created and “asked, answered none” is recorded. kg-contribution-offer carries the option set and the question that identifies a design-memory asset. | It goes in the OWNING layer’s docs/ — a cat-harness feature’s reasoning in cat-harness/docs/, a folio’s subject matter not in the platform at all. placement decides where inside it: architecture/ for why it is shaped this way, guides/ for how a person does something with it, reference/ for generated material that is never hand-edited. | Not fsh-guts. That is the declared non-rendered trashcan and its content may be thrown away or lost. A design record’s whole value is that it survives the conversation that produced it. | . What separates the record from the skills the same phase produces: a skill carries what a competent practitioner needs in order to do the task; everything past that line — background, options not taken, how to reach a data source, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls — is documentation. Both directions fail silently, so state which one you are writing before you write it. A harness feature’s documents: proposed in docs/proposals/, filed in docs/requirements/ (STRICT) . When the feature is the harness’s own, the documents this process produces (initial analysis, MVP, the options, the agreed requirements) live and are updated under docs/, in two declared sub-graphs of it. | stage | where | what it is | checked by | . | Phases 1–5, and while building | docs/proposals/<slug>.md | the argument: needs, options, MVP, what was agreed | — | . | the feature ships | docs/requirements/<slug>.md | the promise: its front matter is a Requirement | check:requirements | . The directory says what KIND of document it is; the stage is a field. The requirements document is a RequirementSet whose stage (draft … accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded) is recorded in the set and moved only by a recorded sign-off. The directory follows the stage — a set reaching accepted is when its proposal is filed — but does not stand in for it, because a file’s location records neither the decision nor who made it. Both kinds, proposals and requirements, declare within: "docs". Every list of kinds (the navbar’s Folders among them) therefore draws them inside the Docs row, folded shut until the reader opens it. That is general behaviour for any kind declaring within, not a special case for these two. One proposal per feature, updated in place, never forked. A later phase edits the same page rather than writing a second one, so the history of the argument is git log on one file. Filing on ship is a MOVE, never a copy. In Phase 6, once the owner has said to merge: . | git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md, so git log --follow walks the requirement back through its argument. | Add the Requirement fields to its front matter, from bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>. The id IS the file name. | status: in-force | proposedIn: the old path. | actors, description. | statements: one per agreed requirement, each with a key, a conformance level (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY or SHALL NOT) and one requirement sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to. A functional statement may add activity, capability (“I want”) and benefit (“so that”). A non-functional one may add a category. Keep the body: the reasoning stays with the promise it produced. | . | Point the feature’s test runs at the statements they check, in folio-test-run/v1’s requirements array, as req:<slug>#<key>. The test points at the requirement, never the reverse. | bun run cat check:requirements. It refuses a slug that is in both sub-graphs (a copy, or a proposal landing on an existing requirement), an id that is not its file name, and front matter the schema rejects. | . The schema names no outside concept. It lives in bootstrap, so every harness has it, and check:bootstrap-concepts fails if any bootstrap schema names a derivative’s content model, layer names, organisation or interchange standard. A harness that follows a particular standard maps that standard’s fields onto these fields in its own layer, never in the base. How filed requirements are organised, traced, superseded, and retired: . | The assessment of open requirements standards is in methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md, and the literature search, adopted/rejected methodologies, and the BPMN filing workflow (Process_RequirementsFiling, sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) are in methodologies/requirements-filing-and-organisation.md. | Physical files stay flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md (id: req:<slug>, statement keys req:<slug>#<key>), organised in docs/requirements/index.md under the eight canonical concern groups (code-lists/concern-group.json), with three-axis traceability (proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, beans, skills, processes, test/attestations/) and an immutable lifecycle (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired, never git rm). | . A folio’s features are not filed here. This applies to the harness’s own feature work. A folio’s subject matter lives in the folio, as Phase 5 already says.

580.title: Phase 6 — Iterative development
580.content: Input: work items . For each work item: . | Create feature branch — always, no exceptions. Before the first edit, run the collision review in coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Starting new work”. | Implement — following the accepted requirements, and, where a requirement changes a rendered surface, against the wireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4. The delivery summary links the chosen candidate beside the after-screenshot. | Open PR — link to the work item and the parent issue | Deploy staging preview — the feature-staging.yml workflow auto-deploys to branches/<branch-slug>/ on gh-pages. The magenta “FEATURE BRANCH” banner at the top of every page links to the source branch and provides a “compare with main” link. | Post before/after comparison to issue — use the staging-review skill. Every changed page gets a before (main) and after (staging) URL pair in a Markdown table. See schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json for the schema: | Page | Before (main) | After (staging) | What changed |---|---|---|---| Landing | [main](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) | [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) | Added badge | . | Iterate on PR feedback — code review is on the PR; visual review uses the staging preview URLs. When the change touches a folio’s blocks, the page a reviewer opens is the preview’s review page, branches/<slug>/review/: every changed block before and after, with the heat map and outline. The review itself runs through content-change-review.bpmn. The review coordinator slices the change and assigns the slices, reviewers work them in review-task, disagreements go to adjudication, and the coverage gate must pass before sign-off. | Ask user for explicit confirmation before merging to main. This is the merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) sub-process, called from crdm-close.bpmn (Call_MergeToMain) once the sign-off is recorded and before the issue is closed, and run the same way for any increment the owner asks to land earlier. A stakeholder sign-off or the BA’s confirmation is acceptance of the feature, not authorisation to merge it. | Update documentation — the OWNING layer’s docs/ pages and the workflow BPMNs. For the harness’s own feature, file its proposal as its requirements once the merge is agreed: see “A harness feature’s documents” above. If Phase 5’s offer chose a docs/ destination, this is where that page is written and kept true; if the implementation diverged from what was agreed, the divergence is recorded there rather than smoothed. | Staging cleanup — a merged PR’s preview goes away on its own: the merge is the confirmation, since the main site now shows the same thing. Everything else is retained by default. While a PR that will not be merged is open, the user adds the staging:cleanup label; once it is closed the label can no longer reach it, and removal is a feature-staging.yml dispatch the user runs with cleanup_slug and a matching cleanup_confirm (see staging-review). Never remove a staging preview any other way, and never on your own initiative. | . Theme and UI review is NOT a Phase 6 step — it happens at ingestion . theme-ui-review runs only at ingestion of graphical assets for a website or app design, from ingest-theme.bpmn. GW_StakeholderOK’s accepted branch in crdm-deliver.bpmn closes the phase directly. Accessibility, branding and locales for a UI are checked there, not here, because at ingestion a finding is a decision about what the assets will be rather than a defect in something that shipped. When a round of implementation is complete (one or more work items resolved): . | Post a round summary comment on the issue — addressed to the BA and stakeholders, containing: . | What was accomplished in this round | What remains to be accomplished (open work items) | Links to updated content for review (staging URLs, docs pages) | Before/after comparison table for changed pages | . | Never close the issue without explicit authorization — the BA or stakeholder closes it, or the agent closes it only when the BA explicitly says to. An agent must never assume completion. | .

596.title: Criterion adjudication
596.content: Process_CriterionAdjudication · advisory · 4 step(s) . Two reviewer entries for ONE QA criterion disagree: ask the adjudication, then do the one of three things that a criterion disagreement admits. You are in this process when the disagreement is about a criterion — a script failing what a reviewer passed, an agent and a person reading the same block differently. If what disagrees is not a criterion, this is the wrong process and adjudication.bpmn is the one to call directly, with your own outcomes. The three outcomes are legitimate in the same way, and it is not which one is chosen: the finding stands, the criterion does not apply here and should be scoped, or it applies and this is a stated exception. All three converge on A_RecordEntry, because what makes an outcome sound is that its reason was recorded. ADVISORY at the process level, for the reason the adjudication itself is: a judgement cannot be gated, since the whole reason it was entered is that the mechanism ran out of facts. What is NOT relaxable is A_RecordEntry. A judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run, so the judgement is free and the record is not. i i i i

602.title: dak-l1-library
602.content: Skill dak-l1-library: Build a DAK’s library from the L1 sources its Component 1 cites, and the L1 knowledge graph that records them. Read when starting or extending a DAK library, when a DAK’s guidance changes, and before writing any L1 graph for a DAK. Covers fetching a cited WHO IRIS item, ingesting it, deciding whether it is L1 (declared > context > inferred), extracting the Component 1 graph, the L1 graph of each L1 source as a specialisation of its library entry, and the layering rule: the library is upstream of L1. Named by: L2 DAK authoring, Phase 1: Planning, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: dak-l1-library · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn step Build the L1 library from Component 1, in the Business analyst lane. Every library built for a DAK starts from the DAK’s own Component 1, “Health interventions and recommendations”: §1.1 lists the interventions, and §1.2 names the WHO guidelines and guidance the DAK operationalises, each with a printed (n) into the DAK’s reference list. Those sources are the DAK’s L1. Without them the library cannot answer what an L1 graph is for: which recommendation does this decision rule implement? .

603.title: Input and output
603.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: where to look: the useCase (stage 1 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, guideline-use-case’s output), a dak whose Component 1 cites the sources (l2-dak-authoring.bpmn), or both; and whether to ingest what is not in library/ yet. | Out: l1Sources: the candidates, Component 1 sources first, then WHO IRIS and the jurisdiction’s own, each in-library, in-kg or not-yet, included or not with a one-sentence reason. Stage 2 (recommendation-extraction) takes it as its l1Sources. | .

604.title: The layering rule
604.content: Every layer points only upstream: L3 → L2 → L1 → library. An L1 node may name the library node it was read from; nothing in the library names L1. So an L1 document’s publication, sections and elements are specialisations (prov:specializationOf) of its library entry, sections and blocks, and L1 inherits whatever sectioning the ingest produced: an outline, inferred contents, or pages. The schema is smart-base’s l1-library layer (smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts), which imports smart-kg L1 3.0 unchanged.

605.title: L1 or not — three sources, one precedence
605.content: A document is L1 when it is WHO guideline content: a guideline, implementation guidance, a summary table, a position paper, a classification. A DAK is not (it is L2); neither is a technical specification. The answer is a classifications[] entry on the document’s intake.json (scheme https://smart.who.int/kg/layer, code l1), from up to three sources: . | source | written by | smart-kg derivation | . | declared | a person, with by and at | decided | . | context | this step: §1.2 introduces every card as guidance the DAK draws on (--record-context) | — the publication stays inferred | . | inferred | l1-membership.ts from the IRIS Dublin Core record (series, title words) | inferred | . declared > context > inferred. A lower record that disagrees is reported on every run, never dropped: the immunizations DAK’s §1.2 cites DDCC (28), so context says L1, and a declaration says it is not. With no record at all the document is undetermined: the L1 step does nothing and says what to record.

606.title: The pattern
606.content: The DAK itself is library-only: it is L2, so it gets no L1 graph. Reading its Component 1 is how the L1 sources are found; each of those is ingested individually and gets its own L1 graph. | Fetch the DAK from WHO IRIS with bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/fetch-dspace-item.ts <handle URL> --out uploads. It writes the PDF, the item’s Dublin Core record (folio-dublin-core/v1) and an intake.json whose licence is the record’s dc.rights, stated only when the repository states it. | Ingest it: bun run cat ingest uploads/<doc_id>/<doc_id>.pdf --library <lib>. A WHO PDF with no outline goes to pdf-structure, which keeps its inferred contents only if they pass the trust tests, else falls back to pages. | Read Component 1: bun run smart-base/scripts/extract-dak-l1-references.ts --entry library/<doc_id> --context-only. It lists §1.2’s citations and the reference each printed number names, with its URL, and flags those that rest on the printed number alone. Those references are the fetch list. | Fetch every L1 source, one by one, by where it lives: . | an IRIS or PAHO IRIS handle → fetch-dspace-item.ts; | a who.int item page (/publications/m/item/…) → bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/fetch-who-publication.ts <URL> --out uploads, which reads the page’s title, date, type, overview, page count and copyright into the Dublin Core record and takes its one PDF; | a reference whose URL is a listing (the summary-tables page lists Tables 1–4, each cited by its own card) → fetch each listed item, and record on each intake how it was reached. | . A source that is not a publication (a data portal, a blank reporting form) is not fetched; say so. Then ingest each (step 2). | Record the context decision: run step 3 again with --record-context. Each held source’s intake gets §1.2’s context classification, matched by handle or by its record’s dc.identifier.uri. | For each held source that is L1, run the L1 step: bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-specialise.ts --entry library/<doc_id> --validate-zod <smart-base checkout>. It writes smart-kg-l1-library.jsonld beside the entry. A source that is not L1 gets no L1 graph; its library entry is its only representation. | Check the edition. A who.int page serves the CURRENT edition, which may be newer than the one the DAK cites (“updated in 2024” against a 1 December 2025 table). Note it on the intake; do not treat them as one. | Leave fidelity to a person. The run lists each citation whose words differ from its reference title. Someone opens the DAK page and the source and confirms it; nothing marks that check passed automatically. | .

607.title: What an L1 graph holds
607.content: smart-kg-l1-library.jsonld, beside each L1 source’s entry: publication, publication-section (one per library section, front matter excepted, with the ingest’s confidence in its note) and publication-element (each figure, table and box the ingest’s figure reader found), joined by contains, each specializationOf its library-node. Section IRIs use the number as the contents page prints it (Annex 1, Section 2), so an annex does not collide with a chapter of the same number; a heading printed many times (“Analysis” under every chapter) takes its position among its namesakes. A publication with no ISBN or handle is identified by its page URL. It is JSON-LD that survives as RDF. Its @context is http://smart.who.int/kg/l1-library.context.jsonld, the layer’s identity, never fetched at run time. smart-base/kg/ generates that context from the same Zod source as the FHIR models and serves it through src/loader.ts; expand a graph with jsonld.js and that documentLoader. smart-kg’s own L1 context would drop every node class and property name and any predicate it does not know; the library context keeps all three (@vocab, properties as @nest with Dublin Core terms, predicates by declared IRI). A citation resolves by its printed number into the numbered list that holds every cited number with the most title agreement; a DAK has several numbered lists. Title agreement is only corroboration: a card often describes its source rather than naming it, so low agreement is flagged for step 8, not treated as a miss. publicationType comes from a declaration or the title’s own words (summary tables, guidance, position paper, classification). A guideline’s subtype turns on its GRC history, which a title does not carry, and a data portal has no type at all; neither is forced into the nearest code.

608.title: Where the files go
608.content: Each L1 graph is written beside its entry; smart-kg-l1.json is the recommendation extractor’s (extract-smart-kg-l1.ts). The DAK repository holds the library: library/<doc_id>/ for each entry, and uploads/<doc_id>/intake.json plus the Dublin Core record for each fetched item. The PDFs are pinned by sha256 and not committed.

609.title: What it cannot do yet
609.content: . | Element types the library does not extract: table rows, footnotes, charts, images, flowcharts, lists. L1 3.0 defines nine; the L1 step emits the three the ingest finds and names the other six in the publication’s note. | Recommendations in an L1 source are extract-smart-kg-l1.ts’s, which writes L1 1.0 and finds only printed labels. For a source with none, and for each recommendation’s scenario (persona, process, user story), see recommendation-extraction. | The position papers behind a summary table. (29) in the immunizations DAK is the routine-immunization summary tables, which cite the WHO vaccine position papers; following them is a fetch per paper, not automated. | Sources neither fetcher reads. fetch-dspace-item.ts speaks DSpace 7 and fetch-who-publication.ts reads who.int item pages; a PAHO IRIS item behind a different network policy, or a spreadsheet, is recorded with its URL and reported, not fetched. | .

610.title: Schemas this rests on
610.content: . | L1 3.0 and the l1-library layer: smart-base/kg/ — Zod, from WHO smart-kg main 3f5e477, generating the KG* logical models, code systems and value sets; | IRIs: smart-base/scripts/l1-kgid.ts, smart-kg’s kgid.mjs as tested; | the Dublin Core record: folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts; | the intake, its licence and its classifications: cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/intake.ts, cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/source-licence.ts. | .

617.title: dak-postprocessing
617.content: Skill dak-postprocessing: What the DAK post-processing phase produces after the IG Publisher runs — the JSON/JSON-LD surface, the DAK API hub, and the metadata-to-Liquid bridge — and how an IG repository’s own site gets the same sidecars from the cached AST (ig-site:sidecars). Read before changing a post-processing step, and before assuming the Publisher produced something it did not. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: dak-postprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind, except the two Library strippers, which are fhir-harness — see §”One step is not WHO’s”. Everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between publisher.jar finishing and deployment, gated by do_dak and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json (see dak-preprocessing, which also says where the scripts come from). Each step runs inside the Publisher’s Docker container (docker exec -w /work ig-run python3 …), against output/.

618.title: The steps, and what each accomplishes
618.content: | # | script | what it produces | . | 1 | strip_library_binaries.py | removes base64 content.data from Library resources | . | 2 | strip_library_content.py | replaces inline CQL/ELM with a URL reference | . | 3 | generate_logical_model_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per logical model | . | 4 | generate_valueset_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per ValueSet, plus the enumeration-response schemas | . | 5 | generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py | JSON-LD vocabularies from the ValueSet expansions | . | 6 | generate_dak_api_hub.py | dak-api.html — the hub page, and the .openapi.json / .displays.json sidecars | . | 7 | update_translated_image_refs.py | rewrites image references inside translated HTML pages | . | 8 | generate_smart_liquid.py + inject_smart_liquid.py | IG metadata → Liquid variables, and the include injected into every markdown page | . Steps 3 and 4 share one workflow step. Steps 1–5 belong to fhir-harness, not to this overlay: they only transform what the Publisher emitted and add no constraint or profile. They stay in this table because ghbuild.yml still runs them in this phase. check:fhir-harness-exclusions reads the script names from this table and dak-preprocessing’s and refuses them in fhir-harness, except these five. Steps 6–8 are the WHO surface.

619.title: Step 8 is the seam
619.content: generate_smart_liquid.py reads the Publisher’s output/. It scans it for {ResourceType}-{id}.json and, for each, emits Liquid assignments named . smart__<ResourceType>__<id_normalized>__<category>__<key> . with categories url__canonical, url__page, url__json, text__display, link__html, and elements__<key> for scalars (name, title, description, status, version, …). Ids are normalised by replacing every non-alphanumeric character with _. This already turns IG Publisher metadata into variables Jekyll processes, aimed at the Publisher’s own Jekyll. Moving to just-the-docs re-points this bridge rather than building a new one. It is one build behind . The script writes input/pagecontent/smart.liquid.md, which the Publisher only processes on the next build, and also writes output/smart.liquid.html directly so the page exists in this one. A surface that needs two builds to converge cannot drive an incremental staging loop; under just-the-docs the variables are computed and consumed in one pass.

620.title: One step is not WHO’s
620.content: Steps 1 and 2 strip base64 binaries and inline CQL/ELM out of Library resources. Nothing in either is DAK-shaped: any FHIR IG that embeds CQL (any IG using hl7.fhir.uv.cql) produces oversized Library resources. By the smart-stack-layering test — would a non-WHO FHIR IG need this? — they belong in fhir-harness. The deploy phase’s “Delete files >100MB before deployment” step is the same concern one layer down.

621.title: Steps 3–6 are the DAK API
621.content: The schema, vocabulary and hub steps produce the surface the artefact index binds (ig-artifact-ingestion): .schema.json, .displays.json and .openapi.json per artefact, .jsonld vocabularies, and the enumeration schemas (ValueSets.schema.json, LogicalModels.schema.json). No IG publishes an artefact-index instance: an enumeration schema is a schema of a response, whose example happens to hold the list. On an IG repository’s own site: ig-site:sidecars . An IG repository whose index.config.json names smart-base as its site’s landing declares no steps of its own. The site route (cat-harness-tools stage-local.ts) runs the landing layer’s ig-site:sidecars, which is ig-site-sidecars.ts: . | It runs fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of steps 3–6’s generators, over the cached AST. This layer passes only the label and its data types’ JSON-LD prefix. | The per-artefact sidecars, including <stem>.openapi.json, go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/sidecars/. The enumeration schemas and the Swagger UI page openapi/index.html go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/site/, which fhir-harness serves at the site root without replacing a path the site already holds. | $SITE_WORK/ig-api/ig-api.json says {"label": "DAK API"} when the IG declares a DAK (index.config.json contentTypes.dak, or a legacy dak.json; scripts/ig-dak-metadata.ts). Otherwise fhir-harness’s default label, “IG API”, stands. | . fhir-harness binds and serves the sidecars (ig-repo-site.ts, fhir-harness ig-build-pipeline §”The IG repository’s site route”) and never learns the DAK name. ig-index:build runs the same step when it builds an IG’s artefact index. The hub page is fhir-harness’s: ig-api-hub.ts draws it from the artefact index’s bound sidecars, with one loader, on the docs site, an IG site and an IG repository’s own site. This layer names only what WHO calls it: ig-api.json gives the label and the marker an IG’s own dak-api.md holds (<!-- DAK_API_CONTENT -->), and fhir-harness puts the hub at that page.

622.title: Step 5 depends on expansion, which depends on a terminology server
622.content: generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py reads ValueSet expansions, which exist only if the Publisher expanded them, which depends on tx, the optional terminology server input. With a dead or restricted tx the step produces fewer vocabularies, warns and fails nothing. A thin vocabulary output is not evidence of a thin ValueSet: check the expansion first.

623.title: Step 7 renders nothing and is not translation
623.content: update_translated_image_refs.py rewrites <img> references inside translated HTML that has already been built. Where the locale layer is part of rendering there is no built HTML to patch, and the step has nothing to do.

624.title: What the QA reports say, and where they go
624.content: Every script here uses the same QAReporter as the pre-processing scripts and emits a phase report: successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, and a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. qa.json from the Publisher run is uploaded as a workflow artifact. The qa-report graph typology (cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes the shape these scripts emit. Its schema enforces three rules: a summary may not disagree with the details it counts; files_missing must be a subset of files_expected, so an empty result stays distinguishable from a not-found; and running is never a pass — qaReportVerdict returns unknown for a script that died before finishing, not ok.

625.title: Binary artefacts on deploy and on release
625.content: The generic rule and the measuring Tool are ig-binary-artefacts and ig-binary-audit. What the WHO workflows do: . | ghbuild.yml deploys output/ with its binaries. The only binary step is “Delete files >100MB before deployment”, and no Publisher binary is that large. Each branch build deploys to branches/<branch>/, so each preview carries another full copy, full-ig.zip included. | On a GitHub release, release.yml hands off to smart-html. It runs only if publication-request.json exists, then calls WorldHealthOrganization/smart-html/.github/workflows/release.yml (pinned by commit). That runs smart-html’s scripts/ig_publisher.py, which builds and publishes into the smart-html webroot, leaves ig-build-zips/ out of the sitepreview copy, moves only files over 100 MB plus a copy of output/package.tgz into release-assets/, and uploads that to the release tagged GITHUB_REF_NAME. So a release gets package.tgz and, in practice, nothing else; every other binary goes to the webroot. | create_package_release.py is called by no workflow. It would cut a release and move the 19 named binaries out of output/. | downloads.md lists 19 release assets that no release carries, and leaves out full-ig.zip, the largest. fix_release_links.py correctly rewrites its WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base release links to the building repository; the list itself is what is wrong. | . These workflows belong to the WHO repositories and are not changed here.

626.title: Where the counterparts are
626.content: dak-preprocessing — the steps before the Publisher, most of which only populate sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu:. ig-publication — the Publisher run and the authority to release. ig-artifact-ingestion — the artefact index that binds what steps 3–6 produce.

628.title: dak-preprocessing
628.content: Skill dak-preprocessing: What each DAK pre-processing step does before the IG Publisher runs, which steps exist only to feed the Publisher’s page index, and how the phase runs as the overlay on fhir-harness’s AST cache refresh (dak-pre-export.sh). Also which files in a DAK repository are authored and which are generated, and the SEMVER rule for DAK and IG versions. Read before changing, assuming or moving a pre-processing step. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: dak-preprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind (smart-stack-layering), with two steps that are not pre-processing at all — see §”Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing”. DAK Preprocessing is everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between checkout and publisher.jar, gated by the do_dak input and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json. Every script reads and writes that section through input/scripts/dak_index.py. An IG that still carries a legacy dak.json keeps building: dak_index.py --adopt-legacy reads it into the index for that build only, with a warning. Nothing is committed back. ghbuild.yml runs the copy in the IG’s own input/scripts/ when there is one, and otherwise downloads the script from litlfred/smart-base at a commit pinned in the workflow (SCRIPTS_BASE_COMMIT). Step names and script names are the stable handles; re-read the workflow before relying on a detail.

629.title: The steps, and what each one accomplishes
629.content: | # | script | what it actually does | . | 1 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py | writes contentTypes.dak into index.config.json from sushi-config.yaml plus branch/repo context — only when smart.who.int.base is a dependency and the section is absent | . | 2 | update_sushi_config.py | registers pages and menu entries in sushi-config.yaml, and writes placeholder markdown — see below | . | 3 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py, again | re-runs step 1 “with current branch context” | . | 4 | dmn_questionnaire_generator.py | emits FHIR Questionnaire resources from the DMN decision tables | . | 5 | transform_dmn.py + dmn2html.xslt + dmn.css | renders each DMN file to HTML for inclusion in a page | . | 6 | inject_translations.py | substitutes translated strings into the diagram sources before they are rendered | . Steps 1 and 2 share the workflow step “Prepare DAK environment”; steps 3–6 each have a step of their own.

630.title: What “get it into the IG index” meant — step 2, precisely
630.content: update_sushi_config.py does four things: . | Scans for resources — fsh-generated/resources/ (SUSHI’s output) and input/resources/ (static JSON), collecting every ValueSet and every logical-model StructureDefinition. | Writes a placeholder markdown page per resource into input/pagecontent/, as ValueSet-<id>.md and the logical-model equivalent, each carrying a <!-- DAK_API_PLACEHOLDER: … --> marker. A file that already exists with real content is left alone; the marker is how the script tells its own placeholder from an author’s page. | Registers dak-api.md in sushi-config.yaml’s pages: map, creating the pages: key if the IG has none. | Registers Indices → DAK API → dak-api.html in the menu: map, creating menu: and the Indices subsection if absent. | . So the “index” is sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu: maps: the IG Publisher’s Jekyll renders a page only if the file exists in input/pagecontent/ and pages: names it. Step 2 supplies both halves. Under the just-the-docs pipeline navigation is derived from sushi-config.yaml directly and the pages are folio pages, so this step has no job there. See ig-render-jekyll for what replaces it.

631.title: Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing
631.content: Steps 4 and 5 — dmn_questionnaire_generator.py and transform_dmn.py — mint artefacts rather than prepare a renderer: . | the questionnaire generator emits FHIR resources, which the Publisher validates, indexes and publishes like any other. Without it the IG is missing Questionnaires, not a page. | the DMN transform produces the only human-readable rendering of a decision table the IG has. | . They depend on nothing the Publisher does. They are content generation and belong upstream of the Publisher, as authoring steps of the DAK document kind. transform_dmn.py outputs HTML, which the JSON-only render contract does not take. Whether it gains a structured output or its HTML is treated as an embedded asset is still open.

632.title: Step 6 is conditional on who renders
632.content: inject_translations.py rewrites diagram sources before rendering because the Publisher offers no later hook. When pages render through just-the-docs, this platform’s locale layer does that for pages. Diagram sources are still rasterised outside Jekyll, so the step is still needed for them: do not remove it on the page argument alone.

633.title: Steps 1 and 3 — one fact, computed twice
633.content: generate_dak_from_sushi.py runs twice in ghbuild.yml; the second run (“Regenerate DAK configuration with current context”) recomputes the same section after the branch has been resolved. The DAK section is this platform’s own declaration, so compute it once, in the right order. Do not reproduce the double run when lifting this step.

634.title: What a QA report already exists for
634.content: Every one of these scripts instantiates a QAReporter and writes a phase report — successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, plus a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. The qa-report graph typology (qa-report/v1, holds: "state", cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes exactly that shape, upstream’s snake_case field names included, so no translation step sits between WHO’s producer and this platform’s consumer.

635.title: In the AST lifecycle: the overlay on fhir-harness’s refresh
635.content: smart-base’s IG is published from the AST on its cache branch (cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>), like every smart-* IG. The one writer of that branch is fhir-harness’s reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml (skill ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). The plain AST exporter does not run this phase, so smart-base supplies it as an overlay; fhir-harness never names it. | The command is smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh (bun run cat smart-base:dak-pre-export). It runs steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, in that order, from this checkout’s own input/scripts/. It does not repeat step 3. Steps 4–6 run only when the IG declares contentTypes.dak. Any failure fails the run. | The caller is smart-base’s .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml: fhir-harness’s template plus pre-export: bash smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh. It runs by hand, and on every push to main that changes sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini or input/**. | What the cache records. This phase rewrites the IG’s inputs (sushi-config.yaml’s pages:/menu:, placeholder pages under input/pagecontent/). fhir-harness takes the clean commit’s input digest before the command runs, puts the inputs back after the export, and records the AST against the clean commit; the prepared tree’s digest goes under the manifest’s preExport. So the cache verifies on any clean checkout, and a merge that changes no input does not make it stale. | The counterpart after the export is fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of the post-processing schema and vocabulary generators, run over the AST by ig-site:sidecars (dak-postprocessing). | . ghbuild.yml keeps its own copy of these steps for downstream repositories; it does not write smart-base’s cache.

636.title: Source of truth versus generated artefacts in a DAK repository
636.content: This extends the base IG rule in ig-build-pipeline §”Source of truth versus compiled, cached and rendered output”. Two rules: . | Across knowledge layers, authority flows L1 → L2 → L3 → compiled AST / rendered site (smart-guideline-end-to-end §”The order is a rule: L1, then L2, then L3”). L1 narrative guidelines and referenced tables (library/<bib>/l1-extraction/) ground the L2 DAK components (business processes, decision-support logic, core data dictionary, L2 form wireframes, personas, scenarios, indicators, functional/non-functional requirements); those ground the L3 FHIR artefacts (input/fsh/, input/cql/). Never patch an L3 artefact or a rendered page to contradict its L2 source, or an L2 table to contradict L1 without an L1 citation. | Within the repository, hand-edit only the authored inputs — never files written by DAK pre-processing, row generators, SUSHI, the AST refresh or DAK post-processing. dak-pre-export.sh and the QA suite (qa-checkers-dak.ts isGeneratedArtefact) both draw this line: | . | Authoritative source (edit here) | Generated, cached or rendered output (never hand-edit; overwritten on build) | Producer | . | sushi-config.yaml (id, canonical, name, title, description, version, status, license, effectivePeriod, publisher, contact) and index.config.json contentTypes.dak | Legacy dak.json (read-only fallback via dak_index.py --adopt-legacy; never committed back) and fsh-generated/resources/ImplementationGuide-*.json | dak_index.py, generate_dak_from_sushi.py | . | input/fsh/**/*.fsh (ValueSet, logical-model StructureDefinition, profiles, extensions, hand-authored instances) and authored input/pagecontent/*.md | Placeholder pages input/pagecontent/ValueSet-<id>.md and input/pagecontent/<Model>.md carrying <!-- DAK_API_PLACEHOLDER: … -->, plus dak-api.md in sushi-config.yaml pages: and Indices → DAK API in menu: (reverted after AstExportCli in ig-ast-refresh.yml) | update_sushi_config.py, dak-pre-export.sh | . | Authored L2 decision-support tables (input/decision-support/**), data dictionary / requirements workbooks and L2 form wireframes | Generated Questionnaire JSON/FSH resources, rendered DMN HTML tables, and row-generated .fsh instances carrying generated from row N, Automatically generated from DAK artifacts or Autogenerated from DAK artifacts | dmn_questionnaire_generator.py, transform_dmn.py, qa-checkers-dak.ts (isGeneratedArtefact) | . | Authored BPMN / diagram sources (input/business-processes/**, input/images-source/**) and gettext .po catalogues (input/translations/**) | Translated diagram copies and rewritten <img> references in output/ | inject_translations.py, update_translated_image_refs.py | . | Cached AST (cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>) and sushi-config.yaml | DAK API sidecars ($SITE_WORK/ig-api/sidecars/*.schema.json, *.displays.json, *.openapi.json, .jsonld vocabularies), dak-api.html, openapi/index.html, stripped Library JSON (strip_library_binaries.py, strip_library_content.py), and input/pagecontent/smart.liquid.md / output/smart.liquid.html (generate_smart_liquid.py) | dak-postprocessing, ig-site-sidecars.ts | .

637.title: Version numbering: DAK SEMVER and how an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s
637.content: index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version (schemas/dak.ts DakDeclarationSchema, mirroring input/fsh/models/DAK.fsh) and sushi-config.yaml version both use exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: . | Increment | Bumps the DAK (contentTypes.dak.version) | Bumps the L3 IG (sushi-config.yaml version) | . | major (X+1.0.0) | Breaking L2 change in any of the nine DAK component types (DAK.fsh): removing or incompatibly redefining a core data element (dataElement), business process (businessProcess), decision-support table (decisionSupportLogic) or clinical rule, indicator (indicator) numerator/denominator, persona (healthInterventions), scenario (userScenario), L2 form wireframe (form), or functional/non-functional requirement (requirement); or rebasing onto a new L1 WHO guideline edition that invalidates prior L2 logic or data elements | Breaking L3 conformance change per ig-build-pipeline §”Version numbering: SEMVER for a FHIR IG” (removing/renaming a canonical resource, tightening cardinality or bindings, incompatible CQL/operation signature change, fhirVersion change, or breaking dependency major bump), or any major bump in the DAK it encodes | . | minor (X.Y+1.0) | Backward-compatible L2 addition: a new persona, scenario, BPMN workflow, DMN decision table or rule row, optional data dictionary element, L2 form wireframe, indicator or requirement; or extending an L2 value set without invalidating existing rows | Backward-compatible L3 addition (new profile, logical model, extension, ValueSet, CodeSystem, Library, PlanDefinition, Measure, Questionnaire, optional element/slice, or narrative page), or any minor bump in the DAK it encodes | . | patch (X.Y.Z+1) | Backward-compatible L2 editorial or bug fix: typos, descriptions, labels, translations or diagram layout; correcting a DMN cell or data dictionary description to match the existing L1 source without changing data-element semantics or workflow structure | Backward-compatible L3 fix (narrative prose in input/pagecontent/**, translations, example fixes, CQL/FML bug fixes preserving declared inputs/outputs and clinical intent, or rendering fixes), or any patch bump in the DAK it encodes | . How an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s: . | DAK and L3 IG in one repository (contentTypes.dak + contentTypes.ig) — lockstep. index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version, sushi-config.yaml version (and publication-request.json version on a release) carry the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and matching status (draft | active | retired). Both move to the higher of the two increments: L2 minor with L3 patch is minor; an L3 major with L2 unchanged is major. | Update both files in the same commit. Step 1 seeds contentTypes.dak from sushi-config.yaml only when it is absent (if read_dak_section(repo_root) is not None: return), so editing version or status in sushi-config.yaml alone leaves contentTypes.dak stale. | . | Standalone L2 DAK and downstream L3 IG (l3-fhir-authoring). When the DAK (contentTypes: { dak }) and the IG (contentTypes: { ig }) live in separate repositories, each has its own MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH series; a major or minor bump in the DAK requires at least the same bump in the IG release that adopts it. | Adapted / country DAKs and IGs (l2-dependency-choice, l3-dependency-choice). The adaptation pins the upstream WHO DAK and IG in sushi-config.yaml dependencies: (and index.config.json dependencies) at an exact released version (bun run cat check:published-refs); its own contentTypes.dak.version and sushi-config.yaml version follow its own release series. | .
