833.title: When to use this skill
833.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

834.title: How it works
834.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

835.title: Agent workflow
835.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

836.title: Staleness detection
836.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

837.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
837.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

838.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
838.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

839.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
839.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

840.title: Staging links
840.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

841.title: feature-staging (skill)
841.content: The skill feature-staging as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/feature-staging.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

842.title: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe
842.content: Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Process: questionnaire-wireframe-review.bpmn (Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview). Show a built FHIR Questionnaire the way a person will meet it — a mid-fidelity wireframe at web and mobile width, and a live form — have it reviewed as a design, check that it says what the wireframe it was derived from says, and take change requests on either side back through authoring. Sourcing. What a Questionnaire means is defined by the FHIR specification and the Structured Data Capture IG; what the live form supports is defined by NLM’s LHC-Forms. This skill states how the two are wired in this harness.

843.title: Rules
843.content: . | The renderer is NLM LHC-Forms, vendored into the site: never a CDN at runtime. Its BSD-style notice travels with the vendored files. | The field ↔ item check is scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts (Tool check-wireframe-questionnaire). It knows nothing about any one IG; a layer above uses it by name. | Either side may be edited. A change request says whether the Questionnaire or the wireframe was changed, and the agent brings the other back in line. Neither is regenerated from the other. | .

844.title: Inputs and outputs
844.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-questionnaire-wireframe/: . | in — questionnaire (required: one built JSON path; several are several runs), mode, wireframe, renderer, assetDir, suggest, issueForm, channels, branch | out — the output shape of wireframe-design-review (use, topic, assetDir, candidates[] each with its source HTML, web and mobile screenshots and their staging links, chosen, changedAssets, stagingLinks), plus renderer, fidelity[] (the checker’s findings per layout), sdcChecks[] (step 4b) and changeRequests[] (issue URL, which side was edited, status). | . stagingLinks is an inline copy of cat-harness schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json, as every contract carrying it keeps one; changedAssets is the staging preview graph’s changed-assets record, with three kinds of its own: questionnaire-wireframe, questionnaire-rendering, questionnaire-screenshot.

845.title: Roles
845.content: | role | does | . | fhir-modeller | authors: renders, runs the checks, applies change requests | . | business-analyst | reviews the form against the workflow it serves | . | clinical-sme | reviews what the form asks and in what order | . | build-pipeline | the mechanical steps: rendering, screenshots, the fidelity check | .

846.title: Steps
846.content: . | Read the built Questionnaire JSON, never FSH: fsh-generated/resources/Questionnaire-<id>.json, or the IG’s published Questionnaire-<id>.json. FSH is what the author wrote; the JSON is what every renderer and reader receives, so it is what is judged. | Render. | A mid-fidelity wireframe: one field per answerable item, in item order, each carrying data-element="<id>" (the item’s definition, or its code) and sitting in a data-layout="web" or data-layout="mobile" subtree. Monochrome, the item’s own text, no placeholder text — the rules of wireframe-design-review step 2. | A form view: the same JSON in <lhc-forms>, from the vendored LHC-Forms build, on the IG site’s Questionnaire form page (build-ig-site). | . | Screenshots at web and mobile width with the cat-harness Tool wireframe-check (1280×800 and 390×844; renders, no-overflow, no-placeholder). A candidate missing either viewport does not enter review. | Fidelity, when an L2 wireframe exists — the form was designed first and the Questionnaire derived from it: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts <wireframe.html> <Questionnaire.json> . Each layout is judged on its own: a field with no item, an item with no field, an item naming no data element, a data element twice, the first place the order differs. Exit 0 faithful, 1 a finding, 2 cannot tell — and 2 is never a pass. The findings go in fidelity[], per layout. This is fidelity, not design: a faithful form can still be a poor one. 4b. SDC build checks, with CSIRO’s libraries (Apache-2.0; used for checks, not UI), Tool sdc-checks: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/sdc-checks.ts --ast output-ast --fixtures input/tests/questionnaires [--out <dir>] . | check | library | passes when | . | assemble | @aehrc/sdc-assemble 2.0.3 | an assemble-root’s sub-forms all resolve in this IG; --out writes the assembled Questionnaire, so assembly is a build step too | . | template-extract | @aehrc/sdc-template-extract 1.0.16 | extraction from the fixture’s response.json yields every resource in extract-expected.json | . | populate | @aehrc/sdc-populate 4.7.2 | FHIRPath pre-population from populate-context.json gives the answers in populate-expected.json | . | behaviour | @aehrc/questionnaire-test-toolkit 0.1.0 | the IG’s behaviour.test.tsx passes. Warn-only: the toolkit is early, and needs its React and Smart Forms peers installed with the IG’s tests | . The fixtures are the IG’s, one directory per Questionnaire id. Nothing is fetched from a server. not-applicable, no-fixture and could-not-determine are said, and never read as a pass. The results go in sdcChecks[], one entry per Questionnaire. | Review by wireframe-design-review, as-is use for a form that exists, design use for one being designed: blind, per criterion, at both viewports, adjudicated where reviewers disagree. That skill is the method; this one does not restate it. | Stage by feature-staging, and ask for review with staging-review: one deep link per rendered Questionnaire and wireframe, before and after. Where the request goes — the conversation, an issue, the pull request — is a judgement, and more than one may be right: staging-review’s deep-link rule, point 5. | Change requests come in in one of two ways, and both end as an issue: . | ✍ suggest, in its Questionnaire mode, on the form page: the reviewer edits the Questionnaire or the wireframe and the editor opens an issue; | the questionnaire-change issue form, filled by hand. | . Each goes to content-feedback for triage (to public-comment when a review round is open), then to l3-fhir-authoring, which edits the side the request did not touch so the two agree again, then back to step 1. changeRequests[] records each issue, which side was edited, and where it stands. | .

847.title: The change-request payload
847.content: What the ✍ editor writes into the issue’s body, and what the issue form asks for, by these field ids, when it is filled by hand: . | field id | holds | . | questionnaire | the Questionnaire’s canonical URL or Questionnaire/<id> | . | edited | questionnaire or wireframe: the side the reviewer changed | . | patch | an RFC 6902 JSON Patch over the built Questionnaire, its paths annotated with the item’s linkId | . | items | a readable before/after table of the items that changed | . | source | the FSH file and line the item comes from, when known | . | rationale | why | . The issue form is templates/ig-repo-site/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/questionnaire-change.yml, which an IG repository copies to .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/, as it copies the workflows beside it. It is for people filing by hand: the ✍ editor does not open it, because GitHub ignores a prefilled body when template= names an issue form, and the patch would be lost. The editor opens a plain issue whose body carries everything. A pre-filled link longer than about 7000 characters is too long for GitHub; the body then goes to the clipboard and a stub issue opens, as the ✍ runtime does.

848.title: The form view and the ✍ Questionnaire mode
848.content: build-ig-site writes one page per Questionnaire in the IG’s AST, Questionnaire-<id>-form.html, through scripts/questionnaire-form.ts: . | the form, drawn by the vendored LHC-Forms build (scripts/assets/vendor/lhc-forms/<version>/, its NLM LICENSE.md beside it, vendored.json recording the npm tarball and a SHA-256 per file) from a rendered copy of the built JSON, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.json. The source Questionnaire is never changed. Nothing is loaded from another origin; | ✎ (the FSH source the AST names), 📣 (feedback) and ✍ (suggest a change), through the platform’s edit-links recipe and a #fa-edit-cfg block whose suggest.profiles names the mode for the ✍ runtime’s mode registry, [{ id: "questionnaire", module, extensions: [".json"], kinds: ["questionnaire"] }], beside the mode’s own builder, sw, fhirVersion, source and slug. The form host carries data-suggest-mode="questionnaire" and data-block="questionnaire:<id>"; | a plain open in CSIRO Smart Forms link-out, as a rendering cross-check. Nothing of it is embedded. | . The ✍ Questionnaire mode is scripts/questionnaire-mode.js, a plain ES module with no build step. It exports the three roles the ✍ suggest runtime’s mode registry calls (cat-harness-tools EDIT_LINKS_RUNTIME), by these names: . | export | does | . | open(host, ctx) → { get, dispose } | ctx is { text, sourceText, sourcePath, why, src, path, label, kind, repo, branch, config, status(msg) }: text the BUILT Questionnaire JSON (the host’s data-suggest-text), sourcePath / sourceText the FSH it was built from, why the reader’s reason (live). A panel: which side was edited (the Questionnaire or its L2 wireframe), and a raw-JSON fallback; with config.suggest.builder, the self-hosted NLM Form Builder in a window, its updateQuestionnaire / closed result kept (its API.md hand-back). Progress goes to ctx.status. get() is awaited on Submit, never polled, and is ctx.text itself while nothing was edited; dispose() closes the builder window | . | check(before, after, opts) | findings [{ severity, message }], from checkSuggestion below; an error blocks Submit | . | issue(before, after, ctx) | { title, body } and no template: the side edited, the FSH source link (ctx.sourcePath, anchored on the Instance: line found in ctx.sourceText), the page, the item table and the JSON Patch with each operation’s linkId. Not the Why: the runtime appends **Why:** to a mode’s body that lacks it, so the mode writing one too would file it twice | . The side edited and the builder’s round-trip baseline reach check and issue through the session open keeps. Everything else is ctx’s: the mode reads no Why from the dialog’s DOM and does not re-derive the source path from the page. Which path opens it. The form page’s host names the profile (data-suggest-mode), the source in the repository (data-src, the .fsh file) and the URL of the BUILT text the mode edits (data-suggest-text, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.source.json, the unexpanded copy the IG compiled; not the copy LHC-Forms renders, whose value sets were expanded). A runtime with the mode registry serves any host that names its mode: it fetches the built text as ctx.text, reads the source as ctx.sourceText, and its dialog offers a Form | FSH switch: the Form pane is this mode, the FSH pane edits the source as text and files a source diff with the reader’s Why. Without such a runtime, the form page’s loader (scripts/templates/ig-pages/questionnaire-form.js) opens the mode itself, with the same ctx (built text fetched from data-suggest-text, sourcePath, a live why; no sourceText), its own Why field, withWhy to append the Why as the runtime does, and issueUrl for the link. Where the runtime has put its ✍ link in the host, the page’s own link hands the click to it. The self-hosted Form Builder, and no cross-site call . The editor is the NLM Form Builder (formbuilder-lhcforms 12.9.0), self-hosted. The site makes no cross-site call. | The builder is vendored unmodified (scripts/assets/vendor/formbuilder-lhcforms/). The site serves a rewritten copy of its index.html, also as window-open.html (its hand-back route): jQuery from this site (vendor/jquery/3.6.0), the Google font rules removed, and a guard that registers the service worker and reloads before anything else loads. | The service worker (scripts/terminology-sw.js, scoped to the builder; the mapping is the pure scripts/terminology-map.js) answers every request to another origin from this site: . | request | answer | . | clinicaltables /api/loinc_items/v3/search | the IG’s terminology index, in the CTSS shape. LOINC comes only from the IG’s cache; a code it does not hold shows “not in this IG’s terminology cache; add it via the FSH source” | . | clinicaltables /api/ucum/v3/search | the full UCUM list (vendored @lhncbc/ucum-lhc definitions) | . | lhcforms-static /lforms-versions/… | the vendored LHC-Forms | . | lforms-fhir.nlm.nih.gov (import and export), anything else | a local error saying it is disabled on this site | . | The terminology index is written at build time by scripts/terminology-index.ts (Tool terminology-index) from the IG’s own restored cache: output-ast/expansions.json and input-cache/txcache/ (ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). | The form view needs no terminology server either: each item’s answerValueSet that the expansions hold becomes answerOption in the rendered copy. The source Questionnaire is unchanged; a value set the cache does not hold is reported. | A code the cache lacks is added through the FSH source. A ✍ change request can carry it as free text. | .

849.title: The suggest checker
849.content: checkSuggestion(before, after, { wireframe }) in check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts is the checker a suggest editor runs on the reviewer’s edit, in the editor-checker shape { errors, warnings }: . | errors are syntax only — not JSON, not a Questionnaire; | warnings never block, and only what the edit introduces is reported, computed against the editor’s own round-trip of the original: a duplicate linkId, an enableWhen naming no item, and the fidelity findings of step 4 when a wireframe is given. | . It is not declared as an editor-checker profile (contentType: questionnaire; a folio-editor-checker/v1 node naming open, check and issue with extensions: [".json"]): the editor-checkers typology is declared by folio-assistant-sci, which this layer does not need. The page config names the profile directly (QUESTIONNAIRE_PROFILE in questionnaire-form.ts).

850.title: What this skill does not do
850.content: . | It does not build the IG: l3-fhir-authoring and ig-publication do. | It does not regenerate one side from the other on its own. Which side is the source of a change is the change request’s to say. | A clean fidelity check is not a design review, and a clean design review is not conformance: fhir-validation still decides that. | .

852.title: fhir-validation
852.content: Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Incremental IG build, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, L3 FHIR IG pipeline . Skill id: fhir-validation · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Validate against profiles, Build pipeline — SUSHI · validator · IG Publisher lane) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (Validate the cone (fhir_validate), Publisher + validator services (JVM) lane). Validate an IG’s FHIR artefacts against the profiles and packages they claim to conform to. Sourcing. Conformance is defined by the FHIR specification and by the packages an IG depends on; the validator is HL7’s. This skill states how it is invoked in this harness and what each outcome is allowed to mean.

853.title: Inputs and outputs
853.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-validation/: . | in — igRoot (required), validationLevel, targetProfiles | out — overallStatus (required), sushiResult, publisherResult, conformanceResults | . SUSHI compiling is not conformance. FSH can compile to JSON that the validator then rejects, so a green sushiResult with an unrun publisherResult is not a pass.

854.title: The binaries
854.content: The package declares these capabilities (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json); each is defined, with its detection command, in scenarios/capabilities/: . sushi --version # sushi-compiler (requires node-runtime) java -jar "${FHIR_VALIDATOR_JAR}" -version # fhir-validator (requires java-runtime) java -jar "${IG_PUBLISHER_JAR}" --version # ig-publisher (requires java-runtime) . fhir-validator is the standalone validator, distinct from ig-publisher, which builds a whole IG. An authoring loop runs the validator on single resources between builds; a release is cut from the publisher.

855.title: When a package host refuses you
855.content: SUSHI and the Publisher resolve the IG’s dependencies: from packages.fhir.org. Where that host is refused, the failure looks like a broken IG and is not one. Ask for the remedy: . bun run cat tools:remedy packages.fhir.org # → fhir-cache-seed-npm, with its command . Every network-dependent Tool declares remedies per host it reaches (check:tools enforces it), and fhir-harness/scripts/ig-cache.sh doctor prints the same answer for each host it finds unreachable. For packages.fhir.org it is fhir-cache-seed-npm --sushi-config sushi-config.yaml, and for versions npm does not carry, --mirror from a repository that fhir-package-mirror filled on a machine that reaches the host. Pin that repository with --mirror-commit <full 40-character SHA>: git cannot fetch an abbreviated SHA from a remote, and the seeder refuses one. A cloud session can fill the mirror without a person’s device, through a GitHub Actions runner: push a claude/mirror-* branch that edits packages.txt in the mirror repository, wait for its mirror.yml run, merge, re-seed. SUSHI also adds packages that sushi-config.yaml does not list, such as hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r4#latest. A #latest needs the registry to name a version, so offline it fails with errors that look like the IG’s own (for example logical-target … does not exist), even with the package in the cache. Serve the mirror as a registry on localhost, answering GET /<name> with dist-tags.latest and GET /<name>/<version> with the tarball, and run FPL_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sushi build .. Check which version latest resolves to: it is the mirror’s highest, which is only right when the mirror holds the current release. Do not report “SUSHI cannot run here” before running tools:remedy. A refusal that tools:remedy answers with none is “could not determine” in the sense of the next section: say so, with the reason it gave.

856.title: A capability that is absent did not pass
856.content: If a probe fails, overallStatus is not a pass with an empty findings list. It is “could not determine”, and it is reported as such: a clean run over a validator that never started looks exactly like a clean IG.

857.title: Validating a cone
857.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn validates a restricted cone — the artefacts a change touches — rather than the whole IG, and reports the cone it chose. That is a latency optimisation for the authoring loop. It does not gate a release: the full publisher build in l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn does. Do not let a green cone stand in for a green IG: a profile the change did not touch can still be broken by it.

858.title: After validation
858.content: Quality gates on the aggregate are quality-control; publishing is ig-publication. A validator’s verdict is an input to the QC reviewer’s decision, not the decision.

860.title: Folio getting started — content-type triage and routing
860.content: Skill folio-getting-started: The content-folio half of the harness’s getting-started skill: binds processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn and decisions/folio-intent.dmn, interprets describeRepository() content-type markers (folio, harness, dak, sushi), and routes new-content and specialised IG/DAK creation requests. Named by: Getting started . The harness skill getting-started governs repository triage (isFolio, repoHasContent, statedIntent), selectable options via interaction-modality, and gh-pages provisioning before GitHub Pages is switched on. In a content folio or a layer stacked on folio-assistant-core, apply these rules alongside it. Process: processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn. Decision table: processes/conduct/decisions/folio-intent.dmn.

861.title: 1. Repository membership vs. isFolio
861.content: describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. | folio and harness are distinct memberships. The declaration (<name>.json) says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType (<name>.config.json or inline in index.config.json) says this authors folio content. isFolio in folio-intent.dmn tests membership of folio specifically. | Multiple markers do not perturb the five branches. A folio that is also a DAK or carries a sushi-config.yaml takes the same branch in folio-intent.dmn as one that is not: use describeRepository() to inspect what the repository is, and isFolio to drive Gateway_Intent. | .

862.title: 2. Content-type routing on new-content and specialised harnesses
862.content: . | new-content branch: stop the onboarding process immediately and hand off to the folio’s content authoring workflow (such as document-authoring for a document folio, or the paper authoring skills in a paper folio). Scaffolding anything on new-content is a defect. | Specialised IG or guideline creation: when the user asks to create a domain Implementation Guide or guideline in a harness that specialises this layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill discovered via skill_list. In a harnessed repository, default to staging the new sub-KG in place first (sub-kg-lifecycle) until the owner confirms creating or writing to an external repository. | .

864.content: Skill folio-init: Scaffold a new folio layer from the harness — the instantiate affordance of the knowledge graph. Covers when to run folio-init vs remote-mount, what the scaffold writes, the builder shim, state branch seeding, write capability requirements, and –dry-run degradation. relocate content to the trashcan, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . folio-init is the instantiate affordance of the knowledge graph (kg-affordances): standing up a new folio repository or adding a folio layer so an author has a conformant workspace (folio/, uploads/, library/, declarations, agent instructions, and work-plan state branches) linked back to the harness. |   | where | . | the Tool node | tools/folio-init/folio-init.json (id: "folio-init", MCP folio_init, CLI bun run cat init-folio) | . | the entry processes | getting-started.bpmn (new-repo and add-folio branches), repo-conversion.bpmn (overlay branch) | . | companion skills | getting-started, repo-conversion, index-config, remote-mount | .

865.title: When to use folio-init
865.content: Reach for folio-init when triage in getting-started or repo-conversion has settled that a new folio structure should be created: . | new-repo — a brand-new repository is being stood up to author a paper, document or DAK folio. | add-folio — an existing repository wants a new folio added alongside its existing directories (overlay), without overwriting its tracked files. | . Do not run folio-init when: . | The repository already has a <name>.json declaration and only needs a lower harness layer brought in at a pinned SHA — that is materialise, served by remote-mount (bun run cat mount:remote). | The user is converting existing prose in place (convert in repo-conversion.bpmn) — that uses ingestion, not a blank scaffold. | . Because folio-init runs before the target repository has a content type, the Tool is registered among the generic harness tools rather than inside a content-type adapter.

866.title: Write capability requirement and read-only degradation
866.content: folio-init is a writing verb: it creates directories, writes manifests and agent stubs, and (when git is available) prints the command that seeds the cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos orphan state branches. Before invoking folio-init to write, check that at least one write capability is present (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — local filesystem write plus git remote push capability for the target repository and its state branches. | github-api — GitHub API token (gh / REST / GraphQL) able to create or populate the target repository and refs. | github-connector — MCP GitHub connector able to push the scaffolded files into the target repository. | . When no write capability is available (a read-only container or an unauthenticated session), folio-init degrades cleanly via --dry-run (dry_run: true on the MCP tool): it computes and returns the complete Markdown report of every directory, manifest, builder shim and config file it would write, without touching the filesystem or git refs. Never attempt a partial write when write capability is absent, and never report a failed capability probe as a completed scaffold.

867.title: What folio-init writes
867.content: Given title and one or more authors (plus optional content_type, slug, dir, link, assistant_path, force, dry_run), folio-init lays down: . | The folio directories and initial manifests — folio/ (or content/), uploads/, library/, the root <slug>.json layer declaration and <slug>.config.json, and the root index.config.json that instantiates it (index-config). | The builder shim (content/schema/builders) — block manifests in the folio import ../schema/builders rather than importing the platform path directly. Writing the path to the harness once in the shim means re-linking a folio (submodule ↔ sibling ↔ remote mount) is a two-file edit rather than a sweep across every block manifest. | The link back to the platform (--link) — links the harness via sibling (--assistant-path ../folio-assistant) or submodule, and writes .mcp.json and the .claude/ session-start hook (bun run cat state:mount) pointing at that link. | The agent instructions — AGENTS.md and the one-line CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md stubs pointing to it. | The work-plan state branches — declares beans and todos on the cat/<slug>/beans and cat/<slug>/todos branches and prints the seed command; once it has been run, bun run cat state:mount mounts a working store on the first session start (directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”). | .

868.title: What to check afterwards
868.content: . | bun run cat check:declaration-resolution — every directory and asset the new <slug>.json declares resolves on disk. | bun run cat index:render:check — the generated AGENTS.md matches the new index.config.json and layer declaration. | bun run cat state:status — the beans and todos stores are mounted and writable. | .

870.title: Folio repository conversion — markers, orphaned evidence, and intake handoff
870.content: Skill folio-repo-conversion: The content-folio half of the harness’s repo-conversion skill: outside-content evidence and refutation candidate scanning, content-type marker declarations, and dispatching library and content buckets to document-intake and folio authoring. Named by: Getting started . The harness skill repo-conversion governs the read-only repository scan (scan-repo-content.ts), the three selection questions (Q1–Q3), marker selection (--markers), merging existing AGENTS.md / README.md / .gitignore, and provisioning gh-pages. When converting an existing project into a content folio, apply these rules alongside it.

871.title: 1. Preserving outside-content evidence and refutations
871.content: In repositories with formal, scientific, or analytical content, crucial evidence and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/). Carrying only the content tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts classifies outside-content artifacts into read-only candidate classes with their linkStatus: . | classification | description | examples | . | math_proof | Formal proof or theorem outside content tree | docs/audits/*.lean, math/*.lean, Coq .v, Isabelle .thy | . | computation_script | Numerical or symbolic calculation / verification script | docs/audits/*.py, computations/*.py, .sage, .ipynb, .jl | . | macro_definition | TeX macros, custom commands, environments, or math tables | macros.tex, tables/*.tex, preamble.tex, defs.tex | . | audit_refutation | Audit refutation or counterexample falsifying a claim | docs/audits/*is-false*.lean, audits/counterexample.py | . | derivation_note | Informal derivation note or scratchpad | docs/notes/derivation*.md, derivations/*.md, scratchpad.md | . | linked: referenced by at least one block or manifest in the content tree (linkedBy). | unlinked: orphaned evidence not linked by any content block — present these candidates to the author before importing so refutations and computations are linked or ingested rather than left behind. | .

872.title: 2. Dispatching the converted buckets

880.title: /getting-started — what did they actually ask for?
880.content: Skill getting-started: Triage what a person means when they ask to create a folio, and route them. Five requests share one sentence — a folio in a new repo, folio-assistant overlaid on an existing repo, a second folio in a layer that already has one, a content object they called a folio, or something the filesystem cannot tell apart. Reads the repository facts, runs them through the folio-intent decision table, asks a selectable question for what facts cannot settle, scaffolds, and reports the published URL. Use whenever a user asks to create, start, set up, or initialise a folio, a paper, a DAK, an IG, or “folio-assistant” itself. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, KG to public portal, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan, SMART Guideline end to end . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn. Decision table: the content core’s decisions/folio-intent.dmn.

881.title: The landing page is the layer’s own description
881.content: A folio’s home page opens with its description inside its backdrop, both declared in the repository’s declaration. Nothing about any particular layer is written into the template, so a downstream folio does not inherit the platform’s grumpy cat. Where the markdown node is: description in <name>.json. It is markdown and it is rendered as-is. There is no separate landing page to keep in step with it, because a description in two places will disagree with itself. How the picture is declared: an image with role: "landing" and a layout (laptop, mobile, card), plus a textRegion giving, as fractions of the image, where words may safely be drawn. textRegion is authored, not computed. It states where the composition is quiet, which is a judgement: find it by rendering candidate boxes over the image and looking at them, not by deriving a number from the aspect ratio. Run bun run cat docs:harness after editing, and --check in CI. Three states: . | declared | rendered | . | backdrop with region | description drawn inside it | . | backdrop, no region | picture shown, words placed below it | . | no backdrop | words alone | . An undeclared region means do not overlay, never anywhere is fine, because text positioned by guesswork lands on the picture. A folio with no art is ordinary. A viewport with no variant falls back to the widest available, and the fallback is reported — that crop’s region is wrong for a narrow screen, so a consumer can decline to overlay rather than place text somewhere nobody chose. Reader-facing walkthrough: docs/start/getting-started.md §8. A new layer’s beans/ and todos/ are not written into its checkout. By default folio_init declares them on their own branches, cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos, and prints a one-time seed command. Say so when you hand the scaffold over: until the seed has been run and mounted, an empty beans list means not mounted, not no work. The rule, the branch naming and the override live in directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”.

882.title: 0. Why this skill exists
882.content: folio_init scaffolds a folio, and it does it well. What it cannot do is know whether scaffolding is the right move, because the sentence that reaches it — “create a folio”, “set me up with folio-assistant”, “I want to start a paper” — is spoken by at least five different people: . | they mean | what they have | the wrong move costs them | . | new-repo | nothing yet, or an empty directory | — (this is the safe default, and the only one an agent may assume) | . | overlay | a repository with their own work in it | a folio scaffolded on top of a project the agent never looked at | . | add-folio | a folio-assistant layer already | a second repository they did not want, and a split corpus | . | new-content | a folio, and they wanted a document in it | an entire empty folio, and the chapter they asked for still not written | . | ask | any of the above, undeclared | — | . Four of these five states look identical from the user’s sentence, and three of them look identical from the filesystem, so the triage always runs.

883.title: 1. Read the facts — mechanical, read-only, before anything is written
883.content: Three facts, and nothing else. Gather them by looking, not by asking: . # isFolio — does an instantiated config here declare a contentType? # The root <name>.config.json files, and index.config.json, whose instances # may carry contentType inline (index-config skill). grep -lq '"contentType"' ./*.config.json 2>/dev/null && echo isFolio=true || echo isFolio=false # repoHasContent — does the tree hold somebody's project, as opposed to being bare? # Ignore VCS bookkeeping and editor droppings; count anything else. git ls-files | grep -vE '^\.(git|github|vscode|idea)/' | head -1 . statedIntent is the third, and it is a fact about the conversation: one of new-repo, overlay, add-folio, new-content, or unstated. It is unstated until the user has actually said which — never inferred from tone, from the repo, or from what would be convenient. A user who says “I want to add a chapter” has stated new-content; a user who says “create a folio” has stated nothing, because that sentence is what the five requests have in common. isFolio is ONE MEMBERSHIP of a set, and the set is what a repository is. describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. folio and harness are different types. The declaration says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType says this authors folio content. That config is a root <name>.config.json, or its entry in index.config.json, where inline fields overlay the imported file (index-config). Listing a layer in the index makes it instantiated, not a folio. cat-harness/ carries the first and not the second — it is a harness and is not a folio. isFolio is exactly membership of folio: the DMN documents the input as a config in the working directory that declares a contentType, not its mere presence. So a repository being several things at once does not perturb the five branches. They key on folio-ness alone, and a folio that is also a DAK takes the same branch as one that is not — it is still already a folio, still has content, and the user has still either stated an intent or not. Use describeRepository when you want to know what a repository is; this probe when you want to know which branch to take. isFolio is about the working directory, not about the user. Somebody who has used folio-assistant before, in another repo, is still in an isFolio=false directory. Their experience is not a fact this table reads — it changes how much you explain, not which branch you take.

884.title: 2. Let the table decide
884.content: Feed the three facts to workflow_complete on Gateway_Intent, or read folio-intent.dmn directly. Do not supply an outcome: the gateway is computed, and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied answer there on purpose. The table returns one of five branches. Two of its seven rules return ask, and that is a result, not a failure to produce one: . | already a folio, intent unstated → ask. add-folio, new-repo and new-content are all consistent with what is on disk. | not a folio but has content, intent unstated → ask. overlay and new-repo are both consistent, and overlaying somebody’s repository on a guess is not recoverable by a git checkout. | not a folio, nothing here → new-repo. The one state that answers itself. | .

885.title: 3. Ask — as options, never as prose
885.content: When the branch is ask, put the question as a short list of selectable options. Not a paragraph, not an open “what would you like to do?”, and not a question whose answer has to be typed out. Load interaction-modality first; it decides the form the question takes, and for some users free text is not an available input at all. The list, phrased in the user’s terms rather than the branch names: . | Start a new folio in a new repository — nothing here gets touched. | Add folio-assistant to this repository — keeps what is here; I’ll look through it first and show you what I find before importing anything. | Add another folio to this repository (offer only when isFolio=true). | Add something to the folio that’s already here (only when isFolio=true) — a chapter, a document, a DAK component. | Tell me more — for the user who wants to describe it in their own words. | . Then ask what they want to get started on, offering the top-level content types this platform knows about, because “a folio” is not something anybody actually wants: . | content type | what it is | profile | . | paper | a scientific paper or book, with formal claims backed by Lean and typeset through LaTeX | paper | . | document | structured prose — policy guidance, a standard, a report. No Lean, no required TeX | document | . | WHO SMART DAK | a Digital Adaptation Kit (L2): personas, business processes, data elements, decision tables | dak | . | WHO SMART IG | a FHIR Implementation Guide (L3) built from an L2 DAK | dak | . Record the answer as statedIntent and evaluate the table again. The user’s answer is a fact like any other — it feeds the gateway, so the loop in the diagram runs back to Task_ReadFacts rather than jumping straight to a branch. When a remote repository is involved, ask which mode — and never infer it from push access. A remote git repository is assumed read-only (read-from). Having push access to a remote is never permission to modify it, and instantiating on a remote repository writes nothing there without the user’s explicit permission for that repository. Ask which mode they want, with materialize-or-reference as its own question: . | Keep it here (read-from) — build and render from the remote KG in this repository (stage-ig-sites into /<instance>/), and ask whether to materialize its assets locally or reference it in place (materialize-remote / materialize-on-demand). | Put a harness on the remote repository (written-to) — instantiate the harness in that remote repository itself and build in its own CI (stage-ig-sites --only <instance> --source .), only after explicit permission for that repository. | .

886.title: 4. Route
886.content: | branch | do | . | new-repo | Ask for the name. Create or use the empty directory, then folio_init. | . | overlay | Hand off to repo-conversion — scan first, import second, and never in the other order. The scan’s markers are offered as picks (§2a, Task_ChooseHarnessed): the harness declares only what the person chose — declare, don’t slurp. | . | add-folio | folio_init against a new top-level slug in the existing layer. Do not re-link the platform; it is already linked. | . | new-content | Stop. This process ends here. Hand off to the active content type’s authoring skill. Scaffolding anything on this branch is the bug. | . An empty repository gets main before any feature branch. GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default, so run init-folio (it seeds main first) or push main yourself before pushing anything else. A specialised content type is routed by its own creation skill. When the answer to step 3’s second question names a domain content type shipped by a higher harness layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill (discover it via skill_list). It reads the same facts and adds the in-repository staged sub-KG option — staging inside the current repository first so nothing outside the repository changes until the owner confirms. Where folio_init does not handle that content type directly, the new-repository route scaffolds with --instance. A second folio can leave later. What add-folio creates, and any staged sub-KG, may later move to a repository of its own. That is sub-kg-lifecycle: stage it in place, then create the repository and delete the in-repo copy, each only on the owner’s confirmation.

887.title: 5. After scaffolding — seed the plan, then publish
887.content: . | Seed the work plan. One work item per top-level thing the author named in step 3. Run the exact-title existence check in todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Check before you create” first — beans create is not idempotent. | Provision gh-pages — before Pages is switched on. This is Task_ProvisionGhPages in the process, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn (the gh-pages Tool’s subprocess — render-kg-to-cdn): a gh-pages branch must exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision: it checks git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages and, only if the branch is absent, pushes an orphan gh-pages holding a placeholder index.html and .nojekyll. It is idempotent and never forces a push; without --provision the script creates no remote branch, it only reports unprovisioned with the exact command. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — not “GitHub Actions”, when the publish workflow pushes gh-pages (the script prints the source it expects). Every publishing route reaches this step: new-repo, add-folio, and the overlay route through repo-conversion — including an overlay or new repo that remote-mounts its dependencies, which never reaches this section by itself. | Start the Pages build and report the URL. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --wait. It checks the branch first, derives the site address, says whether a publish workflow exists and which Pages source it needs, and probes until the site answers. | Say which of the four states you got, and never blur them: . | unprovisioned — there is no gh-pages branch (exit 3). Go back to step 2; nothing later can succeed until it exists. | live — hand over the link, and say what is on it. | not-yet — a measured 404. Give the address, say the first build has not landed there yet, and say roughly how long it takes. | unknown — no URL could be derived, or the probe failed. Say that. “Should be live shortly” is a claim you do not have evidence for. | . | Tell them the corpus is by reference, and how to change that. A fresh harness holds references, not the remote content itself, which can be hundreds of gigabytes. When they need part of a remote subgraph locally, that is an ask made later, as the need appears. Name the skill (materialize-on-demand) and the one command that shows what is already held (bun run cat cache:index), so they learn the option exists here rather than by finding a schema. Do not materialize anything now. | .

888.title: 6. Anti-patterns
888.content: . | Scaffolding on ask. The table returned a question; answering it yourself with the convenient branch defeats the table. | Treating “I’ve used this before” as add-folio. Experience is not a filesystem fact and not an intent. | Asking in prose. “Could you tell me a bit about what you’re hoping to build?” is a wall for a user who types with difficulty, and it produces a worse answer than the numbered list. | Announcing a Pages URL you have not probed. See step 5. | Going straight to folio_init because the request seemed obvious. Every one of the five requests seems obvious to the person making it. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” as the source for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. Step 2 first; the source is “Deploy from a branch”. | .
