1108.title: ig-render-jekyll
1108.content: Skill ig-render-jekyll: Rendering a FHIR IG’s content through the just-the-docs pipeline instead of mounting the IG Publisher’s finished HTML — the JSON-only representation contract, navigation derived from sushi-config.yaml, and the LHS rail. Read before adding a representation, a menu entry, or a page kind. Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs . Skill id: ig-render-jekyll · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . Render an IG’s pages as folio pages — markdown with front matter, through Jekyll and just-the-docs — from the Publisher’s structured output, never its finished HTML. Publisher HTML has no front matter, so the navbar, language bar, QA badges and translation surface cannot reach it; a folio page gets them all. Whether an IG repository gets this rendering is asked when it is adopted (default yes); see ig-build-pipeline §”Who starts a build”.

1109.title: The three contracts
1109.content: 1. JSON only . The Publisher emits JSON, XML and Turtle; only JSON is taken, wrapped in JSON-LD / JSON Schema. RDF, where needed, is projected from the JSON-LD. A representation that arrives and is not taken is recorded as a refusal. Not linked either. The site does not link a resource’s .xml or .ttl copy: JSON-LD nodes carry only JSON encodings, and the site.data artefact variables only url.json. The refusal record still counts what each IG published in those forms. 2. Navigation is derived, never authored . sushi-config.yaml already carries both maps the site needs: . | pages: — an ordered map of source file to title. That is the page order. | menu: — the grouping, including nested subsections. | . Derive the navigation from them. Do not hand-author a nav file or write entries back into sushi-config.yaml. When the config names a page that does not exist, that is a finding, not a reason to create a placeholder. 3. LHS rail, and the theme is captured rather than replaced . Navigation goes in the left-hand rail, not the FHIR IG’s top bar. The rest of the IG theme — CSS, typography, resource-page furniture — is captured into the theme layer rather than discarded. Nav position is a layout setting; nav contents are derived per build.

1110.title: What the render reads in the IG repository
1110.content: Only what the repository declares. Every reader on this path (build-ig-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, ingest-ig-chrome, ig-repo-site) goes through scripts/ig-read-scope.ts, which honours contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json; anything outside it is not rendered. A repository with no section is read whole, with a warning. See ig-build-pipeline §”What this layer reads”.

1111.title: Where the variables come from
1111.content: artifactVariables (build-ig-site.ts) writes the per-artefact Liquid variables from the artefact index to _data/, read by the same Jekyll run: site.data.fhir.artifacts.<ResourceType>__<id> with url (canonical, page, json), text, link.html and elements.<key>, plus artifact_categories, artifacts_listed and artifact_lists. An element key the index does not hold is reported as not sourced, never written empty. The families and keys follow WHO’s generate_smart_liquid.py, a build script outside this layer, without its smart__ prefix: that prefix is WHO’s, and this layer does not know about WHO.

1112.title: What parity means, and what it does not
1112.content: Parity is a checklist of asset types and page kinds. A page kind the Publisher emits no data for cannot be rendered.

1113.title: Thin pages, the default (--full-pages to opt out)
1113.content: Every IG page is a thin HTML shell that loads its content from the JSON-LD graph, unless a build passes --full-pages. The shell is cat-harness-tools’ thinPageHtml. Artefact pages (gen-ig-pages.ts) . | Page address: artifact/<Type>-<id>.html, self-canonical. | The asset is a JSON-LD node, artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld, with no .json twin (every reader fetches the .jsonld), written by ig-artifact-jsonld.ts from the index (kind ig-artifact-jsonld; QA ig-artifact-jsonld.ts check over the built site). It uses the FHIR RDF class, dcterms, schema.org and PROV, and mints nothing. The page names the node as alternate. Its encodings list the reduced <Type>-<id>.json at the site root first (local), then the full copy in the AST cache by raw URL (mirror), then the IG’s published file (upstream); artifact/index.jsonld names each root file on its entry (schema:contentUrl; fhir-harness#359). | One shared renderer. assets/ig-artifact.js fetches the node, then the resource’s full copy (the mirror, else the local one), draws the description, facts, identity table and elements, concepts or includes, and hands the narrative and JSON to ast-resource.js. The page carries only its title, key and a <noscript> link to the node and resource. | The rail is linked: folio-navbar: linked, and the rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts) links its style and scripts rather than inlining them. | The tab views are thin pages too, written beside the page wherever the site serves the artefact’s JSON: a compiled copy (--compiled-data) or, failing that, the Publisher’s own <Type>-<id>.json carried as data (--publisher-data <dir>, from the docs root). An IG repository’s site (ig-site:compose) passes only --compiled-data .: the AST’s copy, served once at the root as <Type>-<id>.json. Each view keeps the Publisher’s file name: . | -definitions: the snapshot’s element table, differential marked; | -mappings: each mapping declaration with the elements mapped to it; | the JSON view (.profile.json for a StructureDefinition, else .json), drawn by ast-resource.js; | -examples, for every StructureDefinition: the instances claiming it in meta.profile, or a note that there are none. | . Each uses the same shell (thinArtifactView) and renderer; the artefact’s page links them in a tab bar, and the narrative’s links to them are relinked. The change history, testing, XML and Turtle views are neither rendered nor published. The IG API view pages stay full pages. | Nothing under comparison-v*/ is published. ig-site:publisher-pages serves the AST’s data and reads no Publisher output. | In an IG site the docs root is the site root, so --compiled-data . points each resource at ../<Type>-<id>.json from artifact/. No ast-data/ mirror is published. | . The artefact list and the table of contents (build-ig-site.ts) . | One index node, artifact/index.jsonld (family folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1, same kind), lists every artefact once, in the Publisher’s order, each entry naming its node and carrying only what a list row shows; check holds it to the artefact index and each node. | artifacts.html is a thin shell over that node: a jump list of categories, a filter, then every category open (nothing collapsed), anchored #artifacts-<slug>. | What a list draws: . | The IG’s own ImplementationGuide is “This guide”, drawn first (#artifacts-this-guide), never as a “Not categorised” row; the toc lists it first too. | A category that mixes resource types is sub-headed by type (#artifacts-<category>-<type>; the Publisher’s “Other”: Basic, Questionnaire, DocumentReference…), and the jump list counts each type. | A table draws only the columns its rows fill. An instance (an artefact with no canonical URL) has no description, so the index copies what the resource states: its meta.profile (dcterms:conformsTo, drawn as the last path segment, linked when it is in the same IG) and its code (dcterms:subject). A definition’s core profile (shareablevalueset) is not shown. | . | toc.html is a thin shell. The IG’s own pages (sushi-config.yaml pages:, landing page first) stay in its HTML; the artefacts under each category are drawn from the index node. | Both are written by stageIgSite when StageOptions.artifacts.index is given, which stage-ig-sites.ts does unless --full-pages. Staging thin a site whose artefact pages were generated with --full-pages (no index node) is refused. | . The narrative pages (composeIgSite) . | The IG’s prose stays in the HTML, rendered by Jekyll; composed into a host site, the page wears thinIgLayout (_layouts/ig-thin-<instance>.html) instead of the host’s layout, so none of the host’s chrome (harness bar, SVG sprite, sidebar nav, inline scripts) is written into it. | Everything around the prose is linked: assets/ig-artifact.css, assets/ig-topbar.css, assets/ig-source-links.js and the rail (folio-navbar: linked). The IG’s top bar, edit links, footer and TOC declaration stay. | The thin page has no host search box or QA badges; it has its own search box and language picker block (below). | . The footer stays in view . Every IG page ends with the Publisher’s footer (ig-footer.liquid on the Jekyll pages, ig-artifact.js on the thin pages, one igSiteFooter object for both): publisher and copyright year, package#version, FHIR version, the build day, and Links: Table of Contents | QA Report | Version History | License, each value read from the IG’s package, sushi-config.yaml or AST and left out when none holds it. Unlike the Publisher’s, it stays at the bottom of the window (owner, 2026-11-06): it is the body’s last box, after <main> on every IG page, position: sticky (ig-artifact.css), so it spans the width beside the rail, the page scrolls under it and nothing is left behind it at the end of the page. The body is a column at least the window’s height with <main> taking the free space, so on a page shorter than the window the footer lands at the window’s bottom too. In print both are off: the footer is static, once, at the end. “QA Report” is qa.html, the harness’s QA report (ig-qa-page.ts): the FHIR QA the build holds (the Publisher’s qa.json carried with the AST, the AST’s record and validity) and the knowledge graph’s (cat-harness-tools kg-qa-report.ts). Search and the language picker . The folio rail replaces the theme’s side menu (#site-nav is dropped; IG_DROPPED in stage-local-ig.ts), and the IG’s top bar carries a search box over the IG’s pages and artefacts (ig-search.ts): . | ig-repo-site.ts compose writes the index, assets/ig-search.json (each IG page’s title and full text; each artefact’s title, id, name, key, canonical and description), and the client, assets/ig-search.js. The index is fetched on the box’s first focus, never on page load. | The box (form.ig-search, input #search-input) is in the composed pages’ .ig-topbar and the thin pages’ header.iga-top. It is not .search, so docs-ui leaves it in the top bar. A build that does not write the files (gen-ig-pages without --search, StageOptions.search unset) writes no box. | Any other built page lacking a box (for example an IG API hub page or openapi/index.html) gets one: publisher-pages puts a bar at the top of its body (header.ig-search-top: the IG’s name, the box, the picker’s slot; stampSearchBox, withSearchBar). The pass skips assets/ and runs only when the site serves a search index. | The language picker sits beside the box, in the empty <span data-fa-slot="locale"> that follows it, which docs-ui fills. A site with no IG bar keeps the picker in docs-ui’s band. | docs-ui draws the picker from a page’s fa-translation-meta block, which publisher-pages writes (cat-harness-tools lib/translation-meta.ts) into every built page lacking one, from the IG checkout’s translation declaration; set-html-lang.ts reads it afterwards. | Translated pages (fhir-harness#382). When the IG declares translations/ in contentTypes.ig.include, each catalogue translations/<locale>/pagecontent/<page>.po is injected into its page (cat-harness-tools injectMarkdown, the segmentation the catalogue was extracted with) and staged at <locale>/<page>.md, the path the picker opens. The page and its translations carry lang, available_locales and, on a translation, translation_status and translation_source; the thin layout writes the picker’s block from them, so the picker links each language that exists. A span with no translation stays in English. A locale is verified only when translations/<locale>/status.json records a sign-off; otherwise unverified, and docs-ui shows its notice. Translated pages are out of the menu, and relative links climb out of the locale folder unless they point at a page translated into the same locale (scripts/ig-page-translations.ts). | . Pass both or neither. --thin is a no-op; --thin --full-pages is refused.

1114.title: What this does not replace
1114.content: Which AST the pages are drawn from. An IG repository’s site is drawn from the AST on its cache branch, cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, which a Publisher run on a runner refreshes; the publish refuses an AST not valid for the commit. See ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”. The Publisher still runs: validation, dependency resolution and terminology expansion are its job and are not reproducible from cached output.

1116.title: index.config.json: what this checkout instantiates
1116.content: Skill index-config: index.config.json at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each layer’s config INLINE in its entry (a legacy <name>.config.json is only imported until --inline retires it), and which harness / is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, index.lock.json and its legacy fallback, the reserved index stem, the generated .gitignore block and its gate, and index-config:migrate (with --inline) for separated repositories. Named by: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Remote-mount a dependency . The schema is folio-index-config/v1 in cat-harness/schemas/kg/index-config.ts. The index is the ONE config. Each layer’s config is written inline in its instances[] entry. A <name>.config.json is a legacy file: imported only as a migration step, then retired with index-config:migrate --inline --write. Never create one — not to make a tool find a recipe, not for a new layer. If a reader only finds config in the file, that reader is the bug; fix it to read the index entry first. index.config.json holds three facts about how a checkout is instantiated: which harnesses are instantiated, which one is / (a checkout has one <base>/index.html), and where each one comes from, so each is stated once rather than spread across every root config. When it exists at the root it is authoritative. When it is absent, readers fall back to the root *.config.json files, their site.landing flags, and remoteMounts on the root declaration. { "$schema": "folio-index-config/v1", "instances": [ { "name": "folio-assistant", "source": { "local": { "at": "." } } }, { "name": "cat-harness" }, { "name": "my-ig", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "owner/my-ig", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "overrides": { "my-ig": { "whole": true } }, "trust": { "consent": { "...": "..." } } } } }, { "name": "my-guide", "contentType": "document", "site": { "build": { "sourceSteps": ["site:document"] } } } ], "site": { "landing": "cat-harness" } } .

1117.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
1117.content: A declaration (<name>.json) says what a layer declares. It travels with the harness into every checkout that uses the harness. An index.config.json entry says the layer is instantiated in this checkout. Without an index, a <name>.config.json at the root says the same thing. Tiles, the landing and the hub listing are all drawn from the instantiated set, which instantiatedHarnessNames(root) returns. Never derive that set from declarations or from a directory listing. The dependencies of an instantiated harness are not instantiated just because a mount’s closure brought them in. They keep a group of their own rather than disappearing. A harness that a KG subscription chose is instantiated the same way: kg:instantiate adds its entry, with its config inline, when the checkout has an index (and only without one writes a root <name>.config.json).

1118.title: Inline, over a legacy import while one remains
1118.content: Each entry’s effective config is built like this: . | Start from a legacy imported file, while one remains. That is import when it is given, else <name>.config.json, and only if the file exists. The target state is that no such file exists. | Overlay every other key of the entry (everything except name, import, source and _comment) as an inline HarnessConfig field. Objects merge key by key, and arrays and scalars are replaced. Inline fields win. | . effectiveInstanceConfig(root, name) computes it. readHarnessConfig(dir) returns it for any layer that an index lists, walking outward from the layer root and stopping at the first directory that holds either the index or the layer’s own config. A layer the index does not list is read from its own config file. Readers that are handed a root and a name (the site recipe in build-instance-site.ts) use readInstanceConfig in cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-config.ts, which reads the same way and REPORTS every legacy file it reads. Retiring the files is index-config:migrate --inline --write: each imported file is folded into its entry by exactly the overlay above, so no effective config changes, and the file is deleted. index-config:inline:check fails while one remains.

1119.title: Local or remote
1119.content: . | source absent: local, at <name>/. | source.local.at: local, at that path. Use . for the layer declared at the root. | source.remote: a remote mount. It is a remoteMounts entry minus harness, which is the entry’s name. It reuses RemoteMountSchema instead of restating it, so it has ref (not pin), overrides.<name>.whole and .path, note, trust.consent and track, and every field added to RemoteMountSchema arrives with no edit here. | . There is one read path and one write path for remote mounts: . | Read: readDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot) returns the index’s remote entries when an index exists, else the declaration’s remoteMounts. If both carry mounts it throws and names both files. It never picks one. | Write: writeDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot, mounts) always writes index.config.json, seeding the index from the checkout first if there is none. It refuses while the declaration still carries remoteMounts. Nothing writes remoteMounts on a declaration. | .

1120.title: Which harness / is
1120.content: resolveLandingInstance(root) is the only reader. It applies these rules in order: . | condition | / is | . | the index is unreadable | invalid: the gate fails. There is no fallback to the flags, because the index was written to override them | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it lists | that layer (by: "index") | . | the index’s site.landing is "hub" | the neutral hub: the harness listing and the todo panel | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it does not list | invalid: the gate fails, and it is never a silent fallback | . | no site.landing (or no index), one layer | that layer (sole) | . | no site.landing, several layers, exactly one config flags site.landing: true | the flagged one | . | several flagged | the hub | . | none flagged | ambiguous: check:landing-instance fails, because the answer is never guessed | . | nothing instantiated | none: a state of its own, not a default | . gen-landing-data.ts and sync-docs-harness.ts ask this resolver. They do not use their own location. check:landing-instance also checks that the index and the root *.config.json files agree: . | A root config that the index does not import fails the check: without the index it would instantiate a harness, with it it does not, and nothing picks between them silently. | An import that names a missing file also fails the check. | An entry with no config file at all is the target state, and passes. | A legacy file an entry still imports is reported every time. It passes while it is a pending migration (every key it holds is either not inline or inline with the same value). It fails when the entry overrides one of its keys with a different value: the file’s value is then dead text that a reader of the file alone takes for the config. | .

1121.title: A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests
1121.content: Instantiating a harness in a repository includes turning its checks on there, through one reusable workflow the harness owns, never a copy per repository, so a layer is judged on its own pull requests and not only when an index re-pins it. Switching off a repository’s builds must not switch off its gates. The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml. A repository calls it from a workflow of about fifteen lines that runs on pull_request: . jobs: checks: uses: <owner>/<tools-layer>/.github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml@main with: mode: layer # or `index`: the repository is its own index instance: <instance> # layer mode: its directory in the folio-assistant index path-in-repo: <instance> # where the instance sits in the repository ('.' at the root) . | layer mode is for a repository that an index mounts, such as cat-harness or the DAK layer. The workflow checks out folio-assistant and puts the PR in place of the locked mount. | index mode is for a repository that is its own index: an IG repository over the DAK layer, smart-ra, or a folio. Its own index.lock.json is replayed. | The gates are the harness’s graph checks over the repository’s own layer, plus every check:* / *:check script of that layer and its whole dependency harness (its transitive needs). Each is named <owning-instance>:<script>. | A PR fails only on what it newly breaks. Each gate and test runs on main and on the PR. Anything already red on main is listed, never hidden, and never counted against the PR. | . A layer PR that declares a new directory is red on two index gates it cannot clear. The index README lists every declared directory, so the PR leaves index:render:check and readme:sync:root:check stale, and only the index re-pin that takes the PR regenerates the README. Read those two as expected when they are the only new failures, and run them green in the index re-pin instead. Disabling a repository’s automatic builds is not disabling its checks. When an IG repository’s automatic gh-pages or IG Publisher triggers are switched off (the onboarding question in the FHIR IG layer’s ig-build-pipeline), the harness caller stays on.

1122.title: The exemptions of the index’s own workflows
1122.content: .github/workflows/ belongs to the index, so the steps CI runs there that the local gate set does not are exempted HERE, under gateExemptions.steps, each with a kind and a reason (GateExemptionsSchema, the same shape an layer declaration carries). They land in the same change as the workflow step, never ahead of it in a layer: an exemption for a step CI does not yet run matches nothing, and gates-workflows.test.ts refuses a stale exemption as it refuses an unclassified step. "gateExemptions": { "steps": [ { "match": "bun run cat state:push -- --id health", "kind": "ci-only", "reason": "…" } ] } . A layer still exempts its OWN scripts and steps in its own declaration.

1123.title: index.lock.json, and the legacy name
1123.content: The lock records what the declared mounts resolved to. It is generated by mount:remote and kept as a separate file. The legacy name is <root-instance>.mount-lock.json. The rules for each reader and writer: . | Writers write index.lock.json. mount:remote first renames a legacy lock onto the new name, so the old file is moved, never dropped. | Readers take index.lock.json first, then fall back to the legacy *.mount-lock.json, so downstream folios and old branches still replay. The readers are: . | mount-from-lock.ts | mountedInstanceRoots | mountedUnder in git-corpus.ts | mount:remote:check | . | Both files present is an error that names both. Two locks are never merged. | . mount-from-lock.ts imports only node:*, so it restates the rule inline and its test holds it to lockFilesIn. A re-pin ends with one commit per layer, and moves pins only forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). Every layer the change needs is pinned in the same re-pin, and the re-pin PR holds the pins and nothing else: a change that needs the new pins stacks on it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). The one exception is a change mutually dependent with the re-pin, where neither passes alone. It may share the PR, and the body says why. The rules are in remote-mount §”Re-pinning”.

1124.title: The reserved index stem
1124.content: index.config.json ends in .config.json, so a scan that treats “each root *.config.json is a harness” would find a harness called index. The index stem is therefore reserved across the board: . | rootConfigStems skips every index.* file. It is the one root scan; every other reader calls it or instantiatedHarnessNames. | findDeclarationFile skips every index.* file too. | The index schema refuses a layer named index, and hub, because that is the landing keyword. | . Do not add another copy of the scan: a new copy is how the reserved name leaks back in.

1125.title: The generated .gitignore block
1125.content: # BEGIN index mounts (generated from index.config.json — do not edit) /my-ig/ # END index mounts . The block holds one /<path>/ line per remote layer in the index, where the path is overrides.<name>.path, else <name>/. After those it lists every further layer root the lock records, because a mount’s closure can land layers that the index never names. Three things write the block: . | mount:remote | writeDeclaredMounts | index-config:migrate --write | . check:index-ignores fails when the block is missing or disagrees with the index. When an index exists, mount:remote does not append to .git/info/exclude: a local exclude rule is invisible to every other clone, so a path the committed block does not cover is reported as not ignored. Without an index, it still appends there.

1126.title: Converting a checkout: index-config:migrate
1126.content: bun run cat index-config:migrate # print the index it would write, and its findings bun run cat index-config:migrate --write # write it; move remoteMounts; write the block; rename the lock bun run cat index-config:migrate --check # exit 1 when --write would change anything (a gate here) bun run cat index-config:migrate --inline --write # also fold each <name>.config.json into its entry, and delete it bun run cat index-config:inline:check # exit 1 while any imported <name>.config.json remains bun run cat index-config:migrate --root <clone> # a separated repository's standalone checkout . The converter reads only the files under --root, so it runs on a standalone clone of any separated repository. | Which root configs it imports: a root <name>.config.json is imported only when name is a layer the checkout declares (at the root or one level down) or mounts. Anything else becomes an unmatched-config finding and is not imported. A repository cut from a fork, for example, can carry the fork’s own <fork>.config.json; importing it would instantiate a harness the repository does not hold. | Re-runs: it is idempotent. A re-run moves only the remoteMounts entries that the declaration has gained since the last run. An entry the index already holds identically is dropped from the declaration. An entry the index holds differently throws, and you reconcile it by hand. | .

Code and a skill, not folio content: the folio reader reads only `folio/*.json`, and the renderer skips this directory. 4 files . | README.md | file-list.test.ts | file-list.ts | folio-file-list.md | . upstream/ cat-harness-upstream . The pinned-upstream registry, `upstream-pins.json` (`"$schema": "folio-upstream-pins/v1"`): one row per upstream dependency the build pins — such as the just-the-docs theme and the Bun runtime — naming the file the pin is READ from (`pinnedIn`, resolved against this layer's root), the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to the dependency and the MVP that must pass before it moves. It deliberately holds no version: that lives in the file the build reads. Read by `bun run cat check:upstream-pins` (weekly, `.github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml`) and worked by the `upstream-pin-watch` / `upstream-version-adoption` processes and skill this layer owns. Moved here from the repository root on 2026-10-06 (bean `ar1s`, phase 3: tooling leaves the root before the repo split). HERE rather than in the tool layer because this layer's processes, skills and scripts name it, and a harness file naming a file in the layer above is a wrong-direction reference (`check:reference-direction`). `code`: the checker's input table, authored beside the processes that read it, not content any reader renders. 2 files . | README.md | upstream-pins.json | .

1221.content: Measured from who-iris/translations, that instance's own translation-sources directory. Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1424.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1424.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1425.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
1425.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. How to use this handbook > 2.2 Targeted users, p.11 (pdf 23) — this handbook is written for those who will fill the business analyst role on the teamwho-iris/library/9789240101197-eng, Introduction > Who this handbook is for (Table 1), p.8 (pdf 18) — This handbook is for countries, organizations and teams that want to plan and implement digital transformation of the public health supply chain.who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng, Introduction > How to use this handbook, p.8 (pdf 17) — This handbook provides a stepwise approach to implementing standardized NPC and product master data management processes.https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/en/cat-harness/library/dpi-h-ra/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/, 1.1.4 Who can benefit from this guidance, pdf p.23 — Enterprise Architects and Technical Teams: This reference architecture provides TOGAF-based methodology, formal architecture patterns, and systematic requirements frameworks | . | 2 | Position in the DIIG process and SMART Guidelines layersdiig-and-smart-alignment | required | Which phase of the DIIG's "planning and implementing a digital health enterprise" process the handbook supports, and its alignment to the SMART Guidelines layers. The seven phases have ONE source, DIIG §1.1 Fig. 1.1.1 (owner, 2026-10-03, #1984: "use one DIIG seven phase figure as source"); a DTH cites that figure for them, and the copies the handbooks print (PHC Fig. 6, SC Fig 5, PC Fig. 4) are reproductions of it, not further sources. The primary health care DTH places itself in Phase 5, determining health content requirements; the Reference Architecture's Figure 1, which adapts the DIIG figure, places the supply chain and product catalogue handbooks in Phase 7, and the Reference Architecture itself across Phases 1-4. Its SVG rendering, drawn from the DIIG PDF's own vector layer with its provenance inside the file, is who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/figures/vfig-p017.svg (bean 70zt); the reproductions are listed 1426.title: WHO guideline (L1) l1-guideline
1426.content: An L1 publication containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy, structured as the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd ed.) §12.1 "Guideline format" requires, with the SMART additions Mehl 2021 names: uniquely identified recommendations and data recommendations. Sections modelled by smart-kg L1 classes are the ones a smart-kg L1 graph of the guideline holds (bean 8pzh). semi-fixed structure · 16 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/l1-guideline.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Executive summaryexecutive-summary | required | A stand-alone summary that states the key recommendations, each with its strength and the certainty of its evidence.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — All guidelines should have an executive summary, a main body and appendices. The executive summary should contain the key recommendations of the guideline.who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — the strength of the recommendation and the quality of the evidence for each recommendation should be specified in the executive summary | . | 2 | table-of-contents | required | Navigational listing of the main-body sections.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — The main text of the guideline should include a table of contents, introduction, methods, recommendations and conclusions. | . | 3 | Target audience and persons affectedtarget-audience | optional | Who will apply the recommendations (end-users), distinguished from the people who receive the interventions.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §2.2.3 Who is the target audience?, PDF p.29; sections/sec-030-223-who-is-the-target-audience.md — Guidelines must have a clearly defined target audience (end-user) which is identified early in the guideline development processwho-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §2.2.3 Who is the target audience?, PDF p.29; sections/sec-030-223-who-is-the-target-audience.md — the end-users are those who will apply the guidelines, not the recipients of the recommended interventions.who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §4.5 Table 4.1 Essential components of the planning proposal, PDF pp.53-55; sections/sec-075-44-when-should-the-planning-proposal-be-develope.md — 3. 1430.title: Document kinds
1430.content: . | All instances | smart-base | . A document kind is a named structure of sections that a document authored with a harness follows: fixed (exactly these sections) or semi-fixed (these required, others allowed). Every kind and section names its sources.

1431.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1431.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1432.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
1432.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. Only the frame a WHO guideline and a Digital Transformation Handbook BOTH carry is here; what each puts in its body is a sub-kind — l1-guideline (recommendations, evidence, GRADE) and dth (a digital transformation handbook). 1581.title: Beans in Process_TestPlanExecution: cat-harness-tools
1581.content: cat-harness-tools's work plan · beans by process · every instance . BPMN workflow instances recorded in cat-harness-tools's work plan, joined with the beans they name. Ages are measured on 2026-11-13 (UTC, the day this page was built); an instance is stalled when it is running and has not moved for more than 7 days. A finished instance is marked where it ended. Beans that no instance names are listed under "Beans in no process"; the store page has every bean. A running subprocess is followed on each instance's own page. Refresh every 5 s from the local bean store . 1667.title: Glossary
1667.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the layer's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Auditorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/auditorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. A system lane — it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, which is exactly why every decision in board-open-close.bpmn and board-relocate.bpmn sits in the reader's lane instead. It is NOT the build pipeline: it runs where the reader is, once per request, and publishes nothing.notation role/board-rendererfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Boardsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/boardsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/bootstrapfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapping Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/bootstrapping-agentfirst seen 2026-09-23status current | . | Build pipelineglossary-ledger.json | Validates, renders and publishes, and watches whether that actually worked. A system lane: it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, so anything needing a decision belongs in a different lane. It carries todo-manager for the two CI-watcher dispatch points in content-change-review, which claim and note a bean and never resolve one -- claim is idempotent and note appends, both fixed programs, while deciding that a publish SUCCEEDED is the judgement this lane must not make (bean xom7: docs-site.yml failed 30 times while reporting its own exit code).notation role/build-pipelinefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Building blocksglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/building-blocksfirst seen 2026-11-05status current | . | Business analystglossary-ledger.json | Turns a stated need into a modelled requirement. A specialisation of stakeholder — accountable sign-off — but NOT judgementOnly: the exit criteria are a table it applies, and only the decision on top of them is the judgement (owner ruling, 2026-10-01). It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. | core-processes folio-assistant-core/processes … | library-processes cat-harness/library/processes … | processes cat-harness/processes … | . | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Detangled?cat-harness/processes/kg/decisions/detanglement-gate.dmn | An unassigned column above zero means the measurement is incomplete. A low edge count over an unclassified corpus is the same false comfort as a green check over an empty one — and this rule is FIRST so no cross-edge count can outrank it. | . | Stands alone?cat-harness/processes/kg/decisions/isolation-gate.dmn | No declaration of its own: the directory moves and nothing downstream can resolve it. | . | Ready to seed?cat-harness/processes/kg/decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn | A PR marked as moving much of the tree is still open over this layer: the seed would snapshot one side of it. | . | Declared in place?cat-harness/processes/kg/decisions/subgraph-declared-gate.dmn | Could not determine. 1787.title: auto-docs index
1787.content: Derived documentation over a declared sub-graph. Each entry below is generated from the repository on every build, so it is what the tree actually holds rather than what anybody remembered. These are indexes, not the documentation. They say what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a thing is for, when you would reach for it, and what it is not, is authored beside them and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. | Decisions …every DMN decision table a declared `processes` graph holds, with the decision's own name | Docs …every AUTHORED documentation page an instance publishes, with the title and description its own front matter declares | Processes …every BPMN process, with its own documentation, its lanes, and the skills its activities name | Roles …every role a declared `scenarios` graph defines, with the description it declares | Schemas …every schema module a declared `schemas` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | Skills …every skill markdown file, with the description it declares in its own front matter | Tasks …every named activity in a declared `processes` graph — task, user, service, manual, script and call activities | Tools …every Tool module a declared `tools` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | .

1791.title: The catalogue, as a graph
1791.content: The replica pages show what IRIS looks like. This one shows what this catalogue knows — and, more usefully, what it records that it does not know. The gap is the point, not a backlog. This instance models 235 node(s) against 273,559 items across 1,057,223 files upstream. Cataloguing by reference means recording that something exists without holding it, so a small number here is the design rather than a shortfall.

1797.title: Every process — one page each

1858.title: Strict, advisory — and nobody said
1858.content: Three states, not two. loadProcessModel reads an undeclared policy as strict, which is right for the engine — “a process that forgot to say is governed, not exempt” — and hides a fact a reader wants. Somebody chose strict and nobody said, so the engine assumed strict are different, and the second is 23 of 114 here. | enforcement | declared | defaulted | . | strict | 44 | 23 | . | advisory | 47 | 0 | .

1859.title: Findings
1859.content: 3 diagram(s) have no rendered SVG. bun run cat render:bpmn. | folio/dth-sc/ch04-traceability/bp-sc-bp-03-centralized-track-and-trace.bpmn | folio/dth-sc/introduction/bp-sc-bp-01-stepwise-dhsc-transformation.bpmn | folio/dth-sc/introduction/bp-sc-bp-02-end-to-end-supply-chain-processes.bpmn | . Activities carrying no <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> — a census, not a gap list . 69 across 24 diagram(s). This section reported them as defects in its first version, and that was wrong: beans luke and uuhu worked this corpus from 90 down to this remainder and settled what is left. luke: “coverage is deliberately NOT gated — a human sign-off step has no skill”. uuhu added the call-activity exemption and recorded that its own remainder “are not gaps”. 15 are call activities, which delegate to a subprocess — the skill is named there, and naming it twice would be one fact in two places. The other 54 are listed by lane, because the lane is what says whether a person, a pipeline or an agent performs the step, and only the last of those has a skill to run. | lane | steps | . | Agent | 6 | . | Stakeholders | 4 | . | Central warehouse | 3 | . | Enterprise & solution architect | 3 | . | Health facility | 3 | . | Patient / individual | 3 | . | Contributor | 2 | . | DHSC traceability hub | 2 | . | Owner | 2 | . | Project manager & analyst | 2 | . | Regional warehouse | 2 | . | Regulatory authority | 2 | . | Steering committee & sponsor | 2 | . | Agent (playing the machine) | 1 | . | Build pipeline | 1 | . | Community health | 1 | . | Content Author | 1 | . | Developer, integrator & QA | 1 | . | Editor / author (person) | 1 | . | Folio-Assistant Agent | 1 | . | Logistics provider | 1 | . | Manufacturer | 1 | . | Manufacturer & distributor | 1 | . | Ministry of health | 1 | . | Ministry of health (MOH) | 1 | . | Procurement agency | 1 | . | Publication manager | 1 | . | Requestor | 1 | . | Reviewer | 1 | . | Reviewer / SME | 1 | . | Sysadmin, support & trainer | 1 | . No verdict is offered on which of these is a gap, and that is the honest state rather than a hedge: distinguishing a person’s judgement step from an agent step somebody forgot needs the lane’s actor KIND, which a free-text lane name does not give — process-model.ts notes sixty lanes spell two dozen positions. The lane’s partitionElementRef is the join that would answer it, and it is present on 54 of these 54 steps — which is the measurement, not an impression. An earlier draft of this sentence said few of these and was counting whether the lane had a NAME, a different question with a different answer.

1882.title: Refresh an IG’s AST cache on a runner
1882.content: Dispatch an IG repository’s ig-ast-refresh.yml, which calls fhir-harness’s reusable .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml: mount the layers the IG’s index.lock.json pins, restore and judge the cache for ref, and when it is not valid (or force) run the caller’s optional pre-export overlay command and build the IG with the pinned Publisher AST exporter (the AST is recorded against the clean commit’s inputs, the overlay’s changes put back), check the new AST is valid for its commit, and seed cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id> with ig-cache seed --push — only from a commit on the default branch with the tip’s inputs. 1883.title: Skills it satisfies
1883.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. 1923.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. 1982.title: Skills it satisfies
1982.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. 2014.title: Skills it satisfies
2014.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. 2022.title: Skills it satisfies
2022.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. 2053.title: Build an IG repository’s own site from its cached AST, with no instance declaration
2053.content: The three checkout scripts the platform’s site build runs for a repository that holds an IG and only mounts layers (index.config.json): ig-site:ast restores the AST from the IG’s cache branch (ig-cache.sh restore) and judges it, refusing a stale, cannot-tell or absent one (a stale one is accepted for a preview by default, refused with SITE_ACCEPT_STALE_AST=0, and never accepted for the root); ig-site:compose derives the artefact index from the AST (binding any IG API sidecars a layer above left in $SITE_WORK/ig-api/), writes the thin artefact pages, stages the IG’s input/ and sushi-config.yaml (menu read at build time, palette from the webpage theme of the top layer the repository mounts, edit links from its origin) and composes it at the ROOT of the host site source; ig-site:publisher-pages serves each of the AST’s resources once, as <Type>-<id>.json at the root (no ast-data/ mirror) — reduced (minified, no narrative, no ELM data, the ELM attachment pointing at the full copy) when the pages read the full resources by raw URL from the AST cache commit, and off with SITE_ROOT_RESOURCES=0 — the artefact index (or fhir-artifact-index/index.ref.json, pointing at the cache’s copy) and the sidecars (or none, read from the cache), refuses a page wearing the IG Publisher’s chrome, repairs repeated element ids and stamps folio-build.json. Never runs the Publisher and never reads its output. Compose lists the pages it puts in the site in FOLIO_SITE_UPSTREAM_PAGES, so the site build reports the IG’s own dead links rather than refusing the publish over them. |   |   | . | Tool | ig-repo-site | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/tools/ig-repo-site.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/fhir-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | fhir-harness | . | source | fhir-harness/tools/ig-repo-site/ig-repo-site.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2069.title: Cut an IG release as a GitHub draft that carries its packages and AST, and report a version left untagged or unreleased
2069.content: Gather a release’s files from a full Publisher build (package.tgz and its R4/R4B variants, and ast-data.zip, the IG’s AST with the Libraries’ ELM), say from sushi-config.yaml whether it is a pre-release, and make or refresh the GitHub DRAFT release for the tag with the files uploaded. 2093.title: Build each IG instance’s artefact index from the IG’s cached AST
2093.content: Write each IG instance’s fhir-artifact-index/ at publish, so no IG instance commits one. 2188.title: Skills it satisfies
2188.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. publish-extracted-statements . The standard step of adding source documents to a folio’s working artifact: every statement extracted from a library source is published readably in the artifact’s own pages AND in the shared extraction viewer, each with a link to its library entry and to the section it came from, and CI fails when the generated pages are stale. Generic across content types; each type’s adapter says only how its pages look. Executable form: processes/library/publish-extracted-statements.bpmn. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/library/ingestion/publish-extracted-statements.md. Also satisfied by: publish-extracted-statements. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/publish-extracted-statements/{input,output}.schema.json).

2286.title: L1 recommendations → L2 user-scenario candidates

2330.title: Apply a vocabulary mapping table
2330.content: Carry one source record into a target vocabulary by a declared folio-vocab-mapping/v1 table: each source field becomes the predicate its row names, in the table’s order, with a DERIVED target (such as dcterms:title rendering skos:prefLabel) copied from its authoritative one so the two cannot drift. A table is shaped like a FHIR ConceptMap: an existing ConceptMap, R4 or R5, is representable as one without loss (fromConceptMap), and a table can be produced as a ConceptMap (toConceptMap), which returns every loss rather than dropping anything silently. 2339.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. kg-separation . Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. Also satisfied by: mount-from-lock, package-exports, rewrite-moved-paths, separation-cutover-check. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/kg-separation/{input,output}.schema.json). kg-affordances . The four affordances of a conformant knowledge graph — browse, materialise, instantiate and copy-into-folio — which capabilities each requires, how each writing verb degrades cleanly when no write capability is available, and how copying an asset stamps KgAsset.source provenance. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/kg-affordances.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/kg-affordances/{input,output}.schema.json).

2371.title: Check that an ArchiMate model’s fhir-actor tags point at the IG’s FHIR ActorDefinitions
2371.content: Actors come first: the IG’s ActorDefinitions are written from the DAK’s personas, and an ArchiMate model only points at them. For one model a layer’s cat-archimate.config.json names, this reads every element carrying the Archi property fhir-actor, whose value is an ActorDefinition’s canonical URL, and the IG’s ActorDefinitions: FSH InstanceOf: ActorDefinition under input/fsh/, and FHIR JSON under fsh-generated/resources/ or input/resources/, each canonical being <sushi-config canonical>/ActorDefinition/<id> unless its url says otherwise. It fails on a value that is not a canonical URL, a tag that names no ActorDefinition, an element kind that cannot be an actor (a data object, a goal), and a type mismatch (a #person actor on an application or technology element, a #system actor on a business actor or role). It warns about each ActorDefinition no element realizes; --strict makes that a failure. --json prints element → actors and actor → elements, for page back-links. It never writes an ActorDefinition or any FSH, and never matches boxes to actors by name. |   |   | . | Tool | archimate-actors | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/archimate-actors.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/archimate-actors/archimate-actors.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2545.title: Skills it satisfies
2545.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. repo-conversion . Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/repo-conversion.md. Also satisfied by: instantiate-harness. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/repo-conversion/{input,output}.schema.json). getting-started . Triage what a person means when they ask to create a folio, and route them. Five requests share one sentence — a folio in a new repo, folio-assistant overlaid on an existing repo, a second folio in a layer that already has one, a content object they called a folio, or something the filesystem cannot tell apart. Reads the repository facts, runs them through the folio-intent decision table, asks a selectable question for what facts cannot settle, scaffolds, and reports the published URL. Use whenever a user asks to create, start, set up, or initialise a folio, a paper, a DAK, an IG, or “folio-assistant” itself. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/getting-started.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/getting-started/{input,output}.schema.json). folio-init . Scaffold a new folio layer from the harness — the instantiate affordance of the knowledge graph. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/folio-init.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/folio-init/{input,output}.schema.json).

2553.title: Skills it satisfies
2553.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. kg-separation . Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. Also satisfied by: declaration-resolution, mount-from-lock, package-exports, separation-cutover-check. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/kg-separation/{input,output}.schema.json).

2602.title: Publish a built site to gh-pages as a full replace
2602.content: Lay a built _site onto a gh-pages checkout as a FULL REPLACE and push it, keeping the open pull requests’ staging previews: each attempt re-reads the branch, re-runs restore-staging and keep-shared-payloads against what is on it now, replaces the tree, commits docs(gh-pages): site from <sha> and pushes. A rejected push is rebuilt, never rebased (a rebase would re-apply the replace over a preview a sibling just deployed), up to three attempts. A restore that cannot read the branch stops the publish. A site that matches the branch is a no-op, not a failure. It publishes and does not verify: the workflow’s verify step runs after it. |   |   | . | Tool | publish-gh-pages | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/publish-gh-pages.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/publish-gh-pages/publish-gh-pages.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2667.title: Mount remote harnesses at a pinned commit, only when trusted
2667.content: Lay down each declared remote mount — a source.remote layer in the root index.config.json, or, in a folio with no index, a remoteMounts entry on its declaration (both at once is refused) — and its dependency closure, from another repository at a full commit SHA. Write the lock, index.lock.json (a legacy <name>.mount-lock.json is read, and renamed onto it when rewritten), and, with an index, regenerate the root .gitignore block that ignores each mount path. It READS the declared mounts and never writes them: a tool that changes a mount writes through writeDeclaredMounts into index.config.json. Before anything is checked out, each mount must pass the trust gate (schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts, rule H8): a person’s consent recorded for THIS pin, or a signature in a declared trust network. No signature verifier exists yet, so a signature alone is could-not-determine and does not mount. Unsigned and unconsented is refused. --staging mounts for a preview and needs neither. A directory id an override or mountDefaults names may be one the layer declares in its <name>.json or one it declares FROM WITHIN a declared directory (skills/skills.json naming voices), resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories; an id in neither is refused at plan time. tools on an override names Tools by id and mounts each one runnable: its definition (<tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts), its implementation (the inProcess.module, or the script its bun run cat <key> resolves to) and their import closure, walked by bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (the one closure walker), as every declared directory that closure touches — the lock still records directories only. A hydrated mount lays each chosen directory down as its published index.hydrated.jsonld only: read from the pin’s git tree when a commit carries it, otherwise fetched from the pin’s subgraph index package (the subgraph-index-<sha> release asset subgraph-index-package publishes), its tarball checked against its folio-binary-release/v1 record, its manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, and each file against its sha256, SubgraphHydratedSchema and the subgraph IRI; the lock records the package’s URL and sha256 so a replay fetches the same bytes. --check compares the disk against the lock and never fetches. When a run CHANGES the lock, it then re-renders the agent surface (skill:commands → .claude/commands/, agent-memory → .claude/agent-memory/ and .agents/) from the checkout root, so a re-pin commit carries the skills and memory the new layers define; a generator that fails fails the run, and --no-agent-surface opts out. |   |   | . | Tool | remote-mount | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/remote-mount.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/remote-mount/remote-mount.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .
