2684.title: Where to drop a file — the queue’s upload URL
2684.content: Compose the forge URL a person can drop a file at, from the layer’s own declaration: the uploads graph’s directory, resolved against the ROOT its scope names, expressed relative to the repository, and appended to the origin remote as GitHub’s /upload/<branch>/<path>. Every failure is NAMED and no URL is guessed — no declaration, no declared uploads graph, a declared queue absent from disk, no origin remote, and a non-github.com remote each return a reason and a remedy instead. The declared path is relative to the LAYER and a forge URL needs it relative to the REPOSITORY, so pasting the declared path can mint a 404. |   |   | . | Tool | upload-url | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/upload-url.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/upload-url/upload-url.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2713.title: Instantiate a harness over a repository that has none: pin, mount, open the setup-only PR, render the preview
2713.content: The scripted step of the initiation process (getting-started.bpmn, the repo-conversion skill §4). Reads the harness’s declaration at its pin and every needs, transitively (a need beside the layer that needs it unless –repo-of says otherwise, at its default branch’s tip unless –pin says otherwise, its declaration’s name checked), seeds them all into the repository’s index.config.json with the consent given (remote-mount --seed --whole), sets site.landing to the harness, site.agentRun and mountApprovers, mounts the closure (remote-mount: index.lock.json and the .gitignore mounts block), installs it as root workspaces with the hoisted linker, writes the root bootstrap (.github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh from cat-harness-tools templates/root-bootstrap/) and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so bun run cat … mounts the layers itself on a later fresh clone, re-renders the agent surface from the mounted generators, runs the harness’s instantiate:<harness> checkout script when a mounted layer declares it, and commits on a branch (default harness/). Then, unless --local, pushes the branch, provisions gh-pages when absent (`pages-bootstrap --provision`), opens the setup-only PR, runs `prepare:` when declared (what the site is built from and nobody commits, such as an IG's AST) and renders the branch's preview at gh-pages branches// (`stage-local`); with --local the site is built and composed and nothing is pushed. It imports only node:*, so it runs from a fresh clone of cat-harness-tools before anything is mounted: it lays the platform's own closure, at the pins the repository will mount, into a temporary root to run the mount from. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run the same file from a fresh clone: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht && bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts …`. Two more flags, not declared as ports because no constrained type carries them yet: `--pin =` pins one layer of the closure, `--repo-of =<owner/repo>` says where a need lives. |   |   | . | Tool | instantiate-harness | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/instantiate-harness.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/instantiate-harness/instantiate-harness.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2714.title: Skills it satisfies
2714.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. repo-conversion . Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/repo-conversion.md. Also satisfied by: folio-init. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/repo-conversion/{input,output}.schema.json). remote-mount . Bring a harness, and every layer it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/remote-mount.md. Also satisfied by: build-instance-site, index-config-migrate, kg-retrieve-npm, mount-from-lock, npm, subgraph-index-package. 2763.title: Lower the tangles in ArchiMate views: re-route lines and swap same-size boxes in a row
2763.content: Searches for a less tangled drawing of each view: a line may be re-routed straight or orthogonally (an L, or a Z through a free lane between boxes), and two same-size boxes in the same parent and row or column may swap places. A change is kept only if it lowers crossings + lines through boxes + lines drawn on top of each other. Without --apply it reports before and after per view; with it, the model is written back in place, only the moved boxes’ bounds and the re-routed lines’ bendpoints changing. |   |   | . | Tool | archimate-detangle | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/archimate-detangle.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/archimate-detangle/archimate-detangle.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

2796.title: Screen a hand-over for injected instructions, field by field
2796.content: Before a model reads a sub-agent’s report, a delegated prompt, a tool result or a comment from someone who is not the principal, screen it against a declared schema whose top-level fields are control (steers what the receiver does) or data (content it reads). A finding in a control field, or any field the strict schema does not declare, is REFUSED, so a report cannot extend the delegator’s plan. A finding in a data field is QUARANTINED: the original is kept and marked, never stripped. The patterns are a deterministic tripwire (instruction overrides, role and turn spoofs, fence breaks, tool-call syntax, hidden Unicode, exfiltration links, pipe-to-shell), a mitigation and not a guarantee. 2974.title: Convert a checkout to a root index.config.json
2974.content: Write the root index.config.json (folio-index-config/v1) that says which layers the checkout instantiates, where each comes from (source.local or source.remote) and which owns / (site.landing), from the root *.config.json files and the declaration’s remoteMounts. With --write it moves remoteMounts off the declaration into source.remote entries, writes the generated .gitignore block, and renames a legacy <name>.mount-lock.json to index.lock.json. Without a flag it prints the index it would write. Idempotent: a re-run merges what the declaration gained, and refuses an entry the index already holds differently. 2990.title: Draw a document’s tables and figures from its ArchiMate data, and check the model against the document’s relationship rules
2990.content: For each table a layer’s cat-archimate.config.json lists under tables, rewrites the block’s Markdown table from an archimate-relationship-rules/v1 file (relationship-rules: source, relationship, target, note; relationship-types: picture, verb, meaning), keeping the caption and footnotes. 3088.title: Build, check and (on request) publish a layer’s own site, or a branches/ preview
3088.content: From a checkout whose layers arrive by remote mount: mount the pinned closure, install, run the layer’s own gates (--pre), compose the harness chrome for THIS layer, run its source steps, build with Jekyll at the base path read from the git remote (/<repo>, or /<repo>/branches/<branch> for a preview), run the post-build steps (mount-instance-docs, pdf-viewer, set-html-lang, publish-id-lookup, rail-standalone-pages), and check that every relative or base-rooted link in every page resolves to a file under the site, reading each page with an HTML parser. Any failing step stops the run; a link that does not resolve means nothing is published. It never decides to publish: only --publish does, and then a root publish keeps branches/ and _render-log/ on the branch, and a preview replaces only its own branches/<branch>/. |   |   | . | Tool | build-instance-site | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/build-instance-site.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/build-instance-site/build-instance-site.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

3130.title: Replay a committed mount lock with nothing but Node
3130.content: Lay down every remote mount index.lock.json records — each layer fetched at the lock’s full SHA (sparse, blob-filtered), each directory verified against its treeDigest, a mismatch undone and reported — importing only node:*, so it runs on a fresh clone before any layer is present. It never decides what to mount: remote-mount writes the lock (and checks trust); this only replays it. Refuses to write over a path with tracked files or bytes that no longer hash to the lock. 3139.title: Is this repository’s cutover from the monorepo complete? Measured, condition by condition
3139.content: Run in a separated repository. Six conditions, each decided by an existing gate: mounts (every declared layer on disk at its pin — remote-mount --check), declarations (every path a declaration names resolves — declaration-resolution), monorepo-paths (no wiring still names the monorepo: livesAt on it, a submodule of it, a reusable workflow called from it, a path into its old checkout — the one condition implemented here), import-direction and reference-direction (no layer reaches a layer above it), and site (the site builds from the mounts alone, every link resolving — build-instance-site --no-mount, only with --site). Findings inside a MOUNTED layer are listed and not counted: a defect in a layer pinned from upstream is fixed upstream and re-pinned. Exit 0 complete, 1 a condition failed, 2 a condition could not be determined or was not run — without --site the answer is never 0. |   |   | . | Tool | separation-cutover-check | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/separation-cutover-check.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/separation-cutover-check/separation-cutover-check.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

3140.title: Skills it satisfies
3140.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. kg-separation . Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. 3247.title: Journeys viewer
3247.content: Draw every journey (user-scenario) and workshop (workshop) in the checkout as static pages at the route of the visualiser a layer declares for this Tool, <locale>/<instance>/<id>/: an index of all journeys, grouped by layer (each a sub-graph page), each parent’s parts nested under it in its order with optional and repeating parts marked (an older file’s partOf children after them, ordered along follows), and a plain DAK user scenario with no steps listed as one; one page per journey, its parts in order and the journeys it is a part of, a journey map with a lane and a feeling curve per persona, then each step, linked to the journey it includes, with its BPMN drawing (the step’s flow nodes highlighted), user stories, requirements, FHIR examples, building blocks, the DAK assets it uses (data sets, decision tables and indicators, linked into the IG) and ArchiMate views; and the workshop layer, the questions for the room on each step, a page per workshop and per module, job aids, and printable A3/A4 sheets; and each device screen (device-screen) that shows a step a workshop presents, drawn as a static device mock (phone, tablet, scanner, desktop, kiosk) with its owner beside it, in the workshop’s Device Demo, linked both ways with the walkthrough. A persona’s picture (meta.persona.avatar) is drawn wherever the persona appears. 3272.title: Pin third-party GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs
3272.content: Rewrite every third-party uses: owner/repo@ref outside the declared staging-only workflows to @<full commit SHA> # <ref>, so Dependabot keeps the pair current. A tag resolves to its PEELED commit (an annotated tag’s object is never pinned), else a branch head, by git ls-remote with argv. A ref that resolves to nothing, or to more than one commit, is refused and reported, never guessed. This repository’s own reusable workflows are first-party and left alone. A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. 3354.title: Every reference a journey or a workshop names resolves
3354.content: Read every user-scenario and workshop node in the checkout through the layers’ declared directories, with the journeys viewer’s own resolver, and resolve what each names: actors (personas, a step’s lead, experiences[].actor, handoff.from/to, illustrationStyle.cast[].actor), user stories, realisedBy BPMN files (instance-relative) and the element ids in them, uses blocks in a directory declaring building-blocks, req: requirements, FHIR examples and a step’s dak assets (data sets, decision tables, indicators) in a fhir-artifact-index (could not determine while the index is built at publish), illustration.src files, follows/partOf/parts/includes journeys (parts and includes forming no cycle; an includes held against the call activity its step’s realisedBy names, could not determine when the call names no process), the trustLadder code list and each record.state code of it, and ArchiMate views; and each workshop’s scenarios, steps[] {scenario, step} and <scenario>#<step> refs; each device screen’s owner and personCard actors, its steps[] {scenario, step}, and the FHIR examples its qr and recordList blocks name; and every persona’s avatar image path. Every journey is a DAK user scenario (the kind specialises it): its DAK personas, the roles its persona actors play, must be non-empty and each a declared role; a persona may be an actor or (0.4.0) a role. What is derived is not also written: a listed part’s follows or partOf, personas equal to the parts’, a lead equal to the lanes’ first actor, are each a redundant finding, and a 0.4.0 step with no experiences whose lanes no persona plays is a finding. A node that does not parse is a finding. One line per finding, naming the layer, file and step. 3370.title: Publish a folio’s or an IG’s site from the agent’s own checkout — the one agent publish path
3370.content: Build a repository’s site in the agent’s checkout and push it to the publish branch, as a preview or as the main site, without an Actions runner. Which build is read from the repository: a declared site.build recipe (built by build-instance-site), else the reusable workflow its own workflow files call — folio-staging.yml for a folio, the WHO SMART Base IG’s ghbuild.yml for a FHIR IG, whose build job is planned step by step and run as written. For an IG it then applies the harness chrome over the built output (sync-docs-harness, then rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site --instance <the IG>): every page gains the rail and the icon row #fa-navbar-row, and the IG’s own content is left byte for byte. A root publish is REFUSED when the chrome cannot be applied, and a clean root deploy is refused over any root whose index.html wears the icon row unless the new output does too, so a chromed root is never replaced by bare IG Publisher pages. Every run prints its plan first, and the plan lists the chrome step; --plan stops there, --dry-run composes the commit in a temporary worktree and pushes nothing, --artifact writes a claude.ai Artifact bundle instead. |   |   | . | Tool | stage-local | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/stage-local.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/stage-local/stage-local.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

For one model a layer’s cat-archimate.config.json names, this reads every element carrying the Archi property fhir-actor, whose value is an ActorDefinition’s canonical URL, and the IG’s ActorDefinitions: FSH InstanceOf: ActorDefinition under input/fsh/, and FHIR JSON under fsh-generated/resources/ or input/resources/, each canonical being <sushi-config canonical>/ActorDefinition/<id> unless its url says otherwise. It fails on a value that is not a canonical URL, a tag that names no ActorDefinition, an element kind that cannot be an actor (a data object, a goal), and a type mismatch (a #person actor on an application or technology element, a #system actor on a business actor or role). For each figure under figures that names an svg, writes the view as SVG (the same drawing as the view’s page). For a rules table that names a model, reports the rules the model never uses, the relationships no rule covers, the rules ArchiMate’s relationship table refuses, and the relationship types the rules use without a meaning. The rules are in charge: nothing is rewritten from the model. | cli | archimate-models | 3 in / 1 out | qa-reports | . | archimate-checkCheck a layer’s ArchiMate models against its config | The ArchiMate gate (graph typology archimate): every model a layer’s cat-archimate.config.json names is held, parses (Archi’s native XML or its zipped archive), and resolves — every box in every view draws an element the model holds, every relationship’s ends are in the model — and no .archimate file is held that the config does not name. | cli | archimate-models | 1 in / 1 out | qa-reports | . | archimate-crossingsCount the tangles in ArchiMate views: lines crossing lines, and lines through boxes | For each view, as render-view.ts draws it, count the pairs of lines that cross and the lines that run through a box they do not connect (groups, and boxes that hold one of the line’s ends, excepted). 3511.title: Check a review log and its repository’s issues for changes
3511.content: The mechanical check a review-log watcher runs on every poll. Given a drafting sheet’s Contributor Feedback values and the folio repository, it reads the repository’s open and closed issues (leaving out pull requests, issues labelled no-sheet and, with --author, issues someone else opened) and compares a digest of them and of the cells people set (Title, Selected Sections, Contributor Feedback, Disposition, Ready for agent, Ready for merge, Dispositions confirmed; on a public-comment log also Committee Feedback, TWG (CS), TWG (human) and Change Set (human)) with the last check’s. Unchanged: it prints {"status":"unchanged"} and exits 0. Changed: it exits 10 and lists what changed (issue opened, updated or closed; a cell’s old and new text), the Contributor Feedback rows to append, one per issue that no row’s Issue cell links yet (Title the issue’s title, the first Contributor Feedback column @login (#N): first paragraph, Issue the issue’s URL; a closed issue’s row marked closed), and closedRows, the rows linking a closed issue, which the watcher hides with their text struck through. A read with no Issue column (a public-comment log’s Review Change Sets) tracks only issues labelled change-set unless --label says otherwise, and appends no rows: each open issue is reported as an issue-unlinked change instead. It writes no sheet and no issue: the watcher appends the rows and does the agent pass. With --accept it stores the new state for the next poll to compare against. |   |   | . | Tool | review-log-watch | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch/review-log-watch.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. 3570.title: Spreadsheet tabular metadata
3570.content: Read a workbook into a folio-tabular-csvw/v1 record, one CSVW table per rectangular block of cells. Blocks are split on empty rows, then on empty columns, so several tables on one sheet are found, each anchored at its real top-left cell (fac:anchor: sheet, A1 cell, row, column). Dates are read through the number formats in styles.xml, not misread as integer serials. A malformed part is refused rather than half-read. Reads the ZIP with node:zlib and SpreadsheetML with fast-xml-parser. 3626.content: For every figure a source publication declares, report whether the folio built from it has a block and how computable it is: missing, excluded (signed off), picture (a PNG crop), linked (a picture linked to a model view), computable (a diagram, a table or a figure rebuilt by ArchiMate, BPMN, DMN, Mermaid, a class diagram or a generator), or cited (a picture kept on purpose, signed off). Turn a figure into a computable diagram: every figure of a source publication when a folio is built from its L1 entry, and any hand-drawn figure in a folio, an IG or a demonstrator that is redrawn from a source. Every declared figure gets a block, and each one is rebuilt in the form its type calls for: an ArchiMate view, BPMN, DMN, a FHIR logical model, or an SVG generated from data, always from one schema-backed source. The PDF crop stays beside the rebuild as the cited source, and the rebuild keeps the original’s layout. The figure-coverage check counts what is missing and what is still only a picture. 3634.title: Rank candidate glossary terms in prose by C-value
3634.content: The scoring step of the automatic-term-extraction method: count the word n-grams of one or more Markdown or text files (not across punctuation, front matter or code), and rank them by C-value as Frantzi & Ananiadou 1996 define it, so nested multi-word terms are not swamped by the longer phrases that contain them. Tested against the paper’s own worked example (Table 2). 3650.title: ArchiMate model from the glossary
3650.content: Make an ArchiMate model agree with the instance’s folio-glossary/v1 terms whose focus is an ArchiMate element: elements matched by their skosConcept property (never by name) take the term’s prefLabel and definition, a term with no element gets one on no view, and the relationships the terms list are added. A type that disagrees is reported, never changed. A relationship between two linked elements that no term lists is reported, and removed with --prune along with the lines that draw it. No box or line is moved. Without --write it only reports; --check fails when anything would change. --seed goes the other way once, and only from an ingested model held under library/ (--from): an authored model is never a source of the glossary. |   |   | . | Tool | archimate-from-glossary | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/archimate-from-glossary.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/archimate-from-glossary/archimate-from-glossary.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

3675.title: Skills it satisfies
3675.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. review-comments . Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. Use when a reviewer asks how to comment on a block, when the review page shows no comments or a wrong one, when editing the ingestion, or when a folio’s staging workflow is set up. 3722.title: Build the review sheet’s Apps Script and a document’s Config tab
3722.content: Builds Code.gs (--script), the one Google Apps Script every review sheet runs (from review-sheet.gs), and one document’s Config tab rows (--config), filled from the folio’s review/public-comment/sheet-sync.json, its review anchors and the draft’s pdf-line-map.json. The script keeps a public-comment review sheet’s links and joins current: each comment No. links to its comment page; Sections, Page and Line no(s) link to the page of the frozen review draft; Review Change Sets joins its comments, suggested revisions, feedback and dispositions, each No. n linking to its row; and on both tabs Agentic status lists each pull request of the change-set, linked, with its status and what it changed, from the Agent tab. It reads the document’s URLs, tab and column names and data from the sheet’s Config tab (visible, locked to the owner), which the agent writes from these rows. A person pastes the script (one file) into the sheet once (Extensions > Apps Script) and runs installTriggers; from then on the sheet rebuilds itself within about a minute of an edit, with no agent. With "mode": "drafting" in the config it builds the drafting sheet instead: one Contributor Feedback tab where each row is a change set (ids assigned by the script), Sections picked from the document’s table of contents and linked to it, and Issue and Agentic status from the Agent tab. |   |   | . | Tool | review-sheet-sync | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync/review-sheet-sync.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

3761.title: Tools
3761.content: As an API: OpenAPI document · MCP tool list · API reference. A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 227Tool nodes 95skills satisfied 205invoked as a shell command 23reachable over MCP

3763.title: Who declares each specification
3763.content: A user declares the specification it depends on; the record names no user. That is data-modelling step 8 — the dependent holds the pointer — and it is why this list cannot drift from the code: a file that stops declaring stops being listed. Four forms are read: a @conformsTo tag, a conformsTo: front-matter list, an xmlns binding, and a graph typology whose typing module declares the spec (bean u63y). Every declaration names a record on this page.

3764.content: Read from diagram files (BPMN and DMN), metadata records, and JSON-LD contexts — 34 namespace IRI(s) are in use across the corpus. Derived rather than listed, so an artefact that adopts a new vocabulary shows up here instead of going unnoticed. Every namespace the corpus declares is covered by a record above. 3 declared and not in use. Not a defect on its own: a record may cover a namespace only some artefacts carry. Note. reads, not conforms: these records describe external metadata (DSpace), so a DCMI revision is a compatibility question rather than a migration. The transcription came first, which was the defect: dublin-core.ts was written from one captured IRIS record and carries the prefix string dc with no namespace URI and no edition, recording what one deployment spells rather than what the standard defines. A transcription with no cited edition cannot distinguish a missing field from one absent in that edition. The operative terms below are derived from the catalogue records, so they are what IRIS actually sends (DSpace also mints dcterms, local and other prefixes this repository has not met). A term absent here is undeclared, not unsupported. The persistent identifiers DSpace mints (<prefix>/<suffix>, e.g. WHO IRIS’s 10665/332098), written as IRIs through the global HTTP resolver https://hdl.handle.net/. Emitted by schemas/kg/prov-jsonld.ts for PROV prov:used: owner decision 2026-10-01 (option A) links a catalogue item at its Handle, the identifier that outlives the publishing host, rather than at the host’s own item URL. folio-assistant-core’s catalogue schema (HandleSchema, handleIri) applies the same rule to catalogue records. The RFCs are Informational and define the identifier system; the hdl.handle.net proxy is the resolver its operators run, not a namespace in the vocabulary sense. Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) . omg-bpmn-2.0 — OMG, edition 2.0 — conforms, meaning this repository’s artefacts are valid against it. Namespaces. | http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL | http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL# | http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/DI | . Note. The 20100524 in every namespace is BPMN 2.0’s release date and is how the edition is identified in an instance document — the diagrams have carried it since the first one was drawn, and until 2026-09-20 nothing in this repository said which specification that was. conforms rather than reads: these are our instance documents, so a version bump is a migration of the corpus rather than a compatibility question. No XSD is held and none is fetched — referenced, per the owner’s “dont need to materalize, but should reference specific version being used”. That means nothing validates a diagram structurally against OMG’s schema; check:workflows and kg:audit check the things this repository cares about (lanes bind declared roles, activities name skills) and are not a substitute for it. The MODEL# form is the RDF spelling of the same namespace: OMG publishes no RDF vocabulary for BPMN, so a graph that states a sequence flow’s sourceRef/targetRef or a node’s incoming/outgoing (kg-export, and bootstrap-tools’ export-graph.ts) names BPMN’s own attribute by appending # to its XML namespace — the model’s name for the relation, rather than a second one minted here (owner, 2026-09-30, bean xsqm). Namespaces. | http://www.omg.org/spec/DD/20100524/DC | http://www.omg.org/spec/DD/20100524/DI | . Note. Separate from BPMN even though the release date matches: DD is its own OMG specification and BPMN’s DI namespace builds on it. Recording them as one would make a DD bump invisible. DD/.../DC is Diagram Common — NOT Dublin Core, which is dcmi-terms in this registry and shares nothing with it but a two-letter prefix. That collision is exactly why a namespace URI is the identity here and a prefix is not. 3767.title: DIIG — the investment path from a health system bottleneck to a costed plan

3768.title: What it is, in one sentence
3768.content: A nine-chapter sequence taking a health programme from we have a problem to we have a budgeted, governed, monitorable digital implementation, in which each chapter’s output is the next chapter’s input.

3769.title: The nine chapters, as the Guide numbers them
3769.content: |   | chapter | what it produces | . | 1 | Introduction | scope, key terms, and when the Guide applies | . | 2 | Form the team and establish goals | roles and responsibilities; a shared statement of the programme’s needs and goals; an understanding of operations across levels of the health system | . | 3 | Identify health system challenges and needs | a map of the current state, bottlenecks confirmed and prioritized, and those bottlenecks mapped to generic health system challenges | . | 4 | Determine appropriate digital health interventions | selected interventions, an enabling-environment assessment, functional requirements and user stories, a future-state workflow | . | 5 | Plan the implementation | infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; leadership and governance; workforce and training; services and applications | . | 6 | Link the digital health implementation to the enterprise architecture | an assessment of the architecture, the common and enabling components (the digital health platform), and the investment linked to both | . | 7 | Develop a budget | phases of implementation, cost drivers, a budget matrix | . | 8 | Monitor the implementation and use data effectively | a logic model, an M&E plan, a culture of data use, adaptive management | . | 9 | Value proposition and next steps | the case made to whoever pays | . Chapters 4 and 8 close with a progress check, the Guide’s own gate.

3770.title: It builds on CRDM, and this platform already carries CRDM
3770.content: Chapter 3 says so in its own words: . This process builds on the Public Health Informatics Institute’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM), a commonly used approach for defining the problem, identifying how it could be improved, and describing how the improved process would need to function (50). — library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-043.md (PDF page 43, printed page 31), introducing Fig. 3.1. Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges . CRDM’s three areas of concentration, verbatim from the same page: . | Business process analysis | Business process redesign | Requirements definition | . cat-harness runs CRDM (skills in cat-harness/sdlc/skills/crdm/, processes including cat-harness/processes/process/crdm-needs.bpmn and crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn), so DIIG Chapter 3 and the platform’s requirements process descend from one published method. DIIG adapts CRDM for health system challenges; it does not restate it. Where the two disagree, neither overrides the other and they are not merged (methodology-adoption: never blend two methodologies). Pick one per decision, name it, follow it.

3771.title: Where this adoption stops
3771.content: . | The annexes are named, not rendered. DIIG’s fourteen worksheets and templates (the planning and implementation charter, the persona worksheet, the process matrix, the budget template, the logic model template, the adaptive management checklist, and more) are instruments a programme fills in, not steps an agent performs. They are cited to the ingested sections. | Figures are cited, not described. The Guide’s figures are in the ingested entry as figures/vfig-p<PDF page>.png (Fig. 3.1 is vfig-p043; Fig. 1.1.1 also as SVG, by smart-base:diig-figure); where this file mentions a figure it quotes the text around it. | Chapter 5’s country-specific and intervention-specific considerations (Annexes 5.3, 5.4) are a reference table of scale, not a method. Left in the library. | .

3772.title: Refusals
3772.content: methodology-adoption’s refusals bind. The first has a concrete target in this method. Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. DIIG Table 3.3.1, Formula for scoring and ranking bottlenecks (sections/page-050.md, PDF page 50, printed page 38), scores each bottleneck on three criteria, each 1–3: . | How much impact does this bottleneck have on the process? | What is the likelihood of overcoming this bottleneck? | Is this important to a wide range of stakeholders? | . — and combines them into a Score and a Prioritized Ranking. This platform adopts the three criteria and refuses the arithmetic. Three ordinal judgements on incommensurable scales, summed with equal weight, give a number whose precision is invented. An agent applying DIIG Chapter 3 records each criterion’s answer and its reason, and orders the bottlenecks by argument; it does not print a score. The summed score is kept as an alternative: the DTH for health supply chain architecture repeats the tally in its Annex 3 (9789240101197-eng, sections/page-068.md: “Adding the scores yields the prioritized ranking.”), and DIIG Table 3.3.1 and SC Annex 3 are both recorded beside this refusal in smart-base/findings/dth-terms.md. The refusal still governs what an agent applying this method does. Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. DIIG Chapter 4 selects interventions against prioritized challenges. The interventions considered and not chosen are part of the output, with why. Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A DIIG citation with no rendered step is an appeal to authority no reader can check. Never blend DIIG with CRDM, MAPS or the M&E guide. All touch digital health implementation; they are parallel tracks selected by context, not a toolkit to assemble from.

3773.title: Its neighbours in this library, and what each is for instead
3773.content: |   |   | . | Classification of Digital Health Interventions (v1.0, v2.0) | the controlled vocabulary DIIG Chapter 4 selects from; not a method | . | Digital transformation handbooks (primary health care; substandard and falsified medical products) | DIIG applied to one domain — worked instances, not the method | . | The MAPS Toolkit | assessment and planning for scale, which begins where DIIG’s first implementation ends | . | Monitoring and Evaluating Digital Health Interventions | the full treatment of what DIIG Chapter 8 compresses into one chapter | .

3774.title: DIIG — Digital Implementation Investment Guide
3774.content: ← All methodologies . diig — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Planning, costing and monitoring a DIGITAL HEALTH IMPLEMENTATION inside a health programme — from forming the team through to the budget and the monitoring plan. It is a programme-investment method, not a judgement method: it does not grade evidence (that is grade), does not choose between design options (kepner-tregoe), and does not constrain how a decision is recorded (madr). Reach for it when the question is what shall we build, with whom, at what cost, and how will we know it worked — and specifically when the answer has to survive a funder. Origin. World Health Organization, International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Foundation Digital Health Initiative, Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG): integrating digital interventions into health programmes (2020), ISBN 978-92-4-001056-7. Ingested at who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/; every citation below resolves to a section there. Ingested sources: . | library/9789240010567-eng · view · item page | . Node file: diig.md .

3776.title: 1. The scheme for each slot

3777.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3777.title: 2. The reuse-first precedence
3777.content: An agent or terminologist coding any slot walks the four-rung ladder and stops at the first rung that yields an exact or well-scoped match: . | Rung 1 — Target guide’s own declared vocabulary (exactMatch in guide). The target guide’s own personas (personas.md), business processes (business-processes.md), data dictionary (C5) and local code lists. If one defines the concept and its scope covers the statement, reuse its identifier verbatim. | Rung 2 — Layer base vocabulary (smart-base generic personas, FSH CodeSystems, and shared code lists). When the target guide does not declare the concept, or declares it more narrowly than the statement needs (an immunization guide’s health worker cannot be stretched to cover inpatient clinical management): . | smart-base generic personas (DAK.Persona.* in input/fsh/actors/, extracted in smart-base-generic-personas.json); | smart-base FSH CodeSystems (ISCO08, CDHIv2, CDHIv1, CDSCv2, CDSCv1, KGTerminologySystem and KG*); | shared folio-code-list/v1 lists (smart-base/code-lists/*.json, folio-assistant-core/code-lists/*.json) and SKOS glossaries (folio-assistant-core/glossary/guideline-domain.glossary.json). | . | Rung 3 — External authoritative standard (WHO-FIC / ILO / HL7 / W3C). A standard clinical, occupational or ontological term not in Rungs 1–2 is resolved against the external authority in vocabulary-authority and §1 above (ICD-11, ICHI, CDHI, ISCO-08, ATC, SNOMED CT, LOINC), recording the mapping predicate (skos:exactMatch or skos:closeMatch) per ontologist. | Rung 4 — Local candidate or explicit third state (citing glossary-terms). When Rungs 1–3 hold no match: . | For a persona or domain concept: mint a local glossary entry in <instance>/glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json following glossary-terms with status: "candidate", source: "extracted" (citing the doc_id and section / quote), and emit WARNING <slot>-glossary-candidate. An agent writes only status: "candidate"; promotion to status: "authored" is a person’s, in the terminologist/ontologist lane. | For a business process: never invent a process. Record could-not-determine with WARNING process-not-determined and the basis quoting the statement. That warning is the work list for the guide or domain process catalogue. | . | .

3778.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3778.title: 3. Provenance and review status on every coding
3778.content: Every classification or coding link records two independent facts: . | How the coding was obtained (source): . | declared — a person acting in an authorised role explicitly stated the code or link (must carry by); | context — the printed section heading, table header, or structural container in the source document settles the classification without inference; | inferred — an agent or author read the statement text and matched it against the scheme’s definitions. | . | Where it sits in review (status): . | candidate — proposed by the authoring-agent (using terminology-lookup and classify-and-code-content); | reviewed / authored — checked and signed off by a person acting in the terminologist (or l1-extraction-reviewer) role in classify-and-code-content.bpmn. | . | .

3779.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3779.title: 4. Adjudicating L1 coverage exclusions (l1-extraction-reviewer)
3779.content: When l1-recommendation-candidates scans an L1 source, every sentence carrying a normative marker (should, shall, must, recommend*, may be …) must either become an L1 node (recommendation, implementation-practice, remark, or part-of) or be excluded with one of the five closed reasons (background-fact, manufacturer-statement, editorial, research-question, duplicate-of:<id>). An agent may propose an exclusion in exclusions.proposed.json ("signerRole": {"role": "l1-extraction-reviewer"}) and never signs it. A person acting as l1-extraction-reviewer, in classify-and-code-content.bpmn, reads each candidate sentence in place on the printed page (sections/page-NNN.md), checks that it is non-normative under the stated reason, and either signs it (signedOffBy) or rejects it back to extraction curation, so no guidance is silently dropped.

3780.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3780.title: 5. Refusals
3780.content: . | Never invent a business process to make coverage look complete. When no process in the target guide or a published domain catalogue realises a scenario, the only valid value is could-not-determine with a warning. | Never stretch a narrower code as exactMatch. If a guide’s persona or a code list entry covers only part of the concept, use skos:closeMatch (or skos:broadMatch / skos:narrowMatch per ontologist) or fall through to the next rung. | Never self-approve a candidate term or an L1 exclusion. An agent writes status: "candidate" on glossary terms and leaves signedOffBy absent on exclusions; only a person in the reviewer lane records sign-off. | .

3781.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3781.title: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
3781.content: ← All methodologies . terminology-coding — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Classifying and coding L1 narrative content (guideline recommendations, implementation practices, remarks) and L2 Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) artefacts (personas, user scenarios, business processes, data-dictionary elements, decision-table concepts and indicators) against authoritative vocabularies and local code lists. Reach for it whenever a slot requires a code or SKOS concept (condition, intervention, persona/role, medicine, guideline domain, business process, or GRADE rating), or when deciding whether to reuse an existing term, fall back to a generic base concept, or propose a local glossary candidate. It does NOT grade evidence (that is grade), does NOT model BPMN/DMN control flow (bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring), and does NOT plan programme investment (diig). Origin. World Health Organization, SMART Guidelines: Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) (Mehl et al., BMJ Global Health 2021;6:e004908, ingested at smart-base/library/mehl-2021-who-smart-guidelines/); Classification of digital health interventions, services and applications in health (CDISAH) v2.0 (WHO, 2023, ISBN 978-92-4-008194-9, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240081949-eng/, superseding CDHI v1.0 at who-iris/library/who-rhr-1806-eng/); Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture (WHO, 2024, ISBN 978-92-4-010119-7, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/); and Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025, ISBN 978-92-4-011619-1, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/). 3782.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3782.title: Zero trust architecture
3782.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-10-07 (issue #2389, work item pk0z). The adversarial pass over the earlier draft (work item 1ygp, finding L3.1) showed that the draft was mostly this platform’s own rules presented as a method. The owner chose to split it, and asked to “make it a proper methodology” and to “ingest completely”. So this node holds only the method, as SP 800-207 states it. This platform applies it in the skill zero-trust-handover: the hand-over rules H1–H9, the hand-over screen and the sink-based risk table. That skill names this node and does not restate it, and this node does not restate the skill (methodology-adoption, §”Node, skill, or both?”).

3783.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3783.title: What the method is
3783.content: The operative definition (sec-003-2-zero-trust-basics): . “Zero trust (ZT) provides a collection of concepts and ideas designed to minimize uncertainty in enforcing accurate, least privilege per-request access decisions in information systems and services in the face of a network viewed as compromised.” . The aim is stated as uncertainty to be reduced, not removed: “To lessen uncertainties (as they cannot be eliminated), the focus is on authentication, authorization, and shrinking implicit trust zones” (same section). The abstract model (Figure 1) puts one policy decision / enforcement point between an untrusted subject and a resource. The implicit trust zone behind that point is what the method shrinks.

3784.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3784.title: The seven tenets (sec-004-21-tenets-of-zero-trust)
3784.content: NIST calls these “the ideal goal”, and says “not all tenets may be fully implemented in their purest form for a given strategy.” . | “All data sources and computing services are considered resources.” | “All communication is secured regardless of network location.” — “Network location alone does not imply trust.” | “Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis.” — “authentication and authorization to one resource will not automatically grant access to a different resource.” | “Access to resources is determined by dynamic policy”, drawn from the observable state of identity, application and asset, and possibly from behavioural and environmental attributes. | “The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all owned and associated assets. No asset is inherently trusted.” | “All resource authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed”: a constant cycle of obtaining access, assessing threats, adapting and reevaluating trust. | “The enterprise collects as much information as possible about the current state of assets, network infrastructure and communications and uses it to improve its security posture.” | . The tenets’ own scope limit. They “apply to work done within an organization or in collaboration with one or more partner organizations and not to anonymous public or consumer-facing business processes. An organization cannot impose internal policies on external actors” (same section).

3785.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3785.title: Six network assumptions (sec-005-22-a-zero-trust-view-of-a-network)
3785.content: . | The whole private network is “not considered an implicit trust zone”. Assets should “always act as if an attacker is present”. | Devices on the network may not be owned or configurable by the enterprise. | “No resource is inherently trusted.” Its posture is evaluated by a PEP, continually for the life of the session. | Not all enterprise resources are on enterprise-owned infrastructure. | Remote subjects and assets “cannot fully trust their local network connection”. | Assets and workflows moving between enterprise and nonenterprise infrastructure keep a consistent security policy and posture. | .

3786.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3786.title: The logical components (sec-006-3-logical-components-of-zero-trust-architecture, Figure 2)
3786.content: . | Policy engine (PE). “responsible for the ultimate decision to grant access to a resource for a given subject”. It takes enterprise policy and outside inputs into a trust algorithm, and “makes and logs the decision”. | Policy administrator (PA). Establishes or shuts down the communication path and issues session-specific credentials. It “relies on [the PE’s] decision”. The PE and PA together are the policy decision point (PDP). | Policy enforcement point (PEP). “responsible for enabling, monitoring, and eventually terminating connections between a subject and an enterprise resource.” It may be split into a client-side agent and a resource-side gateway, or be a single portal. | The inputs to the PE. Continuous diagnostics and mitigation, industry compliance, threat intelligence, network and system activity logs, data access policies, PKI, identity management and SIEM. | Two planes. The components talk on a control plane separate from the data plane that carries application data. | . Four deployed variations (sec-012 to sec-015; Figures 3–6) arrange the same components: . | device agent with a gateway; | an enclave behind one gateway; | a resource portal with no agent on the subject; | application sandboxes on a possibly compromised asset. | .

3787.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3787.title: The trust algorithm (sec-016-33-trust-algorithm, sec-017-331-trust-algorithm-variations, Figure 7)
3787.content: The PE’s decision process. Its inputs are: . | the access request; | the subject database and its history; | the asset database and the asset’s observable status; | resource policy requirements; | threat intelligence and logs. | . NIST distinguishes algorithms on two axes: . | Criteria-based or score-based. A criteria-based algorithm grants access “only if all the criteria are met”. A score-based one computes a confidence level from “values for every data source and enterprise-configured weights” and compares it with a threshold. | Singular or contextual. A singular algorithm judges each request alone, with the “risk that an attack can go undetected if it stays within a subject’s allowed role”. A contextual one also weighs the subject’s recent history. | .

3788.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3788.title: The threats NIST names for a ZTA itself (sec-026 to sec-033)
3788.content: . | 5.1 subversion of the decision process: “any configuration changes must be logged and subject to audit”; | 5.2 denial of service or network disruption; | 5.3 stolen credentials and insider threat; | 5.4 visibility on the network; | 5.5 storage of system and network information; | 5.6 reliance on proprietary data formats or solutions; | 5.7 use of non-person entities (NPE) in ZTA administration. This is the one written about agents (sec-033-57-use-of-non-person-entities-npe-in-zta-adminis): . “Artificial intelligence and other software-based agents are being deployed to manage security issues … The associated risk is that an attacker will be able to induce or coerce an NPE to perform some task that the attacker is not privileged to perform. … If an attacker can interact with the agent, they could theoretically trick the agent into allowing the attacker greater access or into performing some task on behalf of the attacker.” . NIST calls how such agents authenticate “an open issue”. Its stated mitigation for their errors is “regular retuning analysis to correct mistaken decisions”. It names false positives and false negatives as “the biggest risk” of automated enforcement. | .

3789.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3789.title: Migration (sec-042 to sec-052, Figure 12)
3789.content: A ZTA is introduced as a cycle laid against the NIST Risk Management Framework, not switched on: . | identify the actors; | identify the assets; | identify key processes and evaluate the risks of executing them; | formulate policies for a candidate; | identify candidate solutions; | deploy and monitor initially; | expand. | . “Incomplete knowledge will most often lead to a business process failure where the PE denies requests due to insufficient information” (sec-045-73-steps-to-introducing-zta-to-a-perimeter-based).

3790.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3790.title: Where this rendering stops, and what is refused
3790.content: . | The enterprise network machinery is not adopted. That covers the CDM program, TIC 3.0, EINSTEIN, FICAM, micro-segmentation and software-defined perimeters (§3.1, §6). This platform is not an enterprise network. It adopts the decision structure (a named decision point, a named enforcement point, per-request policy, no implicit trust by location) and applies it to agents, tools and graphs. Deciding which components map to what is the skill’s business, not this node’s. | The score-based trust algorithm is refused. A score from “configured weights” reads as a measurement, and the weights are invented. That is methodology-adoption §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”. Of NIST’s two kinds, only the criteria-based trust algorithm is adopted. | NIST’s applicability limit is kept as NIST states it. The tenets do not govern anonymous public participants, and an organisation cannot impose its policy on them. How this platform handles text from such participants is the skill’s business, not this node’s. | No performance or efficacy claim rests on this source. SP 800-207 is an architecture and guidance document. It reports no evaluation, and none is attributed to it here. | .

3791.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3791.title: What the source does not establish
3791.content: . | How an agent should authenticate to the decision components. NIST leaves this “an open issue” (5.7), and so does this node. | Whether a pattern-based screen of agent input is adequate. NIST does not discuss prompt injection by name. The screen in the skill is this platform’s mitigation, judged against prior work held separately (CaMeL, DataFilter, DefensiveTokens), and is not an application of anything 800-207 says. | .

3792.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3792.title: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
3792.content: ← All methodologies . zero-trust-architecture — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A participant is about to act on something another participant gave it, and the question is whether to trust it. That covers an access decision at a boundary, a hand-over between agents, a tool or a dependency graph reaching this platform, and the design of a check that decides any of these. It answers how trust is decided: never by location, per request, by policy, at a named decision and enforcement point. It is NOT a method for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe), for recording a decision (madr), for a recurring business rule (dmn), or for who is involved (raci). It is also not a threat-modelling or risk-scoring method: it says where trust is decided, not how likely an attack is. Origin. NIST Special Publication 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, by Scott Rose, Oliver Borchert, Stu Mitchell and Sean Connelly, August 2020, doi:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207. The primary is held, in full, at library/nist-sp-800-207: 59 pages, 55 sections and all 12 figures described. The owner supplied it on 2026-10-07 after this container’s network policy denied both NIST hosts. It is a US-government work: the PDF states it “is not subject to copyright in the United States” (p. i). Every quotation below is from that copy, cited by section id. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/nist-sp-800-207 | . Applied by skills: . | zero-trust-handover | . Node file: zero-trust-architecture.md .

3793.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3793.title: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — generate the rule, then execute it
3793.content: Adopted 2026-09-23. The source was uploaded, ingested whole through the pdf-structure rung (12 outline entries, structure read rather than inferred) and read before this node was written.

3794.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3794.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3794.content: Have the model emit a RULE that deterministic machinery then validates and executes — not the RESULT. The paper’s schema-mapping half is the clean case (§III-B): rather than asking the model to transform a document, it asks for a JSONata expression, checks that expression parses, and then runs it deterministically over the data. The model never touches the data at scale. Its output is a program, and a program can be checked before it is trusted in a way a transformed dataset cannot. That inversion is what makes the rest of the method work, and it is the part worth carrying anywhere. A generated result must be verified by inspecting every item; a generated rule is verified once and then applies at any volume.

3795.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3795.title: The five safeguards, as the source enumerates them
3795.content: §III-A, numbered there and renumbered nowhere here: . | # | safeguard | what it refuses | . | 1 | Prompt construction and context management — the tool builds the prompt, sets the model’s role, and states the expected output format | an ad-hoc prompt nobody can reproduce | . | 2 | Integrated validation and visualization — output is validated and shown immediately | an unvalidated artefact entering the system | . | 3 | Scalability through targeted context — send the user-selected sub-schema, never the whole thing | degradation the model will not report | . | 4 | Automated response post-processing — strip code fences and language hints | a wrapper artefact read as content | . | 5 | Human-in-the-loop editing — on incomplete or incorrect output the raw response is shown, and the person corrects, accepts or discards | a silent accept | . Safeguard 5 shows the raw response, and that detail is the method rather than an implementation nicety. A tool that hides the failed output leaves the person deciding whether to trust something they cannot see.

3796.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3796.title: Why the safeguards exist — three cited failure modes
3796.content: The source does not assert that models need guarding; it cites three measurements (§II-B), and they are reproduced here because a reader is entitled to check them rather than take the premise: . | LLMs can be distracted by irrelevant context — Shi et al., ICML 2023. | Accuracy drops on low-probability inputs even for deterministic tasks — McCoy et al., arXiv:2309.13638. | Reasoning degrades as input length increases, before the context window is reached — Levy et al., arXiv:2402.14848. | . The third is why safeguard 3 is about targeted context rather than merely sufficient context: staying under the window is not the same as staying in the range where the model reasons well. These three are second-hand here — cited by the ingested source, not themselves ingested, and marked as such per literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. The source also reports, from Buss et al. on LLM schema mapping, that “due to the difficult nature of data integration, human-in-the-loop approaches are required” — which is safeguard 5 arrived at independently.

3797.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3797.title: Bounded truncation — the one technique worth naming separately
3797.content: §III-B. Where the input is too large, the source does not summarise it and does not silently clip it. It recursively truncates arrays to length n and object properties to 8n, halving n from 64 until the document is under 64 KB or n = 2 — properties trimmed more conservatively than array items, because array items tend to share a schema while properties usually differ. The part that makes it a method rather than a hack: the schema inferred from the COMPLETE document is included in the prompt, so what truncation removed is still described even though it is no longer present. The source states the consequence rather than hiding it — there is an upper bound on document complexity that this supports.

3798.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3798.title: What it refuses
3798.content: . | Never let the model’s output be the thing that is acted on, where a rule could be generated instead. That is the whole method; everything else is support. | Never send the whole context because it fits. Fitting the window is not the criterion — safeguard 3 and the Levy et al. finding are about the range in which reasoning holds, which is smaller. | Never accept silently on failure. Safeguard 5 requires the raw response to be visible to the person who is being asked to accept it. | Never treat syntactic validation as semantic validation. The source is explicit that its JSONata check is “for syntactical correctness (not semantics)”. A method that blurred those would present an expression that parses as an expression that is right. | .

3799.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3799.title: Where this rendering stops
3799.content: methodology-adoption step 2: both halves stated. Adopted — the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards, the three cited failure modes, bounded truncation with schema preservation, and the syntactic/semantic distinction. Not adopted, and deliberately — every tool choice in the paper. MetaConfigurator, JSONata, gpt-4o-mini, jsonhero/schema-infer and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint are one instantiation. The owner’s instruction on ingesting this source, 2026-09-23: “do not need to match tools in paper, start with process, determine most appropriate tools (known or which can be added).” A node that named those tools would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method. Not assessed — the paper’s chemistry application example (§IV) is a demonstration, not an evaluation. It reports no accuracy measurement, no baseline and no comparison, so nothing here rests on a claim about how well the approach performs. The source does not make such a claim, and this node must not manufacture one.

3800.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3800.title: How this platform applies it
3800.content: This repository was already navigating the deterministic-to-agentic spectrum before this node existed, through four mechanisms that do not refer to each other. That application — and the open research questions this source bears on — is in the skill: skills/process/workflow/deterministic-and-agentic.md. The method lives here once; the skill names it and does not restate it.

3801.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3801.title: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
3801.content: ← All methodologies . hybrid-llm-deterministic — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. An agent must produce an artefact that something downstream will act on. Use it when a language model is in the loop and a wrong output would be acted on rather than merely read — a schema, a mapping, a classification, a branch, a judgement. It answers how to get the output safely, never which option to choose: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, who is involved is raci, and situation analysis is swot. Those pick an answer; this one constrains how an answer is produced. Not applicable where no model is involved, and unnecessary where the output is only ever read by a person who will notice it is wrong. Origin. Felix Neubauer, Jürgen Pleiss and Benjamin Uekermann, “AI-assisted JSON Schema Creation and Mapping” (arXiv:2508.05192v2), University of Stuttgart. The authors’ own word for it is a “hybrid approach that combines large language models (LLMs) with deterministic techniques”. Open access, read whole and ingested here — unlike most nodes in this graph, the primary IS held. It is a tool paper reporting one implementation (MetaConfigurator), so what is adopted below is the METHOD it generalises, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2508.05192v2 | . Applied by skills: . | deterministic-and-agentic | . Node file: hybrid-llm-deterministic.md .

3802.doc: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT
3802.title: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms
3802.content: Adopted 2026-09-29 as one of the three decision-methodology sources the owner supplied. What is adopted is the frame — which family of algorithm answers which shape of question, and what its analysis does and does not license — not any algorithm and not any bound.

3803.doc: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT
3803.title: The load-bearing distinction, and it comes first in the monograph
3803.content: Chapter 1 opens on the split between Bayesian and frequentist decision theory, with a quotation about practitioners who “nimbly skip among these different ideas” without saying which they are using. That is the frame worth importing: the two answer different questions. | Bayesian — a prior over the unknown, updated by evidence; the guarantee is about expected performance under that prior. Thompson sampling and Bayesian optimisation sit here. | Frequentist — no prior; the guarantee is high-probability and holds for any fixed problem instance. Explore-then-exploit and UCB sit here. | . An agent quoting a bound has to say which it is, because “regret is bounded by …” means two different things across that line: an average over a prior nobody committed to, or a statement that holds with stated probability for the instance in front of you.

3804.doc: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT
3804.title: What the monograph covers, as a map
3804.content: | part | what it analyses | . | decision theory | Bayesian and frequentist formulations of the same problem | . | concentration inequalities | Gaussian tail bounds and the other inequalities every proof below reuses | . | frequentist bandits | explore-then-exploit, then UCB | . | Gaussian processes | posterior inference, RKHS, information capacity | . | Bayesian optimisation | discrete first, then continuous; GP-UCB high-probability regret, GP-TS expected regret | . Read as a selection aid, the table says the practical question is what you can assume about the reward surface. A finite unstructured arm set gives a bandit; a smooth surface over a continuous domain with a kernel you are willing to name gives Bayesian optimisation; and the GP machinery in the middle is the price of that smoothness assumption.

3805.doc: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT
3805.title: Where this rendering stops
3805.content: . | No algorithm is implemented or recommended. The monograph does not rank them either; it analyses them. | No bound is quoted as a fact about anything here. Every guarantee in it is conditional on assumptions — sub-Gaussian noise, a bounded RKHS norm, a known horizon — and a bound repeated without its assumptions is not a weaker claim, it is a different and false one. | It is a tutorial, not an empirical study. There is no benchmark and no comparison, so nothing in it can support “method X beats method Y”. | The application domain is not inherited. Materials and drug discovery are the author’s motivating examples. | .

3806.doc: Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT
3806.title: What it is evidence FOR, here
3806.content: Chiefly that “adaptive” is a precondition, not a bonus. Every method in this family earns its guarantee by choosing the next trial in light of the last, so the family is simply inapplicable to a decision that is made once — which is the cleanest line between this node and mcdm-aggregation, and the line decision-methodology-selector most needs to be able to draw. Second, and more narrowly: the Bayesian/frequentist split is a worked instance of the rule this repository states as reported, never graded. Two numbers that look alike, mean different things, and cannot be compared — the same shape as m4xy’s declared-versus-placed and LCSHBench’s exact-versus-concept.
