3883.doc: JSON-LD 1.1 — the knowledge graph serialised as Linked Data in plain JSON
3883.title: What the source does NOT establish
3883.content: The Recommendation defines a syntax; it makes no claim that a graph written in it is correct, complete or well-modelled. A document that expands without warning has a well-formed serialisation and nothing more. The two platform rules above (identifier = path; every prefix emitted) are house rules layered on the standard, not part of it.

3884.doc: JSON-LD 1.1 — the knowledge graph serialised as Linked Data in plain JSON
3884.title: JSON-LD 1.1 — the knowledge graph serialised as Linked Data in plain JSON
3884.content: ← All methodologies . json-ld-serialisation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Choosing how a node of the knowledge graph is written to disk or published, so that it is ordinary JSON to a reader with no RDF tooling and RDF to one with it. Use it when adding a generated .jsonld sibling, a term to a published @context, a prefix, or a new exported document. It answers how a node is identified, typed and linked in the serialisation. It does NOT answer what a node means (that is the vocabulary and the schemas), whether a relation is true (uses-editorial-review), or how a table is modelled (CSVW, bound as a vocabulary, not a serialisation). Origin. W3C, “JSON-LD 1.1 — A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data”, W3C Recommendation 16 July 2020 (https://www.w3.org/TR/2020/REC-json-ld11-20200716/), editors Gregg Kellogg, Pierre-Antoine Champin and Dave Longley; produced by the JSON-LD Working Group. Held as the Working Group’s own publication snapshot of the REC (github.com/w3c/json-ld-syntax, commit 029777cf), under the W3C Software and Document License. The companion Recommendations — JSON-LD 1.1 Processing Algorithms and API, and JSON-LD 1.1 Framing — are NOT held. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1 | . 3885.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3885.title: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation: score against where experts agree, and read the panel
3885.content: Adopted 2026-09-26 (work item 0js9). Both sources were ingested through the library pipeline and read before this node was written.

3886.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3886.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3886.content: Experts agree about what a work is about far more than about how to say it, so an evaluation must score those two layers separately. It must also take its answer key from where independent experts agree, not from one of them. The source makes this a measured premise rather than an assumption. Its concordance study (section “Consensus ground truth”) compares the headings that three research libraries assigned independently to 465,187 works that all three catalogued. It finds two layers. At the concept level (the heading’s root, before the first --), the three share a heading 93.3 % of the time and share nothing 0.2 % of the time. At the exact, fully subdivided level, only 39.4 % assign identical sets, and 35.6 % of all assertions come from just one of the three. In the source’s words: “most disagreement is granularity — which subdivisions, how specific — not topic”. Those figures are the source’s measurements on its corpus. They are quoted here as the reason for the design, not as constants this platform relies on.

3887.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3887.title: The method, as the source constructs it
3887.content: 1. The answer key is a consensus of independent judges. A work is admitted only if at least two cataloguing agencies independently assigned headings. The source enforces independence “at the level of the cataloging agency (MARC field 040), not merely the holding library, so that a copy-cataloged record imported from another institution does not count as a second judgement”. The rule is “strict and never relaxed to enlarge the dataset”. 2. Disagreement is kept, not resolved. Each heading carries a vote: the number of judges who asserted it. Three answer views are released: per-judge (the raw evidence), union (the default, which “rewards finding any heading a professional used”), and unanimous (the strictest). Every result states which view it was scored against. 3. Provenance before validity. A heading string can look valid in the vocabulary and still come from somewhere else. The source keeps a heading only when its record says it is from the target vocabulary. That removes “most of a quarter of candidate headings whose strings look like valid LCSH but whose provenance is not — a distinction string-validity checks miss”. 4. Normalise before comparing. NFC, lower-casing, a canonical subdivision separator, collapsed whitespace, and no trailing period, “so systems are judged on substance, not typography”. 5. Two match modes, always both. Every measure is computed under exact match (the full subdivided heading) and concept match (the root only). The gap between them is diagnostic: “a high concept but low exact score means the system found the right topic but not the authorised subdivided form — a different, specifiable error from a topical miss”. 6. A panel, not a headline. “The central methodological commitment is that no single number is trustworthy on its own.” Set metrics (micro and macro precision, recall, F1) for generation; ranked metrics (recall@k, P@k, R-precision, MRR) for retrieval; each under both match modes; and each broken down by language and by heading type, which the source calls “the panel’s most important safeguard”. 7. Never score what the system could not have reached. Retrieval is scored against the gold headings that exist in the retrieval vocabulary. The reachability ceiling is reported explicitly. Records with no reachable gold are excluded and counted, not scored as zero. “So that a heading that cannot be retrieved is never scored as a miss.” . 8. Stage-wise, where the system has stages. Where a system retrieves, reranks and then selects, each layer is scored separately. Recall at the first stage is “the ceiling for everything downstream”. The source rejects a frozen candidate pool because it “would bake in an arbitrary retriever’s choices”. 9. Human agreement is a reference, not a ceiling. One cataloguer reproduces roughly 87 % (exact) or 93 % (concept) of their peers’ consensus, so “a non-trivial share” of a system’s misses are headings a second cataloguer would also have omitted. The source deliberately does not turn this into a recall ceiling, because a ranked list of 200 and a short final set “measure different things”.

3888.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3888.title: Why the panel is not optional: the source’s own worked case
3888.content: The source’s section “The metric panel is necessary” shows a single aggregate getting the answer wrong. Its fine-tuned embedder wins on exact recall@200, but a hosted model wins on concept recall@200. The fine-tune wins on Korean, Arabic, Japanese, Chinese and German, and the hosted model still wins on English and Russian. “A benchmark reporting a single aggregate F1 would have asserted a clean victory and been wrong about its shape.” This is the case for step 6. It is not a claim about either model, and this node makes no such claim.

3889.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3889.title: What it refuses
3889.content: . | Never score against one indexer’s record as though it were the truth. A single library’s headings make “a noisy gold standard”. The concordance numbers are the reason. | Never report one number. Not a headline F1, not one match mode, and not an aggregate without the language and type breakdowns. | Never count an unreachable heading as a miss, and never leave out the count of what was excluded. | Never treat a hashed or held-out answer set as contamination-proof. The source is explicit that hashing over a finite public vocabulary is “a speed-bump, not a guarantee”, and that genuine control “would require a private evaluation server”, “with residual risk reported, not assumed away”. | Never compare results across vocabulary versions as though they were comparable. The vocabulary and cataloguing practice change. The source versions and dates its benchmark for this reason, and notes that the change affects exact match more than concept match. | .

3890.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3890.title: The parallel design, and why it is not this node
3890.content: methodology-adoption: parallel tracks are recorded, not blended. SemEval-2025 Task 5 (arXiv:2504.07199v3) evaluates with a single catalogue as gold: subject annotations by TIB’s own subject specialists, 17 of them across 28 disciplines. Its primary metric is recall, averaged over k from 5 to . | It adds a qualitative track in which subject librarians label each predicted subject as correct (Y), irrelevant but technically correct (I), or wrong. That track is scored twice: once counting Y and I as correct, and once counting only Y. The organisers note that their precision “would never amount to one” at larger k, because records carry about five true subjects. | . This is a sound design for its setting: a single institution, a specialist team, and a shared task with a deadline. What it does not have is steps 1 and 2 above. With one catalogue as gold, the concordance finding says that a large share of “misses” at exact level would be headings another professional would also have phrased differently. The two-case qualitative reading is the part of SemEval’s design that LCSHBench does not yet have. LCSHBench lists “the qualitative expert track” among its deferred components. Where this platform needs expert ratings, it uses SemEval’s protocol as SemEval’s, cited as such. It is not grafted into the consensus method as step 10.

3891.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3891.title: Where this rendering stops
3891.content: methodology-adoption step 2 requires both halves, so both are given here. Adopted: steps 1–9, the refusals, and the two-layer premise as the reason for them. Not adopted: the benchmark itself. Its corpus, its three source catalogues, its answer hashing, its embedders and its fine-tuning recipe are one instantiation for LCSH. The owner’s instruction, 2026-09-23: “start with process, determine most appropriate tools.” Nothing in the method depends on LCSH. A vocabulary without multiple independent indexers cannot supply step 1, and that is a reason to say the evaluation is single-judge, not to pretend otherwise. Not assessed: the source’s fine-tuning result. The source calls it “preliminary”: it was run on a development subset, not the held-out test, and at the first stage only. No claim about any system’s performance rests on this node. The concordance percentages quoted above are the source’s measurements, attributed as such, and nothing here uses them as parameters.

3892.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3892.title: How this platform applies it
3892.content: It does not apply it yet. Nothing here assigns subject terms, so nothing is evaluated this way. The nearest existing machinery is the QA-sidecar discipline. It shares this node’s refusals: never render “could not determine” as clean, and never quote one number without its basis. That is agreement in spirit, not an application, and it is recorded so nobody mistakes it for one.

3893.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3893.title: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
3893.content: ← All methodologies . consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Judging how good a set of controlled-vocabulary assignments is, when qualified people would themselves disagree about the exact answer. Use it to evaluate a subject-indexing system, compare two of them, or decide whether one is good enough to draft for a human reviewer. It is also for any labelling task whose gold standard is expert judgement with a subjective surface. It answers how to measure. It does not answer how to produce the assignment, which is skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, a parallel node. Not for certainty of evidence behind a recommendation (grade), and not for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe). Not applicable where the answer is decidable, meaning a single correct output a checker can verify, because then there is no disagreement for a consensus to absorb. Origin. Kwok Leong Tang, “LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment” (arXiv:2606.04382v1), 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper. The parallel design it is contrasted with is the one used by the shared task the other ingested subject-indexing papers were entered in: D’Souza, Sadruddin, Israel, Begoin & Slawig, “SemEval-2025 Task 5: LLMs4Subjects — LLM-based Automated Subject Tagging for a National Technical Library’s Open-Access Catalog” (arXiv:2504.07199v3), TIB Hannover. It was ingested and read too, so that design is described from its own text. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2606.04382v1 | library/arxiv-2504.07199v3 | . Node file: consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation.md .

3894.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3894.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing: decompose the cataloguer’s stages and validate each
3894.content: Adopted 2026-09-26 (work item 0js9). All three sources were ingested through the library pipeline, and the primary was read whole before this node was written.

3895.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3895.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3895.content: Prior systems found the right topics and still got the headings wrong. The failures were in applying the rules, and a single prompt gives rule application nowhere to happen. The source reviews the earlier LLM studies and states the diagnosis directly (its section “Present Contribution”): the documented accuracy failures “are not primarily failures of topic identification — they are failures of rule application”. The models “produce unauthorized heading forms, omit required subdivisions, use deprecated subfield practices, and fail to verify headings against authority files”, and every prior study “treats subject assignment as a single-step task”. The remedy is structural. A professional cataloguer works through distinct stages, so the pipeline gives each stage its own skill, and each skill passes a structured intermediate output to the next. The source’s own framing is “an externalized, architecturally enforced form of chain-of-thought reasoning”: the intermediate outputs are “inspectable and correctable at each step before proceeding to the next”, and that is what a single prompt “cannot” provide.

3896.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3896.title: The four stages, as the source defines them
3896.content: Section “The Four-Skill Pipeline” and its Figure 1. Each stage names the policy it encodes, which is the point: every stage is small enough to be checked against its own source document. | # | stage | receives → emits | what it encodes | . | 1 | Conceptual analysis | title, abstract, table of contents → an aboutness statement and a flat list of candidate concepts, each justified | Wilson’s four methods of subject determination (purposive, figure-ground, objective, cohesion), Langridge’s three questions, the Joudrey–Taylor framework, via Holley & Joudrey’s review | . | 2 | Quantitative filtering | concept list → an ordered list of candidate headings, each with its intended MARC field | SHM H 180: the 20 % rule, the rule of three, specificity, depth of indexing; H 80: order by predominance; the 2026 LC genre/form policy | . | 3 | Authority validation | candidates → authorised forms, with variants redirected through their UF references | a local index over the LCSH and LCGFT authority files; a live query against LCNAF for names; H 830 for geographic subdivision | . | 4 | Field synthesis | validated headings → MARC 21 6xx fields | H 1075 subdivision order, H 830 indirect geographic subdivision, H 405 and H 430 for name headings, J 105 and J 110 for genre/form | . Two design choices inside the stages are part of the method, not details: . | Stage 1 over-generates on purpose. The source: “The skill intentionally over-generates at this stage — filtering is deferred to Skill 2.” Recall is one stage’s job and precision is the next stage’s. A stage 1 that filtered as it went would be doing stage 2’s job with none of stage 2’s rules. | Authority validation is a lookup, not a judgement. Stage 3 asks whether each candidate exists as an authorised form in the file. It does not ask the model whether the candidate looks authorised. That makes it the one stage whose output is deterministic given its input. | .

3897.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3897.title: How the skills were made: the construction discipline is part of the method
3897.content: Section “Source Material and Skill Construction”: each of eleven LC policy documents and one review article was “read in full and its normative content — rules, exceptions, decision criteria, and worked examples — was translated into structured instructions”. The resulting skills “are not simply prompts; they are multi-section documents that define terminology, enumerate decision steps, specify output formats, and include validation checks.” . This is what makes the method survive a change of vocabulary. The pipeline shape stays fixed, and moving to another vocabulary means re-reading that vocabulary’s policy manual into the same four stages. The source names MeSH, AAT and FAST as the next candidates. A stage whose instructions cannot be traced back to a clause in the vocabulary’s own policy is not this method.

3898.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3898.title: What it refuses
3898.content: . | Never go from the work to the finished fields in one pass. That is the failure the method exists to correct. | Never rely on the model’s internalised knowledge of the vocabulary. The source contrasts itself with single-prompt approaches on exactly this point: it “explicitly encodes SHM rules at each stage rather than relying on the model’s internalized knowledge of LCSH conventions”. | Never emit a heading that stage 3 did not find in the authority file. If a validator is never allowed to say no, the stage is only there for show. | Never ship the output as final. The source’s conclusion: the output “would serve as a draft for review by a subject cataloger rather than as a final product, consistent with the human-in-the-loop workflow advocated throughout the literature”. | Never read a difference from an existing record as an error. The source’s baseline records “may reflect subject indexing decisions made years or decades ago — potentially under different LC policies”. Its largest systematic difference, genre/form in 655 fields rather than as $v subdivisions, is the pipeline applying the current policy correctly. | .

3899.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3899.title: The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node
3899.content: methodology-adoption: parallel tracks are recorded, not blended. Two ingested sources take a different route to the same task. Each is recorded here as it presents itself. Trained extreme multi-label classification, with LLMs in support (Annif, arXiv:2504.19675v2). A toolkit of XMTC backends is trained on catalogued records, and its suggestions are merged by ensemble. Omikuji uses partitioned label trees; MLLM does lexical matching; XTransformer is a fine-tuned transformer. Language models are used around the classifier and do no classifying themselves: they translate records between languages and generate synthetic training records. It placed first in the task’s all-subjects quantitative ranking. It needs a large body of already catalogued records to train on. Chow names this as the line: the skill pipeline “does not require training data or corpus-level pattern learning”. Use Annif’s track where that corpus exists and the vocabulary’s policy is not written down in a form a stage could encode. Retrieve, then let a model judge each candidate (Homa / OntoAligner, arXiv:2504.21474v1). Subject indexing is recast as ontology alignment: embed the record, retrieve the top 30 subjects by cosine similarity, and ask a small fine-tuned model whether each one matches. The authors report that recall held up and precision did not: “the system retrieves a broad set of candidate subjects, but many are not relevant”. The retrieval step does real work. What this track lacks is any stage that applies the vocabulary’s rules: nothing in it filters by policy, orders by predominance, or constructs a subdivided heading. For a flat vocabulary that may not matter. For LCSH, it is exactly the gap Chow diagnoses. Neither is refused as wrong. They answer the same question under different conditions, and which one applies depends on the context. Composing them into “Annif’s candidates, filtered by Chow’s stage 2” would be a house method that cites nobody.

3900.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3900.title: Against hybrid-llm-deterministic
3900.content: These are parallel nodes, and the difference is worth stating because the two look alike. hybrid-llm-deterministic has the model emit a rule that machinery then executes. The model never touches the data at scale, because a generated result would have to be checked item by item. This method has the model emit results, the headings themselves, and checks each one. That is sound here, and it is sound for a reason the other node does not cover: checking a result costs one authority-file lookup when the answer must come from a closed, enumerable vocabulary. The expensive per-item verification that the rule/result inversion avoids becomes a membership test here. Where results come from an open space, that argument fails and hybrid-llm-deterministic is the node to reach for.

3901.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3901.title: Where this rendering stops
3901.content: methodology-adoption step 2 requires both halves, so both are given here. Adopted: the diagnosis (rule application, not topic identification); the decomposition into four stages, each with a structured output; the over-generate-then-filter split; authority validation as a lookup; the construction discipline of reading each policy document into a stage; and the refusals above. Not adopted, and deliberately: every tool in the paper. Claude Code, its skill file format, the local TF-IDF index over NDJSON dumps from id.loc.gov, the LC suggest2 API, and MARC 21 as the output encoding are one instantiation. The owner’s instruction on ingesting a tool paper, 2026-09-23: “do not need to match tools in paper, start with process, determine most appropriate tools (known or which can be added).” The same holds for the specific LCSH rules: they are the content of stages 2–4 for LCSH, and another vocabulary’s policy supplies its own. Not assessed: the source’s evaluation is ten titles, one or two per discipline, compared with existing Harvard records along four dimensions. The source calls the comparison “interpretive rather than strictly quantitative” and says ten comparisons “are insufficient for statistical generalization”. No claim about how well this method performs rests on this node. It also cites a 26–35 % alignment figure for single-prompt approaches from Tang & Jiang (2025). That paper is not ingested here, so the figure is second-hand and is not repeated as a finding. Named by the source as open, and left open here: under-subdivision (geographic $z and chronological $y), choosing among overlapping authorised headings, the missing step of consulting peer records for the same ISBN, and overlapping population groups in conceptual analysis. These are the source’s own stated limitations (section “Limitations and Areas for Improvement”). They are listed so that a skill built on this node does not rediscover them.

3902.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3902.title: How this platform applies it
3902.content: It does not apply it yet, and says so. No skill here assigns controlled vocabulary terms. Library entries produced by the L1 ingest (epic slw1) carry structure, sections, images and labels, but no subject field. This node exists so that the day one is added, the method is chosen by adoption and not improvised. A skill that implements it names this node and does not restate it.

3903.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3903.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
3903.content: ← All methodologies . skill-pipeline-subject-indexing — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Assigning terms from a closed, rule-governed controlled vocabulary to a work: deciding what it is about and saying so in the vocabulary’s own authorised form. Use it when the vocabulary comes with a written policy manual (LCSH has the Subject Headings Manual; MeSH, AAT and FAST are the source’s own named candidates) and an authority file that can be queried, and a wrong but plausible term would be acted on in cataloguing, retrieval or linking. It answers how to produce the assignment. It does not answer how to tell whether an assignment is good: that is consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation, which is a parallel node and is not folded into this one. Not for choosing between options (kepner-tregoe), a recurring decision rule (dmn), or making a model emit a rule instead of a result (hybrid-llm-deterministic); §”Against hybrid-llm-deterministic” explains why the last is a separate method and not this one’s parent. Not for free keywording with no vocabulary to validate against, because the authority step is what the method rests on. Origin. Eric H. C. Chow, “A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing” (arXiv:2605.03537v1), School of Humanities, The University of Hong Kong. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper alone. Two parallel tracks, both entrants in SemEval-2025 Task 5, were ingested beside it and read so that §”The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node” rests on the papers and not on how Chow summarises them: Suominen, Inkinen & Lehtinen, “Annif at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Traditional XMTC augmented by LLMs” (arXiv:2504.19675v2), National Library of Finland; and Bayrami Asl Tekanlou et al., “Homa at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Aligning Librarian Records with OntoAligner for Subject Tagging” (arXiv:2504.21474v1). Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2605.03537v1 | library/arxiv-2504.19675v2 | library/arxiv-2504.21474v1 | . Applied by skills: . | mesh-subject-indexing | mesh-subject-indexing | . Node file: skill-pipeline-subject-indexing.md .

3904.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3904.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3904.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

3905.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3905.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
3905.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan work item → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed work items archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

3906.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3906.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
3906.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

3907.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3907.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
3907.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary 3909.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3909.title: Automatic term extraction: candidates from prose, ranked, judged by a person
3909.content: Adopted 2026-11-10 (cat-harness#1144 follow-up, owner card Q-IDX-1 = A), so that the glossary skills that read prose for terms rest on a published method rather than on a house heuristic.

3910.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3910.title: Its sources: what is held
3910.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | Tran et al. 2023, survey | ✅ library/arxiv-2301.06767v1 | the task and its two steps (§1), the feature families (§5.1, Fig. 2), the evaluation methods and measures (§6, Fig. 4), nested terms as the main open problem (§8.1) | . | Frantzi & Ananiadou 1996 | ✅ library/frantzi-ananiadou-1996-c-value | the C-value measure and its algorithm (§3, equations 1–3), and the human judge as the last step | . | Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000 | ❌ not held | C-value applied to terms, and NC-value’s context weighting. Nothing here depends on them; they are named so that a reader does not take this node’s C-value for theirs | .

3911.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3911.title: The task, in the survey’s words
3911.content: “ATE systems usually employ a two-step procedure: (1) extracting a list of candidate terms, and (2) determining which candidate terms are correct using supervised or unsupervised techniques.” (§1) . The candidates come from preprocessing (tokenisation, lemmatisation, POS tagging, chunking). The second step scores them with features from six families (§5.1, Fig. 2): shape, linguistic, frequency, statistical, contextual and variational. The statistical family splits in two. Some measures need no reference corpus, such as C-value, TF-IDF and lexical cohesion. Others compare the domain text with a general one, such as weirdness, domain relevance and termhood.

3912.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3912.title: C-value, as Frantzi & Ananiadou define it (§3)
3912.content: C-value scores a candidate string a by how often it occurs, how long it is, and how often it occurs inside longer candidates. It exists for nested units: a phrase such as “Wall Street” that occurs mostly inside longer ones (“Wall Street Journal”) and would score low on its own frequency. | case | C-value(a) | . | a has the same frequency as a longer candidate that contains it (it only ever occurs inside that one) | 0: not a candidate | . | a is not a substring of any extracted candidate | (|a| − 1) · n(a) (eq. 2) | . | a occurs inside one or more longer candidates, not always the same one | (|a| − 1) · (n(a) − t(a) / c(a)) (eq. 3) | . n(a) is the frequency of a, |a| its length in words, t(a) its total frequency inside longer candidates, and c(a) the number of those longer candidates. The algorithm visits n-grams from the longest down, after a minimum frequency cut-off, and revises t and c of every substring as it goes. The more different longer candidates contain a, the smaller t(a)/c(a) and the higher its C-value. Two limits the paper states itself. It measured no precision or recall, because those “depend on the definition of collocation and they are domain dependent” (§4). And it presents the method as semi-automatic: “It is the human judge that will give the final decision” (§3). The 1996 paper is about collocations; applying it to terms is its own stated future work (§6), done in the papers that are not held.

3913.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3913.title: How a result is judged (survey §6)
3913.content: Three evaluation methods: human judges, a dictionary, or a gold standard list. Three scopes: all results, part of them, or the top k. With a gold standard the measures are precision, recall and F1. The survey notes that “the performance of different approaches is often not directly comparable” because the setups differ. Here, the gold standard for a layer is its own authored glossary terms: precision is the share of candidates a person accepted, and recall is the share of authored terms that the extractor proposed.

3914.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3914.title: Nested terms are the hard case (survey §8.1)
3914.content: Nested terms are “words or phrases that are both terms themselves and parts of longer terms”. The most common error the survey reports for current systems is that they predict only the shorter, nested term instead of the whole multi-word term, or the other way round. This is the case C-value was built for, and it is why C-value is the statistical measure this node names.

3915.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3915.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
3915.content: Adopted: . | the two steps, candidates then scoring; | C-value as the first scoring measure, because it needs no reference corpus and it addresses nested terms; | evaluation against the layer’s authored terms, reported as precision and recall, and never as one score. | . Refused: . | An extracted term is never a definition. It enters the glossary as candidate, with no definition until a person writes one. This is the 1996 paper’s human judge, and it is glossary-terms’ existing rule. | A score is not a decision. The ranking orders the review queue. A cut-off may shorten the queue, but it never promotes a term. | A measure the sources do not define is not added under this node’s name. NC-value’s context weights, or the log-length variant of C-value, come in with their own held source or not at all. | .

3916.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3916.title: How it is performed here
3916.content: The glossary skills that read prose for terms name this node in their uses-methodology, and the Tool that computes C-value satisfies them. Both live in the content layer, which links down to here. The Tool’s test reproduces Table 2 of the 1996 paper. By default it applies the paper’s method as published, which on ordinary prose ranks function phrases such as “it is” first (the paper: many candidates “may seem unimportant”, §4).

3917.doc: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3917.title: Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide
3917.content: ← All methodologies . automatic-term-extraction — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding which words and phrases in a body of prose are the TERMS of its domain, so that a glossary can be proposed from the text rather than typed from memory. It answers which strings are candidate terms, ranked. Every output is a candidate: a person decides what is a term and writes its definition (glossary-terms: an extractor writes candidate, only a person moves one to authored). Not for assigning terms from a closed controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for keywords that summarise one document against the others (lsi, correspondence-analysis, the keyword graph), and not for reading definitions a source already states in its own glossary section, which are copied verbatim and need no extraction. Origin. Automatic term extraction (ATE) as surveyed by Hanh Thi Hong Tran, Matej Martinc, Jaya Caporusso, Antoine Doucet and Senja Pollak, “The Recent Advances in Automatic Term Extraction: A survey” (arXiv:2301.06767v1, CC BY 4.0), ingested whole and read. The C-value measure for nested multi-word units is Katerina T. Frantzi and Sophia Ananiadou, “Extracting Nested Collocations”, COLING 1996 (ACL Anthology C96-1009, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), ingested whole and read; its equations were checked against the printed page, because the Anthology’s own text layer is a poor OCR. The later C-value/NC-value papers that apply the measure to terms (Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000) are not open access and are not held. 3918.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3918.title: WireGen: from a written intent to a reviewed, mid-fidelity wireframe
3918.content: Adopted in part, 2026-09-23, by the owner’s direction. In the owner’s words: “make methodology/utilize/integrate into existing processes. need both web and mobile layouts in usability reviews. wireframe is part of design process for adjudication”. Integrated into CRDM, 2026-10-14. crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn calls Process_WireframeDesignReview (Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built; the candidates become assets of the request’s proposal, and the requester or BA chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. See wireframe-design-review. Placed in cat-harness (owner, 2026-09-23: “put wireframe in cat-harness, not folio-assist(-core)”). The method is domain-neutral, and methodology-adoption §4 puts a domain-neutral method in the harness. It was first drafted in litlfred/ihris, and its first use was that folio’s data-model site. Issue #1023.

3919.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3919.title: What the method says (rendered faithfully)
3919.content: Section numbers below are the paper’s. | Design intent comes first, as language (§3, §5.2). A short natural-language description of what the screen is for and what it holds. | Mid-fidelity is the target (§3.1.1). The wireframe is monochrome and simplified, but it carries real content, semantic icons and interactive elements, not boxes and placeholder text. | HTML is the carrier (§3.1.2, §3.3). The screen is expressed as a UI-specific HTML-like language. Raw output is post-processed against UI guidance: icons chosen by meaning, typography, and layout guidelines (§3.3). | Evaluation is blind and comparative (§4.3). Independent raters with design background see the description and a shuffled grid of candidates, without knowing which generator produced which. They mark candidates significantly better or significantly worse. | Usefulness is asked separately (§5.2): whether a wireframe is effective for inspiration, whether it relates to the description, and whether the candidates are diverse. These are rated on a 5-point scale. | Refinement is iterative (§6). Intent, then wireframe, then a revised intent, then a revised wireframe. | .

Candidates here may come from a person, an agent or any tool. The method applies to what they produce. | . | blind, shuffled comparison | yes: reviewers are not told a candidate’s author | none | . | better/worse marks and Likert ratings | the structure, not the arithmetic | methodology-adoption refuses scoring and summing. A mean of Likert ratings reads as a measurement of a judgement. Reviewers record per-criterion pass / warn / fail with a reason. | . | mobile only (the paper’s data is Android, §3.1.1) | extended: both web and mobile layouts are required in every usability review (owner, 2026-09-23) | The source’s scope is narrower than our need. We state the extension rather than claim the paper supports it. | . | the reported numbers (77.5%, the user study) | no | They describe the authors’ model and datasets. This is folio-assistant’s existing multi-reviewer primitive. | Disagreement: when entries for one criterion disagree, the candidate set enters Process_Adjudication (processes/process/adjudication.bpmn).
