Accreditation candidate In a health workforce context, the evaluation of educational institutions and programs of study against pre-defined standards required for the delivery of education. The outcome of the process is certification of the suitability of education programmes and the capability of education institutions to deliver initial and/or continuing education. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The handbook cites its reference 69 for this entry. The handbook cites its reference 108 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Institution (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). Candidate definitions (4) . | Active Health Worker (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Occupation (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))The concept of occupation is defined as a “set of jobs whose main tasks and duties are characterized by a high degree of similarity”. A job is defined as “a set of tasks and duties performed, or meant to be performed, by one person, including for an employer or in self-employment”. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). Facility Type candidate Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Gender candidate Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Facility Type (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 5173.content: National Capacity to Monitor Key Metrics for Health Workforce Planning and Global Monitoring Frameworks 4-05 candidate Capacity of national human resources for health information systems to monitor key metrics relevant for national health workforce planning and policy-making and for global monitoring frameworks . NHWA indicator 4 – 05. The definition is the sheet's "Indicator name"; the label is its "Abbreviated name". Candidate definitions (7) . | International Health Regulations (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An international legal instrument that is binding on 196 countries across the globe, including all Member States of WHO. Its aim is to help the international community prevent and respond to acute public health risks that have the potential to cross borders and threaten people worldwide. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 91; PDF page 105). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 109 for this entry. | Subnational Level (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))To be defined according to the specific conditions, governing structures, and constitutional provisions existing in a given country. Disaggregation based on administrative boundaries down to the first or second subnational level is recommended (depending on the structure of administrative boundaries and the size of subnational territories), without overlaps between the administrative units. Examples for subnational administrative units are states, regions, provinces, counties, and districts. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 47 for this entry. | Active Health Worker (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Occupation (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))The concept of occupation is defined as a “set of jobs whose main tasks and duties are characterized by a high degree of similarity”. A job is defined as “a set of tasks and duties performed, or meant to be performed, by one person, including for an employer or in self-employment”. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 58 for this entry. | Status in Employment (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One of two categories of the total employed: (a) wage and salaried workers (employees): workers who hold a job defined as “paid employment”, with explicit (written or oral) or implicit employment contracts that give them a basic remuneration that is not directly dependent upon the revenue of the unit for which they work, and (b) self-employed workers: workers who, working on their own account or with one or more partners or in a cooperative, hold a “self-employment job”, i.e. one in which the remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. Public Health Workforce candidate The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. 5176.title: Q
5176.content: quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. Term page · WHO house terms · https://litlfred.github.io/who-iris/v0/ns/glossary/who-terms/quality-of-the-evidence · source who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng/sections/sec-153-91-what-is-the-quality-of-the-evidence.md .

Remuneration candidate Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 5262.title: Business Process candidate
5262.content: A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3). Also called: business process . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling and referrals (3)." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen.

5274.title: Digital Transformation candidate
5274.content: The process of digitally optimizing and driving systems-level changes by leveraging innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to improve person-centred health systems. Digital technologies are used to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (12,14,15). Also called: digital transformation . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8); identical wording (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which inverts the two sentences: "In the health context, using digital technologies to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (3, 4, 5). The process involves using innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to achieve systems-level changes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

5292.title: Enterprise Architecture candidate
5292.content: The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. Also called: EA, enterprise architecture . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5308.title: Registry candidate
5308.content: A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set. Also called: registry . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Near-identical wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health-care facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores, and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (4) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10, truncated in source PDF): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using predefined canonical minimum data etc." All five are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5312.title: Product Master Data (PMD) candidate
5312.content: Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. Also called: PMD, product master data . PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept.

5317.title: Product candidate
5317.content: A concrete offering, bundling services and data, that is made available to stakeholders. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). 5333.title: Functional Requirements candidate
5333.content: Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). Also called: functional requirements, Functional requirements . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5343.title: Workflow candidate
5343.content: The sequence of activities from one task to another (see section 3.3). Also called: workflow . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and cross-DTH alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-014-33-map-business-processes-and-workflows.md, pp. 35-39): "Workflows are a visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, interactions) performed within a business process (45)." (2) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11, citing DIIG/DAK): "A visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, decision points) in a logical flow illustrating the interactions within the business process (21)." (PHC glossary defines a workflow as the sequence of activities itself; PHC §3.3 and SFP glossary define it as the visual representation of that progression.) All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5351.title: Traceability candidate
5351.content: The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14). Also called: traceability . SC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing the WHO policy paper on traceability of medical products, ref. 14). Internal/substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 4 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-054.md, p. 54, citing GS1): "Traceability is the ability to trace the history, application or location of an object. In a supply chain context, it is the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain." Shared across dth-sc, dth-pc, and dth-sfp; both definitions are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140).

5359.title: Non-Functional Requirements candidate
5359.content: General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8). Also called: Non-functional requirements, nonfunctional requirements . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (without section cross-reference) in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary ('nonfunctional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of how the digital system needs to operate and perform in order to support the tasks that make up the business process." (2) PC handbook glossary ('Non-functional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of the attributes and constraints that the system must have to ensure its quality and performance. These requirements do not specify what the system should do, but rather how the system should perform its functions. (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to support offline mode when network connectivity is not available)" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5381.title: Governance candidate
5381.content: Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure. Also called: governance, governance (health supply chain) . RA §3.4.1 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-029-341-purpose-and-framing.md, p. 64–65). Substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 3 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-045.md, p. 45): "In the context of the health supply chain, governance is the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures and mechanisms to ensure that the supply chain processes and the systems to manage those processes are managed effectively, ethically and in alignment with established objectives and stakeholders’ interests." (RA defines governance as the distribution, exercise, and accountability of decision authority across shared infrastructure; SC defines it as the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures, and mechanisms for supply chain processes and systems.) Also related to `digital-health-governance` in Mehl et al. 2023 (glossary/full-stac.glossary.json, smart-ra#143 P8). Also framed in SFP handbook §2.3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-015-23-establish-governance-and-leadership.md, page-028.md, p. 16) as a structure for coordinating multiple stakeholders, defining clear roles and responsibilities, enhancing transparency, and creating a stable platform for decision-making. Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140, dth-sfp#1 P2).

5387.title: Health Digital Public Infrastructure candidate
5387.content: Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA §1.1.2 body (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-002-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure.md), which adds a second defining sentence: "Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions. These digital resources for health — encompassing both systems and specifications — leverage foundational DPI, are interoperable, reusable, publicly governed and built on open standards." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

5432.title: Interoperability candidate
5432.content: Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively. Also called: interoperability . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and internal alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9), PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "The ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner, through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries. In the health context, this provides timely, safe and seamless portability of information to help ensure good health outcomes (1)." (3) PHC handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, §4.4, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and standards, which should be defined by the EA and independent of a particular solution’s system architecture (22)." (4) PHC handbook §4.4.2 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and data representation standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5436.title: Evaluation candidate
5436.content: The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). Also called: evaluation . SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1).

5445.title: Digital Public Infrastructure candidate
5445.content: A set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. (G20/UNDP) . Also called: DPI . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA §1.1.2 body (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-002-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure.md): "Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) refers to shared digital systems that are secure and interoperable, built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition and respect human rights and fundamental freedoms." (Glossary reads "interoperable, and can be built"; body reads "interoperable, built".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

5449.title: Trade Item candidate
5449.content: Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Also called: trade item, Trade item . Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition.

5465.title: Functions candidate
5465.content: Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." (PHC defines functions as "how features are implemented"; SC defines them as "Business processes within a system that help the system perform".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

5474.title: SMART Guidelines candidate
5474.content: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. Also called: SMART guidelines . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5492.title: Actor (Conformance Model) candidate
5492.content: An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Also called: Actor, actor (conformance model) . Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1).

5523.title: Digital Health candidate
5523.content: The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness. Also called: digital health . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8, citing WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025): "Digital health is the systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG and Global Strategy): "The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (1, 2)." (3) SC handbook Introduction (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-012.md, p. 12, quoting the WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025, same source cited by dth-hrh): "the field of knowledge and practice associated with the development and use of digital technologies to improve health". All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

5527.title: Open Source candidate
5527.content: Open-source software is software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public, enabling anyone to inspect, modify and enhance the code (18). While the source code is open to everyone, this does not mean that implementation of software is necessarily without costs. An open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (19). Also called: Open-source software, open-source software, open source . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary under 'open-source software' (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which adds "within set guidelines": "Software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public so anyone can inspect, modify and enhance the code within set guidelines (8). While the source code is open to everyone, the implementation of the software is not necessarily without costs. Open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (9)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

5544.title: User Story (Requirements) candidate
5544.content: Captures a long list of features from an end-user’s perspective. It describes who the end-user is, with their feature wants or needs, and the reason for that want or need (see section 3.2.3). Also called: User Story, user story . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and platform alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.2.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-013-32-get-to-know-the-users.md, pp. 33-35): "User stories are the start of generating a long list of requirements, in non-technical terms, that will help the technical team to determine the more specific functional requirements of the system." and the template "“As a… [user persona], I want to… [do what I want to be able to do differently using an electronic system], so that… [reason for wanting that functionality].”" (2) Platform glossary `user-story` (folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json), which binds the story to a Role rather than a user persona: "What a reader acting in a Role is trying to do, told as that role: as a <role>, I want <want>, so that <so that>." Also used as the functional requirements template ("As a … / I want … / So that ...") in SFP handbook §4.5 Table 12 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-026-45-gather-requirements.md, page-043.md, p. 31).

5556.title: Health Information System (HIS) candidate
5556.content: A system that integrates data collection, processing, reporting, and use of the information necessary for improving health service effectiveness and efficiency through better management at all levels of health services. Also called: HIS, health information system, Health Information System (HIS), Health Information Systems . DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO 2004 Developing health management information systems; also abbreviated in DIIG page-011.md and HRH handbook who-iris/library/9789240062627-eng/sections/page-006.md). The PHC handbook (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng) has no HIS abbreviation or definition; a wording earlier attributed to it here is not in its text and was removed (smart-ra#200). Referenced in SFP handbook glossary under SMART Guidelines (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) and Ch. 4 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-021-4-determine-the-requirements.md, page-035.md, p. 23). The definition is recorded as a candidate (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 P2).

5569.title: SNOMED GPS candidate
5569.content: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set is a list of basic clinical terms. It is an open and freely accessible subset of SNOMED CT terms that represents the breadth of concepts included in the SNOMED CT International Edition. Also called: SNOMED-GPS, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Global Patient Set . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Expanded in PHC handbook Abbreviations (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-001-abbreviations.md, pp. 7-8) as "SNOMED-GPS" = "Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Global Patient Set" and cited in SFP handbook §4.4 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-025-44-outline-data-requirements.md, page-042.md, p. 30).

5573.content: User acceptance testing (UAT) is conducted to see whether the end-users are satisfied with the end product (24). 5577.title: Point-of-Service Applications candidate
5577.content: Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem. 5581.title: Open Standards candidate
5581.content: Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). Also called: open standards, Open standards . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143).

5671.title: Open Architectures candidate
5671.content: Documentation, using open standards, of reusable enterprise architecture patterns for health systems, describing the diverse digital interconnections of systems and capabilities (including trust networks, services, registries, access controls). Open architectures are designed to be instantiable via open technologies; provide a core infrastructure that fosters an ecosystem of digital health tools; are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes; and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). 5701.title: A
5701.content: Actor (Conformance Model) candidate An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1). Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/actor-conformance-model · source library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md . Adverse Events Following Immunization AEFI candidate Adverse effects following immunisation . Recorded per smart-ra#142 item 4: the PC handbook abbreviations list (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-006.md, p. 6) expands AEFI as "Adverse effects following immunisation", whereas standard WHO immunization terminology expands AEFI as "Adverse events following immunization" (an 'event' is any untoward medical occurrence following immunization and does not presuppose a causal 'effect'). Both expansions are recorded as candidates; neither is silently altered. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/adverse-events-following-immunization · source who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-006.md . Application Component candidate A deployable, modular piece of software that provides a defined set of functionality and holds the data it manages, exposing both through services. The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). 5702.title: B
5702.content: Business Domain candidate A specific focus area or subsystem within a broader business system, characterized by its own essential attributes . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. The draft marks this entry [Under review]. Business Process candidate A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling and referrals (3)." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen. (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG and Global Strategy): "The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (1, 2)." 5705.title: E
5705.content: Enabling Environment candidate Attitudes, actions, policies and practices that stimulate and support effective and efficient functioning of organizations, individuals and programmes. The enabling environment includes legal, regulatory and policy frameworks and political, sociocultural, institutional and economic factors (3). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG), matching DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-139.md, p. 127). Shared DIIG Phase 1 concept across DTHs (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1); recorded as a candidate. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/enabling-environment · source who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md . End-User candidate People who will be using the digital system(s). Identical wording in PHC handbook glossary ('End-user', who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8), PC handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary ('end users', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "People who will be using the digital systems." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1). Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/end-user · source who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md . Enterprise Architecture candidate The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Evaluation candidate The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). Candidate definitions (1) . | Monitoring (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)The continuous process of collecting and analysing data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-141.md, p. 129, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The process of collecting and analysing routinely collected data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results and measure changes in performance over time." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). | . 5706.title: F
5706.content: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources candidate FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by HL7® . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/fast-healthcare-interoperability-resources · source folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md . Features candidate The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording alternatives across the DTH corpus, differing only in domain example and 'a system' vs 'your system' (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “order processing” can be a feature of an order management solution)." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The characteristics of your system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “approval workflow” can be a feature of a product master data management solution)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Candidate definitions (2) . | Functions (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." (PHC defines functions as "how features are implemented"; SC defines them as "Business processes within a system that help the system perform".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1). | Functional Requirements (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | . Full-STAC candidate An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC). Cites Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json) in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#143). Candidate definitions (4) . | Open Standards (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143). | Open Technologies (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Components of configurable and extensible source code, often curated as 'global goods' or 'digital public goods', that perform a distinct function while adhering to open standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Architectures (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "High-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components, such as within a health information exchange."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Content (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open content refers to domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage, such as health guidelines, workflows, core data elements, terminology mappings, and test cases aligned to standards."). Full-STAC candidate Together, open Standards, open Technologies, open Architectures and open Content represent a next-generation ‘full-STAC’ remedy for digital health transformation. Quoted from the abstract. The paper calls it both an approach and a remedy, and names the four as 'four factors'. The DPI-H RA draft (sec-022, footnote 14) cites this paper and presents the four as 'the enabling conditions for REDDHI'. Related terms (1) . | Person-focused Health (Full-STAC: open Standards, Technologies, Architectures and Content)The centre of Figure 1, which the four factors surround. The paper does not define it; the nearest statements are the vision of health data that 'travels with them' and a 'standards-based longitudinal health record that supports the patient over time'. Recorded so the RA can decide whether it matches its own person-centred terms. | . Uses: Open Standards, Open Technologies, Open Architectures, Open Content . Functional Application candidate Functional applications are application components that deliver a specific operational function within a defined domain. Functional Requirements candidate Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9).
