(2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Candidate definitions (3) . | Non-Functional Requirements (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (without section cross-reference) in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary ('nonfunctional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of how the digital system needs to operate and perform in order to support the tasks that make up the business process." (2) PC handbook glossary ('Non-functional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of the attributes and constraints that the system must have to ensure its quality and performance. These requirements do not specify what the system should do, but rather how the system should perform its functions. (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to support offline mode when network connectivity is not available)" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | Features (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS). (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The characteristics of your system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “approval workflow” can be a feature of a product master data management solution)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | Functions (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." 5707.title: G
5707.content: Generic Product candidate In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142). Candidate definitions (2) . | Trade Item (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. | Product Master Data (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . Goal candidate A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired state for an organisation and its stakeholders. The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Depicted in ArchiMate dpi-h-ra 0.3.0-draft.1: Goal (Goal); views: Metamodel, Metamodel vs EIRA, Testing . Governance candidate Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure. RA §3.4.1 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-029-341-purpose-and-framing.md, p. 64–65). Substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 3 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-045.md, p. 45): "In the context of the health supply chain, governance is the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures and mechanisms to ensure that the supply chain processes and the systems to manage those processes are managed effectively, ethically and in alignment with established objectives and stakeholders’ interests." (RA defines governance as the distribution, exercise, and accountability of decision authority across shared infrastructure; SC defines it as the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures, and mechanisms for supply chain processes and systems.) Also related to `digital-health-governance` in Mehl et al. 2023 (glossary/full-stac.glossary.json, smart-ra#143 P8). Also framed in SFP handbook §2.3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-015-23-establish-governance-and-leadership.md, page-028.md, p. 16) as a structure for coordinating multiple stakeholders, defining clear roles and responsibilities, enhancing transparency, and creating a stable platform for decision-making. Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140, dth-sfp#1 P2). Candidate definitions (1) . | Data Governance (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)The structures and standards (policies & legal frameworks) necessary to coordinate and manage the data journey from collection, storage, sharing, analysis to use to produce trusted, secure and quality data for decision making . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. | . Substantive and internal alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9), PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "The ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner, through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries. In the health context, this provides timely, safe and seamless portability of information to help ensure good health outcomes (1)." (3) PHC handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, §4.4, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and standards, which should be defined by the EA and independent of a particular solution’s system architecture (22)." (4) PHC handbook §4.4.2 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and data representation standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. 5711.title: M
5711.content: Monitoring candidate The continuous process of collecting and analysing data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-141.md, p. 129, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The process of collecting and analysing routinely collected data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results and measure changes in performance over time." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). Candidate definitions (1) . | Evaluation (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). | . 5712.title: N
5712.content: Non-Functional Requirements candidate General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (without section cross-reference) in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary ('nonfunctional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of how the digital system needs to operate and perform in order to support the tasks that make up the business process." (2) PC handbook glossary ('Non-functional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of the attributes and constraints that the system must have to ensure its quality and performance. These requirements do not specify what the system should do, but rather how the system should perform its functions. (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to support offline mode when network connectivity is not available)" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Candidate definitions (1) . | Functional Requirements (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | . 5714.content: Person-focused Health could-not-extract The paper uses the phrase but never states what it is. The centre of Figure 1, which the four factors surround. The paper does not define it; the nearest statements are the vision of health data that 'travels with them' and a 'standards-based longitudinal health record that supports the patient over time'. Recorded so the RA can decide whether it matches its own person-centred terms. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Candidate definitions (2) . | Generic Product (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142). | Trade Item (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. | . 5716.title: S
5716.content: SMART Guidelines candidate Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Traceability candidate The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14). SC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing the WHO policy paper on traceability of medical products, ref. 14). Internal/substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 4 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-054.md, p. 54, citing GS1): "Traceability is the ability to trace the history, application or location of an object. In a supply chain context, it is the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain." Shared across dth-sc, dth-pc, and dth-sfp; both definitions are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140). Trade Item candidate Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . All three are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. User Story (Requirements) candidate Captures a long list of features from an end-user’s perspective. It describes who the end-user is, with their feature wants or needs, and the reason for that want or need (see section 3.2.3). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and platform alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.2.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-013-32-get-to-know-the-users.md, pp. 33-35): "User stories are the start of generating a long list of requirements, in non-technical terms, that will help the technical team to determine the more specific functional requirements of the system." and the template "“As a… [user persona], I want to… [do what I want to be able to do differently using an electronic system], so that… [reason for wanting that functionality].”" (2) Platform glossary `user-story` (folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json), which binds the story to a Role rather than a user persona: "What a reader acting in a Role is trying to do, told as that role: as a <role>, I want <want>, so that <so that>." Also used as the functional requirements template ("As a … / I want … / So that ...") in SFP handbook §4.5 Table 12 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-026-45-gather-requirements.md, page-043.md, p. 31). 5732.title: health system strengthening
5732.content: A guideline whose recommendations address how the health system itself is organised and resourced — service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, access to medical products, financing, and leadership and governance — rather than a particular condition or population intervention. 6014.title: Health Supply Chain Information System (HSCIS) candidate
6014.content: A paper-based or software tool that supports the management and/or operations of the health supply chain. Such software tools (e.g., for order management or warehouse management) are also commonly referred to as electronic logistics management information systems. Also called: HSCIS, electronic logistics management information system . Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. smart-ra models the individual systems as ArchiMate application components (sc-workplan.md section 4).

6055.title: Traceability Model candidate
6055.content: One of the three main models for implementing traceability (centralized, semi-centralized, distributed), which differ mostly in how they store traceability data and share them with the relevant health authority and across actors in the supply chain. Assembled from two sentences of Chapter 4 (PDF 54): 'The three main models for implementing traceability are the centralized, semi-centralized and distributed models. They differ mostly in how they store the data and share them with the relevant health authority and across actors in the supply chain.' The handbook does not state it as a definition, and recommends none of the models. Open: not adopted.

6208.title: C
6208.content: Centralized Traceability Model candidate A traceability model that involves a single database or repository for storing all traceability data. The handbook's sentence (PDF 54), with 'A traceability model' put in front so it reads as a definition. Open: not adopted. Candidate definitions (2) . | Traceability (Glossary of the Digital Transformation Handbook for Health Supply Chain Architecture)The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification. Handbook definition, quoted. Open: not adopted, nothing chosen between alternatives. The handbook gives a second definition in Chapter 4 (PDF 54), citing GS1: the ability 'to see the movement of health products across the supply chain'. Both are kept as alternatives; neither is chosen (litlfred/smart-ra#140). dth-pc and dth-sfp link to this term. | Interoperability (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and internal alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9), PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "The ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner, through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries. In the health context, this provides timely, safe and seamless portability of information to help ensure good health outcomes (1)." (3) PHC handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, §4.4, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and standards, which should be defined by the EA and independent of a particular solution’s system architecture (22)." (4) PHC handbook §4.4.2 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and data representation standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." Named in the handbook's abbreviations table, which gives the expansion used as prefLabel. A candidate: no definition has been written. Candidate definitions (1) . | SMART Guidelines (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. Check a review log and its repository's issues for changes candidate, extracted The mechanical check a review-log watcher runs on every poll. Given a drafting sheet's Contributor Feedback values and the folio repository, it reads the repository's open and closed issues (leaving out pull requests, issues labelled no-sheet and, with --author, issues someone else opened) and compares a digest of them and of the cells people set (Title, Selected Sections, Contributor Feedback, Disposition, Ready for agent, Ready for merge, Dispositions confirmed; on a public-comment log also Committee Feedback, TWG (CS), TWG (human) and Change Set (human)) with the last check's. Unchanged: it prints {"status":"unchanged"} and exits 0. Changed: it exits 10 and lists what changed (issue opened, updated or closed; a cell's old and new text), the Contributor Feedback rows to append, one per issue that no row's Issue cell links yet (Title the issue's title, the first Contributor Feedback column @login (#N): first paragraph, Issue the issue's URL; a closed issue's row marked closed), and closedRows, the rows linking a closed issue, which the watcher hides with their text struck through. A read with no Issue column (a public-comment log's Review Change Sets) tracks only issues labelled change-set unless --label says otherwise, and appends no rows: each open issue is reported as an issue-unlinked change instead. It writes no sheet and no issue: the watcher appends the rows and does the agent pass. With --accept it stores the new state for the next poll to compare against. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 346 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 346 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 281 entries say otherwise. 6253.content: hand-back-to-discussion candidate, extracted A sibling agent, spawned during or working beside a live agent-human discussion, hands every card, question, decision, result, blocker or piece of context back to the discussion agent that is talking with the person, and never leaves it only in its own thread. Mapping: fhir unmapped · skos unmapped . harness-projections candidate, extracted Who may write under .claude/, and when. The generated projections of the knowledge graph (.claude/commands/*.md from skill:commands, the assembled agent memory under .claude/agents/ and .claude/agent-memory/) are written by CI, which commits them to the PR branch, and never by an agent. 6271.title: Glossary: Schema fields, A–C
6271.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 522 terms and is 364 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 522 entries say otherwise. CacheSchema.stateInputs candidate, extracted Whether the producer reads MUTABLE STATE the tree does not pin — a branch-kept graph (state:mount: the work plan beans/, qa-reports, fsh-guts…). A producer that reads one must carry that ref's commit in its key, or its entry is never current (#2966: the publish pages read the work plan's finished instances, and a cache keyed on the tree alone served a stale page). REQUIRED, so no node is silent on it: - none: shown to read no state mount (by construction, or by a recorded read set that touches no state path); - keyed: every state ref it reads is in the key (refs); - unkeyed: it reads state the key does not carry — never current; - unmeasured: not shown either way yet — never current. 6276.title: Glossary: Schema fields, M–O
6276.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 232 terms and is 163 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 232 entries say otherwise. 6281.title: Glossary: Schema fields, D–E
6281.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 222 terms and is 156 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 222 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 222 shown . D E

6285.title: Glossary: Schema fields, T–Z
6285.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 525 terms and is 357 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 525 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 525 shown . T U V W

6291.title: Glossary: Schema fields, F–L
6291.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 620 terms and is 428 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 620 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 620 shown . F G H I J K L

6300.title: Glossary: Schema fields, P–R
6300.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 572 terms and is 392 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 572 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 572 shown . P Q R

6305.title: Glossary: Schema fields, S
6305.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 270 terms and is 157 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 270 shown . S

6308.title: Glossary: Schema fields
6308.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2527 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 151 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). Split by first letter. 2963 terms are too many for one page within its budget of 1.0 MB, so they are on 7 pages by the first letter of the label. The ranges are fixed, so a term’s address does not move as terms are added. A label that does not start with a letter is on the first page. | A–C: 522 terms | D–E: 222 terms | F–L: 620 terms | M–O: 232 terms | P–R: 572 terms | S: 270 terms | T–Z: 525 terms | .

6320.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
6320.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 1 | 4655 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 4656 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.

Regional Office for South-East Asia Issued2000-12-31 Typebook PublisherWHO Regional Office for South-East Asia Languageen AbstractInformation, education and communication (IEC) activities can be very effective in bringing about appropriate changes in behaviour, especially among populations with high-risk behaviour. IEC is also important for advocacy to motivate policy and decision-makers to create environments conducive to behavioural change, and to provide much needed services. This guide describes the steps in HIV/AIDS IEC planning and implementation. 6443.doc: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
6443.title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
6443.content: World Health Organization (2023). Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-21 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240085138 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the digital adaptation kit for HIV provides operational, software-neutral requirements to support the incorporation of WHO clinical, public health and data use recommendations into digital systems. Developed within the SMART Guidelines approach, it focuses on the content requirements for person-centred digital tracking and decision support systems used by health workers for HIV services in primary health care settings. The kit is intended to facilitate transparent, consistent and adaptable translation of narrative guidance into digital implementations while supporting interoperability and local customization. The publication organizes HIV-related requirements into eight components: health interventions and associated recommendations; generic personas; illustrative user scenarios; business processes and workflows; core data elements; decision support and scheduling logic; indicators and performance metrics; and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. It covers processes including HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infant diagnosis, diagnostics, client follow-up, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use, with complementary operational resources provided in web annexes. 6449.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
6449.title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
6449.content: World Health Organization (2025). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2025-4-10 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization DOIhttps://doi.org/10.2471/B09341 Languageen AbstractThis web annex to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 3: Diagnosis, compiles the evidence synthesis and analyses used to inform WHO recommendations on diagnostic technologies for tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis. The publication presents systematic reviews, meta-analyses, qualitative evidence syntheses and economic evaluations examining the diagnostic accuracy, safety, cost–effectiveness and implementation considerations of multiple diagnostic approaches, including low- and moderate-complexity nucleic acid amplification tests, targeted next-generation sequencing technologies and Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests. The annex describes the methods applied to identify, assess and synthesize evidence across diverse populations and settings, including adults, adolescents, children and people living with HIV. It addresses the detection of pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis, rifampicin resistance and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis using respiratory and non-respiratory specimens. The document also examines stakeholder and user perspectives, operational feasibility and factors influencing implementation. Developed in accordance with WHO guideline development standards, the annex provides the technical evidence base underpinning updates to WHO policy guidance on tuberculosis diagnosis and drug-resistance testing. 6471.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-12-31 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240099456 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis publication presents the World Health Organization’s digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations, developed within the SMART Guidelines framework to support the implementation of WHO immunization recommendations in digital systems. The document provides operational and software-neutral specifications intended to facilitate the translation of immunization guidance into interoperable digital health applications, particularly person-centred point-of-service systems and electronic immunization registries. It outlines the role of digital adaptation kits in strengthening digital health systems by improving the consistency, transparency and standardization of health content, workflows, data structures and decision-support logic used in immunization programmes. The publication also situates the DAK within broader digital health strategies and interoperability standards. The document describes eight core components of the immunization DAK, including health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and functional requirements. It incorporates WHO guidance related to routine immunization, electronic immunization registries and digital health interventions, while emphasizing adaptability to country-specific policies and implementation contexts. Additional sections address interoperability, data standards, workflow optimization and the use of digital systems to support longitudinal tracking, reporting, decision support and communication within immunization services. The publication is intended for immunization programme managers, digital health teams, software developers and implementers involved in designing and deploying digital immunization systems. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240031593 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThese consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and programme monitoring across the continuum of HIV care. Updating the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, this edition integrates guidance issued between 2016 and 2021 and reflects major advances in clinical practice, diagnostics and service delivery. Developed using the GRADE approach and informed by expert consultation and country experience, the guidelines aim to support countries in implementing high-quality, person-centred HIV services while advancing universal health coverage and progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The publication addresses HIV testing strategies, prevention interventions, antiretroviral therapy, management of advanced HIV disease, care for common coinfections and comorbidities, differentiated service delivery, procurement, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It incorporates updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, dolutegravir-based treatment, rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation, viral load monitoring and community-based models of care. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, policy-makers and health-care providers, the guidelines also serve as a resource for technical partners, community organizations and people living with HIV to support the implementation of effective, equitable and people-centred HIV programmes. 6481.content: Organisation mondiale de la Santé (2022). Lignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de santé. Organisation mondiale de la Santé. TitleLignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de santé AuthorsOrganisation mondiale de la Santé Issued2022-5-19 Typebook PublisherOrganisation mondiale de la Santé ISBN9789240046641 (version électronique) Languagefr AbstractCes lignes directrices de l’OMS présentent des recommandations fondées sur des données probantes concernant l’utilisation des interventions numériques pour renforcer les systèmes de santé et soutenir les progrès vers la couverture sanitaire universelle (CSU). Élaborées en réponse à l’adoption croissante des technologies numériques et à la résolution sur la santé numérique approuvée par l’Assemblée mondiale de la Santé en 2018, elles répondent à la nécessité d’évaluer rigoureusement les interventions de santé numérique afin que les investissements reposent sur des données probantes relatives à leurs avantages, leurs inconvénients, leur acceptabilité, leur faisabilité, leurs implications en matière de ressources et les considérations d’équité. Les lignes directrices soulignent que les technologies numériques doivent compléter, et non remplacer, les composantes fondamentales de systèmes de santé performants. Les recommandations portent sur un ensemble prioritaire d’interventions de santé numérique, principalement accessibles au moyen d’appareils mobiles, notamment la notification des naissances et des décès, la notification des stocks et la gestion des produits de base, la télémédecine entre client et prestataire ainsi qu’entre prestataires, la communication ciblée avec les clients, le suivi numérique de l’état de santé et des services reçus, les outils d’aide à la décision destinés aux professionnels de santé et l’apprentissage numérique. Les lignes directrices présentent également des considérations relatives à la mise en œuvre, recensent les principales lacunes en matière de recherche et visent à aider les ministères de la santé, les responsables des politiques de santé, les professionnels de santé, les partenaires du développement et les autres parties prenantes à prendre des décisions éclairées concernant l’adoption, le déploiement à grande échelle et l’institutionnalisation des interventions de santé numérique efficaces. 6485.doc: WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention
6485.title: WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention
6485.content: World Health Organization (2013). WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention. World Health Organization. TitleWHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2013-11-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241548694 Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies to prevent cervical cancer by detecting and treating precancerous cervical lesions. The screen-and-treat approach bases treatment decisions on screening results, allowing treatment soon or ideally immediately after a positive test, rather than requiring histological confirmation. The guidelines compare strategies using human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and cytology, linked to treatment with cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). They are intended primarily to support policy-makers, programme managers and other health professionals in selecting appropriate cervical cancer prevention strategies according to available resources and existing programmes. Nine recommendations are provided. HPV-based screening is generally preferred where feasible, while VIA is suggested where HPV testing is not feasible; cold knife conization is not recommended as part of a screen-and-treat strategy. Recommendations apply to all women, with specific guidance for women living with HIV. Decision-making and implementation flowcharts support adaptation of the recommended strategies to country and regional contexts. 6491.title: [Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti]
6491.content: Ahmed, A.A.; Latoundji, S. (2007). [Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti]. Title[Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti] AuthorsAhmed, A.A.; Latoundji, S. Issued2007-12-31 Typedocument Languagefr AbstractA cross-sectional survey was conducted among 112 HIV positive patients who had received antiretroviral therapy for > 3 months to assess the efficacy of treatment [viral load < 400 copies/mL]. The median age at enrolment was 36 years, 90% of patients were at the AIDS stage and median CD4 rate was 118/mm[3]. Patients received a combined treatment of 2 NRTI +1 NNRTI [51%], 3 NRTI [45%] and 2 NRTI+1 PI [4%]. Virological efficacy was seen in 74% of the patients, irrespective of the prescribed protocol and the initial clinical and immunological profile. Mean improvements measured were 20% on the Karnofsky index [KI], 2.1 kg/m[2] in body mass index and 82 cells/mm[3] in CD4. The prevalence of side effects was 84%. The predictors for treatment success were quality of care and KI > 70% Sources . | iris.who.int/handle/10665/117378 (canonical) | repository record (repository) | . TitleNational health workforce accounts: a handbook AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-11-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240081291 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Handbook, second edition, provides the conceptual framework, standards, methods and indicators that support the systematic collection, analysis and use of health workforce data for evidence-informed policy-making and planning. Developed by the World Health Organization, the handbook supports implementation of the National Health Workforce Accounts as a country-led system to strengthen human resources for health information systems, improve data quality and availability, and monitor progress towards universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other global health objectives. It describes the rationale, principles and applications of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and outlines a modular approach to health workforce monitoring. The handbook presents guidance on implementation and reporting methods and defines a set of standardized indicators organized into four modules covering workforce stock and flows, education, finance and expenditures, and working conditions, governance and leadership. It explains indicator metadata, calculation methods, disaggregation requirements and reporting standards, and illustrates how NHWA data can be used to support workforce planning, policy development, retention strategies, equity analyses and monitoring of health workforce trends. The revised edition incorporates updated indicators, occupational classifications, tools and guidance to address evolving health workforce priorities and emerging global health challenges. 6503.content: World Health Organization (2023). Pandemic influenza preparedness framework: annual progress report, 1 January – 31 December 2022. World Health Organization. TitlePandemic influenza preparedness framework: annual progress report, 1 January – 31 December 2022 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-8-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240076907 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework: annual progress report, 1 January–31 December 2022 presents technical and financial progress in implementing the PIP Framework, which aims to strengthen the sharing of influenza viruses with human pandemic potential and improve developing countries’ access to pandemic vaccines and other response supplies. The report assesses progress under the High-Level Implementation Plan II (2018–2023), including activities financed through the industry-funded Partnership Contribution mechanism. The report documents achievements and challenges in influenza laboratory capacity and surveillance, virus sharing, disease burden estimation, regulatory preparedness, risk communication and community engagement, deployment planning, and national pandemic preparedness. In 2022, 91% of Partnership Contribution recipient countries reported influenza data to FluNet, 48 countries had implemented regulatory approaches for pandemic influenza products, and 37 countries had developed or updated pandemic preparedness plans. It also presents progress in securing pandemic response products through benefit-sharing agreements, alongside financial allocations, expenditures and implementation milestones. 6513.doc: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
6513.title: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
6513.content: World Health Organization (2016). The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance. World Health Organization. TitleThe use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-8-8 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241511186 Languageen AbstractTuberculosis remains a major global public health challenge, and the WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes the need for early diagnosis and universal drug-susceptibility testing. This policy guidance presents evidence-based recommendations on the use of the commercial loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis. Developed following a systematic review of studies conducted since 2012 and assessment using the GRADE approach, the document evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy, as an add-on test after negative smear microscopy, and in comparison with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, while also assessing the frequency of indeterminate or invalid results. Based on the available evidence, WHO recommends that TB-LAMP may be used as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in adults with signs and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis and as a follow-on test when further investigation of smear-negative specimens is required. The guidance emphasizes that these conditional recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence, apply to sputum specimens from patients with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, and should not replace rapid molecular tests capable of detecting rifampicin resistance. It also highlights the limited evidence for use in people living with HIV, notes the extrapolation of recommendations to children, and provides implementation considerations and priorities for future research. 6515.content: Lundgren, Jens D; Raben, Dorthe; Ерамова, Ирина; et al. (2014). Лечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом в Беларуси: отчет оценочной миссии: январь 2014 г.. Всемирная организация здравоохранения. Европейское региональное бюро. TitleЛечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом в Беларуси: отчет оценочной миссии: январь 2014 г. AuthorsLundgren, Jens D; Raben, Dorthe; Ерамова, Ирина; Ильенкова, Вера Issued2014-12-31 Typereport PublisherВсемирная организация здравоохранения. Европейское региональное бюро Languageru AbstractОценка лечения и ухода в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом выполнена с учетом стратегии или концепции ВОЗ/ЮНЭЙДС «Лечение 2.0», где указаны пять приоритетных областей: оптимизация лекарственных схем, обеспечение доступа к диагностике в местах оказания помощи, снижение стоимости, адаптация систем оказания услуг и мобилизация сообществ или гражданского общества. Для оценки использованы результаты анализа существующих документов и отчетов и страновой миссии, которая состоялась 11-14 ноября 2013 года в гор. Минске и Солигорске, Беларусь. Особое внимание было уделено практике тестирования на ВИЧ, поскольку именно здесь начинается лечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ, а также уязвимым группам и обеспечению доступа к лечению и уходу. Кроме того, была проанализирована устойчивость программ в свете используемых в настоящее время и будущих международных и национальных схем финансирования. 6519.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-11-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240093362 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform primary health care through the development and implementation of person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSS). It addresses the transition from paper-based and fragmented digital systems towards integrated, interoperable digital solutions that support service delivery, continuity of care, data use and health system strengthening. Grounded in WHO recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening and aligned with the SMART Guidelines framework, the publication outlines approaches for translating clinical and public health guidance into digital systems while maintaining fidelity to normative standards. The publication presents a stepwise methodology covering assessment of digital readiness, identification of user requirements, workflow and business process mapping, system design and adaptation, software selection, testing, deployment and scale-up. It emphasizes person-centred care, interoperability, longitudinal health records, decision support and the use of standards-based digital architectures. Through practical tools, worksheets and implementation guidance, the publication supports policy-makers, programme managers, digital health practitioners and software developers in designing and optimizing digital systems that improve service quality, strengthen accountability and enable more effective, integrated and responsive primary health care services. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations: optimizing health worker roles to improve access to key maternal and newborn health interventions through task shifting AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2012-12-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241504843 Languageen AbstractThis WHO guidance provides evidence-based recommendations on optimizing health worker roles through task shifting to improve universal access to key maternal and newborn health interventions. Developed in response to health workforce shortages and inequities in access to care, it assesses whether specific interventions can be delivered safely and effectively by different health worker cadres, including lay health workers, auxiliary nurses and nurse midwives, nurses, midwives, associate clinicians, advanced level associate clinicians and non-specialist doctors. The guidance presents 119 recommendations, ranging from practices recommended for implementation to those requiring targeted monitoring and evaluation, rigorous research, or not recommended. It emphasizes that task shifting should complement efforts to increase skilled care and should aim to expand access while maintaining safety. Implementation should consider health-system capacity and local sociocultural, political and financial conditions, with recommendations adapted through national dialogue and considered as packages of interventions rather than in isolation. 6543.title: WHO implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection: module 13: integrating STI services
6543.content: World Health Organization (2022). WHO implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection: module 13: integrating STI services. World Health Organization. TitleWHO implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection: module 13: integrating STI services AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-9-5 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240057425 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis module of the WHO Implementation Tool for Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV Infection provides operational guidance on integrating sexually transmitted infection (STI) services into HIV PrEP programmes. Developed for programme managers, decision-makers, facility managers and health-care workers, it compiles existing WHO recommendations and evidence to support the planning, implementation and scale-up of integrated, people-centred sexual health services. The document outlines the epidemiology and burden of STIs, particularly among populations who may benefit from or use PrEP, and highlights the public health rationale for strengthening STI prevention, testing, treatment and follow-up within PrEP delivery platforms. The module describes practical approaches to integrating STI services across different service delivery models, including considerations related to workforce capacity, task sharing, monitoring, financing and demand generation. It presents guidance on counselling, health promotion, screening, diagnostic testing, partner services, clinical management, referral pathways and prevention measures such as condom provision and vaccination. Emphasizing differentiated service delivery and human rights principles, the publication aims to improve access to comprehensive sexual health care, enhance service quality and support efforts to reduce the burden of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections through coordinated and efficient health-system responses. 6545.doc: Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019
6545.title: Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019
6545.content: World Health Organization (2020). Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-11-3 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241550581 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations to support countries in delivering high-quality, person-centred HIV testing services (HTS) across diverse populations and settings. Updating and consolidating previous WHO guidance issued in 2015 and 2016, it incorporates new evidence on HIV self-testing, social network-based HIV testing approaches, western blotting, and strategic service delivery to strengthen progress towards global HIV targets. Developed using the GRADE methodology and informed by systematic reviews, modelling studies and expert consultation, the guideline aims to improve the effectiveness, efficiency and quality of HIV testing while promoting timely linkage to prevention, treatment and care. The publication addresses the full continuum of HIV testing services, including demand creation, pre- and post-test services, facility- and community-based testing, implementation considerations for priority populations, strategic planning, diagnostic testing strategies, quality assurance and programme monitoring. It provides updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, provider-assisted referral, social network-based approaches and the use of dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests, while emphasizing the WHO 5Cs of HIV testing services: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection. Intended for policy-makers, national programme managers, health-care providers and implementing partners, the guideline supports the expansion of equitable, evidence-informed HIV testing services to improve diagnosis and strengthen national HIV responses.
