6841.title: WHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee
6841.content: World Health Organization (2017). WHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-10-17 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis publication compiles WHO recommendations on maternal health that have been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee into a single, accessible reference for WHO staff, policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals. It brings together current WHO guidance covering the continuum of maternal care during pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period, with the dual purpose of facilitating access to recommendations and helping identify areas where further guideline updates are needed. The document indicates newly issued and updated recommendations since 2013 and provides, for each recommendation, its strength, the quality of supporting evidence and the corresponding source guideline. The compilation addresses interventions to promote, prevent and protect maternal and perinatal health, including antenatal care, prevention and management of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, peripartum infections, labour and childbirth, postpartum haemorrhage, postnatal care and health promotion, as well as the management of maternal conditions such as HIV infection, malaria and tuberculosis. Developed according to WHO’s guideline development process using the GRADE approach and structured evidence-to-decision frameworks, it presents evidence-informed recommendations intended to support consistent policy development, clinical practice and programme implementation across diverse health-care settings. 6859.doc: Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud
6859.title: Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud
6859.content: Organización Mundial de la Salud (2022). Directriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud. Organización Mundial de la Salud. TitleDirectriz de la OMS: recomendaciones sobre intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud AuthorsOrganización Mundial de la Salud Issued2022-5-19 Typebook PublisherOrganización Mundial de la Salud ISBN9789240046993 (versión electrónica) Languagees AbstractEste documento presenta las recomendaciones de la OMS, basadas en la evidencia, sobre el uso de intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud y apoyar el avance hacia la cobertura sanitaria universal (CSU). Elaborada en respuesta a la creciente adopción de las tecnologías digitales y a la resolución sobre salud digital aprobada por la Asamblea Mundial de la Salud en 2018, la directriz aborda la necesidad de evaluar rigurosamente las intervenciones de salud digital para garantizar que las inversiones se fundamenten en evidencia sobre sus beneficios, riesgos, aceptabilidad, factibilidad, implicaciones en materia de recursos y consideraciones de equidad. Asimismo, subraya que las tecnologías digitales deben complementar, y no sustituir, los componentes fundamentales de unos sistemas de salud sólidos y eficaces. Las recomendaciones se centran en un conjunto priorizado de intervenciones de salud digital accesibles, como mínimo, mediante dispositivos móviles, entre ellas la notificación de nacimientos y defunciones, la notificación de existencias y la gestión de suministros, la telemedicina entre pacientes y profesionales y entre profesionales, la comunicación dirigida a los pacientes, el seguimiento digital del estado de salud y de los servicios recibidos, las herramientas de apoyo a la toma de decisiones para el personal sanitario y el aprendizaje digital para los trabajadores de la salud. La directriz también presenta consideraciones para la implementación, identifica las principales lagunas de investigación y proporciona orientación a los ministerios de salud, los responsables de salud pública, los asociados para el desarrollo y otras partes interesadas para adoptar, ampliar e institucionalizar intervenciones de salud digital eficaces sobre la base de la mejor evidencia disponible. 6863.title: Global hepatitis report 2026
6863.content: World Health Organization (2026). Global hepatitis report 2026. World Health Organization. TitleGlobal hepatitis report 2026 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-4-24 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240122383 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis report provides a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of viral hepatitis and progress towards the goal of eliminating hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Drawing on data reported by Member States and modelled estimates, it analyses trends in incidence, prevalence and mortality associated with hepatitis B and C, covering the period from 2015 to 2024 based on the latest available data. It also situates these trends within the context of global commitments, strategies and targets. The publication reviews the coverage and impact of key interventions for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including vaccination, infection prevention and control, harm reduction and access to antiviral therapies. It identifies persistent gaps in testing and treatment, marked regional disparities, and the need for accelerated scale-up of services, particularly in high-burden settings. The report concludes that progress towards the 2030 elimination targets remains off track despite the availability of effective interventions. Intended for policymakers, programme managers and public health stakeholders, it serves as an analytical and strategic resource to guide national and global responses to viral hepatitis. 6871.doc: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
6871.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
6871.content: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-11-7 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241549912 Languageen AbstractThis guideline presents the World Health Organization’s evidence-based recommendations on routine antenatal care to support a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls. It aims to provide a comprehensive, consolidated framework for antenatal care that complements existing WHO guidance on the management of specific pregnancy-related complications. The recommendations promote a person-centred, rights-based approach that extends beyond the prevention of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality to enhance women’s physical, psychological and sociocultural well-being, support healthy pregnancies, and improve the quality and utilization of antenatal care. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals, the guideline informs the development of national policies, clinical protocols and service delivery models. Developed according to the WHO guideline development process, the document draws on systematic reviews and applies the GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches together with the DECIDE evidence-to-decision framework. It contains 49 recommendations covering nutritional interventions, maternal and fetal assessment, preventive measures, management of common physiological symptoms, and health system interventions to improve antenatal care utilization and quality. The guideline also introduces the 2016 WHO antenatal care model, recommending a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, and emphasizes implementation, dissemination and periodic updating as new evidence becomes available. 6873.content: World Health Organization. Control Programme on AIDS (1986). Guidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV III. World Health Organization. TitleGuidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV III AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Control Programme on AIDS Issued1986-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for preventing and controlling infection with LAV/HTLV-III, the retrovirus recognized at the time as the etiological agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Developed as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, they are intended primarily for public health authorities and health professionals, who are responsible for adapting the guidance to different populations and settings. The document summarizes available knowledge on transmission, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, surveillance, notification and confidentiality, and case definitions for AIDS. The guidelines emphasize routine precautions to prevent exposure to blood and other potentially infectious body fluids, particularly among health care workers, laboratory personnel and providers of home and emergency care. They address prevention and management of needlestick, parenteral and mucous-membrane exposures, safe handling of specimens and contaminated equipment, and precautions for non-health-care workers. Guidance is also provided on disinfection, sterilization, and the safe processing of reusable needles, syringes and other instruments. 6879.doc: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
6879.title: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
6879.content: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia (2006). Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006. WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. TitleEnumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006 AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia Issued2006-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWHO Regional Office for South-East Asia Languageen AbstractDescription: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes is essential for initiation of antiretroviral therapy for a person with HIV as well as for monitoring the response to treatment. The techniques for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes are evolving. The flow cytometry continues to be the gold standard of CD4 T lymphocytes enumeration in spite of the fact that the technology is expensive both in terms of initial investment in sophisticated equipment and running cost. The newer techniques may be economical to procure and maintain. The latter are particularly intended for countries with limited resources. WHO conducted a workshop to orient the nationals about these technologies and integration of a quality system into routine testing, at Siriraj Hospital Bangkok. The report describes the status of CD4 testing in these countries. While Indonesia, India and Thailand have developed a good infrastructure for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka have made a beginning in this direction. The workshop focussed on principles of various techniques and imparted a hands-on training for performing the same. The issues regarding selection of technology, procurement of equipment and their maintenance; ensuring continuous supply and economical use of reagents and biosafety in laboratory were discussed and have been presented in this Report. 7327.doc: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many …
7327.title: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many …
7327.content: There are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many parts of Africa. HSV2 incidence data are also scarce [Kamali et al., 1999; McFarland et al., 1999; Hayes et al., 2001]. Prevalence and incidence data are necessary: i) to estimate population attributable fractions (PAFs) for HIV; ii) as background data to inform future intervention studies, such as HSV2 4. EPIDEMIOLOGY AND NATURAL HISTORY OF HSV2 treatment and vaccine trials; iii) to evaluate the need for changes in syndromic management of GUD due to presence of genital herpes; and iv) to evaluate the need for regular HSV2 seroprevalence surveys. Issued2001 Typedocument As printedThere are currently few data on HSV2 prevalence from many parts of the world, including Asia, South America and many parts of Africa. HSV2 incidence data are also scarce [Kamali et al., 1999; McFarland et al., 1999; Hayes et al., 2001]. Prevalence and incidence data are necessary: i) to estimate population attributable fractions (PAFs) for HIV; ii) as background data to inform future intervention studies, such as HSV2 4. EPIDEMIOLOGY AND NATURAL HISTORY OF HSV2 treatment and vaccine trials; iii) to evaluate the need for changes in syndromic management of GUD due to presence of genital herpes; and iv) to evaluate the need for regular HSV2 seroprevalence surveys. 7671.doc: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior …
7671.title: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior …
7671.content: S-12 (Sassani et al., 1991) 3.2 Immune responses to revaccination Studies have examined presence of antibodies prior to and following the second dose of mumps vaccine. In a prospective study, <1% of subjects were seronegative before a second dose of mumps vaccine and, following the second dose, IgM was detectable in only 2% of individuals, suggesting that most vaccine recipients had mounted a secondary immune response to revaccination (LeBaron et al., 2009). Although up to 30% of individuals were reported to be seronegative prior to revaccination in other studies, 75% to 97% seroconverted following the second dose of mumps vaccine. 9857.content: Punctuation _(no text on this page)_4. Italics Italic type in printed publications is indicated in typescript by under-lining. 15783.title: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
15783.content: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen the Greek letter representing its type, for example IFN-a for alpha interferons. Non-allelic variants can be indicated by an arabic number or capital letter (sometimes subscripted) attached to the Greek letter. The prefixes “Hu” and “Mu” may be used to represent “human” and “murine” respectively. For example: MulFN-y HulFN-B — HulFN-c4. Interferon nomenclature. Journal of immunology, 1980, 125:2353. 16503.title: Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part o…
16503.content: Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part of the name to which it refers (e.g. sodium ('4C]formate); appropriate arabic numerals and prefixes are added as necessary (e.g. L-[2-C]leucine). For simple molecules, chemical formulae may be used (e.g. 4#CO,). Square brackets should not be used when the isotopic symbol is attached to a word that is not a chemical name (e.g. “!*C-labelled”). Terms such as “'![-labelled albumin” should not be contracted to [3!T]albumin since native albumin does not contain iodine. 16887.title: Oncogenes Oncogenes are usually designated by three-letter italic terms, often taken from the names of the viruses wi…
16887.content: Oncogenes Oncogenes are usually designated by three-letter italic terms, often taken from the names of the viruses with which the genes are WHO Editorial Style Manual associated. A roman prefix may be added: “v-” for viral, “N-” for nuclear and “c-” for the gene’s cellular counterpart (proto-oncogene). Other prefixes and various suffixes are common. For example: Ha-ras-1 N-ras v-erb B yes c-abl fes/fps. 17953.doc: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
17953.title: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen…
17953.content: WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen the Greek letter representing its type, for example IFN-a for alpha interferons. Non-allelic variants can be indicated by an arabic number or capital letter (sometimes subscripted) attached to the Greek letter. The prefixes “Hu” and “Mu” may be used to represent “human” and “murine” respectively. For example: MulFN-y HulFN-B — HulFN-c4. Interferon nomenclature. Journal of immunology, 1980, 125:2353. 18137.doc: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to…
18137.title: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to…
18137.content: Genital herpes can also be due to HSV1 infection, and a study in Scotland found that 40% of genital herpes was due to HSV1 in 1991 [Ross et al., 1993]. Both HSV1 and HSV2 are able to infect and reactivate in the same anatomic area, although the natural history of these infections is markedly different, with HSV2 recurring more frequently than HSV1, so most clinical reactivations are likely to be due to HSV2 [Sucato et al., 1998]. In developing countries, the proportion of genital herpes caused by HSV1 is unknown, although assumed to be low. 18753.content: Genetics Genes and chromosomes The International Committee on Standardizing Human Gene No-menclature has developed a system knownas the International System. for Human Gene Nomenclature, but this is not universally accepted. Human genes are generally denoted by italicized symbols composed of capital letters, sometimes with the addition of an arabic numeral (e.g. CF, G6PD). Lower-case letters are commonly still used in blood-group symbols (e.g. Fy, Rh). Phenotype symbols are set in roman type (e.g. ADA 1). 19075.title: CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. Methodological quality Studies evaluating Xpert Ultra on spu…
19075.content: CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. Methodological quality Studies evaluating Xpert Ultra on sputum specimens (15 studies) In the patient selection domain, for MRS, we judged the risk of bias as low for most studies (13/15, 86.7%) and high for two studies (2/15, 13.3%) because in one study participants with definitive tuberculosis were excluded (Liu 2021) and in the other, the sampling method was retrospective and by convenience (Enimil 2022). Regarding applicability, we judged low concern for most studies (12/15, 80%). We judged high concern for two studies (2/15, 13.3%) because participants were enrolled exclusively as inpatients in tertiary care centers. We judged unclear concern for one study (1/15, 6.7%) because the setting was undefined. Issued2022 Typedocument As printedCSF = cerebrospinal fluid; NPA= nasopharyngeal aspirate. 20403.content: Nahmias et al, 1990 1 (f) females; (m) males 2 Age-weighted sample: younger age-groups were over-represented HSV2 AS A MARKER FOR SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR As HSV2 is more readily transmitted sexually than HIV, HSV2 serology may be a useful marker for changes in sexual behaviour in HIV intervention studies. However, the persistent nature of the infection implies that seroprevalence may not be a sensitive marker of behaviour change, although it will be more discriminating at the lower prevalences seen in younger age groups [Obasi et al., 1999]. HSV2 seroincidence would be a preferable marker of behaviour change, especially in countries in sub-Saharan Africa where there is high incidence among young people. 21153.content: Bootstrap terms . | المصطلح | تسميات بديلة | التعريف | . | العقدة | — | ملف، أو جزء من ملف يمكن الوصول إليه بجزء IRI، يُسمّى بمعرّف IRI. | . | المرجع | — | تسمية عقدةٍ لعقدة أخرى بواسطة معرّف IRI الخاص بها. | . | مخطط العقدة | — | مخطط يمكن التحقق من عقدة وفقه: JSON Schema، أو مخطط خارجي منشور مثل مخطط BPMN. | . | نوع العقدة | — | اسم مقترن بمخطط عقدة. | . | النوع الفرعي | — | نوع عقدة يتطلّب مخططها كل ما يتطلّبه مخطط نوع عقدة آخر، فكل عقدة تستوفيه تستوفي الآخر أيضاً. | . | مثيل العقدة | — | عقدة تسمّي نوع عقدتها في $schema أو في الترويسة، وتستوفي مخطط العقدة لذلك النوع. | . | نوع الرسم البياني | — | مجموعة مسمّاة من أنواع العقد. | . | الإعلان | — | مستند JSON باسم <name>.json يحدّد اسماً ويسرد مُدخلات الأدلة ومُدخلات الملفات. | . | الامتداد | — | حقل في الإعلان، أو في أحد مُدخلاته، غير معرَّف هنا. القارئ الذي لا يتعرّف على الحقل يتجاهله، ويبقى باقي الإعلان على معناه. | . | الرسم البياني الفرعي | — | مُدخل دليل في الإعلان: معرّف ودليل وأنواع الرسوم البيانية التي تنتمي إليها أنواع مثيلات العقدة فيه. | . | الأصل | — | مُدخل ملف في الإعلان: ملف واحد عن المستودع نفسه، يبيّن حقلُه role الغرضَ منه. | . | الرسم البياني المعرفي | — | مخططات العقد ومثيلات العقد والأصول التي يسردها إعلان واحد، بحسب نسخة واحدة من المستودع. وعند نشرها بصيغة JSON-LD، تشكّل عبارات مثيلات العقدة في كل رسم بياني فرعي رسماً بيانياً مسمّى واحداً. | . | التبعية | — | مُدخل needs في الإعلان يسمّي رسماً بيانياً معرفياً آخر. يجوز أن تشير المراجع من مثيلات العقدة في هذا الرسم إلى الرسم المسمّى، ولا يجوز العكس أبداً. | . | المحتوى | — | مثيلات عقدة تصف موضوع الرسم البياني المعرفي، كالسجلات والمستندات والفهارس ومصطلحاتها، لا طريقة العمل به. | . | المهمة | — | وحدة عمل، تُوصَف بما تحتاجه لتبدأ وبما تُنتجه. | . | الفاعل | — | شخص أو وكيل أو برنامج قادر على تنفيذ المهام. | . | المهارة | — | A Node Instance stating a responsibility an Actor carries out to complete a Task: as natural-language instructions to follow, as a contract to be tested against, or both. (غير مترجَم) | . | الدور | — | مثيل عقدة يسمّي دوراً يتولّاه الفاعل لتنفيذ المهام، ويسرد المهارات التي يحتاجها ذلك الدور. | . | عقدة العملية | — | عقدة تدفق BPMN: نشاط (مهمة أو نشاط استدعاء) أو بوابة أو حدث. | . | تدفق التسلسل | — | وصلة موجّهة في عملية BPMN من عقدة عملية إلى التي تليها. | . | العملية | — | مثيل عقدة يحوي عملية BPMN تنسّق المهام: تقع عُقد العملية فيها، المرتبطة بتدفقات التسلسل، في مسارات يسمّي كلٌّ منها دوراً. | . | الإطار | — | رسم بياني معرفي تحوي رسومه البيانية الفرعية مهارات أو أدواراً أو عمليات: ما يستخدمه الفاعل للعمل مع رسم بياني معرفي، بما في ذلك هذا الرسم نفسه. | . سائر المصطلحات المحرَّرة، أبجدياً . 21182.title: indicator-extraction
21182.content: Skill indicator-extraction: Extract the indicators an L1 source prints (indicator reference or metadata sheets: name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, data sources) as L1 indicator nodes with every printed field, then draft one L2 program indicator per indicator, derived from its L1 node. Read before adding a WHO handbook’s or guideline’s indicators to a DAK or a DTH, and whenever an L2 indicator has to trace to its source. Part of L1 → L2 extraction for every DAK and DTH, beside recommendation-extraction. Named by: DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: indicator-extraction · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Follows dak-l1-library, which ingests the source. Sibling of recommendation-extraction: that one takes a source’s recommendations, this one its indicators. It is a step of L1 → L2 extraction for a DAK or DTH, bound to Task_Indicators in l2-dak-authoring and Call_Data in dth-authoring.

21183.title: Two layers, kept apart
21183.content: | layer | what | kind / model | written by | . | L1 | the indicator as the source prints it, verbatim | indicator block (folio type smart-base:Indicator; KG L1 indicator, kg/src/l1.ts) | scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py → candidates.json → gen-library-jsonld | . | L2 | the DAK’s or DTH’s own operational measure, a draft that points back | program-indicator (sgkg-l2), logical model ProgramIndicator | scripts/l2-program-indicators.py | . sgkg-l2 keeps them apart: merging them would merge a WHO definition with a country’s implementation of it. The L2 record is a draft with derivedFrom its L1 node, and the L2 author adopts, edits or drops it.

21184.title: Rules
21184.content: . | Ids come from the source. number / indicatorId is the printed indicator number (“1-01”, “4-01.3”). A sheet whose header prints none is reported and skipped, never numbered by an agent. The L2 id is <prefix>.<number> (“NHWA.1-01”); the prefix only namespaces it. | Verbatim. Every field is the printed text: lines joined, letter-spacing artefacts closed up, nothing reworded. A printed list (glossary terms, data sources) is one string joined with “; “. | Every printed field, not only name, numerator and denominator. The L1 node’s meta holds indicatorId, module, abbreviatedName, name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, glossary, reportingFrequency, reportingFrameworks, dataSources, furtherInformation and dimension where printed; a sub-indicator adds parentIndicator and guidingQuestions. These are the keys the structured-block cards read. | No gap is filled. ProgramIndicator makes definition, numerator, denominator and disaggregation 1..1. Where the source prints none (a composite or self-assessed indicator), the L2 draft lists it in gaps and the L2 author decides. Nothing is copied from another source to fill it. | A composite indicator keeps its sub-indicators as their own L1 nodes; in L2 they are the parent’s components, not program indicators of their own. | Read the page layout, not the section text, when the source prints sheets as a label column and a value column: Stage A’s text reads side bars and columns out of order. | .

21185.title: Steps
21185.content: . | The source is in the library (dak-l1-library), with its PDF in uploads/<doc-id>/. | L1 candidates. From the library repository root: . python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --json # look first python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --write . --write merges into candidates.json as the indicators aspect, replacing an indicator candidate with the same number (re-runs are idempotent). Check the count against the source’s own list of indicators (NHWA: the synthesis table, 29 indicators). | L1 nodes. bun cat-harness-tools/pipeline/gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry library/<doc-id> writes blocks/indicator-<section>-NN.{jsonld,md}, each derivedFrom its section, provenance: ingested, with the fields in meta. Existing indicator IRIs do not change when the first candidate of a section stays the same indicator. | L2 drafts. python3 smart-base/scripts/l2-program-indicators.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --prefix <PREFIX> --out <where the L2 author will review them> . | Into the DAK or DTH. The L2 author takes the drafts into the guide’s indicators component (DAK component 8; a DTH’s data elements, indicators and requirements), through the guide’s own review (l2-component-edit-review) and, for a DTH, a change set. | .

21188.title: Inform the client
21188.content: Skill inform-client: A health worker tells the client (or caregiver) what was decided and what happens next, in words and, where the DAK gives one, on a slip or card: a referral, a return date, a result. Input is what to tell and the client’s language; output is that the client was told, and what they were handed. Generic for any DAK step that ends with the client being informed. Named by: Act on decision-support guidance, Capture data with an SDC questionnaire . Skill id: inform-client · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Performed by a person in a health-worker lane. WHO’s immunization DAK has it as IMMZ.D7 “Counsel client” and IMMZ.D9 “Inform client when to return”.

21189.title: Input and output
21189.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the about (a referral, a return visit, a result, a decision), the facts to convey, the language the client understands, and any handout the DAK gives (a referral slip, a vaccination card). | Out: informed (true once said and understood), the handedOver items, and the questions the client raised that need follow-up. | .

21190.title: What the health worker does
21190.content: . | Say what was decided and what happens next, in the client’s language, without jargon; check it was understood. | Hand over the slip or card when the DAK gives one. | Note any question that needs a follow-up. Nothing else is recorded: this step adds no form. | .

21191.title: Success criteria
21191.content: . | The client can say where to go, when, and why. | Every handout the DAK names was given. | .

21196.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Write dublin-core.jsonld (the record of truth)Task_Dublin | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | One standalone Dublin Core record per folder. dcterms is already this corpus’s JSON-LD vocabulary, so this extends a live context rather than introducing one. | . | Write manifest.jsonld referencing itTask_Manifest | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Write manifest.jsonld for the folder: its @id, @type folio:SourceDocument, what it contains and its provenance, referencing the standalone dublin-core.jsonld as the record of truth rather than copying its fields. | . | Record assets[] — local path or remote URLTask_Assets | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | kind / role / url-or-path / checksum / retrieved. A SIBLING of library:, never inside it: LibraryRef is regenerated from the tree, so an authored URL placed there is dropped on the next sync. | . | Bind the folder to its bibliography slugTask_Bind | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Bind the folder name to the document’s bibliography slug, so library/<bib-slug>/ and its citation key are the same string: a citation resolves to a directory without a lookup table between them. | . | Read glossary into candidate termsTask_Glossary | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | glossary-terms | The source’s glossary and abbreviations sections become candidate terms of a folio-glossary/v1 scheme with the Tool glossary-from-source, verbatim, each with source file#line, and an acronym as the notation of the term it expands. Terms a person owns are never changed, and only a person moves a term to authored. A source with no such section skips this step with nothing written. | . | Extract reference listsTask_References | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Each reference list of the source (a References, Bibliography or Further reading section, in any of the six UN languages) becomes folio-reference/v1 nodes with the Tool references-extract: one node per cited work, provenance extracted, derivedFrom the section it was read from, and printed the entry exactly as the source prints it. Only fields read without guessing are set (address, DOI, ISBN, year, access date); a cited IRIS item the library holds gets heldAt. The nodes are the document’s own bibliography on the bibliography page. A source with no reference list skips this step with nothing written. | . | Link L1 nodes into the corpus graphTask_Link | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Anything in library/ is L1 source content. A knowledge-graph reference from any artefact – paper, L2, L3 – resolves to it through library/. | .

21201.title: Steps
21201.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Archive → greppable contents manifestTask_Archive | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | NOT IMPLEMENTED; see docs/document-ingestion.md. An agent opens every image and vector render and records a verdict in the library’s image-verdicts.json: role (figure, logo or decorative), the reason, and a draft description in English plus ar, zh, es, fr and ru, which the apply-image-verdicts.ts arm lays over images.json on every ingest. Images judged figure are kept as WebP, quality 80, at most 1600 px; logos, decorative fragments and page scans are not. Every description stays a draft until a person confirms it with bun run cat narratives. Method: skill document-intake, “Figures and captioned tables: describe, keep, transcribe”. | . | Transcribe and translate audioTask_Audio | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | No Tool yet; the method, and the choice of recogniser, is skill audio-transcription. | . | Sheet names, headers, shape, narrativeTask_Tabular | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Tools tabular-csv and tabular-xlsx, as CSVW (skill tabular-metadata). CSV and spreadsheet: tabs, column and row headers, sizes, and what the dataset is about. | . | Extract figures and tablesTask_FiguresTables | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The pdf-images.py, pdf-vector-labels.py and pdf-vector-figures.py arms extract the raster images and the figures drawn as vectors (grouped and rendered). For every table the document’s structure declares, an agent reads the rendered page, checks cell text against the text layer, and writes tables/<label>.csv plus tables.csvw.json (folio-tabular-csvw/v1), with a draft description in the six UN languages; pdf-tables.py’s grid is a cross-check, not the answer. Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris): “actually extract the figures” and “any tables too”. Method: skill document-intake, “Figures and captioned tables: describe, keep, transcribe”. | . | Footnotes and the marks that call themTask_Footnotes | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | The pdf-footnotes.py arm (owner, 2026-11-11, “also foot notes/marks”): from the page layout, each note at the foot of a page and every superscript mark in the text that calls it, written to footnotes.json (folio-document-footnotes/v1) with the block that holds the page. The section text is not changed. Only a called note is a footnote; uncalled foot-of-page lines and marks with no note are listed, never dropped. OCR’d pages have no fonts and are reported unread. 21205.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Two provenance paths converge on the same Task_Sections output — an embedded text layer extracted directly, or OCR that leaves the fuller text in ocr/ with only a stub in sections/ — and which branch this lane took is invisible downstream except to a grep that knows to check the fourth tier. Task_Candidates stays a proposal: nothing downstream may treat it as an adjudicated verdict. | .

21206.title: Steps
21206.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Extract the text layerTask_ExtractText | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The document has a text layer: extract it with pdf-extract (pdfminer.six, then a zero-dependency content-stream reader). Exit 2 means no text layer — a scan — and routes to OCR; it is not an empty document. | . | Check each page; OCR pages that failTask_PageCheck | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris, card Q-ODD-1 = A): “force OCR when a page’s text layer fails a quality check”. A text layer can hold plenty of letters and still not be the page’s text: accents mapped to Greek letters (“dΘclaration”), Persian set in the wrong Arabic code points, words split by kerning (“au g m ente”), fake-bold words printed twice, mojibake. cat-harness-tools scripts/_text_quality.py checks every page against the document’s languages (dc.language.iso, or –lang-hint); the router then OCRs the document and pdf-structure.py –ocr takes the OCR text for the failing pages only, listing them in structure.json source.ocr_pages with the reason. When most pages of a document with no outline fail, the whole document is read from OCR, as for a scan. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “A text layer that is not text”. | . | OCR to ocr/page-*.txtTask_Ocr | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Each page is read in the document’s languages (–lang-hint, from dc.language.iso), narrowed to the script the page shows. A page Tesseract is unsure of (mean word confidence under 70) is read again with each other installed script added, and the most confident read is kept: a French article’s Arabic abstract, or the Latin URLs in an Arabic document’s references. A document ingested this way keeps its text in ocr/ and only a stub in sections/, which the documented sections/ grep cannot see. That asymmetry is why the corpus-grep checklist has a fourth tier. The run also records WHICH SOFTWARE made the pages, in ocr/run-context.json: a folio-run-context/v1 (cat-harness schemas/run-context.ts, the record test runs and QA reports use for the same question), naming the OCR engine, the rasteriser and each language model with its version and the sha256 of the bytes that ran. Two OCRs of one scan can read differently (“Manual” and “Manval”), and without it neither could be told from the other or reproduced. | . | Split into sections/*.md with doc_brief front-matterTask_Sections | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Contextual retrieval: a chunk in isolation loses what makes it mean anything, so each section carries the document brief. An outline is set aside when its entries are machine bookmark names (_GoBack, _Hlk…, “Blank Page”, a merged file’s name) or when under half of them name a heading the pages print, and the contents are inferred instead (diagnostics.outline_rejected). A section that would hold more than half of a document of 20 pages or more (and over 8,000 words), or over 20,000 words anywhere, is cut at the headings inferred inside it, else one section per page (diagnostics.oversized_split). Owner, 2026-11-11: “split single blocks that hold a whole book”. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “An outline that is not contents, and a section too long to be a block”. | . | Write structure.jsonTask_Structure | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Write structure.json (pdf-structure/v1): doc id, TOC from the PDF outline or inferred from headings, page ranges, metadata, and source{} with the sha256 and a mimetype sniffed from the bytes, never the extension. A structure that could not be determined says so in structure_note rather than being rendered as one. For OCR’d text, source.runContext cites the OCR step’s run context by sha256. A title already known for the document (the catalogue’s dc.title, or one given with –title) is passed through as the raw title, so the sections’ doc_title does not carry a scan’s misreading. | . | Extract claim candidatesTask_Candidates | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | candidates.json holds extracted theorems and definitions. Proposals only – never adjudicated verdicts. | .

21212.doc: Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate
21212.title: Steps
21212.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Is every derived artefact present?Task_CheckDerived | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | L1 source to L1 KG is NOT complete while a required derived artefact is missing. This is the gate that makes the derivation steps obligatory rather than aspirational. | . | Round-trip translation QATask_RoundTrip | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | translation-manageruntainted-verification | Back-translate each localized narrative into its source language and compare the meaning, to catch semantic drift and bad terminology that a forward-only check cannot see. Agentic. Two parties are kept apart under untainted-verification: a back-translator that sees ONLY the target-language text, and an adjudicator that sees the original and the back-translation and rules. The verdict is recorded per block, under criterion translation-semantic-roundtrip in the block’s <block>.<locale>.translation-qa.json sidecar, by the translation-roundtrip-record Tool (translation-manager §5). A terminology miss is a different criterion, translation-terms-preserved (acronyms, numbers, URLs that must survive), so Gateway_Drift can tell the two apart. Never close this step by reversing the PO’s msgid→msgstr map: that returns the source exactly and scores 1.0 always. An empty translation-semantic-roundtrip entry list means “not yet run”, which is never a pass. | . | Adjudicate the flagged passageTask_FlagDrift | Reviewer (SME or editor) | calls Adjudicationdocument-intakeadjudication | A machine can detect that two readings differ. Which one is right is a human call. | . | Record the L1 completeness verdictTask_Verdict | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Record the completeness verdict in three states — met, unmet, or not yet derivable — as bun run cat check:l1-complete reports it. Not-yet-derivable is never a pass. An unmet verdict opens a bean and returns to derivation; only a met one lets the entry into library/. | .

21213.doc: Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate
21213.title: Decisions
21213.content: Every one of the 2 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Drift or bad terminology?Gateway_Drift | Answered by the round-trip translation QA: did it flag semantic drift or a terminology miss? drift sends the passage to a person to adjudicate, since which reading is right is a human call; clean records the verdict directly. | drift → Adjudicate the flagged passageclean → Record the L1 completeness verdict | . | Which reading was right?GW_DriftOutcome | All three converge on Task_Verdict, and that is deliberate rather than the codes being decoration: this lane adjudicates ONE passage while Lane_0 still owns the completeness verdict as a whole, so the outcome of a passage is a REASON recorded against that verdict, never a different next step. The same shape criterion-adjudication uses, where three outcomes converge on one write because what makes an outcome legitimate is that its reason was recorded.What differs is what gets written and what it obliges. real is drift to fix in the translation. spurious is a false positive, and recording it is what stops the same passage being re-flagged every run. source-wrong points at the SOURCE rather than the translation — the one answer that sends work out of this process entirely, because no amount of re-translating a wrong source produces a right target. | the drift is real → Record the L1 completeness verdictfalse positive → Record the L1 completeness verdictthe SOURCE is wrong → Record the L1 completeness verdict | .

21221.title: Every initialization step, as the declarations name them
21221.content: Skill initialization-steps: Walk every initialization step the declarations name (the layer’s own and each one it needs), check each before doing anything, do what can be done, ask for what only a person can do, and report every step as done, not done, could not determine, or stated. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are making sure a harness’s initialization is complete: right after installing it (initialize-harness calls complete-initialization), or because you were dispatched to do exactly this with nothing but the diagram and the repository. Either way the steps are the same, and they are not listed in this file. They are named by the declarations.

21222.title: Where the steps come from
21222.content: Read <name>.json at the root, then each name in its needs, from a sibling checkout at ../<name>/<name>.json. Each step below names the declaration that names it, so a reader can see why it is there. | step | named by | done when | . | declaration | the file itself | <name>.json parses and its name is its file name | . | needs:<name> | needs | the dependency is beside it, and its declaration parses | . | instructions:<name> | FR-4 | stated: <name>/docs/bootstrap/initialization.md was read and followed | . | schemas:staged | each $id / @id under iriBase (FR-11) | the site build stages every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at its IRI | . | schemas:published | the same IRIs (FR-11) | every one of those IRIs answers | . | directory:<id> | directories[] | the declared path exists | . | asset:<id> | assets[] | the declared file exists | . | readme | FR-8 | the root has a README.md | . | readme-sections | the README’s own markers | every section the README opts into is current | . | site:workflow | repository | a workflow commits the rendered site onto gh-pages | . | site:branch | repository | a gh-pages branch exists — it must, before Pages can be switched on | . | site:enabled | repository | Pages is on, serving gh-pages | . | site:live | iriBase, else the Pages address | the address answers | . The two schemas: steps are the primary ones. They are checked first once the declarations are read, and the report leads with them: publish-documents. A harness above bootstrap names more steps the same way. A work-plan store it declares as a directory is a directory: step, and a harness’s own set-up instructions are its instructions: step. Bootstrap does not need to know which harness declares what. The site steps are in publish-site.

21223.title: Four states, not two
21223.content: . | done: checked, and it holds. | not done: checked, and it does not. Say exactly what to do next. | could not determine: the check could not run (no forge CLI, no network). Never reported as done. A check that could not look is not a pass. | stated: the declarations name it but nothing can observe it (reading and following a harness’s instructions). Follow it, say you did, and leave it stated. | .

21224.title: Idempotent by construction
21224.content: Check before doing, every time. A done step is left alone, so running the process twice changes nothing the second time, and an interrupted run is resumed by running it again. Performing is not the same as done: after you do a step, check it again, and only the check says done. Replace nothing. A step that would overwrite what somebody wrote (an existing README, a Pages site built from a branch, a declaration that disagrees with the directories on disk) is a step for the person. Ask through human-agent-discussion, with the exact step written out. Do not create an empty declared directory to make its step pass. Git does not track an empty directory, so the check would pass on your machine and fail on every clone. Put its first file in it, or ask whether the entry should go.

21225.title: Where tools are available
21225.content: A toolset may perform the checks for you — for example https://github.com/litlfred/bootstrap-tools, whose init command reads the same declarations, does what a tool can (regenerating README sections; switching Pages on when an authenticated gh is present), and prints each step in these four states with what to do next: . bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> # from a toolset checkout beside it bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> --dry-run # check only . Where no tools are available, do the same by reading files. The diagram is the same either way, and so is the report.

21226.title: The report
21226.content: One report through log-message, led by the primary step’s state (the JSON Schemas and JSON-LD at their IRIs): then every step, the declaration that named it, its state, what was seen, and for anything not done, what to do and who does it. End with the counts (done, not done, could not determine, stated). An initialization that finished with steps open says which. It is not hidden behind “installed”.

21228.title: Initialize a harness
21228.content: Process_InitializeHarness · strict (defaulted) · 8 step(s) . THE ONLY PROCESS IN BOOTSTRAP AN ACTOR STARTS. A Bootstrapping Agent that has read bootstrap’s README.md is at its start event and has nowhere else to begin. Every other diagram here is reached from this one by a call activity and is never started: discussion determines which harness and where; human-agent-discussion is the one reusable way any diagram asks a person anything; complete-initialization makes sure every step the declarations name is done; log-message records what a step is doing. PRECONDITIONS are DECLARED below as bootstrap.processes:precondition elements rather than asserted here. Three of the four are kind=”stated”: nothing in this repository can observe whether an actor understands what a role is, so they evaluate to could-not-determine, never to satisfied. The fourth is checkable: README.md EXISTS. That the Bootstrapping Agent read it is not observable.
