21765.title: The one fact everything rests on: a comment cites the REVIEW VERSION
21765.content: A reviewer writes “§3.4.5, p.22, l.618–624”. Those numbers exist only in the PDF the reviewer read. Word computes pages and lines at layout time and stores neither. Once an editor changes the folio, the numbers no longer describe the current text. So the review version is frozen in the library, and the folio is extracted from it in two halves: . | docx-structure.py reads the structure from the .docx: headings, lists, tables, figures, footnotes, call-out boxes. | pdf-line-map.py reads the page and line of every item from the line-numbered PDF, by matching letters only. A miss is reported, never guessed. | docx-to-folio.ts writes the editable folio. Every block’s meta.source records its page, printed page and lines. review-anchors.json is the same index in one file, which is what the importer reads. | . Never regenerate the folio over editors’ work. docx-to-folio.ts refuses a non-empty folio without --force. The anchors keep resolving after edits, because they point at the frozen version, not at the current text. Read the alignment stats (pdf-line-map.json → stats) before trusting a comment’s anchor. The unaligned items are listed by method, not hidden.

21766.title: Intake: one store, four routes, nothing dropped
21766.content: The channels a release goes out on (an offline Excel sheet, a Google Form, a GitHub issue form), each limited to the release’s fixed references, and the path each one takes back to these routes, are the public-comment-channels skill’s. | route | command | anchor comes from | . | comment matrix (.xlsx) | import <file> | section, page, line or Table/Figure columns | . | online-form export (.csv) | import <file> --channel online-form | the same columns, per row | . | narrative letter or email | import-narrative <file> --reviewer … | section, page/line, table or quotation in each paragraph | . | committee or editor on GitHub | the github job, from an issue or PR comment | the pc: reference | . A consolidated review log . A secretariat often keeps one workbook for the whole review: a master log, a tab per large submission, and a contributors sheet. import reads every sheet that holds a comment table, records the sheet on each comment, and passes over a blank template tab. Pass --series <id> naming the log. A copy re-sent later is a different file holding the same rows, and each comment carries the log’s own row number (“No.”), so a re-import adds only the rows it has not seen. What the log already says is carried, not re-done: . | Status. “Accepted”, “Partially accepted”, “Not accepted”, “Noted” and “Deferred” arrive decided, with the log’s disposition as the reason and review-log as who recorded it. “Reviewed” arrives triaged. A refusal with no rationale arrives triaged and is listed as held, because the commenter is owed a reason. | Categorisations. Theme, stakeholder type, committee routing, a review question or priority (“Q9 - Conformance and testing”, “P1”) are kept in labels, verbatim and keyed by the column header. The three comment types stay type. | Consent. Read from the contributors sheet by name, and only the name and consent columns are read. “NAIR, Tapas” and “Tapas Nair” are one person. | . Rules that are not negotiable: . | A row that resolves to nothing is unplaced, not dropped. Triage places it (triage <ref> --to <label>) or leaves it as a general comment. | A narrative is split only where it cites something. Paragraphs that cite nothing stay together as ONE general comment. Inventing an anchor for them would put a reviewer’s words on a paragraph they never mentioned. | Re-importing a file is a no-op. Batches are keyed by sha256. | Privacy. The reviewer’s email is never written, and an address typed into a comment’s text is removed too. Their name is written only when they answered the acknowledgement question “Yes”. Keep the original spreadsheets OUT of the folio’s repository, because they hold emails. Record the batch, and keep the file in the review owner’s private store. | . The live review sheet: public comments, change-sets and feedback . A secretariat may keep working in the log after the import, as a shared Google Sheet. The master log is then split into tabs, joined by the log’s own row number, No. Exactly one tab is written by the agent. Every other agent-facing column is a formula over it, so the views stay current without anyone, person or agent, refreshing them. The model. There are two things to review: public comments (PCs) and change-sets (CSs). A PC brings its own Comment / issue and Suggested revision, which are the commenter’s words. Reviewers give feedback on either one, in Committee Feedback (initials) columns: on a PC in Review Public Comments, and on a CS in Review Change Sets. A reviewer may also change which working group (TWG) a CS goes to. “Ready for agent” and “Ready for merge” belong to a CS, so they are only on Review Change Sets. Columns are named here by header, never by letter: people move them. | tab | who writes it | holds | . | Public Comment Source | intake, copied from what each channel returned (locked) | Every column Grey, header and cells: it is the external source, copied mechanically, and nobody edits it. No., date received, channel, reviewer name, organisation, country / region, stakeholder type. Reviewers’ names and emails stay here and never enter the repository | . | Review Public Comments | people, plus formulas and the Apps Script | one row per PC. Grey, mechanical: No. (a link to the comment’s page), Sections, Page, Line no(s) / Table / Figure (each linked to the draft page), Comment / issue, the PC’s own Suggested revision. Green, derived: Change Set (a link to its Review Change Sets row: the agent’s suggestion, or the person’s Change Set (human)) and TWG (agent). Blue, people: Change Set (human) (another change set’s id, several ids, or new; wins over the agent’s, like TWG (human)), TWG (human) (a multi-select dropdown), Comment type, any number of Committee Feedback (<initials>) columns, Disposition, Status. Green, from Agent by the Apps Script (derived agentic content): Agentic status, one line per pull request of the PC’s change-sets, <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed (the repository in the link text, because Sheets’ link popup cuts the URL short) with the PR linked and the status and completion time bold, or the status alone when there is no PR. Green, from Agent: Staging review page (by the PC’s change-set) | . | Agent - Comments | the agent, and only the agent | one row per No.: No., Comment ref (the PC id), Agentic status, Agentic action taken, Agentic applied in, Agentic handled by, Agentic date actioned (a UTC time, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ, when the agent last finished work on the PC; the four Agentic columns after the status are the agent’s log of what it did on that PC; no view reads them), Change-sets (the change set or sets this comment belongs to) | . | Agent - Change Sets | the agent, and only the agent | one row per change-set: Change-set, Title, Pull request (change set) (any number of PR URLs, one per line), Staging review page (change set), What the PRs changed (change set) (one line per PR, in the same order: what that PR changes in the document), Agent completed (UTC, change set) (one line per PR, in the same order: when the agent last finished work on it, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ), Feedback basis (change set), Staging built (UTC, change set), PR head (change set), Staging built from (change set), Staging deploy (change set) (what the agent found on GitHub, so the script can flag a stale preview; skill review-sheet-script, “Checked by commit”). A change-set may have several PRs, and a PC in several change-sets shows all of theirs. A PR belongs to a change-set, not to a PC. A sheet with one Agent tab (comments in A–H, change sets from I) is read when the Config sets AGENT_CS empty | . | Review Change Sets | people, plus formulas and the Apps Script | one row per CS. Blue, people: Title: making a change set is human-controlled. A person makes a change set by typing a Title on an empty row, and the script gives it the next id; the agent’s title is only the first value of a row it adds. Grey: Change-set, and the Apps Script’s Sections and Pages (each linked) and joins: Public Comments (No. n (Status) · comment, status in bold), Suggested Revisions, PC Committee Feedback and Dispositions (No. n · text), each No. n linking to its row. Green: TWG (PCs), the PCs’ TWG (human), else TWG (agent) marked “(AI)”. Blue, people: TWG (CS) (multi-select), Committee Feedback (<initials>) on the CS. Orange: Ready for agent and Ready for merge (Yes/No, editors). Green, from Agent by the Apps Script (derived agentic content): Agentic status, as on Review Public Comments: one line per PR of the change-set, <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed, the status being the change-set’s PCs’ agentic statuses. Green, from Agent: Staging review page | . | RCS joins (live) | formulas (hidden) | live joins over Review Public Comments and Agent, kept for checking the Apps Script’s output | . Splitting an older sheet’s one Agent tab. Duplicate it, delete A–H on the copy and the change-set columns on the original, rename them, set AGENT and AGENT_CS in the Config, and give each an Instructions row. Then, in the same step, repoint every formula that read the old tab’s change-set columns: they become #REF! when those columns are deleted. They are Review Change Sets A3 (FILTER('Agent - Change Sets'!A3:B, ...), the Change-set and Title), the Staging review column of Review Public Comments (its lookup range becomes 'Agent - Change Sets'!A:D), and A2 of the hidden RCS joins (live) tab. Also unmerge row 1 on the copy: the Instructions cell was merged across B1 to the last column, so deleting A–H shifts that merge onto A1 and hides B1 (a write to B1 then lands in the hidden part and seems to vanish). Merge B1 across the new width again. Read row 3 of each tab for #REF! before saying it is done. Colour key. Blue: people decide. Orange: a release an editor gives (Ready for agent, Ready for merge). Grey: fixed, mechanical, or from the knowledge graph. Green: derived or written by the agent. Every green header is the same green; a header does not say “from Agent”. Locks. Grey and green columns, and every header, are protected; only the owner’s account (which the agent’s connector and the Apps Script run as) may edit them. Editors may change the blue and orange cells. Ready for merge is open to editors, so an editor’s Yes makes the agent merge. Why the CS inputs stay with their rows. Review Change Sets’ Change-set and Title are plain values, so people can type a Title and start rows (where they are still a spill of FILTER('Agent - Change Sets'!A3:B, ...), the script turns it into values once). The script keeps the rows: a Title-only row gets the next id, never reused across both tabs, and a change set the agent records that is not on the tab yet is added at the end. Rows are never reordered or deleted, so the typed cells beside them stay put. Once per sheet, the script also turns Title and Change Set (human) Blue and takes them out of the locks on the agent’s columns. A sorted or filtered view of PCs cannot hold inputs. Feedback columns are found by header. The agent and the views read every Review Public Comments column whose header starts with Suggested revision or Committee Feedback, and every Review Change Sets column whose header starts with Committee Feedback. A board adds its column beside the others and puts its own initials in the header. Never write a fixed column letter into a view. People may reorder the Review Public Comments tab, because Review Change Sets finds columns by name (MATCH on the first row). A renamed header that is looked up by name (No., Sections, Page, Comment / issue, Suggested revision, Status, Disposition, TWG (agent), TWG (human)) does break the view, and its formula, or the Apps Script’s sheet-sync.json, must be updated with the new name. How the views update. The formula columns are FILTER, VLOOKUP, BYROW and MAKEARRAY over Review Public Comments and Agent. Setting Ready for agent, adding feedback, or the agent writing an Agent row shows at once. Nothing is run to refresh them. Two things are not automatic: . | A new or retitled change-set reaches the sheet only when the agent rewrites Agent - Change Sets’ Change-set and Title from review/public-comment/changesets/. | A PC’s change-set (Agent - Comments’ Change-sets) is the change-set whose refs hold the comment. The agent rewrites it when a comment is moved between change-sets. | . What the agent watches. Feedback arrives two ways, and the agent reads both on Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets: . | the Committee Feedback cells and Review Change Sets’ TWG categorisation; | cell comments (Google’s Insert > Comment) anywhere on those two tabs, read with the spreadsheet’s comments included. A cell comment on a PC row is feedback on that PC. One on a CS row is feedback on that CS. | . A changed TWG categorisation on a CS is a re-routing, not an edit. The agent records it in the change-set’s record through the tool, and says so in the CS’s agentic status. When the agent runs. A sheet sync runs three ways: . | Scheduled. A scheduled task in the project runs it (for example, every 2 hours on weekdays). Each run is a fresh thread with no memory of earlier ones, so everything it needs is in the sheet, the records and this section. | Manual. Anyone asks for it (“sync the sheet”, “work the ready rows”) in a project thread, or presses Run now on the scheduled task. A thread may also fire the scheduled task itself. | Active mode. On demand only, and it lasts two hours. The owner asks for it in a project thread (“active mode on”). That thread then checks the sheet about every ten minutes, waking itself with reminders rather than a loop. It compares Review Change Sets’ Ready for agent, the feedback columns and the cell comments with what it saw last, and runs a sheet sync, or fires the scheduled task, when something changed. Two hours after it was switched on, it stops and says so in one line. The regular schedule keeps running throughout. A sheet edit cannot wake an agent by itself, so active mode is frequent checking, not a push. | . Each sync does the steps below, in this order. | Reconcile. For every change-set with a pull request (Agent - Change Sets’ Pull request), read each PR’s state from GitHub. Open: PR open, with its staging review page. Merged: Change merged, and clear the staging link, because a merged branch’s preview is gone and its link 404s. Closed unmerged: back to Not started, and say so in “agentic action taken”. Write the status on every PC row of the change-set. Rewrite the change-set columns from the change-set records as above, keeping each change-set’s row and the PR columns beside it. | Work the ready change-sets. For each Review Change Sets row with Ready for agent = Yes whose PCs’ agentic status is Not started or Needs human, or that has new feedback since its PR was opened: . | Find each PC by No.: the record whose public.source names the log’s sheet and that entry. A row with no record is set to Not in comment record, and the agent goes no further with it. | Review all of it before drafting: every PC in the change-set, with its Comment / issue and its own Suggested revision; every Committee Feedback cell and cell comment on those PCs; and every Committee Feedback cell, cell comment and the TWG categorisation on the CS itself. Feedback on the CS weighs on the whole change; feedback on a PC weighs on that PC’s part of it. | Propose the change the way every change is proposed: in its change-set (see Change-sets below), on a branch, with a PR. A PR already open for the change-set is updated rather than replaced. “Ready for agent” says the change-set is ready to draft. It is not the editor’s decision, and a comment’s status still moves only through this tool. Where the suggestions and feedback conflict, or one asks for something the document cannot say without a decision, set Needs human and write what is needed in “agentic action taken”. | Publish the branch’s staging preview (branches/<slug>/). | Write the Agent rows (skill review-sheet-agent-columns, which applies to any work on a change set, in a sync or not), and nothing anywhere else in the sheet: status (Working, PR open, Ready for review, Change merged), what was done, the blocks or sections changed, who acted (the agent and its session) and the completion time (UTC, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ) on each PC’s row; and on the change-set’s row the PR and branches/<slug>/en/review/ (Pull request, Staging review page), one line saying what the PR changes in the document (What the PRs changed) and the completion time (Agent completed), each on the same line as its PR’s URL. The PR body names the feedback it answered by tab, row and column header, never by a reviewer’s name. | . | Merge the released PRs. For each change-set with an open PR whose Review Change Sets row has Ready for merge = Yes (any editor may set it), and whose QA gate has passed for the PR’s head commit, merge it. The gate is run by a reviewer that did not write the PR (review-sheet-script, “The QA gate”); without a pass for the current head, the agent does not merge and its ⏳ line says why. Nor does it merge while any comment’s committee Disposition is still Pending (review-sheet-script, “Unconfirmed dispositions block the merge”). Only a PR in the folio’s own repository is merged, never one on a WHO repository. After the merge, set every PC row of the change-set to Change merged, clear its staging link, and comment on the PR’s issue. If the merge is refused (a session safety check, a conflict, a required review), set the rows to Merge blocked, write why in “agentic action taken”, and say so in the run’s summary. Do not route around a refusal. | . Which PR counts. Only a PR that edits the document for the change-set. A change-set record’s pr can name the PR that proposed the change-set, long merged. That is not a change PR. Read the PR’s diff or body before writing it to a row. The dashboard draws a staging link only for a PR that is open now, for the same reason (openPullRequests in scripts/public-comment-site.ts). Page links. Every page, section and line reference in the sheet opens the frozen review version at that page. The log cites printed page numbers; the PDF page is the printed page plus the front matter, read from the library entry’s pdf-line-map.json (pages.<pdf page>.printed). Use a short link: the folio’s site publishes a draft/ redirect to its library viewer, so a link is <site>/draft/#page=<n> rather than the full assets/vendor/pdfjs/web/viewer.html?src=… address, and a cell with many links stays small. The review sheet’s Apps Script . Links inside a cell’s text (sections, pages, lines, each No. n in a joined column) are kept by a Google Apps Script bound to the sheet, built by the Tool review-sheet-sync. How to build it, install it, check it works, and reuse it for another document’s public comment is the review-sheet-script skill. A change-set that already has an agent PR has Ready for agent = Yes, so the sheet never shows agent work nobody released. The agent never writes the Review Public Comments, Public Comment Source or Review Change Sets tabs except on the owner’s explicit instruction (such as releasing a change-set as above). It never sets “Ready for agent” or “Ready for merge” on its own, and it never copies a reviewer’s name or email from Public Comment Source, a feedback header or a cell comment’s author into the repository. The sheet is reached through the session’s Google Sheets connector. No credential for it is committed. Google cannot stop the owner’s own account editing any tab, so the one-writer rule is kept by the agent, not enforced by the sheet. Two exceptions are the review log’s own tools (skill review-sheet-script): . | Archiving the log. Every night the log is copied to review/public-comment/logs/<log-id>.xlsx beside its review-log/1.0.0 node. The workbook is overwritten, git keeps the history, and no contact details are copied. | Importing offline feedback. An offline copy, or the feedback template returned with the line-numbered PDF, is imported only after it is checked against the template and a person picks the rows. Then only those rows’ human cells are written. The person’s pick is the owner’s instruction for those cells. Imported comment and change-set numbers are hints, never keys. | . Editorial change-sets may be drafted without waiting . A change-set is editorial when it changes only wording, numbering, cross-references, typos or house style, and no meaning: nothing a TWG or committee has to judge. The agent may draft an editorial change-set as a draft PR with a staging preview without waiting for Ready for agent. It records each step in the Agent tab as usual (review-sheet-agent-columns), with “editorial draft” in its status. | It still never sets Ready for merge, and nothing merges without it. | A change-set that mixes editorial and substantive asks is split: the agent drafts the editorial part, and the substantive part (a new definition, new guidance, a rewrite) goes to Needs human. | A house-style choice the document has not made yet (a spelling convention, say) is asked once with options, then followed; it is not guessed. | When unsure whether a change is editorial, it is not: wait for Ready for agent. | .

21767.title: Placing a comment: how much to trust the anchor
21767.content: anchor.method says how the place was found, and confidence says how far to trust it: . | caption (high): “Table 3.1” named a captioned block. | page (medium or low): a page with no usable line. A lines cell such as “Requirement 5” or “A14.01” names an item, not a line, so it is not read as one. Lands on the page’s first block in the cited section. | page-line (high, when the cited section agrees): the page is read as the printed page first, then as the PDF page index. Printed numbering restarts in the front matter, so the cited section breaks ties. “Section does NOT agree” in anchor.note is a triage signal. Check the comment. | quote (medium or low): a quotation found in the text. Low means it occurs more than once. The other places are in candidates. | section (medium): only the section resolved, by its number or by its title or acronym (“PHSP” is the Public Health Surveillance Platform). The anchor is the section label. | manual: a person placed it with reassign. | .

21768.title: The lifecycle, and who moves it
21768.content: received → triaged → assigned → recommended → decided → editing → incorporated, plus duplicate and withdrawn. Every move is a task in public-comment.bpmn or, for edit and incorporate, in its change phase public-comment-change.bpmn. transition() refuses any other move. Do not edit a comment’s status by hand: the dashboard counts statuses, and a hand-closed comment reads as adjudicated when no one decided it. | who (role) | does | how | . | intake agent (intake) | propose change-sets as records, with no issue (below) | public-comment-changesets.ts seed, propose | . | review coordinator (review-coordinator) | triage, place, mark duplicates, assign | triage, reassign, duplicate, assign | . | committee and editor | agree each change-set’s requirements, and change it, on its issue | the issue thread, and cs-* commands | . | committee member (reviewer) | recommend a decision, with a rationale | a GitHub comment pc: PC-0042 / recommend: accepted-modified, or recommend | . | editor (editor) | decide, with a reason unless accepted | decide: … on GitHub (editors only) or decide | . | author (author), human or agentic | once a comment is dispensed with a changing decision, make the edit on a feature branch | edit <ref> --branch … [--to <login>] | . | pipeline (build-pipeline) | build the change set’s staging preview, mark it incorporated on merge | staging workflow, incorporate | . Who can move a comment from GitHub. Both roles are read from the repository itself by default, so nobody maintains a list: . | Editor: the repository’s owner. Only the editor decides. | Committee: the repository’s collaborators (owner, member or collaborator). Adding someone as a collaborator on GitHub is the whole on-boarding. | . GitHub marks every comment with the commenter’s relationship to the repository, and that mark is what is checked. An editors or committee list in config.json replaces that role’s default with exactly those logins. Anyone may discuss a comment there, but the record is not open to everyone. The five decision codes: accepted, accepted-modified, not-accepted, noted, deferred. Every code but accepted needs a reason, because the commenter is owed one.

21769.title: Change-sets: an issue to agree it, a PR to approve it
21769.content: One editorial change often answers several comments, and one comment sometimes needs several changes. So a comment belongs to zero or more change-sets, and a change-set is discussed and made in two GitHub objects with different jobs: . | object | what people do there | . | the change-set’s ISSUE | discuss and agree the requirements: what the document should say, which comments the change answers | . | the PR that closes it | preview the change on staging, review it, approve the merge to main | . Requirements argued on a PR get lost when it is closed and reopened; a diff argued on an issue has nothing to point at. Keep each on its own object. One record, everything else rendered from it . review/public-comment/changesets/CS-012.json is the only record of a change-set: title, requirements, members, status, primary issue, every other issue that discusses it, its PR, and its history. Nothing else stores any of that: . | a comment’s change-sets are derived from the records, never written on the comment; | the change-set section at the top of its issue is rendered from the record, and a hand-edit to it is put back with a pointer to the commands; | the dashboard is built from the records. It reports and never deletes. The agent proposes; nobody is notified . Task_ProposeChangeSets (intake agent). An agent may draft every change-set, and drafting one opens nothing: a proposal has no issue, so 2,000 comments do not become 300 notifications nobody asked for. | seed --out seed.json lists the open or decided comments in no change-set yet, bucketed by section. 21780.title: The documents at their addresses: the primary step
21780.content: Skill publish-documents: The primary step of initializing a Knowledge Graph harness: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document it names an address for (schemas, vocabulary, diagram vocabulary, graph export, each with its @context) is published AT that address, and the address answers. Checked first, right after the declaration is read. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . A Knowledge Graph harness is its JSON and JSON-LD. Its schemas say what a declaration and every node may be; its vocabulary says what each term means; its graph says what it holds. Each names itself with an IRI: a JSON Schema with $id, a JSON-LD document with @id. An IRI that answers 404 is a broken promise to everything that points at it. So this is the first step checked once the declarations are read, before any directory, README or site step.

21781.title: Which documents
21781.content: Read from the files, never from a list: . | every JSON file whose top-level $id lies under the declaration’s iriBase is a JSON Schema published at that $id; | every JSON-LD file whose top-level @id lies under iriBase is published at that @id. For bootstrap that is the vocabulary (ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/ns/) and the diagram vocabulary (processes/ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/processes/ns/, the namespace every diagram binds); | the graph export, built when the site is published, at the address its own @id names (bootstrap-graph-publication). | . Each document carries its @context inline, so publishing the document publishes its context. A harness whose documents name an external context publishes that context the same way, at its own IRI. No iriBase, no addresses. A layer that declares none has nothing here to publish, and says so rather than reporting a pass over nothing.

21782.title: Where each goes
21782.content: At the path its IRI names, with iriBase removed. An address ending in / (…/v0/ns/) gets the document as index.jsonld there, with an index.json copy beside it. A .jsonld gets a .json copy with the same bytes beside it, because many hosts serve .jsonld as a download. The .jsonld stays the real one: it is what the @id names.

21783.title: Two checks, four states
21783.content: | step | checks | done | not done | could not determine | . | schemas:staged | the site build puts each document at its address | every one is there, byte for byte | one is missing, or another file holds its address | the build could not run | . | schemas:published | each address answers | every one answers | one answers 404 | 403, 407, 5xx or no answer: that is about the way from here (a proxy, an access rule), not about the address | .

21784.title: The site is the vehicle
21784.content: The documents get to their addresses by the Pages site (publish-site): its workflow stages each one where its IRI says, and lists them all under “Published documents” on the README page (README.html). When schemas:published is not done, the site steps are how it gets done. The site is not the goal: a site that answers while one schema address does not has not finished initializing the harness. Where a toolset is available, its site check (site.ts --check) lists every address and what is staged at it, and init.ts reports both steps first.

21786.title: Publish extracted statements with source links
21786.content: Skill publish-extracted-statements: The standard step of adding source documents to a folio’s working artifact: every statement extracted from a library source is published readably in the artifact’s own pages AND in the shared extraction viewer, each with a link to its library entry and to the section it came from, and CI fails when the generated pages are stale. Generic across content types; each type’s adapter says only how its pages look. Executable form: processes/library/publish-extracted-statements.bpmn. Named by: L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Authoring a document, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . A statement nobody can read beside its source is reviewed from memory, or not at all. So whenever source documents are added to a folio’s working artifact (a document, a paper, an implementation guide, a guideline), the statements extracted from them are published where a reader of that artifact will find them, each one linked back to where it came from. This is a standard step, not a per-folio choice. It is the sub-process Process_PublishExtractedStatements, and every process that brings source documents into an artifact calls it: . | caller | when | . | l1-document-ingestion | right after the entry is promoted, which is where it becomes complete | . | authoring-a-document, and each content type’s authoring process | before the artifact is rendered, so a source taken up since ingestion, or a statement changed since, is published too | .

21787.title: What is published
21787.content: A statement is a sentence or row captured verbatim from a library entry, whatever kind the extraction gave it: a recommendation, a requirement, a candidate a person has still to rule on. It is published as captured, with its status. This step neither promotes nor edits it. Each statement carries two links: . | the library entry: the entry’s own page in the library viewer; | the section: the section of that entry the statement was read from, labelled with the section’s title and its locator in the source’s own unit, read off the entry’s structure.json. For example “Catch up schedule, slide 7”, “Annex 2, page 41”, “Setup, cells 3–9”. | . The link is a library reference (instance, libraryId, sectionId), so a statement from another layer’s library resolves through that layer’s declaration and never through a relative path. A statement whose section does not resolve is reported, never published without a link: an untraceable statement is the failure this step exists to prevent.

21788.title: Where it is published — both places, from one list
21788.content: | place | what a reader gets | . | the artifact’s own pages | the statements of the sources this artifact draws on, inside the artifact, so a reader need not leave it | . | the shared extraction viewer | every source and every statement extracted from it, whichever artifact uses them, reached from the site’s Sources menu | . Both are generated from one collected list, so they cannot disagree about what was extracted or where it came from. Neither is hand-edited: a person corrects the extraction or the source, then regenerates.

21789.title: What the content type supplies, and nothing more
21789.content: The step is the same for every content type. What differs is how the artifact’s pages look, and that is the content type’s adapter’s business, declared in its content profile (folio-content-profiles): . | a document (a handbook, policy guidance): pages of the document; | a paper: an appendix or a section of the paper; | an implementation guide or a guideline built as one: pages of the guide. | . The platform layers name no folio, no content type and no level of a guideline. A folio’s own names for its pages (for example “L1 Recommendations” and “Scenario Candidates” in an immunization guideline) are the folio’s, set in its own configuration.

21790.title: Run it
21790.content: bun run cat statements:pages --page <spec>.json [--page <spec2>.json] [--check] . Each page is declared in a committed page spec (folio-statement-page/v1): the statement lists it publishes, the page it writes, its title and introduction, the URL prefixes of the library viewer (entryBase) and of the sources (sectionBase), and the content type’s table look (tableAttr). A spec rather than flags, because those are free text, and free text is never a command-line word. A spec names one or more statement lists (folio-extracted-statements/v1, schemas/extracted-statement.ts): each statement’s id, its text verbatim, its kind and status as the extraction records them, optionally the id of the statement it was derivedFrom (a scenario candidate written from a recommendation names it, and the page shows a “Derived from” column), and its source, a library reference with either a sectionId or the page (or slide) it was read from. With only a page, the section is the one that starts latest at or before it. When several sections start on that page (a one-page poster), the label names only the page. The front matter the PDF rung synthesises (sec-front-matter) is used only when no authored section starts at or before the page. A collector writes the list, and the collector is not core’s. A folio’s extraction has its own format (a guideline’s recommendation rows, a DAK layer’s requirement candidates, a paper’s quoted claims), so the content layer or the folio that owns the format turns it into a statement list. Core resolves, labels, renders and checks. Declare two specs over the same lists, one for the artifact’s page and one for the shared viewer’s, so the two cannot disagree.

21791.title: Staleness fails CI
21791.content: --check regenerates in memory and fails on any difference from the committed pages, and on any link that does not resolve. CI runs it, so a change to an extraction or a library entry that was not republished fails the build instead of leaving a page that says something the extraction no longer does.

21792.title: Nothing to publish is a result
21792.content: A referenced source (its licence forbids a copy), a dataset, or a source with no normative content yields no statements. The sub-process ends at “Nothing to publish”, which is a determined zero, recorded as such, not a skipped step.

21801.title: The site: a layer rendered for publication, and its address answering
21801.content: Skill publish-site: Give a layer a site: its Knowledge Graph rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answering. Four checks — a workflow publishes it, the gh-pages branch exists, Pages serves that branch, the address answers. How the rendering is staged and pushed is the toolset’s own process, not this skill’s. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . One abstract step. A layer with a repository is rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answers. How the rendering is staged, committed and checked is the toolset’s own subprocess (its render-to-GitHub-Pages skill and diagram), so this skill stays a list of checks. The site is how the documents reach their IRIs (publish-documents, the primary step), not the goal. Where the README page lands. At <site address>README.html, and the site address itself (index.html) is the landing page: by default a plain redirect to README.html, so a Harness that wants a different front page puts its own index.html or index.md at its root and changes nothing else. A page generated from the layer’s files says so at its top, and its footer points to what it was generated from, never to an editor for the published copy: that copy is replaced on every publish. The site address is the declaration’s iriBase when it declares one, otherwise https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/.

21802.title: The checks (initialization-steps)
21802.content: | step | done when | . | site:workflow | a workflow commits the rendering onto gh-pages: one under the layer’s own .github/workflows/, or one in the toolset that publishes it from outside. bootstrap’s own workflow writes only its JSON-LD context to gh-pages; its site is published from outside | . | site:branch | a gh-pages branch exists. It must exist before Pages can be switched on; where it does not, the step says how to create it (an orphan branch with a placeholder page) | . | site:enabled | Pages is on, serving gh-pages at /. Only after site:branch passes for this repository (see Order below). Switched on only by an authenticated forge CLI once the branch exists; otherwise the person gets the one step below | . | site:live | the address answers 200, and so does its README page, README.html. 404 after Pages is on usually means the workflow has not run yet. A 403, 407, 5xx or no answer is about the way from here: could not determine, never done | . Order: create gh-pages, then switch Pages on. Never the reverse. site:enabled is not attempted, and not asked of a person, until site:branch has passed for that repository, checked at the moment of asking (a read of the branch, not a remembered publish run). A first publish that is still running, or that failed, has not created the branch. When several repositories are set up together, the ask lists only those whose gh-pages exists now; the others are asked later, once their branch exists, and never ahead of it “for when it appears”. Owner, 2026-11-10: “you need to create gh-pages first … create gh-pages THEN update settings. you make this mistake a lot.” . When site:enabled cannot be done here, it goes to the person through human-agent-discussion, written so it can be followed without opening anything else: . Open https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/pages. Under “Build and deployment”, set Source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). It is free for a public repository. Then re-run the workflow that publishes the site from its Actions tab. If Pages is already on but serves something else, do not switch it yourself: that changes how an existing site is built, so ask. Never silent: a step that could not be checked is said to be unchecked.

21803.title: Cost
21803.content: Pages on a public repository, and the Actions minutes its workflow uses, are free. Nothing else is switched on.

21805.title: quality-control
21805.content: Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Draft, review and publish, DTH authoring . Skill id: quality-control · Package: content-lifecycle-ext · Named by draft-to-publication.bpmn here, and by the QC gates of processes in the layers built on this one — which bind it from above, so this skill names none of them. Apply the publication quality gates to an aggregate of QA output, and decide whether it clears.

21806.title: Inputs and outputs
21806.content: folio-assistant-core/schemas/skills/quality-control/: . | in — checkType (required), targetPath (required), checklistSections | out — overallResult, findings, checklistResults | .

21807.title: Two of the three lanes are human, and that is the design
21807.content: A QC gate is a decision, and the processes put it in a reviewer’s lane — QC reviewer, PR reviewer / QC reviewer — not the build’s. The build’s lane runs the checks; the reviewer’s lane rules on them. The qc-reviewer role holds qa-reporting as a permission, and qa-reporting is also held by ci-pipeline and ig-publisher-service. That a build system and a human share a permission is deliberate: emitting a QA report is mechanical, ruling on it is not. editing-hci-validation.bpmn marks Task_ReviewFindings and Gateway_EditorDecision relaxable="false": the editor seeing the findings, and the decision itself, are the gate.

21808.title: Compute the gate, do not assert it
21808.content: Where a gateway carries <cat-harness.processes:decision/>, pass the facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and let the DMN table return the branch. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. decisions/draft-qa-gate.dmn is the table; dmn-authoring is how to change it.

21809.title: Severity is the gate’s vocabulary
21809.content: The corpus-wide convention, and what the tables read: . | critical — a broken reference: something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. Blocks. | major — a missing join: intact, but a question has no answer. | minor — coverage. Has legitimate instances, so it must not gate; forcing a fake entry onto a real step is worse than the gap. | . unknown is never counted as a pass, and it is not promoted either — it counts at its own criterion’s severity: a check that did not run has not cleared.

21810.title: What to run
21810.content: qa_sweep for content, bun run cat kg:audit for the process/role/skill graph, and the content type’s own conformance validator where its layer provides one (for a FHIR IG, that layer’s validation skill). checklistSections narrows the pass; findings and checklistResults are what the reviewer reads — not overallResult alone, which is a summary of them rather than a substitute.

21818.title: Questionnaire wireframe review
21818.content: Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview · advisory · 10 step(s) . A built FHIR Questionnaire shown the way a person will meet it — a mid-fidelity wireframe at web and mobile width, and a live LHC-Forms form view — checked field for field against the L2 wireframe it was derived from, reviewed as a design, staged with deep links, and changed through requests that say which side was edited. Operating skill: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe. WHERE IT SITS. After SUSHI has compiled the Questionnaire to JSON (l3-fhir-pipeline, Task_Sushi), and wherever a layer above reviews a Questionnaire’s fidelity to its wireframe. It reads JSON only, so it can run on any IG that produces a Questionnaire. WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM. A faithful Questionnaire is not therefore a good form, and an accepted form is not therefore conformant: wireframe-design-review judges the first and fhir-validation the second. i i i i i i i i i i

21824.title: RACI — involvement, over the graph that already exists
21824.content: Skill raci: RACI over this repository’s processes — who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity. Three declared edge kinds over the roles and BPMN activities that already exist, not a new party registry. Use it to work out involvement when a project is initiated, and to sketch its breakdown. Named by: Phase 1: Planning . The method is not in this file. It is the raci node in the methodology graph — methodologies/raci.md — which carries the four letters, the exactly-one-Accountable constraint, and what RACI is not for. This file carries how this platform applies it (methodology-adoption’s split): the method’s text lives once, so two skills quoting it cannot drift apart. Read the node first; everything here assumes it. R is already declared, and that is this platform’s contribution. A BPMN lane says who performs an activity; that IS Responsible, so the overlay does not restate it and declares only the other three: . | letter | where it comes from HERE | . | Responsible | read from the BPMN lane, never declared | . | Accountable | cat-harness.processes:raci, exactly one per activity, gated | . | Consulted | cat-harness.processes:raci | . | Informed | cat-harness.processes:raci | . <bpmn:task id="A_Entities" name="Identify entities"> <bpmn:extensionElements> <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="crdm-data-model"/> <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="business-analyst" involvement="accountable"/> <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="stakeholder" involvement="consulted"/> </bpmn:extensionElements> </bpmn:task> . bun run cat raci prints the chart across every declared process; bun run cat check:raci enforces the rule and is a gate.

21825.title: Why an overlay and not a registry
21825.content: RACI needs tasks and parties. This repository already declares both — BPMN activities under the declared workflow directories, and roles in scenarios/roles.json. RACI adds only the relation between them, and only three quarters of it. A RACI implemented as its own table of names would be a second answer to “who is the reviewer”, free to disagree with roles.json. Every letter names a ROLE, not an actor. role-model.md’s rule is that nothing IS a reviewer — somebody acts as one for the duration of a lane — and naming a concrete actor would bind a process to one participant. That holds for informed too, where the temptation to name a person is strongest.

21826.title: Exactly one Accountable — the method’s rule, ENFORCED here
21826.content: The constraint itself is the node’s; what this section adds is that check:raci fails on a breach rather than advising against one. Zero is also a breach, once an activity declares any RACI at all. An activity declaring nothing is n/a, because annotation is incremental: the gate is on what a diagram CLAIMS, never on how much it has claimed so far. That is the platform’s choice; RACI says nothing about partially annotated corpora. A role cannot be both accountable and consulted on one activity, and the gate enforces that too.

21827.title: Using it to initiate a project
21827.content: The chart is the second half. The first is a conversation, and the order matters: . | Enumerate the activities. From the BPMN if a process exists; from the breakdown if it does not. An activity nobody can name is a gap in the breakdown, not a gap in the chart — finding those is the point. | Ask who is Accountable, one activity at a time. Not a list: one question per row. The answer “the team” means the activity is not yet decomposed far enough, and that is the most valuable finding this produces. | Then Consulted, then Informed. In that order, because C is the expensive one — every name added is a round trip before the work can proceed — and a long C list is a signal to re-read step 2. | Read the columns, not the rows. A role that is C on everything is a bottleneck; a role that appears nowhere was not a stakeholder after all, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it late. | . The agent enumerates; the person decides. CRDM states this for stakeholder identification — “the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess” — and it applies here with more force, because a wrong A is invisible until something goes wrong and somebody has to answer for it.

21828.title: What this is NOT — the platform’s half
21828.content: The method’s own refusals are in the node. These three are about the overlay, and each names the declaration RACI must not be mistaken for: . Not an approval mechanism. Gates are BPMN — a userTask in a lane, with the fulfilmentKindsForBpmnType rule that a system actor cannot fill one. Not permissions. What an actor may DO is an ODRL rule in policies/ (actions in skills/permissions/permissions.json), and cross-cuts roles. Being R for a task says who is expected to do it; performing it also needs a rule that permits perform-task there. Not a substitute for the lane. If the chart and the lane disagree about who performs something, the lane is right and the chart is stale — which is why R is read rather than declared.

21830.title: recommendation-extraction
21830.content: Skill recommendation-extraction: Extract the recommendations of an L1 source as L1 3.0 recommendation and remark nodes, then describe each one’s scenario: the persona (role) who acts on it, the business process they act in, and the user story, as smart-kg L2 user-scenario candidates that reuse the target guide’s own vocabulary. Read before extracting recommendations from a WHO guideline or position paper with no printed “Recommendation N” labels, before linking a recommendation to a DAK persona or process, and whenever a recommendation has to say who does it and where. Covers the hybrid extraction (mechanical candidates, agent structuring, verbatim and 100 % coverage gates), the reuse-first precedence for personas and processes, the WARNING format, and sign-off. Named by: Classify and code content, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: recommendation-extraction · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Follows dak-l1-library, which builds the library and the layout graph this extracts from. A recommendation that does not say who does it, and during what, cannot be implemented. This skill extracts each recommendation verbatim and records, per recommendation, the persona who acts on it, the business process they act in, and whether the guideline is clinical, public-health or health-system-strengthening, before any L2 asset is drawn. It reuses existing vocabulary and processes first, and warns when none fits.

21831.title: Input and output
21831.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: l1Sources, dak-l1-library’s output, and the targetGuide whose personas and processes the scenarios reuse first. | Out: l1Kg: per included source, its extractionPath (library/<bib>/l1-extraction/), sourceVersion, the recommendation, remark, practice and scenario-candidate counts, the coverage and every WARNING. Stages 3 (l2-dependency-choice), 4 and 5 take it as their l1Kg. | . As stage 2 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, a source is skipped only when it is already in a KG: its extraction directory exists, is declared, and is at the same source version (skipped: true). A library entry with no extraction still needs it, after bun run cat ingest and dak-l1-library’s generic-document layer have put it in library/. Skipping is per source.

21832.title: The two halves
21832.content: | half | produces | layer | schema | . | extraction | recommendation and remark nodes, verbatim — or, for implementation guidance, implementation-practice nodes | L1 | L1 3.0, smart-base/kg/src/l1.ts (KGRecommendation); implementation-practice is the l1-library extension, smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts (KGImplementationPractice); not smart-kg 1.0 | . | scenario | one user-scenario candidate per recommendation, joined to persona and business-process | L2 | smart-kg ontology/l2/l2.json, unchanged; smart-base UserScenario.fsh | . No L1 field carries the scenario: L1 holds what WHO says; who does it, and during which process, is adaptation, which is L2’s. Implementation guidance prints practices, not recommendations . A recommendation is a GRC-approved normative statement made by a guideline. A publication whose publicationType is implementation-guidance or methodology (a “how to” document, such as a digital transformation handbook with its own “Best practices” lists) makes no recommendations of its own (handbook for guideline development §1.9). What it prints as normative is an implementation-practice node, never a recommendation with a new kind code. | Record the type in the curation as publication.publicationType. With implementation-guidance or methodology, every as: recommendation decision emits an implementation-practice node at <publication>/implementation-practice/<key>, and the graph names l1-library.context.jsonld so the validator scopes L1 + the extension. | The class lives in smart-base/kg/src/l1-library.ts; l1.ts stays the L1 3.0 layer, unextended. | It carries identifier, statement (verbatim) and contentHash; no kind, direction, strength or certainty. A kind on such a decision is refused. | No remark. L1 3.0’s remark is minted under a recommendation, so a remark decision in such a publication is refused: exclude the sentence or make it its own practice. | smart-base/kg/src/validate.ts refuses a recommendation defined in an implementation-guidance or methodology publication. | The output graph is l1.json. | .

21833.title: Part 1 — extraction (hybrid)
21833.content: Candidates are mechanical, structure is the agent’s, and the gates are mechanical. | Ingest the source (see dak-l1-library steps 1–2): bun run cat ingest uploads/<doc_id>/<doc_id>.pdf --library <lib>. | Fast path — a guideline that prints labels. When the source prints Recommendation N: labels, bun run smart-base/scripts/extract-smart-kg-l1.ts --entry smart-base/library/<id> extracts them by label (it writes L1 1.0). A source with no labels, such as the measles position paper, takes the hybrid path below. | List the normative sentences. Run core’s l1-coverage with an empty capture list; every sentence carrying a marker (should, shall, must, recommend*, should not, may be given/administered/offered/…) comes back as unaccounted, with its page: . echo '[]' > captured.json bun run cat l1:coverage --text pages.json --captured captured.json --out candidates.json . --text is body text only, page-tagged; strip references and running headers first. | Structure them. The agent turns each candidate into an L1 3.0 recommendation (identifier, statement, kind, population, intervention, setting, …) or a remark (text, remarkType) attached by hasRemark: . | statement and text are verbatim: the printed words, line breaks joined, nothing else changed; | a sentence that is history, background or a manufacturer’s statement is proposed for exclusion (step 5), not forced into a node; | GRADE strength and certainty are set only where the source prints them; | every node is inferred, with a note and evidence (page and quote). | . | Gate: 100 % accounted for. The curation is the agent’s step. The script hints (licence-or-imprint, glossary-page, layout-fragment) and proposes the publication’s identity from the printed ISBN; it never decides. Per candidate location (p<page>:s<n>, l1-coverage’s own), the agent records one of: . | as | means | fields | . | recommendation | an L1 recommendation node | key; statement only to narrow a joined list to one bullet, or to join a split sentence; kind only where printed | . | remark | a remark of a recommendation, by hasRemark | of, remarkType | . | part-of | inside another recommendation’s statement | of | . | exclude | a PROPOSED exclusion, one of the fixed reasons | reason; signedOffBy is a person’s acting as l1-extraction-reviewer, never an agent’s | . Every decision carries a basis. A location may carry a list of recommendation decisions: the splitter reads a bulleted list as one sentence. Provenance. The work list cites it by reference. --check ignores it, as it ignores generatedAt. Declare every output directory, in the same commit. 21834.title: Part 2 — the scenario
21834.content: Its mechanical step is the named skill recommendation-scenarios (Tool l1-recommendation-scenarios). The shape: L2 nodes, reused unchanged . Per recommendation, one user-scenario (smart-base UserScenario: title, id, description, personas[]) joined by three edges smart-kg L2 already licenses: . recommendation implementedBy user-scenario user-scenario involves persona business-process realises user-scenario . The description is a user story: . As a <persona>, during <process>, I <act> so that <outcome>. Each link records its source, as an intake classifications entry does (cat-harness-tools/schemas/library/intake.ts): . | source | meaning | smart-kg derivation | . | declared | a person said so; names by | decided | . | context | the section the statement is printed under settles it | inferred | . | inferred | an agent’s reading of the statement | inferred | . and a status: candidate until a person reviews the entry. Reuse first, stop at the first hit . Persona, business-process and guideline-domain coding apply the terminology-coding methodology (backed by classify-and-code-content, the terminology-lookup Tool, and glossary-terms): . | what | 1st | 2nd | otherwise | . | persona | the target guide’s own personas | smart-base’s generic DAK.Persona.* (input/fsh/actors/, ISCO / CDHI) | a glossary candidate, and a WARNING | . | process | the target guide’s own processes | a domain process catalogue — none exists yet (smart-base-clinical holds no processes): report “catalogue absent” | could-not-determine, and a WARNING | . | domain | clinical | public-health | health-system-strengthening, per scenario, with its source |   |   | . Never invent a process. A process not in the guide is could-not-determine, and the warning says why: it is the evidence that the guide (or a catalogue) is missing one. Choose the persona who acts on the statement, not the one it is about: “Vaccine should be offered to travellers” is acted on by the health worker. A persona a guide’s description does not cover (an immunization DAK’s health worker treating measles) falls to the next rung rather than being stretched. Read the statement, not its section: “Countries should achieve ≥95 % coverage” sits under WHO position and is acted on through coverage analysis (IMMZ.I), while “MCVs should not be given to individuals with … severe immunosuppression” is a per-client check (IMMZ.D, IMMZ.D5). A national policy, schedule-design or programme decision is not a per-client process. Run it . | The vocabulary. For the target guide, read its business-processes.md and personas.md from a guide checkout; for the generic rung, read smart-base’s ActorDefinitions: . bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-scenario-vocabulary.ts --guide <guide checkout> --out guide-vocabulary.json bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-scenario-vocabulary.ts --fsh-actors <smart-base checkout>/input/fsh/actors --out smart-base-generic-personas.json . Each file records the repository, the commit, and the file and line of every entry. The guide’s name, namespace and repository come from the checkout’s <name>.json and sushi-config.yaml canonical. Persona ids are slug(title) where the guide prints none (as smart-kg kgid.mjs mints a persona IRI); process ids are the printed Process IDs. | The mapping (l1-scenario-mapping/v1, YAML), authored: per recommendation, its personas (an id, or a candidate term), its process (an id, or could-not-determine), act, outcome and domain, each with a source and a basis quoting the statement, the vocabulary row or the person’s ruling. | The candidates: . bun run smart-base/scripts/l1-recommendation-scenarios.ts \ --l1 <recommendations.yaml | l1-graph.json> --vocabulary guide-vocabulary.json \ --generic smart-base-generic-personas.json --mapping mapping.yaml --out <dir> [--check] . It writes scenario-candidates.l2.json (an L2 graph document) and scenario-warnings.md, and refuses: . | an id the vocabulary does not hold; | a recommendation with no mapping entry (coverage is 100 %); | a mapping entry for a recommendation the source does not hold; | a declared link that names nobody. | . | Tier 2. node tools/validate.mjs <l1-graph.json> scenario-candidates.l2.json in a smart-kg checkout; give it the L1 document too, or every implementedBy edge reads as dangling. | . The WARNING format . One line per warning, greppable, in the report and on stderr: . WARNING process-not-determined <key>: no <guide> process (<ids>) realises this; domain process catalogue absent. <basis> WARNING persona-glossary-candidate <key>: persona "<term>" is a glossary candidate — … <basis> . A warning is not a refusal: the run succeeds, and the warnings are the work list for whoever owns the guide’s processes or the glossary. Review and sign-off . Everything this skill writes is a candidate. A person reviews an entry and records it in the mapping (review: {by, at}); the run then marks that entry’s links reviewed. A person may also turn a link declared (with by). An agent never writes either. Part 1’s exclusions are signed only by a person acting as l1-extraction-reviewer.

21835.title: What smart-kg L2 could not hold
21835.content: user-scenario declares only id, title, description, sourceKind, source and resolutionStatus, and tier 2 refuses any other node property. So domain, each link’s linkSource and the reviewStatus go on the edges’ open properties; the act and outcome live only inside description.

21836.title: What it feeds, later
21836.content: The scenarios are the hinge to L2. Each realises edge names the process, and so the BPMN whose lane is the persona, a scenario will be drawn in; the recommendation’s conditions become DMN rules (for measles, the IMMZ.D2.DT.Measles.* and IMMZ.D5 tables); and the user story becomes a functional requirement (functional-requirement fulfilledBy persona). None of that is drawn here. could-not-determine scenarios have no process to draw into yet.

21837.title: The worked examples
21837.content: An ingested handbook, end to end. smart-base/l1-extractions/9789240116191-eng/ is the Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025; its sections are in who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/) run through both tools: 48 normative sentences. It is implementation guidance, so the curation took 22 implementation practices and proposed 30 exclusions (licence text, glossary definitions, background on SMART Guidelines, chapter checkpoints, and the definition of the data owner on page 26), each naming l1-extraction-reviewer as signer and none signed, so coverage reads 18/48 until a person signs them. The scenarios reuse the handbook’s own roles (data owner, custodian, steward, project manager, solution architect: 18 links), one generic DAK.Persona.DataManager, and 3 glossary candidates (the national regulatory authority, twice, and the master data governance group). The handbook prints no business process with an id and no health-system catalogue exists, so all 22 are could-not-determine: 26 warnings, one of them practice-implementedBy-unlicensed (smart-kg’s L2 licenses implementedBy from a recommendation only, so from a practice it is a proposal for L2). The test l1-recommendation-candidates.test.ts keeps it current. An authored L1, scenario half only. The 75 recommendations of the WHO measles position paper (WER 92(17), 2017), mapped against the immunization guide’s personas and processes, with the vocabulary, mapping, output and warnings, live in that guide’s library with the check that keeps them current: https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations/tree/main/library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/measles. smart-base holds no guide’s example. The generic rung it was run with is smart-base/scripts/fixtures/l1-recommendation-scenarios/smart-base-generic-personas.json, shared with the handbook example. An authored L1 from pictures. When the source prints its recommendations only as images (a schedule poster, a slide deck), Part 1 finds nothing and the L1 is authored from the inspected image narratives and transcriptions of the rendered page. Its check is the step skill transcription-verbatim (Tool l1-transcription-verbatim): every statement verbatim in the narrative or transcription it names, every transcription word corroborated by the text layer unless listed under inspectionOnly with its basis. The Uganda schedule poster and UNEPI deck (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations-uganda/tree/main/library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/uganda) are the worked example.

21849.title: Record a decision rationale (optional)
21849.content: Skill record-decision-rationale: OPTIONAL and never blocking: a health worker who chooses to may note why they accepted or declined decision-support guidance, in one tap plus an optional coded or free-text reason. Input is the decision; output is one FHIR Provenance (or nothing, when skipped, which is the default). The care plan is updated whether or not this is ever done. Named by: Act on decision-support guidance, Capture data with an SDC questionnaire . Skill id: record-decision-rationale · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Task Task_Rationale of act-on-decision-support.bpmn (Process_ActOnDecisionSupport), lane health-worker, reached only through Event_AddReason, a non-interrupting boundary event on the review that happens when the health worker taps “add a reason”. Opt-in, skippable, and skipped by default. It is never required to finish the review, the visit or the process: the diagram starts it from a non-interrupting boundary event on the review, which takes nothing from the review, so the care plan is updated without waiting for it. A DAK must not make it mandatory; a programme that needs a reason recorded every time is asking for a different, blocking step, and should draw one. Performed by a person: the health worker who made the decision.

21852.title: Why a Provenance
21852.content: FHIR R4 Provenance is the lightest standard artefact that says who decided what, about which guidance, and why: target the request the decision is about (or the RequestGroup, on a decline), agent the practitioner, entity (role source) the PlanDefinition, reason the coded or free-text reason (a CodeableConcept, whose text carries free text), recorded the time. It adds no workflow state, unlike a Task; it is not a clinical finding, unlike a DetectedIssue; and it needs no recipient, unlike a Communication. When the guidance came as CDS Hooks cards, the system also sends the service the feedback its card asks for (accepted or overridden, with the overrideReason when one was given): that is the CDS service’s copy, the Provenance is the record’s.

21855.title: Refresh materialized remote content
21855.content: Process_RefreshMaterialized · strict · 8 step(s) . Keep a materialized copy of remote content current: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both did — an archival copy is never re-fetched and gets a fixity check instead. One general process, used everywhere. REFRESH IS NOT RE-IMPORT: it needs three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally since, and what to do when BOTH did. upstream-pins.json answers the first for one caller and nothing answers the other two anywhere. An ARCHIVAL copy is not refreshed. Re-fetching it would defeat it: the copy exists to survive the source, so replacing it with whatever the source says today discards exactly the state it was keeping. What an archive gets instead is a FIXITY CHECK — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy. i i i i i i i i

21856.content: . | Called by: Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph | Calls: Adjudication | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

21857.title: Lanes — who acts
21857.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Contributor (human or agent) | user | Reached only when both upstream and local changed, which is the one case this process refuses to resolve by rule: which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, a fact only this lane has. | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Runs whichever of the two paths Gateway_Purpose selects. On the working path it answers the two comparisons — upstream and local — whose combination Gateway_Both reads to decide whether a human must adjudicate; on the archival path it never compares to the source at all, since fixity asks only whether the copy itself rotted. | .

21858.title: Steps
21858.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | ARCHIVAL verify fixity — never re-fetchTask_Fixity | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Re-compute the digest and compare. An archive is NEVER re-fetched — the source is what it exists to survive, so replacing it with today’s version discards the state it was keeping. A mismatch means OUR copy rotted, and the remedy is restoration from a backup, not re-download. | . | WORKING what changed upstreamTask_Upstream | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Compare the recorded upstreamVersion against the source. could not reach the source is a THIRD answer and is never reported as unchanged — an unreachable source is the sourceLoss gate firing late. Reachability is asked by bun run cat sources:liveness <instance> against the node’s resolvable IRI, its Handle first: live, gone, or could not determine, never live on an error. | . | What changed LOCALLY sinceTask_Local | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The half nothing answers today. A materialized copy that was edited in place is not a copy any more, and overwriting it silently destroys work whose existence the process never established. | . | Adjudicate the conflictTask_Adjudicate | Contributor (human or agent) | calls Adjudicationmaterialize-remoteadjudication | A human or agentic decision, never a merge rule. Which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, and a process that picked automatically would be choosing without the one fact that decides it. | . | Reconcile the two by handTask_Reconcile | Contributor (human or agent) | materialize-remote | Neither side wins whole: the contributor produces content that is neither the local copy nor the remote one, and THEN it is applied. Drawn as a separate step before Task_Apply rather than folded into it, because Task_Apply re-asks the five import gates against what is being materialized — and what is being materialized here is a hand-made artefact, which is exactly the case those gates should see rather than be told about. | . | Re-materialize and record new fixityTask_Apply | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The gates are re-asked, not inherited: a licence can change, and a collection can grow past the size a caller agreed to.AND THE NEW FIXITY IS RECORDED IN THE SAME CHANGE. This step rewrites bytes that a materialization record describes, so leaving the old digest behind would make a CORRECT run of this process fail check:materialized-fixity as a mismatch — the gate reading “somebody edited held content without saying so” about the one process whose job is to replace it.This is the publication exception, stated as a rule rather than as a carve-out, because a list of permitted writers goes stale when a writer is added. The exception is NOT “these actors may skip the rule”; it is “say what you did”. A writer that updates the digest alongside the bytes passes, and the record then describes what is actually there. A writer that does not fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream silently. | . | Keep the edit, re-pinTask_KeepLocal | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The local edit wins, so nothing is re-materialized — and the pin moves to the upstream revision that was compared against. Re-pinning is the half that is easy to forget and is the reason this is a step rather than an absence: without it the same upstream change is detected as new on every cycle, and a contributor is asked the same settled question for ever. The record says the copy is deliberately divergent FROM a named revision, which is a different claim from being stale against an unknown one. | . | Record the conflict: no decision, no re-pinTask_RecordConflict | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Both copies stay and the conflict is written down with what each side says. Deliberately does not re-pin, which is the one thing separating it from Task_KeepLocal: the question is unresolved, so it must be asked again next cycle. Recording is not optional here for the reason A_RecordEntry is not optional in an adjudication — a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a check that never ran, and a DEFERRAL nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a refresh that silently did nothing. | .

A process that could only decide would force a contributor with no answer today to invent one. | the remote wins → Re-materialize and record new fixitythe local edit wins → Keep the edit, re-pinneither whole — reconcile → Reconcile the two by handnot decidable today → Record the conflict: no decision, no re-pin | .

21861.title: External registry — confirming a source’s authority
21861.content: Skill registry-authority-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to when a candidate source is checked against the body that publishes it: resolve the identifier through its own API and return the record, so authority is a resolved fact. When the answer is uncertain or absent the verdict is not invented here; the work plan records the citation as unverified. A role played by an external party is held to a contract, not handed instructions. Named by: Evidence for a recommendation . external-registry (declared below this layer) is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this layer’s control. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s evidence diagram relies on, and nothing more.
