22033.title: Review task
22033.content: Generated from cat-harness/processes/content/review-task.bpmn by gen-processes-viz.ts — do not edit here. All processes · cat-harness processes .

22034.title: Roles are swimlanes
22034.content: Skill role-model: Actors, roles and skills — who performs a BPMN task, under which swimlane, with which skills. How a role’s skill set is resolved through inherits and through a subprocess call chain, how a lane binds to a declared role, and how kg:audit finds a dangling skill, lane, role or decision. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration . One sentence carries the whole model: . An actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Six objects, each with a home: . | object | what it is | declared in | . | Actor | a concrete participant. Human, agentic or mechanical. Persists across every process. | scenarios/actors/*.json (the declared scenarios graph, beside the roles) | . | Role | the swimlane — a persona an actor takes on because of the lane it is acting in. Carries a collection of Skills. | scenarios/roles.json | . | Skill | an instruction body: what the actor needs to know to perform the task it was handed. | skills/<pkg>/*.md (naming its input:/output: contracts, usually under schemas/skills/<name>/); JSON SkillDefinitions in each owning layer’s skills/skill-definitions/ | . | Process / Decision | BPMN and DMN. Lanes bind roles; activities name skills; gateways may compute their branch from a table. | processes/**/*.bpmn, processes/**/decisions/*.dmn | . | Requirement | a conformance obligation, pointed at by what discharges it: a skill or capability names the statement in satisfies: req:<id>#<key>. The requirement points at actors (who is bound) and derivedFrom (the broader requirement it specialises). | skills/requirements/*.json | . | Permission | what an actor is allowed to do. Cross-cuts roles. A W3C ODRL 2.2 rule, scoped by Process, Task or Role when it needs to be. | actions: skills/permissions/permissions.json; who holds them: policies/*.jsonld | . WHO’s “actor” is this model’s Role. An actor in the WHO DPI-H Reference Architecture’s conformance model (§3.7.2, an abstract information-processing role) and a DAK generic persona each map to a folio-assistant Role, never to an Actor. The RA’s system realising an actor maps to a mechanical Actor taking on that role. The comparison is on the DAK layer’s findings/dth-terms.md. Schema: schemas/process/role-graph.ts. Audit: scripts/kg-audit.ts, sidecar schema schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts. Not every skill is PERFORMED — consulted: true . Reference material belongs in no lane, by its nature. build-pdf and proof-triage are tasks somebody carries out; directory-conventions, untrusted-input and turn-reporting are what the performer READS. Both kinds are skills; only the first can sit in a swimlane. A skill that is reference material declares consulted: true in its front matter. Absent means performed: the exception is annotated, not the rule, because an axis whose default costs an edit in every skill file does not get adopted. No mechanical signal (a sibling SkillDefinition, an allowed-tools: line) tells the two kinds apart, so it must be declared. It is checked in BOTH directions, which is what stops it being an opt-out. skill-in-role-or-process skips a consulted skill; the separate consulted-skill-not-performed reports one that a role carries or an activity names, because a skill cannot be reference material and a step somebody performs. Which of the two declarations is wrong takes a person, so the criterion reports both rather than choosing. A skill does not carry roles: front matter . Do not write roles: in a skill’s front matter. bun run cat check:retired-front-matter fails if it appears, because copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings the field back. To learn who performs a skill, read scenarios/roles.json; the registry is the only answer that resolves. A role→skill edge for a skill above the harness is an extensions entry in that layer’s role graph (§”A higher layer EXTENDS a role by id”). roles: in a folio-memory/v1 entry is a DIFFERENT field and stays. memoryForRoles filters on tags.roles, and an untagged entry would be seen by every lane. Sharing a key name across graph typologies is not sharing a field, and check:retired-front-matter keys its exemption on $schema, never on the directory. Whether a skill should declare its performer is undecided; if it ever does, the field is declared in the schema before it is written.

22035.title: Why a lane names a role, and the role is not the person
22035.content: A lane is not itself a role: a lane names the Role its tasks are performed in, not an Actor. The same actor is a different thing in two diagrams, and two different actors are the same thing in one. In crdm-requirements.bpmn the session agent acts in Lane_Agent. In bean-lifecycle.bpmn that very same session agent is, from the other diagram’s point of view, the sibling session — the lane that exists precisely to mark what is not yours to close. The skills differ because the lane differs, not because the actor did. So nothing is “a reviewer”. Somebody acts as reviewer, inside a process, for the duration of a lane. An actor carries roles[], never inherits. “Can review” and “can push” are properties of a position, not of a person, so the inherits lattice lives in the role graph. An actor lists the roles it may take on. roles: [] and an absent roles mean different things. [] says the actor takes on no role, which is the honest value for a read-only identity that never appears in a swimlane; absent says nothing has been asserted. The actor-is-not-a-role criterion reports an actor that carries inherits, because a registry written by hand reaches for inherits again. Roles played by mechanical actors are real roles, because the diagrams hand them tasks. Work plan (beans), Corpus, Publish target, a build pipeline and the external registries are roles a machine or an outside party plays. Their skills are their contract: the responsibilities they must perform, which a test can hold them to — a contract skill names its tests in front matter as tested-by:. The QA report lists a mechanical role whose skills name no test as mechanical-role-untested, and role-has-actor asks what actor plays each such role. A store is a mechanical role with a store block, and is drawn as a data store, not a lane. work-plan, corpus, log and session-record keep things rather than do them. Each stays a Role, so its skills are still its contract, and adds store: what it holds (typology ids), its api (one entry per transport, in that transport’s own format: openapi, fhir-capability, graphql, cli tools, json-schema-files, git), what it is realisedBy, and whether it is published. Only a role played by system or external actors may declare one. The role id is the store id: each layer declares <bpmn:dataStore id="<role id>"> once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn, and a process draws a dataStoreReference pointing at it, with dataInputAssociation for a read and dataOutputAssociation for a write. A system that does its own step (validates, decides, returns a result) keeps a lane; one that only keeps what others write is a data store. The same store is an ArchiMate application component (its interfaces, data objects and services hang off it) and, in a FHIR layer, an ActorDefinition of type system whose capabilities or reference points at its API. Some roles perform, but by judgement. stakeholder carries judgementOnly: true: somebody really does sign off, deliberates and is accountable — they simply cannot be handed a procedure that produces the answer. That is a different thing from a mechanical role, which has no judgement to exercise and whose skills are a contract it can be tested against. Do not give such a role a skill. The flag exists because a decision recorded only in a role’s summary is one the next agent re-litigates. activity-names-skill records n/a for activities in its lane, which lets that criterion gate on the undeclared ones.

22036.title: An actor is one of three kinds — human, agentic, mechanical
22036.content: { "id": "ci-pipeline", "title": "CI pipeline", "kind": "system", … } . kind takes one of four values, and three of them are the classification that matters. external is the fourth: a participant outside this layer, which is not ours to task at all. | kind | the kind it names | what it can be handed | . | person | human | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | agent | agentic | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | system | mechanical | a program to run, and nothing to decide | . | external | outside this layer | nothing | . The line is judgement. An agent and a person can both be handed an instruction body and asked to decide something; a mechanical system executes a procedure and decides nothing. That says whether a given step may be given to a given participant, so one value covering an LLM agent and a CI runner alike would leave “which tasks can this actor perform” unanswerable. The vocabulary is declared once, in schemas/kg/skill-package.ts (the zod-only base both the registry schema and the role graph import), and re-exported from schemas/process/role-graph.ts, where it is ACTOR_KINDS. A legacy type still loads, and is never read as agent. An unmigrated downstream registry has not said whether its non-person actors exercise judgement, so they read as system — the reading that refuses a judgement task rather than granting one on a guess. Guessing from an id ending in -agent would put an unreviewed claim into the graph wearing the appearance of data. An unrecognised kind throws: coercing a typo to system would silently disqualify an actor from every task it exists to perform.

22037.title: A task declares which actor kinds may fulfil it — mostly without saying so
22037.content: Tasks can be fulfilled by only certain actor types. activity-fulfilment-kind checks that against the lane’s role, and almost no diagram has to declare anything, because BPMN already answers it and nothing was reading the answer: . | task type | who may perform it | from | . | bpmn:userTask | person | the spec: “performed by a human being with the assistance of a software application” | . | bpmn:serviceTask | agent, system | the spec: “uses some sort of service … a Web service or an automated application” — no human in the loop | . | bpmn:task | nothing asserted | the abstract task says nothing, so neither does the check | . | bpmn:callActivity | nothing asserted | the constraint belongs to the called process’s own steps | . fulfilmentKindsForBpmnType returns undefined for the last two, never []. An empty list would read as “no kind may perform this” and fail every activity drawn as a plain task — the third state, in the place it is easiest to lose. Scoped like activity-names-skill. An activity whose lane is unbound or absent is already reported by lane-binds-role and activity-in-lane, so it is not reported twice here. Override it only when the derived answer is genuinely wrong: . <bpmn:extensionElements> <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment kinds="person agent" reason="a person or an agent drafts this; a pipeline cannot." /> </bpmn:extensionElements> . The reason is required at load time and a reasonless declaration does not parse — the same rule <cat-harness.processes:no-skill reason> follows, and for the same reason. Widening kinds is the cheapest way to make this criterion pass, so silencing it has to cost a sentence somebody reads in the diff. Read a failure as a question with three answers, not one. The task type may be wrong, the lane may be wrong, or the step may really admit that kind — and only the third is a <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment/>. Reaching for the exemption first turns it into a rubber stamp.

22038.title: Three questions about an actor, and only two are answered on the actor
22038.content: // cat-harness/scenarios/actors/admin.json { "id": "admin", "roles": ["programme-manager", "publication-manager", "editor", "author", "reviewer"], "capabilities": ["git-push"] } // policies/folio-defaults.jsonld: a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set { "permission": [ { "assignee": "admin", "action": "role-management" }, … ] } . | question | answered by | scope | . | what may it act AS? | roles on the actor | per lane | . | what may it DO? | ODRL rules in policies/ naming it as assignee | everywhere, or as narrow as a rule’s cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints | . | what does its machine have? | capabilities on the actor | the environment | . What an actor may DO is not on the actor. It is a W3C ODRL 2.2 rule per action in policies/: . | Inheritance. Each action in permissions.json says which broader actions it is includedIn, ending at ODRL’s own (odrl:display, odrl:modify, odrl:execute, …). A grant of a broader action permits everything included in it. The graph need not be a tree and may have cycles. | Scope. A rule may be limited to a Process, a Task or a Role. No constraint means everywhere. | One question, three answers. permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts returns permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. Performing a task in a lane needs the permission and the lane’s role, so eligibility (roles) and permission stay separate, as below. | Anyone. cat-harness:anyone is an unauthenticated reader: a person with no login, whoever they are. It may visualize and render, and nothing else. | . Identity is not here. Which login is which actor is the data store’s to know. No actor file and no policy carries a login, and workflow history names the actor, never the login: the repository owner’s steps are recorded as owner, and the data store maps the login to owner. Who reads all three before a task runs: the BPMN executor. Before any task or decision is recorded, authorizeTask asks whether the actor is authenticated, eligible for the lane’s role (roles), and permitted by policy to perform-task here and on this content. A role mismatch or a deny refuses, and so does unknown, because the engine runs strict. The HTTP routes ask the same policies through src/core/rbac.ts. See task-authorization. Adding a permission: declare the action in permissions.json with its includedIn, then add a rule to a policy in policies/. Never add a permissions list to an actor file: the audit reads it (an unmigrated downstream registry still works), but a list there is invisible to every scoped decision. Permissions do not belong on Role either. A permission cross-cuts: one action is held by actors taking on several different roles, and not by every actor sharing a role. The line that does hold: a skill answers what the performer of this task needs to KNOW, and belongs to the lane. A permission answers what this participant may DO, and travels with the participant through every lane it enters. Both are audited and both are critical — actor-permissions-resolve (which also checks that every policy rule names a declared action and a declared actor or cat-harness:anyone) and actor-capabilities-resolve.

22039.title: Requirements are the fifth node kind, and they only point
22039.content: A requirement is not a skill and not a role. It is an obligation about them, kept in the kg graph so that every agent reads it and its joins are audited: . { "id": "req:commit-hygiene", "derivedFrom": ["req:agent-workflow"], "actors": ["author", "admin"], "statements": [ { "key": "no-secrets", "conformance": "SHALL", "requirement": "Commits SHALL NOT include secrets, API keys, tokens…" } ] } . and a skill that discharges a statement says so in its own front matter: . satisfies: - "req:commit-hygiene#no-secrets" . The statement names no satisfier: a requirement is written once, and what discharges it arrives later, so the pointer lives on the arrival. The references are audited. satisfies-resolves, requirement-actors-resolve and requirement-derived-from-resolves are critical, because a reader following a broken one gets nothing — the same test as a dangling <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>. requirement-statement-satisfied is minor coverage: a statement nothing claims is visible only from the requirement’s side. requirement-statements-graded is major: an ungraded statement is readable, it just cannot be conformance-tested, and SHALL-vs-SHOULD is the whole reason to write a requirement rather than a note. Do not fold a requirement into the skill that satisfies it. The grading, the derivedFrom lattice, the actor binding and the many-to-many satisfies are the only machine-checkable things about it, and prose in a skill doc carries none of them. satisfies is many-to-many in both directions — one skill discharges statements in several requirements — so inlining duplicates rather than relocates.

22040.title: Two compositions, and they are not the same
22040.content: inherits — a role IS-A role. qc-reviewer inherits reviewer and gets its skills everywhere, in every process, forever. Static. resolveRoleSkills closes over it breadth-first, so a skill’s reported via is the nearest ancestor that supplies it. The subprocess stack — a role acting INSIDE another role’s task. A process calls a subprocess and the actor keeps acting: it does not stop being the outer role, it additionally takes on the inner lane’s role. The skills available at that task are the union along the whole call path. resolveRoleStack takes the path outermost-first and keeps each skill’s provenance, because a reader needs to know not only that a skill was available but which level supplied it. resolveRoleSkills(graph, "qc-reviewer") // static: + everything reviewer has resolveRoleStack(graph, ["editor", "viewer"]) // scoped: the union for this call only . Do not merge them. A flat union would make reviewer permanently hold every skill any caller ever had, and a closure that broad cannot fail an audit, which is the same as not having one.

22041.title: A higher layer EXTENDS a role by id — it never edits it
22041.content: A third relation, across layers rather than within one graph. When a skill belongs above the harness (a core cataloguing skill, a sci Lean skill), the role→skill edge naming it must not stay in cat-harness/scenarios/roles.json — that is an upward reference. So the dependent holds the pointer, the way a voice points at the role it addresses and a story at the role it is told as: . // <content-core>/scenarios/roles.json { "name": "<content-core>", "roles": [], "extensions": [{ "role": "librarian", "skills": ["filing-dublin-core"] }] } . | a dependent’s scenarios/ may | it may NOT | . | add skills to a lower role (extensions) | change its title, description, inherits, actorKinds or persona | . | add a NEW role, which may inherits a lower one | redeclare a lower id — refused, “extend it instead” (one exception, below) | . | extend a lower actor: actors/<f>.json with "extends": "<id>", adding roles / capabilities | carry any other field on an extension | . | extend a capability: "extends" adding requires; or add a new probe | point an extension UP or sideways — only at an id declared below it | . The one exception — a move in flight. Moving a role, actor, capability or policy up a layer is two pull requests: the higher layer adds it, then the lower layer removes it, and in between both declare the id. A redeclaration that only adds — every field the lower declaration carries is there unchanged (the same scalar, every member of an array, a nested object by the same rule), and it may carry more, such as the skills it used to add by extension — is accepted with a warning that names the id and both layers, and the higher declaration is used. The warning is the move’s to-do: remove the lower copy. A redeclaration that changes or drops anything the lower one said is still refused. schemas/process/scenario-overlay.ts applies it (checkoutRoleGraph, checkoutActors, checkoutCapabilities, checkoutPolicies; the exception is onlyAdds); the layers are the checkout’s layers that depend on the role’s owner, deepest first. Resolved alone, the harness sees only its own roles. kg:audit, check:raci, check:fallback-roles, check:actor-reach, kg-export and the stakeholder map read the checkout’s view on the platform’s own run. The edge stays on a role graph — the graph of the layer that owns the skill — never in skill front matter.

22042.title: A lane binds its role with partitionElementRef
22042.content: Lane names are free text, and several spellings name one position, so a name alone joins a lane to nothing and an undefined lane is a silence rather than a finding. So a lane binds its role itself, with BPMN’s own partitionElementRef: the role is declared once per diagram as a top-level <bpmn:resource> whose id is the role id verbatim and whose name is its title, before the collaboration and the process. The role lists no lanes: a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one, and a general node never names its users (data-modelling step 8). <bpmn:resource id="reviewer" name="Reviewer"/> ... <bpmn:lane id="Lane_Reviewer" name="Reviewer" partitionElementRef="reviewer"> ... </bpmn:lane> . A <bootstrap.processes:role ref="reviewer"/> in the lane’s extensionElements is read, with a warning, only when partitionElementRef is absent (laneRoleRef in schemas/process/role-graph.ts); the QA report lists it as lane-role-legacy-binding. <bootstrap.processes:role variable="true"/> stays: it declares a performer who is whoever invoked the process. An explicit binding wins over name matching: a diagram that has said which role it means must not be second-guessed by a string table. A ref naming no declared role is a critical finding — it is not quietly name-matched instead.

22043.title: The audit — bun run cat kg:audit
22043.content: One criterion per join in the sentence at the top. The list below is the actor→role→skill→task core; KG_CRITERIA in schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts is the registry, and it is longer — it also covers requirements, skill bodies and the graph as a whole. activity ──names────▶ skill skill-ref-resolves critical gateway ──computes─▶ decision decision-ref-resolves critical lane ──is───────▶ role role-ref-resolves critical activity ──sits in──▶ lane activity-in-lane major task type─can be done by▶ kind activity-fulfilment-kind major lane ──is───────▶ role lane-binds-role major role ──carries──▶ skill role-carries-activity-skill major decision ──is used──▶ gateway decision-outcomes-used major role ──carries──▶ skill role-skills-resolve critical role ──is-a─────▶ role role-inherits-resolves critical activity ──names────▶ skill activity-names-skill minor role ──is used──▶ lane role-binds-a-lane minor actor ──takes on─▶ role role-has-actor minor skill ──any way in▶ anything skill-has-entry-point minor skill ──modelled?▶ role/task skill-in-role-or-process minor actor ──is not a─▶ role actor-is-not-a-role minor . | command | does | . | bun run cat kg:audit | write the sidecars, print the summary | . | bun run cat kg:audit:check | fail on a critical finding, or on a stale sidecar | . | bun run cat kg:audit:strict | …and on major too | . | bun run scripts/kg-audit.ts --json | the full report set, for a tool | . Why sidecars rather than a console report . check-workflow-refs.ts prints and exits, so its previous answer is gone. That makes “this lane has been unbound since the day it was drawn” and “this lane broke in the commit under review” indistinguishable, and a reviewer cannot separate a new defect from inherited debt. The sidecars are committed, under kg-qa/ beside whatever they audit, so the diff says exactly which findings a change introduced. Same argument and same file shape as the block sweep’s *.qa.json and the script sweep’s *.script-qa.json. Where the sidecars for another layer go — hosted, not written into it . A layer that declares no qa directory does not receive sidecars inside its own tree: kgQaHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts them in the auditing harness’s qa directory under the layer’s stub — cat-harness/test/results/bootstrap/ for bootstrap (a working copy, stored on the qa-reports branch with the rest of that qa directory; a JUDGEMENT about it is hosted the same way, under test/attestations/). A verdict ABOUT an layer is the auditor’s output, and bootstrap is the layer that must read cleanly with no harness present. The same holds once bootstrap is its own repository: the verdicts stay with the harness that computed them, against the pinned bootstrap (kg-separation §”The pair”). Three states, and what unknown costs . A criterion returns pass, fail, n/a (does not apply to this subject) or unknown (could not be evaluated — the file would not parse, a dependency was absent). unknown is never written as a pass. It counts as a failure at its criterion’s own severity. It is not promoted to major either: a diagram that will not load records unknown against its critical criteria too, so it still fails the gate, while an unevaluable minor criterion does not gate the build: a gate that fires on something nobody agreed was blocking gets switched off. Severity, and why coverage is only minor . critical is a broken reference — something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. major is a missing join — the graph is intact but a question has no answer, e.g. a lane bound to no role. minor is coverage: a real gap with legitimate instances. A human signing something off is not implemented by a markdown file, so failing on activity-names-skill would force a fake ref onto a real step, which is worse than the gap. Never quote a count from prose — run the audit . A number written in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. Two criteria ask different reachability questions, and only one of them is about the role model: . | skill-has-entry-point — is there ANY way in: servable, in the harness, carried by a role, or named by an activity? The servable clause alone covers nearly the whole corpus, so this passes near-trivially; its green is not an answer to the coverage question. | skill-in-role-or-process — what does the actor → role → task model actually reach? This is the real coverage question, and it must never gate. A skill invoked directly by name is doing its job without appearing in any diagram, and driving the number to zero would mean inventing roles and activities to absorb tools that do not want them. Watch it move; do not read it as a defect list. | .

22044.title: What counts as a skill
22044.content: scripts/known-skills.ts is the single answer, shared by kg-audit and check-workflow-refs so the two cannot disagree. Not every group under a skills directory holds skills: actors/ holds participants, capabilities/ holds environment probes (docker, pandoc, python3), roles/ holds an assignment table and hooks/ holds a shell script. NON_SKILL_GROUPS excludes them, so <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="viewer"/> does not resolve. It is a deny-list of groups known not to hold skills, not an allow-list of local/, so a new group of real skills is picked up automatically and a new group of something else is a one-line addition.

22045.title: Administration IS a swimlane
22045.content: The role graph is the substrate every diagram’s lanes bind to. Changing it — adding an actor, opening a role, granting a permission, retiring a participant — is therefore a process like any other, and it is drawn: actor-role-administration.bpmn, in the administrator lane. Do not invent a role to make a diagram drawable. A role minted for a picture is a role no audit can fail, because nothing was ever true of it — the closure-widening failure of §”Two compositions”, from the other end. What follows from administration being a lane: . |   |   | . | administration is a lane | so role-management is exercised somewhere a reader can find | . | the lane is person-only | a permission grant is a standing decision, not a task; the agentic/mechanical line is judgement, and this one is authority | . | the mechanics are NOT re-drawn | the diagram calls code-change-review; a second description of branch-gates-review is a second thing free to disagree with the first | . | the audit runs after | every criterion is a join, so what an administrative edit breaks is never in the file it edited | .

22046.title: Adding a role
22046.content: . | Add it to scenarios/roles.json with a description that says what the position is, not what it is called. actorKinds is a SET drawn from person, agent, system and external — human, agentic, mechanical, or outside this layer. It is what activity-fulfilment-kind checks the lane’s steps against, so it is a claim about who can actually stand there, not a label. Use title/description (the two labels every knowledge-graph node carries), never summary, and actorKinds, never actorKind: Zod strips an unknown key, so a misnamed field type-checks, parses, and is silently lost. | Bind its lanes: each diagram declares <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> once, and each lane that names this role carries partitionElementRef="<role id>". The role lists no lanes, since a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one (data-modelling step 8). 22049.title: The root README, and the one fact it must carry
22049.content: Skill root-readme: Write the repository’s root README when there is none, carrying a link to the harness that was installed and the overall install status. Never replaces one that exists. It runs only once the install has succeeded. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are the Bootstrapping Agent, and the install has just succeeded. The repository now is a layer instantiating a harness, and — unless somebody wrote one before you got here — nothing at its root says so. People and agents read README.md first, so the README says it.

22050.title: Writing it is not the write the layer rule forbids
22050.content: An instance-readme is read at session start and never written by a running process. That rule governs a process operating on a layer that exists; initialization brings the layer into being, so it may create the README.

22051.title: When it is absent — write it
22051.content: Two things, and no more: . | A link to the harness that was installed. Whatever reference the Requestor gave when the harness was confirmed, resolved to something clickable. | The overall install status. Not one line per location dug out of a log — the question a reader has is “is this repository set up, and as what”, and that is what you answer. Say how many locations the install touched and whether every one of them succeeded. | . Write nothing else: the harness’s own README tool fills the rest, in marker pairs, once it is installed. Say which locations, when there is more than one. “Installed” over three locations where one failed is a false statement about the repository, and the reader who acts on it is the person who set it up.

22052.title: When one is already there — do NOT replace it
22052.content: Add the link and the status inside a marker pair instead, so the harness’s README tool owns that region from then on and the rest of the file stays the author’s. If you cannot tell whether an existing file is authored or a leftover, it is authored: that is the assumption whose failure mode is a duplicated sentence rather than a lost page.

22053.title: What you do not decide here
22053.content: Whether the install succeeded — the install step decided that, and you are on the path where it did. Which harness it was — the Requestor decided that. What the README should eventually say — its author decides that, and you are not its author. If the write fails (no permission, a read-only checkout), say so and end installed anyway: the harness is installed.

22055.title: Sample import
22055.content: Skill sample-import: Testing an import of a SAMPLE of a remote source into a knowledge graph or other structured store: scope it, let materialize-remote gate it, land it in the library (permanent) or the kept, unpublished trashcan (trial), import it, and test the import. The gates are called, never copied. Named by: Sample import into a structured data store . The SDLC for trying out a remote source before committing to it: take a sample, land it, import it into the store you care about, and find out what breaks. The process is cat-harness/library/processes/sample-import.bpmn. IRIS is the worked instance (the IRIS replica); nothing here is WHO-specific.

22056.title: The gates are not here
22056.content: Size, restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss are asked once, by materialize-remote, and this process only reads the outcome. A second copy would be a second answer free to disagree with the first. What each gate refuses on is in that skill. What this skill adds is what happens around it.

22057.title: 1. Scope — three answers before anything is fetched
22057.content: | question | why it is asked first | . | Which items? By the source’s identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning instance’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | the size gate needs a request to measure | . | Which store? The graph or database the import is tested against. | the test in step 4 is against this store’s schema | . | Permanent or trial? | it decides where the copy lands, and moving a landed copy later means moving it under the wrong obligations | . There is no default for the third. An unscoped sample goes back to the person who proposed it.

22058.title: 2. Materialize — call, and branch on the outcome
22058.content: Call Process_MaterializeRemote. referenced (any gate refused or unknown) ends the sample: nothing is imported, and the refusing gate’s reason is recorded so the next attempt does not re-litigate it.

22059.title: 3. Land it where its permanence says
22059.content: A sample that is not intended to be permanent is materialized to fsh-guts/. |   | permanent | trial | . | destination | library/ | fsh-guts/ | . | published | yes, with the library | no — kept, addressable, exported, never rendered | . | refreshed | yes, by refresh-materialized | no — it records what the source looked like when tried | . | provenance | the materialization record | $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1, plus the work item or issue it was written under. Never a movedFrom: it was not moved from anywhere, and inventing one is false provenance. | . Promoting a trial means running the process again with permanent. The gates are asked afresh; a trial’s answers were given for a trial.

22060.title: 4. Import and test
22060.content: Load the landed sample into the store and check: . | completeness — every requested item arrived (count against the request); | identifiers — the descriptor’s authoritative identifiers survived; | structure — each node validates against the store’s schema; | provenance — source, revision and fixity are attached to each node. | . A check that could not run is a failure, not a pass. That is the whole reason the gateway is labelled “no, or could not run”.

22061.title: 5. Record the outcome — every path
22061.content: . | passed → where it landed and what was checked; | failed → which check, on which items, with the evidence. The landed copy stays: a failed import is information about the source or the store, and removing the copy destroys it (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

22070.title: Secure agent permissions
22070.content: Process_SecureAgentPermissions · strict · 6 step(s) . Secure the permissions a coding agent needs to take part in this harness’s processes, from the human who can grant them, and write each grant into the agent Tool’s own configuration through that Tool’s adapter. Nothing in this diagram names a vendor’s file; the adapter for the Tool in use does. Skill: agent-permissions. An agent that edits its own permission configuration is self-modification. MERGE IS NOT A GRANTABLE PERMISSION HERE. 22076.title: Serving a rendering — endpoints, MIME types, and what each host can enforce
22076.content: Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A rendering is what a layer publishes about itself. Running it produces one or more endpoints under that layer’s stub, and every endpoint has a media type that says what it is. This skill is about serving: the rendering already knows what it produced, and the server must say so, or a .jsonld arrives at a client as text/plain.

22077.title: One stub, several endpoints, per layer in the tree
22077.content: artefactStub() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts is the stem: stub when declared, otherwise name. Every artefact a layer publishes is named with it, so a reader who knows the repository knows the filename. The dependency tree is a set of overlaying layers, and each renders under its own stub, so an overlying layer depending on cat-harness means both are present, and both publish. <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld the knowledge graph application/ld+json <base>/<name>/<stub>.json the same bytes application/json <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> each subject's page text/html <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json its declaration's schema application/schema+json <base>/<stub>/ the viewer text/html . So …/folio-assistant/harness.jsonld is the cat-harness layer’s rendering, served from a tree whose root happens to be folio-assistant. A consumer asking for one layer’s graph must not be handed another’s because the paths collided. The graph sits under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included. There is one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document, so a subject’s page <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> sits next to the document that names it. Where each document goes: instance-publication §”What each layer publishes”. <stub>/ is a directory because an extensionless URL has to be. GitHub Pages resolves <base>/<stub> only to a directory index, so the viewer is what makes the bare stub openable. It climbs to the site root and reads the document’s own path, <name>/<stub>.jsonld (exportIdentity’s docPath). It never composes a neighbour’s name, because that relation is not stable across layouts. One function computes all of this, renderingPath() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts. A path a consumer dereferences — or mints as an $id — is never written out as a template literal elsewhere, so moving the renderings is one edit rather than a hunt for copies.

22078.title: Every endpoint declares its media type
22078.content: The declaration is part of the rendering, not of the server. A server is one consumer of it; an MCP server is another; a Link: header generator is a third. Writing the type at each of them is three places to disagree. | extension | media type | why not the obvious one | . | .jsonld | application/ld+json | not application/json. A JSON-LD processor keys off this type to know the document carries a @context | . | .schema.json | application/schema+json | application/json parses, but loses that it is a schema | . | .json | application/json |   | .

22079.title: What each host can enforce — three states, and they are not degrees
22079.content: A local HTTP deployment enforces it. It reads the declared type and sets Content-Type. This is where the declaration is honoured exactly. An MCP server enforces it. When it serves a rendered artefact it uses the declared default media type rather than guessing from the extension — the declaration is right there, and guessing is how .jsonld becomes application/octet-stream. GitHub Pages does not, and cannot be made to. Pages serves by its own extension table with no per-file configuration: no .htaccess, no headers file, no way to say application/ld+json. An unknown extension is served as application/octet-stream or text/plain depending on the extension. That third row is not a failure to fix. It is a property of the host, and the honest handling is the one this repository applies everywhere else: . | Do not pretend. A tool reporting “served with the declared type” must not say so for a Pages URL it did not check. | Do not fall back to a guess that looks authoritative. “Probably application/json” is worse than “this host does not declare one”, because the first is quoted and the second is investigated. | Report “could not enforce” as its own state, distinct from “enforced” and from “enforced wrongly”. | . The architectural boundary between what a static host and a local dynamic server can enforce is part of deployment awareness — see deployment-awareness (opt-in cat-harness.platform-ui) for the four deployment surfaces, their constraints on tool usage, and why render-time escaping is the required line of defence on static hosts.

22080.title: Consequences a consumer must expect
22080.content: A client fetching <stub>.jsonld from Pages will receive the wrong Content-Type. A strict JSON-LD processor may refuse it. That is a known and accepted cost of publishing there, and the remedy is the local deployment. <stub>.json is an alias, not a rename. The same bytes are served at BOTH extensions: .jsonld stays canonical and is what every @id in the document names, while .json is the one path by which a correct Content-Type can come out of a static host. Renaming the artefact to .json instead would trade a wrong type for a wrong name, and the name is the part a reader uses. What that does not license is a .json whose bytes differ, or an @id pointing at it. Two documents asserting the same IRIs is the defect --base-url exists to prevent, and an alias is only an alias while it is byte-identical — which is why the staging build copies it after stamping, so the two cannot disagree about which build they came from.

22081.title: Running one — serve-rendering
22081.content: The media types and the per-host rules are the contract, in code; the server is one implementation that reads it. bun run cat serve:rendering --dir docs/_site # one site at / bun run cat serve:local --repos <repo-a>,<repo-b> # several, fetched from gh-pages . The default address is http://127.0.0.1:4007 (port 4000 is jekyll serve’s). Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost: the two are different origins, so cookies, storage and service workers split between them, and localhost may resolve to IPv6 ::1 first. The server sends localhost and [::1] requests to 127.0.0.1. Several sites on one origin, as Pages lays them out . --mount /<repo>=<dir> (repeatable) serves each built site under its own prefix, so root-relative links and IRI paths line up with https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/. It copies the Pages behaviours links depend on: <dir> redirects to <dir>/, /page serves page.html, and a miss serves the site’s own 404.html. branches/<branch>/ previews in a gh-pages checkout need no extra rule. Published IRIs open the local copy . For each mounted repo, text responses have the published base <origin>/<repo> replaced by the local one as they are served. Files on disk never change. Whole path segments only (/a never touches /ab), and a repo that is not mounted keeps its live links. <origin> is the declared canonicalUrl’s origin; --iri-origin overrides it and --iri /<prefix>=<base> adds a base on another host. Accept: application/ld+json on an extensionless IRI serves its .jsonld sibling, which Pages cannot do. Rewriting changes bytes. Check signatures and digests with --no-rewrite; a rewritten response carries X-Rendering-Rewritten: iri. One command — serve:local . --repos a,b fetches each repo’s gh-pages branch into a cache (shallow, blob-less, sparse, updated each run) and serves them all. branches/ is left out unless --staging <branch> names a preview; a repo with no published main site lists its previews. --site <repo>=<dir> serves a site you built yourself, for changes not yet published. --offline uses the cache as it is. RENDERING_MEDIA_TYPES and renderingMediaType() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts are the table, beside renderingPath(), because where a rendering LIVES and what it IS are the same kind of fact, and a table in code is one no consumer has to re-derive from prose. Obligations are skills/requirements/serving-a-rendering.json, so a second implementation is checkable against the requirement rather than against this one’s source. What a general-purpose static server actually gets wrong . Less than is often assumed, and overstating it is how a working setup gets ruled out: Python’s mimetypes and Bun.file().type both resolve .jsonld to application/ld+json. The gap is one row: .schema.json resolves to application/json in every OS table, because .json is the suffix that matches and nothing knows the compound extension means a schema. Hence longest-extension-first, and hence a declared table rather than the filesystem’s. Containment is part of the contract . A symlink inside the served root can point at a file outside it: the URL is clean, so a lexical path check passes, and resolve() never touches the filesystem. Real paths must be compared. This matters most for the self-sovereign topology, whose published directory sits beside data nobody intends to publish. The server binds loopback unless told otherwise, for the same reason.

22083.title: Session context
22083.content: Skill session-context: What a state machine tracks across a session, as against one process instance. What the record carries, why actor is required and the rest are not, why the session’s view of a node is advisory, and what a sibling session reads it for. A session is one actor working, from the moment it picks up until it stops. A process instance is a token’s position in one diagram. They are not the same object and the difference is load-bearing: . A session starts before any instance, may open several, switches between them, and outlives each. A session with nothing open is the commonest state there is. Model the session as a field on an instance and the first process opened owns facts that belong to the actor — and the idle session, which is most of them, becomes unrepresentable. So it is its own record, referencing instances rather than containing them. Shape: schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts. Graph typology: session-state, layer state — a session writes its own record as it goes, which is exactly what content-context-and-state-graphs means by live state.

22084.title: The fields — read them off the schema, never off this page
22084.content: SessionContextSchema in schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts is authoritative. A field list in prose beside a Zod object is a second answer, wrong the first time somebody adds a field, so this page gives no field count; the sections below say what the main fields are for.

22085.title: actor is required, and it is the point of the record
22085.content: Every other field can be recovered by looking at the repository. Open instances are in the work item graph; claimed work items carry their own status; timestamps can be reconstructed from commits. WHO is acting cannot be derived from anything. The machine keeping the session cannot infer it, which is also why log-message takes actor. A sibling session needs to know who is answerable before it touches the same work item. It is a reference with a declared flag, not an ActorDefinition. An agent may act without a node under the actors graph, and requiring one would make the field unfillable in exactly the cold-start case the record is most useful for. The two facts — an id that resolves and a name nobody declared — are kept apart because a consumer acts differently on each: an audit can follow the first to a role and a permission set, and can only quote the second. And declared is written, not inferred at read time. A reader resolving it themselves gets a different answer than the writer did if the node was added or removed in between, and the record says what was true when the session acted.

22086.title: The rest of the fields, and what each is for
22086.content: | field | for | notes | . | id | naming this session | stable for its life | . | startedAt / updatedAt | telling a live session from an abandoned one | ISO-8601 UTC | . | open[] | which instances this session is inside | empty is normal, not a gap | . | claimed[] | which work items this session announced | by reference, never copied | . | waitingOn | why nothing is moving | what + since, together | . open empty is the normal state. An agent answering a question, reading, or deciding what to do next is in no process at all, and process-state calls that idle rather than broken. A record that treated empty as a defect would report every reading session as one. claimed is by reference because a claim announces rather than reserves. The work item is the authority on its own status (bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)); a status copied here would be free to contradict it, and a sibling reading the copy would act on a claim that had already been released. waitingOn carries since or it carries nothing. A wait with no start cannot be told from abandoned work — the same argument bean-blocking makes for requiring an expiry. what is free text on purpose: a human answer, a CI run, a sibling’s PR is an open set no enum would survive.

22087.title: The session’s view of a node is ADVISORY
22087.content: open[].atNode is what the session believes. The instance wins. The instance is the authority on its own token; this can be stale by exactly one step — the gap between a step completing and the session noticing. It is recorded anyway for two reasons. The commonest question about a session (“what is it doing”) should not need a second file read. And a disagreement between the two is itself worth seeing: a session whose view has drifted from the instance is a session that lost track, which is one of the detectors process-state names for being out of process.

22088.title: Who reads it, and why it is parsed rather than trusted
22088.content: A sibling session, deciding whether a work item is genuinely being worked or was claimed by someone who stopped. A person, asking what is in flight. The session itself on resume, in a fresh container, where the alternative is starting a second session beside the one that already exists. The writer may be an LLM playing the part of a state machine, so the shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary, which is what makes a non-deterministic writer safe to read from. The general rule: where a machine may be played rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced.

22089.title: What this is NOT
22089.content: Not the work plan. A work item says what is being worked on and survives the session; this says who is working and where they are right now. Delete every session record and the plan is intact. Not a log. log-message records what an actor DID at a moment, append-only. This is the current position, overwritten as it moves. A log tells you how you got here; this tells you where you are. Not interaction preferences. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json holds how a person wants to be asked — durable, read at session start, never written by a process. That is context, and this is state: the two are on opposite sides of the layer line and must not be merged, however adjacent they look. Not a store yet. The kind is registered and the shape is defined; nothing writes one, so no directory is declared for it: a declared-but-empty directory makes a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run.

22091.title: Playing a state machine
22091.content: Skill session-state-machine: An agent PLAYING a state machine rather than an engine executing one. Where the non-determinism actually lives, why the diagram stays strict, the cat-harness.processes:judgement marker that makes a judgement point countable, and what the machine must never do on the actor’s behalf. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . An agent can play a non-deterministic state machine as a tool, managing state during a human and agentic discussion. The diagram is processes/process/session-state-machine.bpmn. It keeps a session’s context current across a discussion: establish who is acting, open the record, and on each turn decide whether anything changed.

22092.title: The non-determinism is in the TRANSITIONS, not the shape
22092.content: A machine whose shape were non-deterministic could not be drawn here. The interpreter supports nine BPMN element types and throws on the rest, on purpose: skipping an unrecognised element yields a process that runs, reports progress, and is silently not the process on the diagram. So the shape is strict and enumerable. What varies is which enabled branch the agent takes, and what it writes. An exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision> is computed and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome; one without it means the caller supplies the answer.

22093.title: Saying that a judgement is deliberate
22093.content: A gateway with no decision table can be two different things: . | somebody’s call, which no table can make, and | a table nobody has written yet. | . <cat-harness.processes:judgement reason="…"/> declares the first, with the same three rules as cat-harness.processes:no-skill on activities: the reason is required and a declaration without one does not load; it is refused on anything but an exclusive gateway; and it is refused alongside cat-harness.processes:decision, because a gateway claiming both that a table decides it and that a person does leaves a reader unable to tell which the author meant. Why this matters more than the activity case. A step with no skill is a documentation gap. A gateway with no table is a point where an LLM decides the branch — and how many of those there are, and which, is exactly the question the deterministic-to-agentic spectrum is about (deterministic-and-agentic), and a mechanism that cannot enumerate its own judgement points cannot answer it. check:workflow-refs prints the three-way split (computed, declared judgement, undeclared) from the models. Ask the checker, not this page. An undeclared gateway is a backlog entry rather than a defect: every gateway that predates the marker lands there, and a gate that failed on an un-annotated corpus would be turned off.

22094.title: What the machine must never do
22094.content: It claims nothing. No cat-harness.processes:bean appears anywhere in the diagram. The process RECORDS that an actor claimed a work item; it does not claim one. A machine that claimed on the actor’s behalf would make the claim’s owner unrecoverable — and a claim announces rather than reserves precisely so a reader can tell who announced it. It closes nothing but itself. A_CloseSession records that the actor stopped. It does not resolve work items or complete instances: those outlive the session by design, and a machine that tidied them away on exit would be asserting that work finished because somebody went away. It is advisory, not strict. An agent keeping its own session record must never be refused. A missing update is a gap in a record, not an unauthorised write — and the base content processes are the ones that gate.

22095.title: The two judgement points, and why each is safe to be one
22095.content: Gateway_ActorKnown — only the discussion says who is acting, and it rarely says so in a field. A table would need a name to read; this branch is the reading. Gateway_TurnEffect — whether a turn changed the session’s state is a reading of intent. “I might look at X later” and “start X” differ by nothing a table can key on. Both are safe to be judgement for the same reason, which will not hold everywhere: getting one wrong is recoverable. The next turn corrects it, and nothing downstream has been authorised in the meantime. Contrast the steps the base processes mark relaxable="false" — the editor seeing the findings, the decision, the write, the release authorisation — where a wrong branch authorises something that cannot be un-authorised. Recoverability is one candidate criterion for where judgement is admissible; whether it is the right one is open research (deterministic-and-agentic).

22096.title: Writing state a non-deterministic machine produced
22096.content: The record’s shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care, because the writer is an LLM playing a part. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary. Where a machine may be PLAYED rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced — at the point the value crosses in.

22099.title: Session state machine
22099.content: Process_SessionStateMachine · advisory · 8 step(s) . The shape of a session from the outside: establish who is acting, open a record for them, take each turn in, and write down only what actually changed. You are in this process for the whole of a session, underneath whatever else you are doing — it is the frame the other processes run inside. The first gateway is the one that matters: an agent that cannot say who is acting ASKS, because every later decision about permissions, preferences and language depends on an answer nobody guessed. The distinction between refreshing a timestamp and writing what changed is the diagram’s whole content. A session record that logs every turn as a change cannot be read for what happened, and one that logs none cannot be read at all. i i i i i i i i

22105.title: Site presentation assets — the node is the source, the stylesheet is a rendering
22105.content: Skill site-presentation-assets: A visual fact — a colour, a glyph, a theme — lives in a graph node, and the stylesheet the site serves is a rendering of it. Read before adding a colour, an icon or a theme, before hand-editing any generated stylesheet, and before referencing a generated asset from a page. Named by: Code node review . A visual fact has one home, and it is a node in the knowledge graph. A colour, a glyph, an avatar, a theme’s token set: declared once as data, and the stylesheet the site serves is generated from it: named CSS assets in the graph, never hard-coded colours. Authoring the stylesheet by hand beside the nodes gives two answers to one question, free to disagree silently, because nothing compares a hex triple in a .css file with one in a node.

22106.title: The test
22106.content: Could a reader change this visual fact in one place and be sure the site agrees? . If the answer needs them to remember a second file, the fact has two homes and one of them is wrong.

22107.title: Four rules
22107.content: 1 — Never hand-edit a generated stylesheet. It is build output that happens to be committed, and it is committed only so it is readable on the forge. An edit survives exactly until the next generator run. 2 — Gate staleness, do not trust it. The generator takes a --check arm that compares against the committed copy and fails rather than writing. Put that --check in CI: without it the output drifts, and the drift is invisible because the file looks authored. 3 — A published generated asset needs a Tool that maintains it. Otherwise the provenance is unreachable: nothing can answer “which node produced this stylesheet”, and the asset becomes the third case in covered-is-not-reachable — a mechanism nobody can find. Declare the artefact by its published path, and check that something actually publishes it before claiming so. 4 — An asset reference resolves; it is never composed. A page that names a generated asset must reach it relative to its own location, so the same bytes work at the canonical base and under a staging prefix with no configuration. A page that composes the URL from a base needs a different build per environment, and a staging build that differs from what ships is testing something else. An address may be relativized. A name may not — a JSON-LD @id or a schema $id is an identity, and relativizing it changes what the document claims to be, resolving against whatever URL happened to serve it.

22108.title: Themes are token sets, not stylesheets with branches
22108.content: A theme declares tokens — the named values a stylesheet reads. Light and dark are two valuations of one token set, not two hand-maintained blocks that drift apart. So a new colour is a token on the node, and the generator decides how it reaches CSS. Adding a @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) branch by hand to cover a value the node does not carry is rule 1 broken with extra steps: the node still does not know about the colour, so the next layer to render it gets the light value in the dark.

22109.title: The third state applies here too
22109.content: An asset whose presence cannot be determined — the site not built, a fetch refused — is not present. Report it as could-not-determine and do not let it clear the assets the check did not reach. A generated asset that silently went missing renders as an unstyled page, which looks like a design choice rather than a failure.

22110.title: What this skill does not cover
22110.content: . | Prose voice and tone — one-voice-style-guide. | Whether a rendered block LOOKS right — that is a content question, and the rendering auditor’s. | How a link is spelled — readme-sections §”On link style — raw is not the private-repo answer” (summarised in the agent-memory entry link-style-raw-is-not-the-private-repo-answer). | . This skill is only about the direction of authority: the graph decides, the stylesheet reports. It names no script, because a skill written to give a command somewhere to point passes every check and teaches nothing.

22112.title: Adding a skill
22112.content: Skill skill-registration: Adding a skill is never a one-file change. What a new skill file owes, the one command that performs the derived half, the one declaration it deliberately leaves to you, why running it once is not enough, and the two orphan directions it reports rather than fixes. Read this before adding, renaming or removing a skill. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . One command, before you commit: . bun run cat skill:register . It generates everything derived from the skill and verifies each artefact landed. bun run cat skill:register:check is the same question without writing, and it is a gate — a skill that arrives undeclared fails CI. skill:register, singular. If you find skills:register in older text, it means this.

22113.title: What a skill file owes, and why you cannot see it
22113.content: Three things nothing derives for you, and none of them is in the file you just wrote: . | artefact | where | produced by | . | a skills entry | the package’s package-manifest.json | you — see below | . | a published reference page | the site’s reference/skill-instructions/<name> | skills:docs | . | a kg-qa sidecar | test/results/kg-qa/skills/<pkg>/<name>.kg-qa.json — the working copy | kg:audit | . The kg-qa sidecar is a derived QA result, and its record is not the committed file. The CI job qa-publish stores every run’s test/results/ on the orphan qa-reports branch under main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. The file is also committed on main and kg:audit:check reads it, so skill:register writes it — but a judgement about your skill (an agent’s voice review, a pair attestation) does not go in it: that is test/attestations/kg-qa/…, on main, because no writer can regenerate it. Then a cascade: the schema reference, the glossary and its SKOS export, the auto-docs index and the detangle measurements all read something that just changed. The reason this needs a skill at all is that the feedback arrives somewhere else. CI judges the merge of each pull request’s head into the base, so an undeclared skill on main fails the gate set on every open pull request — and the author who sees the failure is whoever opens the next one.

22114.title: The manifest entry is yours, on purpose
22114.content: skill:register will not add it. Which package a file belongs to is your assertion, not a derivable fact, and a command that guessed it would register files somebody was still drafting. The command names the file and the remedy; you add the slug, sorted. Everything else it either performs (the derived artefacts, and stripping a retired key — see below) or reports and leaves alone. One exception to “commit what it writes”: skill:commands, one of its steps, writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. That directory is a projection CI writes (harness-projections), so leave its changes unstaged and let the workflow commit them.

22115.title: A new folder is a named subgraph of its harness — declare it
22115.content: If what you are adding needs a new folder, decide first which of three kinds of folder it is. Each has exactly one way to be declared, and the place the folder sits decides which: . | A folder directly under the harness root (a new code area, a new graph): an entry in the harness’s own declaration (<harness>.json, e.g. cat-harness.json), under directories, with an id, the path, its graphTypologies and a one-line description. | A folder inside a folder the harness already declares: declared from within, in that directory’s own <dir>.json (as skills/skills.json declares voices). This is not a matter of taste: check:layout-norms fails a new top-level entry whose path lies inside another declared directory (the pairs it only lists are a baseline). Add subgraph: true when the new folder is a subgraph of the LAYER rather than a part of its parent’s graph (voices is the first kind, beans.json’s defs the second). | A folder that holds ONE node — one Tool, one voice: it is not declared. It sits inside the declared graph that owns the node and is found through that graph’s reader, as each voice folder is found by its voice.json. Never declare one Tool’s folder as a tools directory: discovery refuses a harness that declares two tools directories. The Tool’s folder is found by the loader (toolsFromFolders, in the tools layer), as each voice is by its voice.json. | . Both declared forms say what a folder holds the same way, by its graphTypologies: a from-within entry names its own kind (voices.json declares vendors as voice-vendors), it does not inherit its parent’s. One folder per Tool, always. A Tool is declared in tools/<id>/<id>.json ("$schema": "tool-definition/v1") inside the harness’s declared tools directory: the folder, the file stem and the Tool’s id are one string, and the folder also holds whatever is that Tool’s alone (its script, fixtures, tests). toolsFromFolders refuses a folder that breaks the convention. The tools/ directory is data only; the loader and shared helpers live in the tools layer. The JSON-LD of each Tool (<doc dir>/tools/<id>.jsonld, its own IRI) and the JSON Schema of each I/O type are written when the site is published, never committed. Why declaring is part of the process, not tidying: . | A folder nothing declares is a folder nothing reasons about. No check catches it for you: check:undeclared-files sweeps the repository root only, so a new undeclared folder inside a harness passes it. | Declared directories are what can be mounted and exported. A remote mount lays down declared directories only, so an undeclared code folder is missing downstream. A harness’s package exports are derived from its declared, shipped code directories (check:package-exports), so an undeclared one cannot be imported by package name either. A from-within id can be mounted on its own (remote-mount resolves it through instanceDirectories). | bun run cat harness:dirs then materialises every declared directory, so the folder exists in every checkout rather than only in yours. | .

22116.title: Why one pass is not enough
22116.content: skill:register runs each writer and then re-runs every :check on its own to assert the artefact landed. That second pass is the point: a writer can exit 0 over an artefact it failed to update, and only the :check form catches it. Do not re-derive the chain through bun run cat gates. bun test runs the detangle and kg-audit writers, so by the time those checks execute the artefacts are already repaired. A chain measured through gates comes out two steps short, and both omissions look correct. Do not recall the list from memory: recall goes wrong in both directions, naming steps that adding a skill does not stale and omitting ones it does. Each step in the command was measured red-then-green in isolation. Add one only with the same experiment, and put the measurement in the docblock. One pairing is worth knowing because it reads like a typo and is not: glossary:page is verified by check:glossary, which is that same script with --check. glossary:check is a different program over the SKOS projection. Do not “fix” the pairing to make every check end in :check.

22117.title: Do not re-add roles:
22117.content: roles: is retired front matter: nothing reads it, and the actor ids it named do not exist. Copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings it back, so skill:register strips it and tells you it did — safe to perform automatically, since a retired key carries no author intent to guess at. A field saying who performs a skill must be declared in the schema before it is written.

22118.title: Removing or renaming a skill: two orphans, and they are yours
22118.content: skill:register reports these and does not fix them. That is deliberate, not an omission. | A manifest entry with no file. kg:audit calls this manifest-skill-exists at severity critical. Pruning it automatically would decide, on your behalf, that nothing referenced the name — and KNOWN_DANGLING in skill-manifest-coverage.test.ts is empty on purpose “so a future entry is added here consciously, with the reason, instead of the check being loosened”. | A derived artefact whose subject is gone. kg:audit reports SUBJECT GONE and refuses to delete it. That is deletion-requires-confirmation: an agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. No amount of regenerating settles it, which is why the command reports the check as still red rather than looping. | .

22119.title: What this does not decide
22119.content: Whether a skill should exist, what it should say, or which package it belongs in. This is about the declarations a skill owes once you have decided to add it. For where a new thing goes at all, start at where-does-this-go.

22121.title: Skill voice review
22121.content: Skill skill-voice-review: Reviews a skill against a voice that judges skills — the base agent-skill-authoring voice or a vendor override such as Claude’s, Gemini CLI’s or OpenAI’s — rule by rule, with each rule’s citation open, and records the verdicts with voice:review. Use when skill-voice-review-current reports a skill never reviewed or reviewed before the skill or the voice changed, or when asked whether a skill follows a vendor’s authoring guidance. The agent half of that axis; the mechanical half, in scripts/skill-voice-review.ts, only says whether a current review exists. Named by: Code node review .

22122.title: What this axis is, and what it deliberately is not
22122.content: A voice whose rules declare appliesTo: ["skill"] judges skill files. In agent-skills that is the shared base agent-skill-authoring and one override per vendor under skills/voices/vendors/ (vendors/vendors.json lists them), each extending the base. A voice counts only once the harness config activates it (voice.active in its index.config.json entry) — the same switch every other voice uses. The boundary: an agentic review, with no formal gate on rule content. “Best practice” drifts, and a vendor describing its own product is an assertion, not evidence. So: . | the criterion skill-voice-review-current (minor, gated by nothing) asks only whether a review exists for the skill and voice as they are now; | a rule you judge fail is recorded in the skill’s attestation file and printed — it is not a finding, and it must not be turned into one here. | .

22123.title: Reviewing one skill against one voice
22123.content: . | Print the rules you are judging, resolved through extends: . bun run cat voice:review -- --rules agent-skill-authoring-claude . A vendor voice lists its own rules and the base’s, because an inherited rule keeps the scope it was declared under. | Open each rule’s citation before judging it. Every rule carries the library entry, page and quote it was read from. Uphold a verdict from the source, never from the one-line title: the title is a summary, and the rule is what the quote says. | Judge the skill as the platform would load it — the front matter the router sees, the body, and the files the body points to. One verdict per rule: . | verdict | when | note | . | pass | the skill does what the rule asks | optional | . | fail | it does not | required — what is missing, where | . | n/a | the rule cannot apply to this skill (a scripts rule, and the skill has no scripts) | required — why not | . n/a is not a softer fail. If the rule could apply and the skill does not meet it, that is a fail with a note. | Record it — the writer refuses a set that misses a rule, judges one twice, or leaves a fail/n/a unexplained: . bun run cat voice:review -- --sidecar <instance>/test/results/kg-qa/<skill path>.json \ --voice agent-skill-authoring-claude --by agent --verdicts verdicts.json . verdicts.json is [{ "rule": "<id>", "result": "pass"|"fail"|"n/a", "note": "…" }]. The review pins the skill’s content hash and the hash of the voice’s skill rules, and replaces any earlier review of that skill against that voice. --sidecar names the subject, not where the review is written. A voice review is a judgement, so it is kept as voice_reviews in the skill’s attestation file, <instance>/test/attestations/kg-qa/<skill path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main — not in the derived kg-qa sidecar, whose record is on the qa-reports branch. Commit the attestation file. A store that cannot be read is UNKNOWN and the writer refuses rather than overwriting it. | Run bun run cat kg:audit so the sidecar’s criterion reads the new review from the store. | .

22124.title: When the criterion reports stale
22124.content: A review goes stale when the skill changes or the voice’s skill rules change. The earlier review is kept, not deleted — it is evidence of what was checked — and the finding stays until a new review replaces it. Re-review the whole voice rather than patching the one rule you suspect moved: a changed skill can break a rule nobody was looking at.

22125.title: Fixing what you found
22125.content: A fail verdict is information for whoever owns the skill. Editing the skill is a separate change with its own review. Do not edit a skill to make your own verdict pass in the same step: record the verdict first, change the skill, then review again — so the sidecar shows both states.
