22256.title: Theme art intake
22256.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

22257.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
22257.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

22258.title: The constraints
22258.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

22259.title: Refuse, report, or neither
22259.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

22260.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
22260.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

22261.title: Reading the report
22261.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . 22265.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
22265.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

22266.title: What it reviews
22266.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the layer’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

22267.title: What this gives up — accepted
22267.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

22268.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
22268.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

22269.title: Measure; do not assert
22269.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

22270.title: Branding is a question about the LAYER, not about taste
22270.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the layer’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

22271.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
22271.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

22272.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
22272.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

22273.title: What this does NOT cover
22273.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

22274.title: Both viewports, always
22274.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .

22282.title: Todo Review Skill
22282.content: Skill todo-review: Monitor and triage open feedback across all content blocks. At session start, ask the author if they’d like to work on feedback. Provide overview, let them pick a chapter/section, then review and iterate until done. Named by: Adjudication, Wireframe design review, Public comment on a review draft, DTH authoring . Disambiguation: . | todo-review (this file) = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ (paper-scope; persistent across sessions; surfaced via /todos dashboard). | todo-manager = the agent’s session work-plan via work items (durable, committed under beans/). | . Both can be active in one session: the agent’s work-plan (todo-manager) may include “process N feedback items via todo-review” as a single task.

22283.title: Where the feedback came FROM — this skill starts mid-air without it
22283.content: Materialized content (held by reference or materialized from elsewhere) is read-only; a reviewer cannot annotate it in place. The first step of review is copy-out-materialized (diagram: library/processes/copy-out-materialized.bpmn): the reviewer copies the materialized sub-graph into their own folio/, carrying provenance.local back to the original, annotates the copy, and those annotations arrive here. While triaging: . | Feedback is on the COPY, not on the original. Resolving an item edits the copy. The original still hashes to its recorded digest, and check:materialized-fixity fails if somebody annotated held content in place. | provenance.local makes a resolved item traceable to the thing it was about; without it the copy is indistinguishable from original work one rename later. | .

22284.title: Role
22284.content: Monitor open feedback across the manuscript. At session start, offer a structured todo workflow. Provide triage, context-aware selection, and a feedback cycle until the author is satisfied.

22285.title: When to Use This Skill
22285.content: . | Session start (automatic): ask if author wants to work on feedback | User asks: “show todos”, “what feedback is pending”, “review todos” | User asks: “what needs attention”, “any open items”, “work on todos” | After completing a block of work, to check if related items can be closed | .

22286.title: Feedback Storage
22286.content: Feedback lives in feedback/<paper-dir>/ (tracked in git, committed to main via worktree). Each content block with feedback has a TypeScript file: . feedback/ <paper-dir>/ <block-a>.ts <block-b>.ts ... Each file exports an array of FeedbackItem (extends TodoItem with author/authorEmail): . import type { FeedbackItem } from "../../schemas/types"; export default [ { "id": "todo-mn159z53", "summary": "short description of the issue", "comment": "longer description of the issue", "status": "open", "priority": "medium", "origin": "human", "assignee": "editor-agent", "createdAt": "2026-03-22T02:35:33.543Z" } ] satisfies FeedbackItem[]; .

22287.title: Session Start: Todo Workflow
22287.content: When the editor skill enters the session start protocol and open feedback exists, follow this flow: . Step 0 — Offer the todo workflow . Present a brief overview and ask: . You have N open feedback items (X critical, Y high, Z medium). Would you like to work on feedback today? . Options: . | Yes, let’s review feedback → proceed to Step 1 | No, I have something else in mind → exit to normal triage | . Step 1 — Overview and scope selection . Show a quick summary grouped by chapter: . ## Feedback Overview | Chapter | Open | Critical/High | Sample |---------|------|---------------|--------| Ch 1: Introduction | 12 | 3 | "this does not need to hold in general" | Ch 4: Methods | 4 | 1 | "missing cross-ref to prior section" | Ch 11: Results | 6 | 0 | "clarify the derivation" | . Then ask: . Where would you like to start? . Options (dynamically generated): . | High priority first — all critical + high items across paper | **Ch N: ** — one option per chapter that has feedback | Show all — flat list sorted by priority | . Step 2 — Present the selected feedback . Show the filtered items as a table: . ## Open Feedback — Ch 1 (12 items) | # | Priority | Block | Summary |---|----------|-------|---------| 1 | high | initial-conditions | this does not need to hold in general | 2 | high | main-point | need a supporting statement for the claim | 3 | medium | core-definition | clarify notation convention | ... | . Ask: Which item(s) would you like to address? (pick by number or “all”) . Step 3 — Review and address each item . For each selected feedback item: . | Show the feedback — full comment, author, date, priority | Read the block — load content/<paper>/<chapter>/<rootName>.md and .ts manifest for context | Propose a fix — suggest specific edits to the .md content | Ask for approval — show the proposed changes and ask: Does this address the feedback? (yes / revise / skip) . | Apply if approved — edit the file, mark todo as in_progress | Iterate if “revise” — ask what to change, re-propose | . Step 4 — After each item, offer next steps . After completing (or skipping) an item: . Done with “this does not need to hold in general”. What next? . Options (context-aware): . | Next item on this block (if more exist) | Next item in this section/chapter | Back to overview — re-show the chapter summary | Done for now — exit todo workflow | . Step 5 — Wrap up . When the author says “done” or all items in scope are addressed: . Session feedback summary: . | Reviewed: 5 items | Addressed: 3 (edits applied) | Skipped: 2 | Remaining open: 9 | . The addressed items are marked in_progress. You can resolve them from the viewer feedback panel when you’re satisfied with the changes.

22288.title: Resolving Feedback
22288.content: Only the human author may resolve or remove a FeedbackItem. Agents must never set status to resolved or wontfix, and must never delete items. Agents may set status to in_progress after making edits. Resolution happens in the viewer’s feedback panel (click the status badge on any feedback item).

22293.title: Reference
22293.content: The authoritative documentation is docs/guides/translation-support.md. Read it before using this skill. This file is the operational checklist, not the architecture.

22294.title: The two-axis model
22294.content: A content node varies along two axes: . | Format — .md (Markdown), .lean (Lean 4), .tex (LaTeX), .bpmn, .dmn, etc. | Language — BCP 47 locale tags (en, fr, es, ar, zh, ru). | . The format axis is handled by companions. The language axis is handled by the PO/POT pipeline with TranslationNode manifests in translations/<locale>/.

22295.title: TranslationNode — .po/.pot files as KG nodes
22295.content: Each .po/.pot pair is wrapped by a .ts manifest that makes it a first-class node in the knowledge graph: . import type { TranslationNode } from "../../schemas/translation"; const node: TranslationNode = { label: "trans:fr/index", locale: "fr", sourceFile: "docs/index.md", potFile: "translations/fr/index.pot", poFile: "translations/fr/index.po", status: { locale: "fr", official: false, generatedBy: "agent" }, coverage: { translated: 37, total: 37, pct: 100 }, }; export default node; . The manifest carries the status, coverage, and QA results inline — no separate status.json or .qa.json files.

22296.title: PO source resolution (fallback behavior)
22296.content: Content blocks can declare explicit PO sources via poSources[] on BlockBase. When not declared, the pipeline resolves by convention: . | Block-level: translations/<locale>/<block-stem>.po | Chapter-level: translations/<locale>/<chapter-slug>.po | Folio-level: translations/<locale>/global.po | Dependency walk: walk <name>.config.json dependencies depth-first | . When poSources is declared, only the listed files are consulted (no fallback). Later entries override earlier for the same msgid.

22297.title: What is translatable
22297.content: | Content | Translatable? | Notes | . | Block titles | ✅ | From .ts manifests | . | Prose bodies (.md) | ✅ | Segmented by paragraph | . | Chapter/section titles | ✅ | From chapter.ts / section.ts | . | Kind headings | ✅ | “Definition”, “Theorem”, etc. → locale catalogue | . | LaTeX math | ❌ | Universal notation | . | Block labels | ❌ | Structural identifiers | . | Code blocks | ❌ | Programming language content | . | Lean companions | ❌ | Formal mathematics | . | FHIR resources | ⚠️ | Use FHIR’s own designation system, not gettext | .

22298.title: The exported GRAPH per locale
22298.content: The graph a machine consumes is translated per locale, not only the rendered page: bun run cat kg:locale writes it (kg:locale:bootstrap for the nested layer, kg:locale:check in the gate set). Four rules; an implementation breaks the first by default. 1. The core graph must not reference its translations. No hasTranslation, no availableLocales, no translationOf, no per-locale @id, no locale key in the @context. The obvious implementation hangs a pointer off each node; that grows the core by an edge per locale per node and makes bootstrap’s graph reference artefacts it does not own and cannot validate. The arrow runs one way — a per-locale document references the core, never the reverse — and the core is complete with no translation existing. The same relation board-diagram-interchange states for a board and its folio. localeDocumentsUnreferenced checks it rather than trusting it. 2. A translated node keeps its @id. A translation is not a new term. Locale-suffixed IRIs are ruled out by that, not chosen against. 3. The language tag rides the VALUE, never the document. A blanket "@language": "fr" would assert French over every string that fell through — and fall-through is the normal case, because parsePo takes only non-empty msgstr and skips fuzzy entries. A translated value is {"@value": …, "@language": …}; a fall-through stays a plain string under the document’s declared sourceLanguage. Fall-through is then visible in the data rather than inferable from a coverage number. 4. A catalogue is scoped to the asset it was extracted from. Merging every .po under a locale lets a docs page’s "yes" → "oui" translate every BPMN gateway branch label — output that looks right while no diagram catalogue exists, so it can only be caught by provenance, not by reading the output. So a .po is read only when its stem names an asset the graph projects. A residual is accepted and named: a msgid from diagram A applies to an identical string on a node from diagram B — not a new assumption, since kg-export already dedupes lane-derived Role nodes by lane name across every diagram. What the gate is not. kg:locale:check says nothing about how much is translated. Where a diagram template has no .po in a locale, the exporter writes nothing and reports the locale saying so. A locale with nothing to say is reported, never a missing file a reader cannot tell from a broken build; --all-locales emits a source-language copy per locale for the other reading.

22299.title: Workflow
22299.content: 1. Extract (POT generation) . bun run pipeline/pot-extract.ts [--chapter <dir>] [--block <label>] . Or use the translation_extract MCP tool. Produces .pot files at the configured granularity. 2. Build the locale term base, and review it . Before translating, build the term base for the target locale from the layered glossaries, review it, and translate with it. See The locale term base for where each layer’s glossary is and the precedence rule. The term base is the merge translation:glossary:check checks against, so build it the way that check does, not by hand from one layer. Review it before you use it: a term the more authoritative layer has fixed is not re-translated, and a term with no fixed form in any layer is a decision you make once, here, not again in every block. 3. Translate . Translate with the term base open. Options, in order of preference: . | Existing .po from SMART Base — if the DAK already has translations from Weblate/Crowdin, use them. | FHIR/translation-utils — the po-translate CLI for batch machine translation via DeepL/Google Translate. Tags results # fuzzy. | Agent translation — LLM translation of .pot → .po. Also tagged unofficial. | Human translation — the gold standard. | . Modal strength: a recommendation stays a recommendation . A lowercase should is a recommendation, and its translation is the locale’s recommendation form, never its obligation form. Turning it into “must” strengthens the claim, and in a guide it then reads as a conformance rule. Lowercase must, shall and needs to are obligations. The uppercase BCP 14 keywords (RFC 2119, RFC 8174: MUST, SHALL, SHOULD, MAY) keep the fixed renderings the locale’s term base gives them. | locale | should (recommendation) | must / shall (obligation) | . | ar | ينبغي، يُستحسن | يجب | . | es | debería, se recomienda | debe | . | fr | devrait, il est recommandé de | doit | . | ru | следует, рекомендуется | должен | . | zh | 应当, 宜, 建议 | 必须 | . A brief may not normalise one into the other, for consistency or anything else. A lexical round-trip screen cannot see this shift either: the words of a back-translation overlap whether it says “should” or “must”. So the adjudicator reads every string whose source has a modal (see “What counts as drift”). 4. Inject (PO → translated Markdown) . bun run pipeline/po-inject.ts --locale <locale> [--chapter <dir>] . Or use the translation_inject MCP tool. Reads .po files and produces translated .md in docs/<locale>/ for docs pages, or in the content directory for content blocks. 5. Create TranslationNode manifest . After injection, create or update the .ts manifest: . # The pipeline does this automatically, or create manually: translations/<locale>/<stem>.ts . The manifest carries status, coverage, and round-trip QA results inline. Validate with TranslationNodeSchema from schemas/content/translation.ts. 6. Round-trip QA . After injection, run round-trip translation QA: . bun run pipeline/translation-qa.ts --locale <locale> . Or use the translation_validate MCP tool for coverage and staleness. Semantic verification is per block and lives in the sidecar, not in a node-level summary field: TranslationNode.roundTripQA was removed with the numbers it held. See §”Per-block translation QA” below, and route drift to a human reviewer. 7. Glossary consistency . After translating, check that every glossary term was translated the way the term base fixes it, and the same way everywhere: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> . The check enforces a fixed term wherever the source uses it in its glossary sense; see The locale term base for how the sense is decided. It exits 1 on an in-sense use whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation. A use still pending adjudication is listed and fails nothing. To have the pending uses ruled on, list them for the adjudicator and record the answers: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --pending --json bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --record <verdicts.json> . Fix each violation in the .po, not in the injected output, and re-inject. Then include the check’s glossary section in the KG QA report, so the reviewer who signs off sees it. That section lists violations, exceptions, pending uses and other-sense uses. A violation the translator believes is right is not fixed by editing the term base in the layer: a term a lower layer fixes is changed in that layer, or it goes to the adjudicator. 8. Sign-off . A human reviewer signs off at the desired level: . bun run pipeline/translation-signoff.ts --locale <locale> --level <block|section|chapter|folio> [--path <content-path>] . Or use the translation_signoff MCP tool. Updates the TranslationNode manifest with sign-off metadata and source hash. 9. Staleness watch . On every content change, the pipeline checks whether any official translation’s sourceHash no longer matches the source .md. Stale translations are flagged in the viewer and in translation_status output.

22300.title: Translating into several locales as a team
22300.content: The workflow above is one catalogue’s life. When several locales are produced from the same source at the same time, by several translators, the steps are the same and the order around them matters more. The process is multi-locale-translation.bpmn, with its round trip in translation-round-trip.bpmn and its upkeep in translation-refresh.bpmn, whose steps the translation-refresh skill gives as commands. Five lanes: the owner (scope, merge window, sign-off), one source-language lead, one locale translator per locale, a back-translator and a round-trip adjudicator. Extract once, and merge the source first . The source-language lead extracts every template once: the pages, the diagrams (translate-bpmn --extract, which writes this harness’s own diagrams into its own translations/) and the glossary schemes. All of them go into one source PR to main, and it merges before any locale starts, so every translator branches from the same main. A translator never re-extracts. A locale that seems to need a different template has found a defect in the extraction, and that is reported to the lead. Each locale is its own PR to main . Each locale lands as its own PR, based on main and targeting main. Never into the source branch: a PR into an unmerged branch lands only when that branch does, and a branch that has merged and then receives more commits carries work main will never see. Once a source PR has merged, its branch receives nothing more; a later source fix is a new PR. What a locale contributes . | translations/<locale>/**.po, mirroring the templates’ layout. | A translation-node manifest beside each catalogue, official: false, generatedBy: "agent" (or "human"). No status.json: status is a property of the manifest, and officiality is a person’s sign-off, never the translator’s. | FHIR terms as CodeSystem supplements, one file per locale, holding the locale’s designations for every code system it translates. Never an edit inside a resource: an inline designation is a change to the source, every locale’s edits then collide in the same file, and the supplement is the mechanism FHIR has for exactly this. The supplements must compile with no SUSHI error and pass their structural checks (each one names the code system it supplements, at its version, and carries only codes it defines). | Source-text errors are reported, never fixed in the translation. The translator renders the source as it stands and notes the location; the lead files every such note as one issue on the source. A fix to the source is a source PR, and the next refresh carries it to every locale. | . The deterministic gates . Before any round trip, every gate passes: . | gate | command | . | templates current | translate-bpmn:check, and the layer’s page and glossary template checks | . | every catalogue matches its template | translation:drift:check --instance <root>, translation:obsolete:check --instance <root> | . | coverage | translation:status --instance <root>; a published page has its catalogue: translation:catalogue:check | . | placeholders, tags and URLs preserved | translation:page-qa --instance <root> (translation-terms-preserved) | . | officiality agrees | check:translation-officiality | . | the graph per locale | kg:locale:check | . | translated links resolve | translated-links:check | . | supplements compile | the layer’s supplement build: 0 SUSHI errors, structural checks pass | . The untainted round trip, as run . The discipline is untainted-verification and §”The agentic round trip” below; this is how it was run across several locales. | The sample, chosen by the translator before any result is seen: every diagram label, every persona and scenario string, and a seeded random fraction of the rest, with the seed recorded so the sample can be drawn again. A refresh samples only the strings it changed. | The back-translator gets the target strings alone, keyed by an opaque id, and renders them into the source language with no tools. | A mechanical pre-screen over every (source, back-translation) pair flags a pair whose negation, modal, quantifier, number or code tokens differ, and a pair whose word overlap is low. It only orders the reading. | The adjudicator reads every flagged pair in full, with the source and the back-translation and never the target, and rules each drift or not drift with its reason. | Both halves are stated. Drift: a claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed; a term of art swapped for one that means something else; a named entity, number or quantifier moved. Not drift, and the cases that came up most: inflection; a purpose clause rendered in the subjunctive (Russian чтобы + past tense reads back as “so that … would”); an acronym left uninflected in a language that inflects nouns; an acronym spelled out with the acronym kept beside it. | Each drift is fixed on the locale’s PR, and the fix is noted beside the ruling. When two separate parties cannot be dispatched, the producer records “could not dispatch” with the reason: never a pass. | . Glossary precedence, and sense checks . The term base is layered, in this order: the normative reference glossaries first (the standards bodies’ own term lists the layer declares), then each layer in the order the index config lists it, and the layer’s own glossary last. A later layer adds terms; it never overrides a translation an earlier one fixed in the same subject area. translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> checks a locale against that merge. A platform term found in text of another subject area (the harness’s policy, say, in a health guide’s prose) is a sense check for a person to read, not a violation. It fails nothing. The QA report, one per locale . Each locale’s report goes under test/results/translation-qa/: beside the per-catalogue sidecars translation:page-qa writes, a report that names coverage, each gate’s result, the round trip (sampled, flagged, drift, not drift, and every drift ruling with its fix), the glossary violations and sense checks, and the source errors reported. The lead reads it before merging the locale’s PR, inside the owner’s merge window. Harness commands for another layer’s catalogues . Every command here reads a layer through its own declaration, so one composed checkout serves every layer it mounts: . | --instance <dir> on translation:drift:check (each locale’s .po against the .pot beside it, in the layer’s translation-sources directory; a layer with no site has its catalogues compared and its pages reported unreadable), translation:obsolete:check (msgids a catalogue carries that its source no longer yields; exits 2 when the layer declares no catalogue directory), translation:index:check (the layer’s own site; exits 2 when it declares no Jekyll site) and translation:status (prints the per-locale table, writes nothing; exits 2 without a translation-sources declaration). | translation:page-qa (translation-block-qa.ts --catalogues): every <translations>/<locale>/<rel>.po with its .pot beside it, not already measured as a block or page, is measured against its template, with a sidecar at test/results/translation-qa/translations/<rel>.<locale>.translation-qa.json in the layer’s QA tree. --instance <dir> sweeps another layer. | po-inject takes its units from segmentMarkdown in pot-extract.ts, the same segmentation the extractor writes the catalogue from, so a wrapped paragraph, list item or blockquote is looked up as the one msgid it was extracted as. | translation:glossary:check is the glossary-consistency command named above. | . Exit 2 from any of them is “could not determine”, and is reported, never read as clean.

22301.title: Per-block translation QA, and the agentic round trip
22301.content: Two sweeps, two subjects, and confusing them is how a site reports a translation nobody measured. | translation-qa-sweep.ts measures the docs site: how much of each page exists in each language. It writes docs/_data/translation-qa.json and feeds the badge under a page title. | translation-block-qa.ts measures a block, one sidecar per (block, locale): <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, in the block-qa/v1 entry shape, which is what the per-block TR icon opens. | . bun run cat translation:block-qa # write the sidecars bun run cat translation:block-qa:check # fail if any is stale . What a script may claim, and what it may not . Three criteria are deterministic and carry a script witness: translation-coverage, translation-terms-preserved (acronyms, numbers and URLs that must survive translation and did not — the class a fluent mistranslation passes) and translation-not-echo (a “translation” identical to its source; a warn, because that is right for a proper noun and wrong for a sentence). translation-semantic-roundtrip is written with no entry. A round trip asks whether the MEANING survived, and that needs a translator that has not seen the original. The only back-translation available to a script here is the PO’s own msgid→msgstr map read backwards, which returns the source exactly, always: a perfect similarity score measuring the lookup table. Do not fill this criterion mechanically. A green tick nobody should trust is worse than a gap that says it is a gap — a reader who sees the tick stops asking. This was not hypothetical. translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator” — a measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the translation. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. The agentic round trip — an INSTANCE of untainted verification . The discipline is generic and lives in untainted-verification: the two parties, why neither may see what would let it shortcut, the TOOLS_USED declaration that is recorded rather than assumed, which party rules, how both are written as witnesses, the model / model_source rule, and the two traps — a sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself, and a verdict is hashed to what it was about. Read that first. This section is only what translation adds. The round trip was where that discipline was first written down, and generalising it turned up a defect in the generalisation: the spine’s UntaintedDispatch was typed over CompanionRole, and po is deliberately not one — a PO is a companion of a (block, locale) pair, not of a block. So the founding case could not be expressed in the type taken from it. The abstraction was widened rather than the case bent; untaintedPartitionDefects now takes its artefact universe as a parameter. The declaration . ROUNDTRIP_DISPATCH in pipeline/translation-block-qa.ts: . | party | sees | never sees | . | back-translator | po — the target text, and nothing else | md, ts | . | adjudicator | md — the original, plus the back-translation | po | . Disjoint, which is the whole rule in one line. Shown the source, a back-translator writes the source back and the check passes vacuously — measuring the lookup table rather than the translation. That is not a warning here any more: untaintedPartitionDefects reports it, and a test asserts it. What counts as drift, and what does not . Both halves, always. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and every translation fails. Synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift. A claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is; so is a term of art swapped for something that means a different thing, and a named entity or quantifier moved. A modal is a claim’s strength: “should” read back as “must”, or “may” as “should”, is drift, however close the words are. This is the part that does not generalise — the spine requires a drift statement and checks only that one exists, because “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the defect the whole mechanism exists to stop. Recording it . bun run pipeline/translation-roundtrip.ts --payload <file.json> . Where it lands: translation-block-qa writes translation-semantic-roundtrip: [] on every run, and before mergeCriteria an unrelated re-run deleted a round trip a pair of agents had produced — silently, with nothing in the output to say so. That incident is why the spine carries the replace-only-your-own rule. Staleness is per locale here: the entries hash the .md, the .ts and the .po, so editing the source stales every locale’s round trip and editing one translation stales only that locale’s. The instrument, not the translation . translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator”. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject.

22302.title: Automatic badge rendering
22302.content: Translation badges are automatically rendered on every docs page by docs-ui.js. There is no need to manually add badge includes or front matter. How it works . | head_custom.html publishes a <script type="application/json" id="fa-translation-meta"> block on every page, reading from page front matter | docs-ui.js reads that block and auto-injects into the page title: . | 🌐 Language coverage badge — 0/5 languages (grey), 1/5 (amber), 5/5 (green) | ⚠️ Unverified warning — auto-injected when translation_status: unverified | . | . Front matter for the translation pipeline to stamp . The translation pipeline stamps this front matter on generated pages: . # Source pages (English): lang: en available_locales: ["en", "fr"] # every locale the page can be read in # Translated pages: lang: fr translation_status: unverified # or "official" translation_source: index.md # source file available_locales: ["en", "fr"] . The locale term base . A glossary term must be translated the same way on every page, and the same way in every layer that uses it. The term base is the one place that says how. Where the terms come from. Each layer’s glossary is the directory it declares with the glossary graph typology in its <instance>.json (a *.glossary.json SKOS scheme per file); a layer without that declaration has no glossary of its own and inherits its dependencies’. The terms’ translations today are the per-scheme catalogues translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po written from those schemes, and the pins in translations/<locale>/glossary.po below. Subject areas. Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Each glossary scheme declares the subject area its translations bind in, as subject (dcterms:subject, a local id such as harness-vocabulary or digital-health-trust); a term may override its scheme’s. A term with no subject, on itself or its scheme, binds only within its own scheme. Precedence applies within a subject area. The term base for a locale is the glossaries of the layer and every layer it needs, merged in layer order: within one subject area, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation; a layer only adds. A layer may add a term no layer below defines, and may fix its translation. It may not give a term a lower layer has fixed, in the same subject area, a second translation; that is a violation, reported by translation:glossary:check, never an override. A term used in sense keeps its fixed translation. Owner, 2026-11-07: if a glossary term is used in the narrative in the correct context, the translated narrative uses the glossary translation. The same word is not always the same concept. The harness’s policy is fixed as 策略 (an access policy), but a health guide’s “policy” is 政策. So the sense of each use is decided by rule first, then by an agent: . | By rule. A use in a page or catalogue whose subject area is the term’s own is in sense automatically. | By an adjudicator. Any other use is pending until an untainted adjudicator agent rules on it. The agent is given the term, its skos definition and the source sentence. It rules in-sense or other-sense with a one-line reason. Alternatively it records an exception: in sense, but the fixed term is wrong here because of a reason it gives. | What the check does with each state. An in-sense use (by rule or by verdict) whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation is a violation, and the check fails. A pending use is listed and fails nothing. An other-sense use is not checked. An exception passes and is listed. | Keeping the English term. A msgstr that keeps the English term verbatim renders it only where the term is part of a code or resource name. The same term left in English in prose does not render it. | Where verdicts are kept. They are stored durably in the layer, in a committed file beside its catalogues. Each is keyed by the term’s id and a hash of the msgid. Sense is a property of the source, so one verdict serves every locale and each use is asked about once. A changed msgid invalidates its verdict, and the use is asked again. | Who decides. Each verdict names who decided it, an agent or person id, never a model. The check itself never asks a model. | . How a fixed translation is recorded. It is derived, never flagged: a term whose status is authored and whose scheme catalogue (translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po) holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel is fixed. There is no #, fixed flag and no translated label in the glossary JSON, so the catalogue stays the one place a translation lives. Whether a person has signed it off is the term’s translationStatus, per locale, official or unofficial (absent means unofficial). A pinned msgstr in glossary.po below is a QA hint, not a term base entry. The terminology glossary — translations/<locale>/glossary.po . translation-terms-preserved can see that a source term is absent from a translation. It cannot see whether that is a correct localisation or a silent loss: WHO missing from a French sentence is either OMS or a dropped term, and guessing either way is worse than saying so. The glossary is how a folio tells it which. | entry | meaning | when the term is absent | . | msgstr "OMS" | the expected form, pinned | fail — the glossary said what it should be | . | msgstr "FHIR" (identity) | must survive verbatim | fail | . | #, localised | rendered in the target language, form NOT pinned | pass | . | no entry | unknown | warn | . #, localised exists so a glossary needs no translated content. Pinning a form means authoring target-language material; the flag says the one thing the checker needs — this term gets localised, I am not pinning how — and it is reviewable by someone who reads only English. Pin a form when you want the stricter check. It is a reading rule and cannot become a mute button, which is the property to preserve if you touch it. localised only converts a would-be finding about that term into a pass: it never reaches strict tokens (a URL or a number consults no glossary — nothing localises a 3), it cannot act on a term it does not name, an entry with neither a form nor the flag is unfinished rather than permission, and each locale’s file is read alone, so marking a term in French says nothing about Arabic. Every one of those is a test in translation-block-qa.test.ts. The file is hand-authored and has no POT — schemas/content/translation.ts declares that slot, and TranslationNode.potFile is optional for exactly this. Work item he0e. available_locales includes the SOURCE language, and that is not a formality. It is the list a reader’s language bar and coverage badge are computed from — “which languages can I read this page in” — and the page is certainly readable in the one it was written in. It is not the list of translations that exist, which is what availableLocales() in pipeline/po-resolve.ts returns by resolving translations/<locale>/<stem>.po; that lookup can never name the source language, because there is no translations/en/ and there never will be. Use localesAvailableFor() in pipeline/translation-index.ts to go from one to the other. Both halves of the corpus — generated and hand-authored translated pages — must stamp the same meaning, or a badge reads a numerator larger than its denominator. Do not stamp qa_translation_* keys: stamped from a node-level round trip, they publish every string nobody back-translated as semantic drift. Per-block QA is the record: the TR icon beside each block opens <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, where a verdict names the witness that reached it. docs-ui.js injects the unverified-translation warning itself, from the page’s own front matter. There is no include to add: buildLanguageBar renders the six UN languages and greys out the ones not yet translated. Do not add a translation-warning.html, language-selector.html or qa-translation-badge.html include.

22303.title: The navbar filters by locale
22303.content: Translated pages are labelled as translated content in the graph and are not shown in the navbar unless their locale is selected; with no translation, the navbar falls back to the source language. Three rules, and each is enforced somewhere different because each can break somewhere different. 1. A page is a translation because the PAGE says so . Three fields in its own front matter, and nothing else anywhere: . lang: fr # this page is French nav_exclude: true # keep it OUT of the static nav translation_source: index.md # which page it expresses . pipeline/translation-index.ts walks the site and reads those. A page with no lang is the layer’s source language — absent means the default, not unknown. Never match a directory name against a list of language subtags. A layout coincidence is not a contract, and it is wrong in both directions: a folio with a no/ chapter (Norwegian, or the English word) is silently hidden from its own navbar, and a pt-BR/ or translated-fr/ directory is silently shown as source. Neither announces itself — the navbar simply has the wrong entries in it. Put the French page at accueil-fr.md beside its source and it is indexed correctly; put an English page in a folder called fr/ and it is left alone. There is deliberately no translated-content graph typology. A declaration per locale subtree restates what every page already says and grows as O(locales × subtrees). What is translatable is a node’s content (Markdown, BPMN, …), not its schema: translatability is a property of a format within a content type. Each layer that owns a content type declares, under contentTranslations in its own <instance>.json, which formats have an extract/inject pair, and schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects them — Markdown, LaTeX, PlantUML, SVG, ArchiMate, Excel, BPMN, FSH, FHIR JSON — and isTranslatable(contentType, extension) is the predicate. The index asks it rather than inventing a second answer, so a .json beside a page is data and never a language. translations/ is declared, as translation-sources. That one earns a kind: a .po catalogue is not content in any language, so no file inside it can declare one. There is no nav_order on a translated page. It stands where its source stands, because it replaces that item rather than joining the list. A nav_order beside a nav_exclude is two facts that contradict each other, and the check refuses it. 2. nav_exclude is the half that JavaScript cannot do . just-the-docs builds the navbar at build time, from front matter, on a static site serving the same HTML to every reader. It cannot know which locale anybody chose, so a translated page left in the nav is in it for everybody. A script can swap a nav item; it cannot un-render one without a flash of the wrong nav first. So the translations leave the static nav entirely, and a reader with no JavaScript gets the source-language navbar — the correct degraded answer rather than an arbitrary one. 3. The swap, and the fallback that is not a code path . pipeline/translation-index.ts writes docs/_data/translations.json; _includes/head_custom.html publishes it into every page as #fa-translation-index; mountNavLocale in site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js reads it. With a non-source locale selected, each nav item that has a page in that locale is rewritten in place — same position, same parent, translated title, translated href, and its own dir so an Arabic item inside an English column is not laid out backwards. Fallback is the absence of a rewrite. An item with no page in the selected locale is not touched, so it keeps its source-language title and link. There is deliberately no branch for it: a fallback implemented as its own code path is a code path that can be wrong, and this one cannot be. Which locale is “selected”, in precedence order: ?lang= on the URL, then the page’s own lang when the page is a translation, then the remembered fa-locale, then the source language. A locale the index has never heard of is not honoured — labelling the navbar tlh while every item is in English is a claim the page cannot support. Three states, and the third is why the index is published as null . | data-fa-nav-index | when | what the navbar does | . | ok | the index parsed and holds pages | filter it | . | empty | it parsed and holds none | nothing to swap; every item is source language | . | unknown | no island, unparseable, or index: null because the data file was absent at build time | left exactly as built | . empty and unknown produce the same navbar and are not the same answer: one is “this folio has no translations”, the other is “this build could not tell”. A build that could not determine the translation set must never render as a folio that has none — so translation:index exits 2 rather than writing a partial index over a complete one, and the deploy fails rather than publishing it. Adding a locale . | Write the pages, each carrying lang, nav_exclude: true and translation_source. Where they sit is up to you — the convention here is <dir>/<locale>/<page>.md, and nothing depends on it. | bun run cat translation:index and commit docs/_data/translations.json. | . There is no third step and no declaration to remember. The thing that IS easy to forget is nav_exclude, which is why translation:index:check fails without it: a translated page left in the static nav is in it for every reader, whatever locale they chose, which is the bug this section records.

22304.title: Official vs unofficial
22304.content: | Attribute | Official | Unofficial | . | Human sign-off | ✅ Required | ❌ Not required | . | Viewer badge | ✅ Green | 🔄 Grey/amber | . | Source hash tracking | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | . | Staleness detection | ✅ Yes | N/A | . | Can be shown in viewer | Always | Configurable (officialRequired in config) | .

22305.title: Six UN languages
22305.content: The default supportedLocales in the layer’s config (its index.config.json entry): . | Code | Language | Native | . | ar | Arabic | العربية | . | zh | Chinese | 中文 | . | en | English | English | . | fr | French | Français | . | ru | Russian | Русский | . | es | Spanish | Español | . Folios may add or remove locales. The viewer reads the list from config.

22306.title: translations/ directory rules
22306.content: The translations/ directory contains only three file types: . | .pot — POT templates (extractable strings) | .po — PO translated strings | .ts — TranslationNode manifests (KG nodes) | . Do not put .md, .qa.json, or status.json files in translations/. Rendered output lives in docs/<locale>/; QA and status are properties of the TranslationNode manifest. A layer with no translations directory of its own is hosted. translationsHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts its templates in the extracting harness’s translations/<locale>/<stub>/ — cat-harness/translations/<locale>/bootstrap/processes/*.pot for bootstrap’s three diagrams — rather than inside the layer, which holds no translation machinery. The templates are extracted from the bootstrap the harness has pinned; when bootstrap is its own repository they stay here, since a template is the harness’s work over bootstrap’s text, not part of it (kg-separation §”The pair”).

22307.title: A layer that defines its own translator
22307.content: A layer built on this one may define its own translator actor and translation subsystem. Then the rule is load it; never vendor it: the subsystem is invoked from that layer’s checkout, not copied here, and that layer’s skills say how. This skill names no layer above it.

22308.title: IG Publisher i18n
22308.content: For FHIR IG folios, the IG Publisher’s own i18n system is used in parallel: . | i18n-default-lang in sushi-config.yaml — source language. | i18n-lang — target languages. | translation-sources — path to input/translations/{lang}/ containing per-resource .po files. | Run with -generation-off -validation-off flags for fast translation-only builds. | . The prose translation pipeline (this skill) and the FHIR resource translation pipeline (IG Publisher) are complementary and independent.

22309.title: Do not
22309.content: . | Do not manually add badge includes. docs-ui.js renders them automatically from front matter. The include it replaced is deleted, not deprecated — an include that still exists is one somebody adds back. | Do not publish a semantic-QA number a script cannot establish. A back-translation from this repo’s own PO map, or from a word-substitution table, scores the table rather than the translation — and a string with no back-translation at all scores 0 and reads as drift. If no independent back-translator has run, the criterion has no verdict, and saying so is the honest output. | Do not infer a locale from a directory name. docs/fr/index.md is French because it says lang: fr. A subtag match is wrong in both directions and neither failure announces itself — see The navbar filters by locale. | Do not add a graph typology for translated content. It is the same kind of thing as the page it translates, differing by a field the file declares. Translatability is a property of a FORMAT within a content type — schemas/library/translation-tools.ts and isTranslatable — not of a directory. | Do not leave a translated page in the static nav. nav_exclude: true is what keeps it out, and no amount of client-side work substitutes for it: the nav is built once, for every reader, before anybody has chosen a locale. | Do not put non-PO files in translations/. Only .pot, .po, and .ts manifests belong there. Rendered .md goes in docs/<locale>/. | Do not vendor SMART Base translation scripts. Load from checkout. | Do not translate math, labels, or code. Exclude in extraction. | Do not auto-sign-off. Official status requires a human. | Do not re-extract per locale. Templates are extracted once, merged to main in one source PR, and every locale starts from them. | Do not open a locale PR into the source branch, and do not push to a branch whose PR has merged. Each locale is its own PR to main. | Do not fix the source in a translation. Report it as one issue. | Do not edit a FHIR resource to translate it. Its terms go into the locale’s CodeSystem supplement. | Do not re-translate a term a lower layer fixes in the same subject area. Translate with the locale term base, and fix a violation where the term is fixed. A use in another subject area is enforced once an adjudicator rules it in sense; until then it is pending, not a violation. | Do not treat staleness as “wrong”. A stale translation is still useful; it just needs re-review. | Do not conflate FHIR resource translation with prose translation. They are different pipelines with different tooling. | Do not auto-remove staging previews. Require staging:cleanup label. | .

22313.title: Translation refresh — the watcher
22313.content: Skill translation-refresh: The translation watcher: a scheduled fresh session that keeps every locale of every layer current after the source moves. Cold start, then, per layer, detect, refresh the templates, merge them into each locale, translate only the new and fuzzy strings with the fixed terms, run the gates, round-trip the changed strings, write the QA report, open one PR to main, merge it only where the layer declares merge-when-green, and report source mistakes as one issue. Use for “refresh the translations”, “a template check failed”, and when scheduling or running the watcher. Named by: Multi-locale translation, Translation refresh (watcher), Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route . The watcher is the last step of a multi-locale translation, and it runs for as long as the translations exist. It is a scheduled fresh session in the translation-source-lead lane of translation-refresh.bpmn, which multi-locale-translation.bpmn schedules. This page is what that session follows, cold, with nothing remembered from the session that scheduled it. translation-manager is the reference for every term used here; read its §”Translating into several locales as a team” first. Generic on purpose. Nothing here names a layer. Where a step depends on the layer (where its pages live, which extractor writes its page templates, how its terminology supplements are built), the layer’s own AGENTS.md names it, and you read it there.

22314.title: What wakes it
22314.content: . | The schedule set when the watcher was armed. A run that finds nothing to refresh ends at once, and that is the usual run. | A template check that failed, on main or on a PR: a source change that did not refresh its templates. Run the watcher for that layer before anything else touches its catalogues. | .

22315.title: Cold start, once per run
22315.content: . | Clone each layer the run covers, and follow its AGENTS.md cold start to lay down every pinned layer from its index.lock.json. In a composed checkout that is, in order: clone the mounts the lock lists, bun install --frozen-lockfile, bun run cat mount:lock, bun run cat mount:remote:check. Never mount a layer at a floating ref, and never edit a mounted layer: a fix to one is a PR to its repository. | Attach each repository the run may push to. In a hosted session that is the session’s add-repository tool, with push access. A repository the run cannot push to is reported, and the run goes on with the others. | Note the merge policy. Each layer’s AGENTS.md (§ Translations) declares it. The default, when nothing is declared, is open only: the run opens PRs and merges nothing. A layer may declare merge-when-green (step 9). | .

22316.title: Per layer, in order
22316.content: <root> is the layer’s directory in the checkout. Every command below takes --instance <root>, so one checkout serves every layer. | step | command | moves on when | . | 1. detect | translation:status --instance <root>, translation:drift:check --instance <root>, translation:obsolete:check --instance <root>, and the layer’s template checks | any shows something to do | . | 2. refresh templates | the layer’s extractors (translate-bpmn --instance <root> --extract for diagrams; pages and glossary as its AGENTS.md names) | the template checks pass | . | 3. merge into each locale | msgmerge --update --backup=none, or translation:obsolete --instance <root> | every catalogue matches its template | . | 4. translate new and fuzzy | by hand or by agent, with the locale term base | no empty or fuzzy entry is left | . | 5. gates | below | every gate passes | . | 6. round trip | translation-round-trip.bpmn on the changed strings | both drift and not-drift are recorded | . | 7. QA report | translation:page-qa --instance <root>, and the report | it is written | . | 8. one PR | one per layer, based on main and targeting main | it is open | . | 9. merge | only under merge-when-green, all green, round trip no fail | merged, or left open and reported | . | 10. source mistakes | one issue on the source | filed, or none found | . 1. Detect . bun run cat translation:status --instance <root> # new, fuzzy, empty, per locale bun run cat translation:drift:check --instance <root> # each .po against the .pot beside it bun run cat translation:obsolete:check --instance <root> # msgids the source no longer yields . Then the layer’s template checks: translate-bpmn:check for its diagrams, and the page and glossary template checks its AGENTS.md names. Any of them failing, or any count above zero, is a change to refresh. Exit 2 is not “nothing to do”. These commands exit 2 when they cannot determine the answer, for example when a layer declares no translation-sources directory. Report it for that layer and go on to the next; never read it as current. 2. Refresh the templates . Re-run the layer’s extractors, once, for every locale. Diagrams: . bun run cat translate-bpmn --instance <root> --extract . Pages and glossary schemes: the extractors the layer’s AGENTS.md names. A generator that writes below a mounted layer leaves that mount modified; re-lay it from the lock afterwards, as the cold start says. 3. Merge into each locale . Merge each refreshed template into every locale’s catalogue: . | new strings arrive empty: they are the work of step 4; | changed strings arrive fuzzy, with the old translation kept as a hint; | obsolete strings are kept as #~ entries, never deleted, so the translation can be revived if the source comes back. | . With gettext installed, msgmerge --update --backup=none <locale.po> <template.pot> does all three. Without it, bun run cat translation:obsolete --instance <root> marks the obsolete entries, and the layer’s AGENTS.md names how its new strings are added. Then re-run step 1’s translation:drift:check: it fails while any catalogue still differs from its template. 4. Translate only the new and fuzzy strings . Translate the empty and fuzzy entries in every locale, and nothing else. A string already translated is not re-translated, even where you would have worded it differently today. Translate with the locale term base (translation-manager §”The locale term base”): a term a lower layer fixes keeps its fixed form. Clear #, fuzzy only on an entry you have actually re-translated. FHIR terms go into the locale’s one CodeSystem supplement, never into the resource. Translation-node manifests stay official: false, generatedBy: "agent". Write no status.json. A mistake in the source is not fixed here. Translate what the source says, and note the location for step 10. 5. Gates . bun run cat check:translation-officiality bun run cat translation:catalogue:check bun run cat translated-links:check bun run cat kg:locale:check --instance <root> bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <root> --locale <locale> . The first three read the checkout they run in and take no --instance, so run them from the checkout that holds the layer. Then the layer’s supplement build: the locale’s CodeSystem supplements compile with no SUSHI error and pass their structural checks (the command is in the layer’s AGENTS.md). Placeholders, tags and URLs are preserved: translation:page-qa reports a lost one as translation-terms-preserved. A gate that fails is fixed in the .po, the manifest or the supplement, and step 5 runs again. A glossary hit on a platform term in text of another subject area is a sense check, not a violation: read it, note it in the report, and change nothing because of it. 6. Round trip on the changed strings . Run translation-round-trip.bpmn on the strings this run translated, and only those. The method is in translation-manager §”The untainted round trip, as run”. When two separate parties cannot be dispatched, record “could not dispatch” with the reason: it is never a pass, and the PR says so. 7. QA report . bun run cat translation:page-qa --instance <root> . writes the per-catalogue sidecars under the layer’s test/results/translation-qa/. Beside them, write the locale’s report: the strings refreshed, each gate’s result, the round-trip counts (sampled, flagged, drift, not drift) with every drift ruling and its fix, the glossary violations and sense checks, and the source mistakes found. 8. One PR per layer, to main . One branch from main, one PR to main, carrying every locale this run refreshed for that layer. Never push to a source PR’s branch, and never to a branch that has already merged. The PR body links the QA report. 9. Merge, by the layer’s policy . The policy is the layer’s to declare, in its AGENTS.md: . | open only (the default): open the PR, merge nothing, report it. | merge-when-green: merge the run’s own refresh PR only when every check is green and the untainted round trip on the changed strings records no fail. Anything red, uncertain or failing is left open and reported to the owner; the next run looks again. | . Either way the translations stay unofficial: merging is not sign-off. Never merge a PR the run did not open, and never one to a repository the owner has said only a person merges. 10. Source mistakes: one issue . Every source-text mistake the translators noted goes into one issue on the source repository, with the location and the reading the translation took. Not one per locale, and not a fix in the translation: a fix to the source is a source PR, and the next run carries it to every locale.

22317.title: Never
22317.content: . | Never re-extract per locale. Templates are refreshed once, for every locale. | Never re-translate a finished string, and never delete an obsolete one. | Never write official: true. A person makes a translation official (human-translation-workflow). | Never read exit 2 as clean. “Could not tell” is reported, every time. | .

22319.content: Process_TranslationRefresh · advisory · 10 step(s) . Keep every locale current after the source moves: detect, refresh the templates, merge them into each locale, translate only what is new or fuzzy, check it, and land one PR per layer on main. 22325.title: Translation round trip (untainted)
22325.content: Process_TranslationRoundTrip · advisory · 6 step(s) . Did the meaning survive the translation? The untainted round trip on a sample of one locale’s strings, with the two parties kept apart: a back-translator who sees only the target text, and an adjudicator who sees only the source and the back-translation. You are in this process when multi-locale-translation or translation-refresh calls it, after the deterministic gates have passed. It is the translation instance of untainted-verification: the producer (the locale translator) draws the sample and never writes the verdict; the back-translator renders and rules on nothing; the adjudicator rules. GT_RoundTripQa in translation-workflow is the same check drawn as one step; this diagram draws its parties, because the separation between them is what makes the result a measurement. A first run samples every diagram label, the personas and scenarios, and a seeded random fraction of the rest; a refresh samples only the strings it changed. The third state is drawn: when two separate parties cannot be dispatched, the producer records “could not dispatch” with a reason, and that is never a pass. i i i i i i

It chooses what is checked, by a rule stated before any result is seen, and hands on the target strings alone. It may record one thing here, “could not dispatch”, because without that state a producer forbidden from writing a verdict has nothing honest to write. | . | Back-translator | back-translator | Sees the target strings and nothing else: not the source, not the repository, no tools. Shown the source, it writes the source back and the check passes without measuring anything. | . | Round-trip adjudicator | round-trip-adjudicator | Sees the source strings and the back-translation, never the target text, and rules each pair drift or not drift with its reason. Both halves of the drift definition are in front of it, so that inflection and word order are not ruled as drift. | .

22331.title: Translation Workflow
22331.content: Process_Translation · advisory · 12 step(s) . The machine half of translation, end to end: extract the translatable strings, inject a catalogue back, check the result by back-translating it, and track whether the source has moved since. You are in this process whenever translation happens without a person having to be present. Two of its steps are the exception and are drawn in their own lane: a flagged passage is ADJUDICATED by a human, and a translation becomes official only when a human signs it off. human-translation-workflow is what happens when a person is doing the translating rather than checking it. Staleness is an END state that re-enters at the beginning, not a failure. A source change does not invalidate a translation’s accuracy; it invalidates its currency, which is a different fact and is why it is recorded rather than thrown away. i i i i i i i i i i i i

It decides nothing a person would disagree about — every branch it takes is computed from a hash or a file’s presence.It is one lane rather than two because agentic and mechanical is a judgement rather than a line (see the role model), and nothing in THIS process turns on which of the two ran a step. Where that distinction does matter, the process says so by putting the step in the reviewer’s lane instead. | . | Human reviewer / adjudicator | translation-adjudicator | The only lane here that JUDGES. Mechanical translation QA produces candidates — a flagged passage, a terminology miss, a staleness verdict — and a candidate is not a finding until somebody decides it is. This lane is where that decision is made, and it is the lane that signs the translation off, because the actor who resolves a disputed passage is the one who can say the whole is fit to publish.Adjudicator rather than reviewer alone, and the distinction is the accountability: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles. The word is used here because the passage reaching this lane is one where a checker and a translator disagree, and somebody has to choose between them WITH a reason.
