22337.title: Untainted verification — the producer never writes the verdict
22337.content: Skill untainted-verification: The party that produced an artefact does not write the verdict on it. How a checker and an adjudicator are dispatched with controlled context, the three rules that make it a measurement rather than a ritual, and the third state that lets it gate at all. Named by: Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, Wireframe design review, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Make a decided public comment change, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: untainted-verification · Package: sdlc-core . A secret scan, a schema validation, a back-translation and a systematic literature search differ in what they read and in what counts as a finding. They do not differ in this: . The party that produced the artefact does not get to write the verdict on it, and the checking party is given a controlled context rather than the run of the repository. Everything below is that sentence made operational, for any domain, because taking the translation vocabulary out of it changes nothing structural; translation-manager.md §”The agentic round trip” is the translation instance.

22338.title: The parties
22338.content: | party | is given | produces | . | producer | the task | the artefact | . | checker | the artefact’s declared checker_sees, and nothing that would let it shortcut | an independent rendering or finding | . | adjudicator | adjudicator_sees and the checker’s output — never the artefact itself | pass / warn / fail, each drift named | .

22339.title: Three rules, and the failure each one stops
22339.content: 1. Neither party sees what would let it shortcut. A back-translator shown the English writes the English back and the check passes vacuously. An adjudicator shown the French can talk itself into any reading of the back-translation. Neither failure raises an error; both produce a green verdict that measured nothing, which is worse than a red one. 2. The checker uses no tools, and says so. The artefact is in the repository. A checker with filesystem access can find what it was not given, and the verdict then measures its search rather than the artefact. Ask for a TOOLS_USED line and record the answer — UntaintedParty.tools_used. Absent means nobody asked, which is not the same as “no”. 3. One party doing both halves is not this check. It compares a thing with its own paraphrase of itself.

22340.title: The context is declared, not composed
22340.content: UntaintedDispatch on the criterion (schemas/sdlc/block-qa.ts) declares checker_sees, checker_withheld, adjudicator_sees and drift. A caller names a subject and a criterion; it does not hand-assemble a brief. That is not ceremony — the party composing a brief by hand is the producer, and rule 1 then breaks silently, one call site at a time. A declaration is also checkable, and untaintedPartitionDefects checks it: . | defect | what it means | . | undeclared | no untainted block. Reported, never skipped: nobody said is not nothing to check | . | overlap | a role visible to both parties — one of them is grading its own input | . | unpartitioned | a companion in depends_on that is in neither visible set; usually a role added later. Nobody decided | . | phantom | a role named in the declaration that the criterion does not depend on — the declaration describes something else | . Totality is the point of checker_withheld. Without it a newly-added companion role defaults into the checker’s view, or out of it, and either way the separation moves without anybody choosing. With it, the partition simply stops being total, which has a name. drift must say both halves. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and everything fails. The translation round trip states it well: synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift; a claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is. The check verifies the string is non-empty and nothing more — “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the exact defect this skill exists to stop.

22341.title: Three states, and the third is what lets it gate
22341.content: . | verified — the adjudicator ruled. Two entries, adjudicator first. | could not dispatch — no dispatch capability was available. One entry, result: "n/a", metrics.dispatch: "unavailable", and a required reason. The producer may write this one, and only this one. | not attempted — no entry at all. | . Without state 2 the discipline cannot gate anywhere: a producer forbidden from writing a verdict has nothing to write in an environment with no subagents, so the gate reads an absence it cannot tell from negligence. Recording it keeps “could not dispatch” distinguishable from “nobody tried”. It is never a pass. isVerified() is the predicate a gate asks, and it is false for state 2 and for state 3 alike. A consumer that reads n/a as “nothing to see” turns the honest gap straight back into the silent one.

22342.title: Recording
22342.content: Both parties are written as witnesses. The adjudicator leads — the first entry per criterion is the operative one everywhere in this repo. The checker sits behind it with result: "n/a" and its output in notes, because a reader asking on what basis? needs the intermediate and a reader asking who did this? needs both names. Record model with model_source, or not at all. A subagent’s serving model is not observable from the session that dispatched it: it inherits the parent unless the harness overrides, and the hand-back does not say which model served the turn. A bare model string is an inference printed as a fact. Absent both, a reader gets “not recorded”, which is true and acceptable. A sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself. mergeUntainted carries everything else through, so an unrelated re-run never silently deletes another party’s verdict. A human ruling is never superseded here. A verdict is hashed to what it was about. Edit the subject and the verdict goes stale. This matters more for an agent ruling than a script one, because nobody can cheaply re-run it. Where the verdict is kept: the attestation store, not the derived file . Both entries are judgements — reviewer.kind is agent (or human) — so their durable home is the attestations graph, test/attestations/<family>/<mirrored subject path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main. The derived test/results/ file beside them is a working copy whose record lives on the qa-reports branch, and a regeneration cannot reproduce an agent ruling. recordUntainted writes the store first, through the same resolvePrior / finalizeCriteria API as every other attesting writer, and refreshes the derived report only if one already exists — it never invents one. So the verdict lands whether or not the derived file is on the branch, and the store file it returns is the one to commit. What puts a subject in scope is the subject existing (<subject>.md or .ts), not its derived report, which does not live beside it. A corrupt or unreadable store reads UNKNOWN and is refused, with nothing written, rather than overwritten.

22343.title: Why the instrument is the thing to watch
22343.content: A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject — for example a failure count that is really a count of entries missing from the checker’s reference map. Remove such a measurement rather than publish it. translation-manager §”The instrument, not the translation” has the worked case.

22344.title: This is one rule with two homes
22344.content: It is not a platform invention. Guideline methodology separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason, and the identical rule applies to evidence-based literature review for living guidelines. When adding a domain’s rules here, run them through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions first: a rule that fails all three is a folio’s rule, correctly located, and fencing it and saying so is the honest move.

It deliberately does not call a model: the payload is written by whatever ran the parties, so recording works the same for two subagents, two API calls, or two people. | .

22347.title: Upload naming — the name is normalised, not the link escaped
22347.content: Skill upload-naming: What an ingested file may be CALLED. Read before adding anything to an uploads or library graph, before writing a generator that links to one, and before “fixing” a broken link in a generated README. Covers which characters break what, why the name is normalised as well as the link escaped, how a sidecar stays paired with its source, and the one case the fixer refuses. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links, DTH authoring . A file in an uploads or library graph is named by whoever uploaded it, and that name reaches a generated Markdown link. So the name is an interface, not a label. It is a library-core skill, beside uploads-watch and library-ingestion, because what an ingested file may be called is a question about acquiring and ingesting sources. bun run cat check:upload-names reports; check:upload-names:check gates; check:upload-names:fix renames with git mv.

22348.title: The rule
22348.content: A name may not contain any of . space , ( ) [ ] { } # ? & % ' " ` < > | . Everything else is left exactly as uploaded. The fixer replaces a run of those with a single -, trims, and preserves the extension and any sidecar suffix. A name with no unsafe character is returned untouched. Collapsing and trimming happen only to names that were going to change anyway; a double dash, a leading dash or a trailing dash is not this check’s business. Case is not a defect either: README.md stays README.md, because renaming it breaks every link to it and every generator that writes one. Rewriting a name that was already safe breaks whatever looks it up by that name, such as a generator that lists a section file. Both are pinned by tests.

22349.title: What each character breaks
22349.content: | character | what it breaks | . | space, (, ) | a Markdown link target ends at the first ) | . | [ ] | the label half of the link | . | < > \| | the angle-bracket link form, and tables | . | # ? | a fragment and a query to every URL parser | . | & % quotes backtick | escaping in a shell, an href, or both | . | , | nothing — included for the stub convention | .

22350.title: Why the NAME as well as the link
22350.content: uploads/X (2).pdf produces the link target X (2).pdf, which resolves to X (2. Two layers answer this, and neither subsumes the other: . | layer | reaches | fails when | . | linkTarget (in subgraph-readmes.ts) / decodeLinkTarget (in check-subgraphs.ts) | every generated README link, in every graph typology, including directory names | never — it percent-encodes every segment of what the generator writes (parentheses included, because an unbalanced one ends a CommonMark destination as surely as a space), and the check decodes before asking the filesystem | . | this check | uploads and library names, before anything links them | a name reaches something that is not that generator | . The encoder keeps generated READMEs valid. This check keeps a filename usable in a shell, an href, a CI log line, a curl, and any later generator. Escaping is per-generator; a name is per-file, so a name that is safe everywhere is safe once. A rename churns downstream references, and that is accepted: they are repaired, not abandoned. After a rename, repoint the hand-maintained path fields (files[].path in intake.json; container and assets[].path in *.extraction.json; provenance.source in catalogue records; file and source_file in structure.json and manifest.jsonld; hardcoded paths in tests and scripts). Leave a hand-authored wireframe alone: what it depicts is a design decision, not a consequence of the rename. Then regenerate in dependency order: library:graph → library:viz → library:readmes → readme:subgraphs, then skill:register. Out of order, a later writer stales an earlier one’s output, which reads exactly like a real failure. Build the old-name list for a reference sweep from git diff --name-status -M split on tabs (awk -F'\t'), not on whitespace: the filenames being renamed contain spaces. A sweep that finds nothing must be shown to have had something to look for.

22351.title: A sidecar suffix is not an extension
22351.content: X.pdf pairs with X.pdf.extraction.json. Two ways to break that: . | rename the source and not the sidecar → the extraction is orphaned | normalise the sidecar by a different rule than its source → same | . So the fixer strips the sidecar suffix first, normalises the remaining name by the one rule, and restores the suffix. The pair moves together by construction. The stem is normalised and the extension left alone, because a whole-filename slug destroys the extension (…(2).pdf → …-2-pdf).

22352.title: Findings are not the size of a rename
22352.content: The check reports only what is still unnormalised, so once part of the corpus has been renamed its count is the tail of the work, not its size. Measure a rename from git diff --name-status -M.

22353.title: The one case it refuses
22353.content: Two files that normalise to one name. The fixer reports the collision and renames neither: picking a winner silently destroys an upload, and an upload is somebody’s source material. Rename one by hand. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to a rename — a git mv that overwrites is a deletion with a friendlier name.

22354.title: What this does NOT cover
22354.content: . | Directory names. The check reads files; a directory with a space in it is not graded. | Content. It reads names and never opens a file, which is why it is harness-layer rather than folio-layer in the repo partition. | Whether a file should be there at all. That is ingestion’s question, not naming’s. | .

22356.title: Two mechanisms and a persona
22356.content: Skill upload-routes: How a file actually REACHES uploads/ — the two mechanisms that write bytes into a declared queue, the persona that performs one of them on somebody’s behalf, and what each writer owes that the route does not do for them. The step before intake and after acquisition. Named by: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/ . content-acquisition decides what channel a resource comes in on — a file, a link, or a description somebody gives in their own words. This skill starts one step later, where the answer was a file: what writes the bytes into the declared queue, and what does the writer owe? . It ends the moment the file is in the queue. uploads-watch notices it arrived; library-ingestion and document-intake take it from there.

22357.title: The answer is two, not three, and the third is a persona
22357.content: Two mechanisms write bytes: a git commit, and the forge’s web UI. A file handed to an agent in a conversation is route 1 performed by a different actor. A persona inherits every obligation of the mechanism it performs, so the question about an agent is “did the agent discharge the git route’s obligations, and what does it owe on top?” Treating it as a third route would invite a third, shorter list of obligations. What it owes on top is provenance. A commit records its own author and message; a web upload records the account that made it. Neither records “this arrived in a conversation, from this person, for this reason” — that fact exists only in the session, which is ephemeral. If the agent does not write it down when it places the file, it is gone: for the other two routes a commit exists to go back to, and for a conversation nothing does.

22358.title: Route 1 — a git commit from a working tree
22358.content: git add the file under the queue, commit, push, open a PR. A working tree is where the pre-commit hook and bun run cat gates run — if you run them. What you owe. |   |   | . | put it in the declared queue of the layer that will own it | see §”Which queue” | . | run the generators the file stales | uploads/README.md is generated and lists every file, so any addition stales it. bun run cat readme:subgraphs, then bun run cat gates for the rest | . | open a PR | so CI judges it, and so a sibling session can see the queue grew | . | record where it came from | the commit message is the only place this route has for it | . You do not owe ingestion. Placing and ingesting are different acts by different skills, and uploads-watch is explicit that a drop is somebody handing over a file, not an instruction to publish it.

22359.title: Route 2 — the forge’s web UI
22359.content: GitHub’s “Add files via upload”. Never write the URL by hand — run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/upload-url.ts [branch], which composes it from the declaration. The declared path uploads/ is relative to the layer, and a forge URL needs it relative to the repository. There is no working tree, so there is no pre-commit hook and no generator run. The commit is minted server-side from the bytes you selected and nothing else. Two hazards: . | It commits to the path you are LOOKING at. A file outside the declared queue reads as absent to every consumer, because each resolves the queue from the declaration. | It lets you commit to any branch, including the default one. A commit straight to main skips the PR, which is the only place CI would have run: no hook locally and no CI remotely. The generated uploads/README.md is then stale on the default branch, and readme:subgraphs:check — a blocking gate — fails for whoever opens the next pull request. | . What you owe. Everything route 1 owes, discharged afterwards from a checkout, because the web UI cannot discharge any of it: . | choose the branch, not main, unless you are also going to run the generators immediately; | navigate to the declared queue directory before uploading, not to the repository root; | pull, run bun run cat readme:subgraphs and bun run cat gates, and push the result — or ask an agent to, which is the persona below. | .

22360.title: The persona — a file handed to an agent in a conversation
22360.content: This is route 1, performed by an agent. It inherits every obligation above. Three things are the agent’s own: . Materialise the bytes before anything else. A file that exists only in the conversation exists nowhere the repository can see. Write it into the declared queue under a name that will still mean something — not ChatGPT Image Sep 20, 2026, 08_26_47 AM.png or a bare UUID. Write down what the conversation knows and the commit does not — who provided it, when, what they said it was, and why it was wanted. Put it in the commit message at minimum. This is the obligation the other two routes do not have, and the reason the persona is named although it is not a mechanism. Do not ingest on your own say-so, and do not delete. Both are other skills’ decisions — library-ingestion and deletion-requires-confirmation. A processed upload still looks spent and still is not.

22361.title: What the routes are NOT responsible for
22361.content: The same three for every route, stated once so no route’s section can shorten the list: . | deciding the file belongs in the corpus. That is acquisition’s question, answered before this step. | ingestion. A file in the queue is a file in the queue; library/ is a judgement call somebody else owns. | cleaning the queue. uploads/ is the raw record of what was handed over and a derived library/ entry does not replace it. | .

22362.title: Which queue — there can be more than one, and they belong to different layers
22362.content: A checkout that includes several layers can carry several uploads queues — for example uploads/ declared by the layer at the repository root and cat-harness/uploads/ declared by the cat-harness layer. They are not one directory declared twice: they are two layers’ queues that share an id. So “put it in uploads/” is not an instruction — it does not say whose. Resolve the queue from the declaration of the layer that will own the material, which is what queueRepoRelative in scripts/upload-url.ts does and what the upload-url Tool exposes. Pass that layer’s root; do not paste a path.

22363.title: Unsettled
22363.content: . | Which layer owns a given file. Nothing states the rule for choosing between two declared queues. Ask, or follow whatever the surrounding work already uses. | Whether an arrival without an intake record should be refused. A gate would fail main on arrival, which is the opposite of accepting what somebody offers (content-acquisition). Whether the record is owed by the placer or minted by intake is undecided. | .

22365.title: Watching the queue
22365.content: Skill uploads-watch: Notice what has landed in the acquisition queue, and tell an arrival from a backlog. Reports; it never deletes, and never ingests on its own say-so. Named by: Content acquisition . uploads/ is the acquisition queue — content-acquisition puts things in it, library-ingestion takes them out. This is the step between: seeing that something arrived. The queue path is read from the declaration, never written down. It is uploads/ relative to the layer, which is not where a repository-relative consumer would look. queueRepoRelative in scripts/upload-url.ts is the one place that arithmetic lives.

22366.title: An arrival is not a backlog
22366.content: A file sitting in the queue says nothing on its own: it may have landed a minute ago or been waiting since before this session. Do not report a queue’s contents as news: a watcher that does becomes noise that gets ignored, and an ignored watcher reads as coverage. So report against a mark: what was there when this session began, or when the watch last ran. What is new since the mark is an arrival. Everything else is the backlog, and the backlog is mentioned once, as a count. A backlog is still a finding. A queue that has held the same file for weeks means acquisition happened and ingestion did not, and nobody noticed. That is worth one line — not silence, and not a repeated alarm.

22367.title: It reports; it does not act
22367.content: Never ingest on a watcher’s say-so. A drop is somebody handing over a file, not an instruction to publish it: ingestion decides a bib slug, writes into library/, and is a judgement call that library-ingestion owns. Never delete anything from the queue — that is deletion-requires-confirmation applied where it is most tempting, because a processed file looks spent. It is not: uploads/ is the raw record of what was handed over, and the derived entry in library/ is not a substitute for it. Report what could go, with sizes and ages, and wait to be told.

22368.title: What to say when something arrived
22368.content: Name the file, say when it landed, say what it appears to be — and then say the next step is ingestion and whether you are taking it. An arrival reported without a next step hands the reader a fact and a chore.

22369.title: What to say when nothing did
22369.content: Nothing, unless you were asked. A watch that reports every quiet interval trains its reader to skip it, including the round that matters.

document, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

22372.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
22372.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

22373.title: 1 — Watch
22373.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

22374.title: 2 — Impact analysis
22374.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

22375.title: 3 — MVP
22375.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

22376.title: 4 — Review
22376.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

22377.title: 5 — Decide
22377.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

22378.title: Adding a tenant
22378.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

22379.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
22379.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

22381.title: uses[] Editorial Review
22381.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review, Committee review of a content change .

22382.title: The relation you are auditing
22382.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

22383.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
22383.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

22384.title: The prime directive
22384.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

22385.title: Workflow
22385.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

22386.title: Verdict rubric
22386.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

22387.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
22387.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

22388.title: Declaring the second case
22388.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

22389.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
22389.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

22390.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
22390.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

22391.title: One reading is not the standard
22391.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

22392.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
22392.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

22393.content: | Skill | Interaction | . | content-graph | Owns the graph the mechanical checks read | . | prepare-merge | Runs the uses axis as part of the content gates | . A content type’s own skills that consume or extend this relation are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this skill.

22395.title: Vocabulary authority — one fact, one home, N renderings
22395.content: Skill vocabulary-authority: One vocabulary is authoritative for one kind of fact, and every other is a derived rendering reached by a declared mapping. Which vocabulary owns what here, the pros and cons behind each ruling, how DC and SKOS overlap and what stops them drifting, and the normalisation-first rule for any modelling or mapping exercise. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: vocabulary-authority · Package: folio-core .

22396.title: The rule
22396.content: A fact has ONE authoritative vocabulary. Every other vocabulary that carries it is a RENDERING, reached by a declared mapping with stated equivalence — never a second copy of the fact. | the fact | authoritative | why not the others | . | what a term MEANS | SKOS | the only candidate here whose subject IS a meaning | . | a resource’s metadata | Dublin Core | a document has a title; a concept has a preferred label. Different subjects | . | a clinical code’s operational semantics | FHIR CodeSystem / ValueSet / ConceptMap | versioning, designations with a use, expansion-as-release. SKOS has none of these | . | a release of any of the above | DCAT (held, not built) | it is not a term model at all; it describes a published dataset | . ┌──────────────────────────────┐ AUTHORITATIVE ──▶ │ skos:Concept = the MEANING │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ skos:exactMatch / closeMatch / broadMatch / relatedMatch │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ FHIR Code- Dublin Core schema.org TBX DCAT System (resource DefinedTerm termbase (release of (clinical metadata, (SEO / (CAT-tool any of these operations) bib records) discovery) exchange) as a dataset) . SKOS is the hub because its mapping properties exist for exactly this, and because it is the only one of the five whose subject is a meaning rather than an artefact, a record, or a distribution.

22397.title: Pros and cons, as ruled
22397.content: The reasons are measured against this corpus, not read off the specs. SKOS — adopted, authoritative for meaning . |   |   | . | Pro | Native JSON-LD. Multilingual labels first-class. notation is the code — TermGloss’s prefixed names. Mapping properties with stated equivalence. Carries the vocabulary terms and swimlane roles here | . | Con | No versioning model at all. No designation use. No post-coordination. Mapping properties carry no provenance | . The con is why convergence STOPS at SKOS. The failure this exists to prevent: reading “one glossary mechanism” as “one terminology mechanism” and binding an ICD-11 code to a skos:Concept with a notation and no version. That graph validates, publishes, and is wrong the next release. Dublin Core — kept, authoritative for resources . |   |   | . | Pro | ISO 15836. Qualified, repeatable and language-tagged as IRIS actually uses it — the content core’s schemas/dublin-core.ts is shaped by one measured record that does all three | . | Con | Two predicates overlap SKOS (below) | . schema.org — kept at 3 predicates; never a source of truth . |   |   | . | Pro | Search engines consume it. Native JSON-LD | . | Con | A publishing vocabulary, not a terminology one. DefinedTerm has name + description and stops: no versioning, no designation concept at all, no mapping semantics, no deprecation-with-successor | . It has no definitions to speak of. Used for 3 predicates (softwareVersion, codeRepository, text). Measuring usage: a naive grep for schema.org mostly matches json-schema.org (JSON Schema’s $schema keyword) and the schema:viz npm script. Never cite that count. TBX — not closed, and still not adopted . ISO 30042:2019 is published both as an ISO standard and as a free open industry standard; dialects and schemas are public. So “closed” is false and the ruling does not rest on it. |   |   | . | Pro | Genuinely open. Purpose-built for multilingual term entries | . | Con | Its niche is CAT-tool termbase interchange. This repo translates through gettext .po, not a termbase. XML-only | . Legitimate as an export if translators ever ask for a termbase. Rejected outright . SKOS-XL — it reifies labels to fix part of the designation gap and nothing else; the gap it does not fix is the one that matters. OWL — overkill: prose definitions, no reasoner in the pipeline. DCAT — held, for the render of whatever is landed on.

22398.title: DC ↔ SKOS: the overlap, and what stops the drift
22398.content: | pair | relation | . | dcterms:title ↔ skos:prefLabel | real overlap | . | dcterms:description ↔ skos:definition | real overlap | . | dcterms:subject → skos:Concept | not overlap — the designed JOIN. DC points at a concept | . | dcterms:hasPart, dcterms:source | no SKOS equivalent | . DC describes a RESOURCE. SKOS describes a CONCEPT. One object, one type, one naming predicate. They collide only where a node is genuinely both — such as the glossary document, which is a file and a skos:ConceptScheme, carrying both skos:prefLabel and dcterms:title. Two predicates for one fact, with nothing declaring which is authoritative, drift apart. The node is a concept scheme, so skos:prefLabel is the source and dcterms:title is the derived copy for resource-metadata consumers.

22399.title: Guidance for schema and data modelling
22399.content: . | Model in an open standard. Not a proprietary or house schema that happens to be convenient. | Proprietary input is mapped, not adopted. A mapping is a declared artefact with stated equivalence — not a rename in a loader. | Normalise FIRST. The first step of any mapping exercise is data normalisation. Mapping un-normalised data encodes the source’s accidents into the target and they are invisible afterwards. | The exercise runs as a defined process, not as a one-off script. | .

22400.title: Where the pins live
22400.content: cat-harness/external-schemas/ — one record per specification, pinning the edition and carrying the operative terms derived from the corpus, never hand-listed. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/external-schemas.ts --check. A vocabulary can be used in more than one syntax (a BPMN file, a JSON-LD @context); a usage check that reads only one reports the other as absent.

22403.title: Voice editorial review
22403.content: Skill voice-editorial-review: Adjudicate a voice-* finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-voice.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

22404.title: The axis you are adjudicating
22404.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

22405.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
22405.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

22406.title: What the criterion cannot know
22406.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

22407.title: Adjudicating one finding
22407.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

22408.title: Where the open findings are
22408.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

22409.title: Do not
22409.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

22412.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
22412.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

22413.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
22413.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

22414.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
22414.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

22415.title: A mechanical match is a question
22415.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

22416.title: Recording the verdict
22416.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

22417.title: Do not
22417.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

22419.title: Voice overlay review
22419.content: Process_VoiceReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . The voice axis: load whichever editorial voices are active, run each rule’s mechanical half, and decide — for each finding — whether the prose is wrong, the rule does not apply to this content, or this block is a stated exception. You are in this process after the base voice has been adjudicated, and only if a voice is active at all: the first gateway ends the process honestly when none is, rather than reporting a clean review of nothing. Three outcomes, all legitimate, and the third is the one that needs recording: an exception without a reviewer entry is indistinguishable from a rule nobody ran. There is also a fourth path the diagram draws deliberately — if the rule’s own citation does not support it, the RULE is the defect, and that becomes a bean rather than a finding against the prose. i i i i i i

22431.title: Web apps — an app is content, the harness publishes it
22431.content: Skill web-apps: Interactive web apps as knowledge-graph content: a layer holds an app’s source in a directory of kind web-app (one web-app.json), its UI strings go through the harness’s translation process like any template, and the harness’s apps visualiser (Tool web-app-build) builds it at publish and writes it to its own route with no site chrome, loaded only when a reader opens it. Read before adding an app to any layer, before writing a publish script for one (do not), and when an app’s build or translations fail. Named by: Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route . Skill id: web-apps · Package: ui-core · Kind: web-app · Tool: web-app-build (bun run cat web-apps:build) · Process: web-app-publish .

22432.title: The rule
22432.content: A layer that carries an app declares it; it does not publish it. Owner, 2026-11-11 (cards Q-GAME-5 A and Q-GAME-7 A): a content layer with an app (a WHO onboarding game was the first) must not become a harness to ship it, and the one-off route VaxLink used (web/ + its own publish.sh + site.build.keep) is retired. The kind and its visualiser are the harness’s, so every layer that mounts cat-harness gets them. Before writing an app at all, ask whether it is a journey: a walkthrough of people and steps is a user-scenario and a workshop drawn by the journeys-viewer, not an app. An app is for what a page cannot be: a game, a simulation, a 3D world.

22433.title: Declaring one
22433.content: . | Put the app’s source in a directory of the layer, with its package.json and a lockfile (package-lock.json for npm, bun.lock for bun): the build installs exact versions only. | Declare the directory in the layer’s <name>.json with "graphTypologies": ["web-app"]. | Put a web-app.json (web-app/0.1.0, the schema the Tool web-app-build reads) at its root: | . { "$schema": "web-app/0.1.0", "id": "onboarding-game", "title": "Join the Network", "description": "A country onboards to the GDHCN, one choice at a time.", "build": { "installer": "npm", "script": "build", "outDir": "dist" }, "locales": ["en", "ar", "es", "fr", "ru", "zh"], "i18n": { "catalog": "src/i18n/en.json", "out": "public/i18n" }, "contentFrom": ["business-processes", "glossary"], "sizeBudgetMB": 45, "license": "Apache-2.0", "source": { "repository": "https://github.com/carlsbox/gdhcn-onboarding-game", "commit": "bd4c34c" } } . | field | rule | . | id | lower-case kebab; the route segment. Two layers claiming one id is a declaration error naming both. | . | build | defaults npm / build / dist. The app must build with relative asset paths (Vite base: './'), since its route is computed, not chosen. | . | chrome | always none (the default): the app draws its own frame. | . | locales | the first is the source language. A WHO layer ships the six UN languages: ar, en, es, fr, ru, zh. Arabic is right to left: the app sets dir="rtl" for it. | . | contentFrom | the layer’s own directory ids the app reads at build time. An app reads the layer’s content (its BPMN, glossary, actors, instances) at build time rather than copying it into code, so it cannot drift. | . | sizeBudgetMB | the index flags an app over it; the site size review reads it. | . | license, source | for a copied app: keep its LICENSE and a NOTICE naming the source commit. | .

22434.title: Where it is published, and why it loads only when opened
22434.content: | route | what | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/ | the index, in the site’s chrome: one entry per app, its languages and size | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/<id>/ | the app’s build, every page marked <meta name="folio-navbar" content="none"> and rendered-by: web-app-build | . The route is computed by visualiserRoute, as for every visualiser (harness-tiles). No other page embeds an app or loads its scripts: a tile, an IG page or a journey links to it. So a reader downloads an app only by opening its route. Inside the app, put heavy parts (a 3D engine, films) behind a dynamic import() or preload="none" so the first screen paints first.

22435.title: Translating an app — the harness’s process, not a second one
22435.content: An app’s UI strings are one more template to the translation process (translation-manager, translation-refresh, multi-locale-translation.bpmn): . | Source catalog. i18n.catalog is a flat JSON object { key: text } in the source locale. Placeholders are {name}. Nothing else is translatable: no strings hard-coded in components. | Templates. bun run cat web-apps:build --extract writes translations/<locale>/apps/<id>.pot in the declaring layer, one ui-string entry per key with the key as msgctxt. Name this command in the layer’s AGENTS.md §Translations as the app’s “refresh the templates” step, so the watcher runs it. | Translation. Translators fill translations/<locale>/apps/<id>.po exactly as for pages and diagrams: one PR per locale, the fixed terms, the untainted round trip, officiality as the layer declares it. | Injection is the build. Before building, the Tool writes each locale’s translated strings to <i18n.out>/<locale>.json. The app loads its locale’s file and falls back to the source text per string. | Gates. web-apps:build --check fails on a stale template, a translation that drops or adds a {placeholder}, or a translation for a key the catalog no longer has. Untranslated strings are reported, never failed. | . Media that speaks (narration, films) is not a string: list each clip per locale in the app’s own data, and say in the app when a locale has captions only.

22440.title: Input and output
22440.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the use (design or as-is), the topic (for CRDM, the proposal slug), the surface, and, from CRDM, the requirements that change it, the proposal path, the humanReviewer (requester or BA), the channels the candidates are shown in, and the branch. | Out — the renderings: assetDir, intent, and one candidates[] entry per candidate: its source HTML path, its screenshots.web and screenshots.mobile paths (from wireframe-check), their staging deep links, its per-criterion entries, and its outcome with the reason. chosen names the candidate, who chose it and the comment that records it; it is absent until a person chooses. | Out — as changed assets: changedAssets[] lists every wireframe file the branch adds, changes or removes (candidate HTML, screenshots, intent, reviews) in the record shape a staging preview’s graph carries (change, kind, title, before, after, source, pages or pagesUnknown; ChangedAsset in cat-harness-tools scripts/kg-changed-assets.ts). The review therefore lists the drawings the same way it lists every other changed asset. | Out — staging links: stagingLinks, the shape every request for feedback carries (staging-review), copied inline as definitions.stagingLinks. | .

22441.title: Two uses
22441.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

22442.title: 1. Intent
22442.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

22443.title: 2. Candidates
22443.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

22444.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
22444.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

22445.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
22445.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

22446.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
22446.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. 22457.title: State in a running process
22457.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

22458.title: Which store answers which question
22458.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

22459.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
22459.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

22460.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
22460.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

22461.title: What state does NOT buy you
22461.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

22462.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
22462.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

22463.title: Reading the state you did not write
22463.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
